For SQuAD-Open, each document contains several paragraphs, and the reader is fed the top-k TF-IDF ranked paragraphs from within the documents in the search space.

Effectiveness of Sentence-Level Encodings
Our method uses sentence-level encodings for paragraph retrieval.
This approach's significance is tested in Figures 5b and 5c.
Sentence-level encodings appear vital for improving state-of-the-art results on SQuAD-Open, but not on HotpotQA.
Hypothesis: This difference is due to dataset creation methods.
In SQuAD, each paragraph serves as context for multiple questions, leading to questions about less essential facts not encapsulated in a single paragraph representation.
In HotpotQA, most training set paragraphs serve as context for at most one question.

Related Work
Chen et al. (2017) introduced neural methods for open-domain QA using textual knowledge sources with DrQA, a pipeline approach.
DrQA consists of a TF-IDF retriever and a multi-layer neural network to find answer spans.
To improve TF-IDF retrieval, works have used Distant Supervision (DS) for re-ranking paragraphs (Htut et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2018).
Wang et al. (2018a) used reinforcement learning for end-to-end training of a re-ranker and RC component, showing advantages over DS alone.
Min et al. (2018) trained a sentence selector, demonstrating the effectiveness of reading minimal contexts.
DS can lead to wrong labeling; Lin et al. (2018) suggested a denoising method to alleviate this.
These methods improve performance but their re-ranking is limited by the number of paragraphs processed, requiring joint reading of questions and paragraphs.
Our approach pre-computes all paragraph representations for efficient large-scale retrieval.
Lee et al. (2018) learned encoding functions for questions and paragraphs, ranking paragraphs by dot-product similarity.
Many of their improvements are attributed to answer aggregation methods suggested by Wang et al. (2018b).
Seo et al. (2018) proposed phrase-indexed QA (PI-QA), a formulation requiring independent encoding of answers and questions.
Question encodings retrieve correct answers via MIPS, posing a challenge rather than solving open-domain QA.
Das et al. (2019) proposed a framework with multi-step interaction between retriever and reader to refine question representation for more accurate retrieval.
This framework is complementary to ours, enhancing retrieval for single-hop questions but not handling multi-hop domains.
Memory Networks (Weston et al., 2015) are reminiscent of our method.
Memory Networks have an array of cells storing vectors and four modules for memory manipulation.
Variations include end-to-end Memory Networks (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015), Key-Value Memory Networks (Miller et al., 2016), and Hierarchical Memory Networks (Chandar et al., 2016).

Concluding Remarks
We present MUPPET, a novel method for multi-hop paragraph retrieval, showing its efficacy in single- and multi-hop QA datasets.
A difficulty in open-domain multi-hop QA is the lack of supervision, partially alleviated in single-hop QA by distant supervision.
Future work aims to tackle this problem to allow learning more than two retrieval iterations.
An improvement would be to allow the retriever to automatically determine if more retrieval is needed.

Paragraph encodings must not depend on questions for efficient MIPS with pre-computed encodings. Without this, new questions would require processing the entire knowledge source.

For multi-hop retrieval:
1. Encode question Q to get $q \in \mathbb{R}^d$.
2. Transform $q$ into search vector $q_s \in \mathbb{R}^d$ to retrieve top-k paragraphs $\{P^Q_1, \dots, P^Q_k\} \subset KS$ using MIPS.
3. In subsequent iterations, use previously retrieved paragraphs to reformulate the search vector. This yields k new search vectors, $\{\tilde{q}_1, \dots, \tilde{q}_k\}$, where $\tilde{q}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$.
4. These new search vectors are used with MIPS to retrieve the next top-k paragraphs.
5. This process is equivalent to a beam search of width k in the encoded paragraph space.

Figure 2 provides a high-level view.

### 3.1 Paragraph and Question Encoder

The encoder model $f$ is defined as follows:
For a paragraph P with k sentences $(s_1, \dots, s_k)$ and m tokens $(t_1, \dots, t_m)$, where $s_i = (t_{i1}, \dots, t_{il})$ and l is sentence length, the encoder generates k d-dimensional encodings $(s_1, \dots, s_k) = f(P)$. This contrasts with prior work using a single fixed-size representation per paragraph.

Encodings are created by passing tokens through:

**Word Embedding:**
Each token t is embedded into a vector $\mathbf{t}$ using character-level and word-level information.
- Word-level embedding $\mathbf{t}_w$ uses pretrained word embeddings.
- Character-level embedding: For a token t with $l_t$ characters $(t^c_1, \dots, t^c_{l_t})$, each $t^c_i$ is embedded into a fixed-size vector $\mathbf{t}^c_i$. These are passed through a 1D convolutional neural network, followed by max-pooling over the filter dimension to produce a fixed-size character-level representation $\mathbf{t}_c = \max\_CNN(\mathbf{t}^c_1, \dots, \mathbf{t}^c_{l_t})$.
- Final word representation: $\mathbf{t} = [\mathbf{t}_w; \mathbf{t}_c]$.

**Recurrent Layer:**
A bidirectional GRU processes the word representations to obtain contextualized word representations: $(\mathbf{c}_1, \dots, \mathbf{c}_m) = BiGRU(\mathbf{t}_1, \dots, \mathbf{t}_m)$.

**Sentence-wise Max-pooling:**
Contextualized representations are chunked into sentence groups. Max-pooling is applied over the time dimension of each group to obtain d-dimensional sentence representations: $s_i = \max(\mathbf{c}_{i1}, \dots, \mathbf{c}_{il})$.

Figure 3a illustrates the sentence encoder architecture, processing tokens to produce sentence representations.

The encoding $q$ of a question Q is computed similarly: $q = f(Q)$. A single vector is produced for each question by applying max-pooling over all question words, disregarding sentence information.

Figure 2: High-level overview of MUPPET.
(a) Sentence Encoder
(b) Reformulation Component

Figure 3: Architecture of paragraph and question encoder components. (a) Sentence encoder: receives tokens, outputs sentence representations. (b) Reformulation component: receives contextualized question and paragraph representations, outputs reformulated question representation.

**Reformulation Component:**
This component takes a paragraph P and question Q to produce a single vector $\tilde{q}$.
1. Contextualized word representations are obtained for Q and P: $(\mathbf{c}^q_1, \dots, \mathbf{c}^q_{nq})$ and $(\mathbf{c}^p_1, \dots, \mathbf{c}^p_{np})$ using the same embedding and recurrent layers.
2. A bidirectional attention layer (adopted from Clark and Gardner, 2018) processes these representations.
3. Attention between question word i and paragraph word j is computed as: $a_{ij} = w_a^1 \cdot \mathbf{c}^q_i + w_a^2 \cdot \mathbf{c}^p_j + w_a^3 \cdot (\mathbf{c}^q_i \odot \mathbf{c}^p_j)$.

Context: One of the most famous people born in Warsaw was Maria Skłodowska-Curie, who achieved international recognition for her research on radioactivity.

For yes/no-based questions, question-aware context representations are encoded into a fixed-size vector using max-pooling over the outputs of the residual self-attention layer. This vector is then passed through a linear layer to predict a yes/no answer.

**Supporting Fact Prediction**
Context supporting facts are sentence-level. Question-aware context representations are encoded into fixed-size sentence representations by passing the residual self-attention layer outputs through another bidirectional GRU, followed by max-pooling over the GRU's sentence group outputs. Each sentence representation is then passed through a multilayer perceptron with a single hidden layer and ReLU activations to predict if it is a supporting fact.

**Training**
An input sample consists of a question and a single context (Q, P). For HotpotQA, which requires multiple paragraphs, P is the concatenation of these paragraphs. The objective function comprises four loss functions:
*   $L_{span}$: For span-based prediction.
*   $L_{type}$: For answer type prediction (span-based or yes/no-based).
    $L_{type} = -\log \frac{\prod_{j \in P_Q} \text{es}^{type}_j}{\prod_{j \in P_Q} (\text{es}^{binary}_j + \text{es}^{span}_j)}$
*   $L_{yes/no}$: For yes/no answer prediction.
    $L_{yes/no} = -\log \frac{\prod_{j \in P_Q} \text{es}^{yes/no}_j}{\prod_{j \in P_Q} (\text{es}^{yes}_j + \text{es}^{no}_j)}$
    where $P_Q$ is the set of paragraphs for question $Q$. $\text{es}^{binary}_j$, $\text{es}^{span}_j$, and $\text{es}^{type}_j$ are likelihood scores for the $j$-th question-paragraph pair being binary yes/no-based type, span-based type, and its true type, respectively. $\text{es}^{yes}_j$, $\text{es}^{no}_j$, and $\text{es}^{yes/no}_j$ are likelihood scores for the $j$-th question-paragraph pair having the answer 'yes', 'no', and its true answer, respectively. For span-based questions, $L_{yes/no}$ is zero, and vice-versa.
*   $L_{sp}$: Binary cross-entropy loss on each sentence for supporting fact prediction.

The final loss function is $L_{hotpot} = L_{span} + L_{type} + L_{yes/no} + L_{sp}$.

During inference, supporting fact prediction is restricted to the paragraph from which the answer is predicted.

**Metrics**
Three sets of metrics evaluate performance on HotpotQA:
1.  **Answer Span Evaluation**: Exact Match (EM) and F1 metrics.
2.  **Explainability Evaluation**: EM and F1 metrics on supporting fact sentences.
3.  **Combined Evaluation**: Joint EM and Joint F1.
    For each example, given answer span precision ($P(\text{ans})$) and recall ($R(\text{ans})$), and supporting facts precision ($P(\text{sup})$) and recall ($R(\text{sup})$):
    $P(\text{joint}) = P(\text{ans})P(\text{sup})$
    $R(\text{joint}) = R(\text{ans})R(\text{sup})$
    Joint F1 $= \frac{2P(\text{joint})R(\text{joint})}{P(\text{joint}) + R(\text{joint})}$
    Joint EM is 1 if both answer span and supporting facts achieve exact match, otherwise 0. Metrics are averaged over the evaluation set.

**Implementation Details**
Tokenization is performed using the Stanford CoreNLP toolkit. Models are implemented in TensorFlow.

**Architecture Details**
*   **Word Embeddings**: GloVe 300-dimensional embeddings pretrained on the 840B Common Crawl corpus.
*   **Character Embeddings**: 20-dimensional character embeddings, with a 1D CNN (100 filters, size 5), ReLU activations, and a dropout rate of 0.2.
*   **Encoder**: ELMo embeddings (pretrained on 5.5B dataset) concatenated with token representations from the embedding layer. Dropout rate of 0.5. A weighted average of ELMo layers is used.
*   **Vocabulary Caching**: For faster computation, context-independent token representations are cached if they appear in HotpotQA Wikipedia titles or at least five times in the entire Wikipedia. Out-of-vocabulary words are given a fixed OOV vector.
*   **Recurrent Layers**: Variational dropout (same mask across time steps) with a rate of 0.2 is applied to recurrent layer inputs.
*   **Encoding Size**: $d = 1024$.

paper2.title: Answering while Summarizing: Multi-task Learning for Multi-hop QA with Evidence Extraction
paper2.abstract:
Question answering (QA) using textual
                        sources for purposes such as reading comprehension (RC) has attracted much attention.
                        This study focuses on the task of explainable
                        multi-hop QA, which requires the system to
                        return the answer with evidence sentences
                        by reasoning and gathering disjoint pieces
                        of the reference texts. It proposes the Query
                        Focused Extractor (QFE) model for evidence
                        extraction and uses multi-task learning with
                        the QA model. QFE is inspired by extractive
                        summarization models; compared with the
                        existing method, which extracts each evidence
                        sentence independently, it sequentially extracts evidence sentences by using an RNN
                        with an attention mechanism on the question
                        sentence. It enables QFE to consider the dependency among the evidence sentences and
                        cover important information in the question
                        sentence. Experimental results show that QFE
                        with a simple RC baseline model achieves a
                        state-of-the-art evidence extraction score on
                        HotpotQA. Although designed for RC, it also
                        achieves a state-of-the-art evidence extraction
                        score on FEVER, which is a recognizing
                        textual entailment task on a large textual
                        database.
methodology:
Evidence (E) was evaluated using official metrics in FEVER.
Answer Type (AT) was evaluated by label accuracy.
Evidence (E) was evaluated by precision, recall, and F1, measured by sentence ID.
The FEVER score, accounting for both AT and E, was used as a metric. A sample's FEVER score is 1 if the predicted evidence includes all gold evidence and the answer is correct. The FEVER score emphasizes the recall of evidence sentence extraction over precision.

5.3 Results

Our multi-task learning approach achieves state-of-the-art performance.
Table 10 shows QFE achieved state-of-the-art performance in evidence F1 and comparable performance in label accuracy to competitive models.
QFE's FEVER score is lower than other models because the FEVER score emphasizes recall. The importance of precision and recall depends on utilization. QFE is suited for situations preferring concise output.

Our evidence extraction achieved high performance on all metrics. On the test set, it ranked 2nd in precision, 3rd in recall, and 1st in F1. On the development set, QFE extracted with higher precision than recall, a tendency also observed in RC evaluation. The single model showed a larger difference between precision and recall. The ensemble model improved recall and F1. Examples are in Appendix A.2.

6 Related Work

6.1 Reading Comprehension

RC matches context and query. Multiple text RC datasets include MS MARCO and TriviaQA. These datasets combine document retrieval models with context-query matching models. Techniques for understanding multiple texts include connecting texts or coarse and fine reading. However, most RC questions require reasoning from a single sentence containing the answer (over 63.2% in TriviaQA, 86.2% in MS MARCO).

This motivates multi-hop QA. HotpotQA includes supervised evidence extraction. QAngaroo uses Wikipedia entity links; its differences from our focus are (1) no supervised evidence and (2) questions limited by knowledge base construction. MultiRC is an explainable multi-hop QA dataset with gold evidence sentences, but its evaluation script and leaderboard do not report evidence extraction scores, making comparison difficult. Unsupervised evidence extraction is important due to annotation cost. Wang et al. (2019) addressed unsupervised learning for explainable multi-hop QA but were limited to multiple-choice settings.

6.2 Recognizing Textual Entailment

RTE involves sentence matching. FEVER aims for verification and fact-checking on a large database, requiring document retrieval, evidence extraction, and answer prediction. Previous work used pipelined models for these subtasks. Our approach performs evidence extraction and answer prediction simultaneously, treating FEVER as an explainable multi-hop QA task.

6.3 Summarization

Typical sentence-level extractive summarization uses an encoder-decoder architecture. It is also used for content selection in abstractive summarization. The model extracts sentences.

The differences in score between the original implementation and our implementation of Yang et al. (2018) are due to hyperparameters. The primary change is increasing `dc` from 50 to 150.

We evaluated a pipeline model that selects the answer string `AS` only from the extracted evidence sentences, masking outputs of the answer layer corresponding to non-evidence sentences with the prediction of evidence extraction. Although most answer strings in the dataset are within gold evidence sentences, this model performed poorly. We hypothesize that evidence extraction aids QA model learning, but its performance is insufficient to improve the answer layer's performance in a pipeline model.

**2 Task Definition**
We redefine explainable multi-hop QA to include the RC and RTE tasks.
**Def. 1. Explainable Multi-hop QA**
Input: Context C (multiple texts), Query Q (text)
Output: Answer Type AT (label), Answer String AS (text), Evidence E (multiple texts)

Context C is treated as one connected text in the model. If the connected C is too long (e.g., over 2000 words), it is truncated. Query Q is the query. The model answers Q with an answer type AT or an answer string AS. Answer Type AT is selected from answer candidates (e.g., ‘Yes’). Answer candidates depend on the task setting. Answer String AS exists only if there are not enough answer candidates to answer Q. Answer string AS is a short span in C. Evidence E consists of sentences in C and is required to answer Q.

For RC, we tackle HotpotQA. In HotpotQA, answer candidates are ‘Yes’, ‘No’, and ‘Span’. Answer string AS exists if and only if answer type AT is ‘Span’. C consists of ten Wikipedia paragraphs. Evidence E consists of two or more sentences in C.

For RTE, we tackle FEVER. In FEVER, answer candidates are ‘Supports’, ‘Refutes’, and ‘Not Enough Info’. Answer string AS does not exist. C is the Wikipedia database. Evidence E consists of sentences in C.

**3 Proposed Method**
This section explains the overall model architecture, which contains our model as a module, and then the details of our QFE.

**3.1 Model Architecture**
Except for the evidence layer, our model is the same as the baseline (Clark and Gardner, 2018) used in HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018). Figure 2 shows the model architecture. The input of the model is context C and query Q. The model has the following layers:

*   **Word Embedding Layer**: Encodes C and Q as sequences of word vectors. A word vector is the concatenation of a pre-trained word embedding and a character-based embedding obtained using a CNN (Kim, 2014). The outputs are C1 ∈ Rlw×dw, Q1 ∈Rmw×dw, where lw is the length (in words) of C, mw is the length of Q, and dw is the size of the word vector.
*   **Context Layer**: Encodes C1, Q1 as contextual vectors C2 ∈Rlw×2dc, Q2 ∈Rmw×2dc by using a bi-directional RNN (Bi-RNN), where dc is the output size of a uni-directional RNN.
*   **Matching Layer**: Encodes C2, Q2 as matching vectors C3 ∈Rlw×dc by using bi-directional attention (Seo et al., 2017), a Bi-RNN, and self-attention (Wang et al., 2017).
*   **Evidence Layer**: First encodes C3 as [→C4; ←−C4] ∈Rlw×2dc by a Bi-RNN. Let j1(i) be the index of the first word of the i-th sentence in C and j2(i) be the index of the last word. We define the vector of the i-th sentence as:
    xi = [−−−→c4,j2(i); ←−−−c4,j1(i)] ∈R2dc.
    Here, X ∈Rls×2dc is the sentence-level context vectors, where ls is the number of sentences of C.
    QFE, described later, receives sentence-level context vectors X ∈Rls×2dc and contextual query vectors Q2 ∈Rmw×2dc as Y. QFE outputs the probability distribution that the i-th sentence is the evidence:
    Pr(i) = QFE(X, Y = Q2). (1)
    Then, the evidence layer concatenates the word-level vectors and the sentence-level vectors:
    c5,j = [c3,j; xi(j)] ∈R3dc,
    where the j-th word in C is included in the i(j)-th sentence in C.
*   **Answer Layer**: Predicts the answer type AT and the answer string AS from C5. The layer has stacked Bi-RNNs. The output of each Bi-RNN is mapped to a probability distribution by a fully connected layer and the softmax function.
    For RC, the layer has three stacked Bi-RNNs. Each probability indicates the start of the answer string, ˆAS1 ∈Rlw, the end of the answer string ˆAS2 ∈Rlw, and the answer type, ˆAT ∈R3. For RTE, the layer has one Bi-RNN. The probability indicates the answer type.

**Loss Function:**
Our model uses multi-task learning with a loss function L = LA+LE, where LA is the loss of the answer and LE is the loss of the evidence. The answer loss LA is the sum of the cross-entropy losses for all probability distributions obtained by the answer layer. The evidence loss LE is defined in subsection 3.3.

**3.2 Query Focused Extractor**
Query Focused Extractor (QFE) is shown as the red box in Figure 2. QFE is an extension of the extractive summarization model of Chen and Bansal.

Summarization uses an encoder-decoder architecture (Cheng and Lapata, 2016; Nallapati et al., 2017; Narayan et al., 2018). Sentence-level extractive summarization is used for content selection in abstractive summarization (Chen and Bansal, 2018). This model extracts sentences in order of importance and edits them. This model has been extended for evidence extraction, considering evidence must be extracted in order of importance, not original order as in conventional models.

**Conclusion**

The main contributions of this study are:
1. The QFE model, based on a summarization model for explainable multi-hop QA.
2. The dependency between evidence and question coverage achieved through the summarization model.
3. State-of-the-art performance in evidence extraction for both RC and RTE tasks.

For RC, the QFE architecture, a simple replacement of the baseline, achieved state-of-the-art performance. The ablation study confirmed that replacing the evidence extraction model with QFE improves performance. The adaptive termination contributes to exact matching and precision scores in evidence extraction. The difficulty of questions for QFE depends on the number of required evidence sentences. This study is the first to base its experimental discussion on HotpotQA.

For RTE, the QFE architecture achieved a higher evidence extraction score and a comparable label prediction score compared to competing models. This study is the first to present a joint approach for RC and FEVER.

4.3 Results
Does our model achieve state-of-the-art performance?
In the distractor setting (Table 2), QFE achieved the best evidence extraction score among compared models. It also showed comparable answer selection performance, resulting in state-of-the-art performance on Joint EM and F1 metrics, which are the primary metrics for the dataset. QFE outperformed the baseline model across all metrics. Despite not using pre-trained language models like BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) for encoding, it surpassed methods that did, such as DFGN + BERT and BERT Plus. Specifically, the evidence EM score improved by +37.5 points against the baseline and +5.4 points against GRN.

In the fullwiki setting (Table 3), QFE outperformed the baseline in all metrics. However, it was outperformed by Cognitive Graph (Ding et al., 2019), an unpublished model at submission time. HotpotQA exhibits a dataset shift problem (Quionero-Candela et al., 2009), where the distribution of gold evidence sentences and answerability differs between training (distractor setting) and test (fullwiki setting) phases. In the fullwiki setting, questions may have fewer than two gold evidence sentences or be unanswerable. Our current QA and QFE models do not address this dataset shift; future work will focus on it.

Does QFE contribute to performance?
Ablation study results are shown in Table 4. QFE performed best among the compared models. While the primary difference between our overall model and the baseline is the evidence extraction model, answer scores also improved. QFE also outperformed the model using only RNN extraction without glimpse.

QFE defines the terminal condition as reaching the EOE sentence, termed adaptive termination. This adaptive termination contributed to QFE's performance. Compared to a baseline extracting the two sentences with the highest scores (as two is the most frequent number of evidence sentences), QFE achieved better performance.

The Query Focused Extractor (QFE), shown in Figure 2, is an extension of the extractive summarization model by Chen and Bansal (2018), adapted for query-focused settings. While Chen and Bansal used an attention mechanism to extract sentences covering important information from a source document, QFE extracts sentences from context C with attention on query Q, ensuring the evidence covers information relevant to Q. Figure 3 provides an overview of QFE.

QFE takes sentence-level context vectors $X \in \mathbb{R}^{l_s \times 2d_c}$ and contextual query vectors $Y \in \mathbb{R}^{m_w \times 2d_c}$ as input. A "timestep" refers to an operation that extracts a sentence. QFE updates the RNN state ($z_t \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$) as follows:
$z_t = \text{RNN}(z_{t-1}, x_{e_t}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$,
where $e_t \in \{1, \dots, l_s\}$ is the index of the sentence extracted at step $t$, and $E_t = \{e_1, \dots, e_t\}$ is the set of sentences extracted up to step $t$.

QFE extracts the $i$-th sentence based on the probability distribution (Figure 3, light blue box):
$\text{Pr}(i; E_{t-1}) = \text{softmax}_i(u_t^i)$
$u_t^i = \begin{cases} v_p^\top \tanh(W_{p1}x_i + W_{p2}g_t + W_{p3}z_t) & (i \notin E_{t-1}) \\ -\infty & (\text{otherwise}) \end{cases}$
The sentence extracted is $e_t = \text{argmax}_i \text{Pr}(i; E_{t-1})$.

$g_t$ is a query vector representing importance at step $t$, defined as a glimpse vector (Vinyals et al., 2016) (Figure 3, green box):
$g_t = \sum_{j} \alpha_t^j W_{g1} y_j \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$
$\alpha_t = \text{softmax}(a_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{m_w}$
$a_t^j = v_g^\top \tanh(W_{g1} y_j + W_{g2} z_t)$.

The initial RNN state is obtained from a fully connected layer and max pooling over $X$. All parameters $W_\cdot \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c \times 2d_c}$ and $v_\cdot \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$ are trainable.

### Training Phase

During training, teacher-forcing is used to define the loss function. The evidence loss $L_E$ is the negative log-likelihood, regularized by a coverage mechanism (See et al., 2017):
$L_E = -\sum_{t=1}^{|E|} \log \left( \max_{i \in E \setminus E_{t-1}} \text{Pr}(i; E_{t-1}) \right) + \sum_{i} \min(c_{t_i}, \alpha_{t_i})$.
The maximum operation in the first term selects the sentence with the highest probability, implying QFE extracts sentences in predicted importance order. The loss function ignores the order of evidence sentences as there is no ground truth order for extraction. The coverage vector $c_t$ is defined as $c_t = \sum_{\tau=1}^{t-1} \alpha_\tau$.

To learn the termination condition for extraction, a dummy "End Of Extraction" (EOE) sentence is added to the sentence set. When the EOE sentence is extracted, QFE terminates. The EOE sentence vector $x_{\text{EOE}} \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$ is a trainable parameter, independent of the samples. The model is trained to extract the EOE sentence after all evidence.

### Test Phase

In the test phase, QFE terminates extraction upon reaching the EOE sentence. The predicted evidence $\hat{E}$ is defined as:
$\hat{E} = \text{argmin}_{\hat{E}} \left( -\frac{1}{|\hat{E}|} \sum_{t} \log \max_{i \notin \hat{E}_{t-1}} \text{Pr}(i; \hat{E}_{t-1}) \right)$,
where $\hat{E}_t$ is the predicted evidence up to step $t$. QFE employs beam search to find $\hat{E}$.

### Experiments on RC

#### HotpotQA Dataset

In HotpotQA, queries $Q$ are created by crowd workers, requiring reasoning over two Wikipedia paragraphs for answers. Answer types (AT) include ‘Yes’, ‘No’, and ‘Span’. The answer string $AS$, if it exists, is a span within the two paragraphs. The context $C$ consists of ten paragraphs and has two settings:

1.  **Distractor Setting:** $C$ includes the two gold paragraphs used to create $Q$ and eight paragraphs retrieved from Wikipedia using TF-IDF with $Q$. Table 1 shows statistics for this setting.
2.  **Fullwiki Setting:** All ten paragraphs in $C$ are retrieved. $C$ may not contain the two gold paragraphs, in which case $AS$ and $E$ cannot be extracted, preventing perfect oracle model accuracy. The training data for the fullwiki setting is identical to the distractor setting.

#### Experimental Setup

**Comparison Models:** Our baseline model is similar to Yang et al. (2018), with the following differences: We use Equation (1), whereas their model uses $\text{Pr}(i) = \text{sigmoid}(w^\top x_i + b)$, where $w \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$ are trainable parameters. Their evidence loss $L_E$ sums binary cross-entropy for each sentence being evidence. In the test phase, sentences with probabilities above a threshold are selected. A threshold of 0.4 was chosen for the highest F1 score on the development set. Other implementation details are consistent with Yang et al. (2018) and are elaborated in Appendix A.1.

topic: Open-domain question answering involves developing models that can answer questions using information from large, unstructured text corpora, requiring advanced retrieval and reasoning capabilities. What is the better method for open-domain question answering tasks: KGNN or QFE?

paper1.title: Multi-Paragraph Reasoning with Knowledge-enhanced Graph Neural Network
paper1.abstract:
Multi-paragraph reasoning is indispensable for
                        open-domain question answering (OpenQA),
                        which receives less attention in the current
                        OpenQA systems. In this work, we propose
                        a knowledge-enhanced graph neural network
                        (KGNN), which performs reasoning over multiple paragraphs with entities. To explicitly
                        capture the entities’ relatedness, KGNN utilizes relational facts in knowledge graph to
                        build the entity graph. The experimental results show that KGNN outperforms in both
                        distractor and full wiki settings than baselines
                        methods on HotpotQA dataset. And our further analysis illustrates KGNN is effective and
                        robust with more retrieved paragraphs.

2.3 Prediction module
After T-step reasoning, the answer is predicted using the final question-aware paragraph representations ¯P(T). Shared-normalization is used for answer probability comparison among multiple paragraphs.

3 Experiment
3.1 Dataset
HotpotQA, an OpenQA dataset with over 11k question-answer pairs, requires complex multi-hop reasoning over paragraphs. Experiments are conducted on distractor and full wiki settings. In the distractor setting, 2 golden paragraphs are provided with 8 disturbance terms. In the full wiki setting, questions are provided, and answers are extracted from the entire Wikipedia corpus. An information retrieval system retrieves 30 paragraphs from Wikipedia for this setting. Entities are aligned to Wikidata items for relational entity graph construction. Five common relations in question answering are included for message propagation: {director, position held, record label, lyrics by, adapted from}.

3.2 Baseline Methods
KGNN is compared with Yang et al. (2018) and a modified version, Yang et al. (2018)-split, which treats paragraphs individually and uses shared-normalization.

4 Related Work
Open-domain question answering (OpenQA) aims to answer questions using knowledge sources. Early work by Green Jr et al. (1961) introduced the concept. Chen et al. (2017) applied machine reading comprehension to answer open-domain questions using multiple texts. Wang et al. (2018a) selected the most informative paragraph. Wang et al. (2018b), Lin et al. (2018), and Clark and Gardner (2018) focused on aggregating evidence from multiple paragraphs. Existing OpenQA models treat paragraphs individually or concatenate them.

Existing OpenQA models treat paragraphs individually or concatenate them into a single text. Wang et al. (2018b), Lin et al. (2018), and Clark and Gardner (2018) focus on evidence aggregation across multiple paragraphs. Sun et al. (2018), De Cao et al. (2019), and Cao et al. (2019) use entity graph neural networks for KBQA, reasoning over entities. Our work differs by using entities as bridges to reason over paragraphs, providing span-style answers instead of entity-style answers.

Multi-paragraph reasoning is crucial for practical open-domain question answering but is overlooked by most existing OpenQA systems. We propose KGNN, a novel OpenQA model that performs reasoning over paragraphs using a knowledge-enhanced graph neural network. KGNN outperforms strong baselines on the HotpotQA dataset and can handle more informative texts. This work aims to illuminate the combination of knowledge graphs and text for OpenQA.

2 Model architecture
The framework of knowledge-enhanced graph neural network (KGNN) for multi-paragraph reasoning consists of three parts: encoding module, reasoning module, and prediction module. An additional component supports fact prediction.

2.1 Encoder module
The encoder components, as described by Clark and Gardner (2018), include a character-level encoder, self-attention layer, and bi-attention layer. These embed the question (Q) and paragraphs ({P1, P2, · · · , PN}) into low-dimensional representations:
Q = Self-Att(Char-Enc(Q)), (1)
Pi = Self-Att(Char-Enc(Pi)), (2)
Question-related paragraph representations are computed using a bi-attention operation:
¯Pi(0) = Bi-Att(Q, Pi), (3)
where Char-Enc(·) is the character-level encoder, Self-Att(·) is the self-attention layer, and Bi-Att(·) is the bi-attention layer.

2.2 Reasoning module
Unlike existing OpenQA models that treat paragraphs as individuals, KGNN propagates information among paragraphs with entities via a knowledge-enhanced graph neural network to improve multi-paragraph reasoning.

2.2.1 Build entity graph
All entities from paragraphs form the nodes (V) of the graph for multi-paragraph reasoning. Edges are built based on two types of relationships between paragraphs.
Co-reference of entities across paragraphs forms the most common relation. An edge ˆeij = (vi, vj) is added if nodes vi and vj represent the same entity. Relational facts from knowledge graphs are used to enhance reasoning. A relational edge ¯e r ij = (vi, vj) is added if entities vi and vj have a relation r, facilitating relational reasoning.

2.2.2 Relational Reasoning
Using the constructed graph G = (V, E), KGNN performs reasoning.
Graph Representation. For each node vi ∈ V, its initial representation is derived from contextual word representations. If an entity has k mentions (m1, m2, ..mk) in a paragraph, its initial node representation is:
vi = Max-Pool(m1, m2, ..mk), (4)
where Max-Pool(·) is a max-pooling layer and mi is the representation of a mention. The representation of a mention mi from the s-th to t-th word in paragraph Pj is the mean of word representations: mi = 1/(t−s+1) * Σ(l=s to t) FFN(¯Pjl), where FFN(·) is a fully-connected feed-forward layer.

Message Propagation. Messages are propagated from each node to its neighbors to aid reasoning. Relation-specific networks are used for message propagation due to the different roles of edge types. The update function for a node is:
vu_i = Σr (αr / |Nr(vi)|) * Σ(vj∈Nr(vi)) φr(vj), (5)
where Nr(vi) is the neighbor set of vi with relation r.
αr and φr(·) are relation-specific attention weights and feed-forward networks. Relation-specific attention weight αr is computed using the question representation ¯Q: αr = softmax(FFN(¯Q) .). The relation-specific network is designed as φr(vj) = FFN(vj + Er), where Er is a translating relation embedding.

Paragraph Update. After message propagation among entities, question-aware paragraph representations are updated. Question-aware paragraph representations Uij are defined as:
Uij = vu_Idx(ij) if an entity appears at Pij, 0 otherwise, (6)
where Idx(·) is the node index of Pij in the entity graph.
A reset gate controls information retention from the graph-aware paragraph representation:
rij = σ(Wp ¯Pij + WuUij), (7)
Ûij = rij * Uij + (1 - rij) * ¯Pij, (8)
where Wp and Wu are trainable matrices, and σ is the sigmoid function.
A self-attention mechanism shares global information from entities to the entire paragraph, and the output of the reasoning part is added to the input as a residual:
¯P′ij = ¯Pij + Self-Att(Ûij). (9)

Abstract

Multi-paragraph reasoning is crucial for open-domain question answering (OpenQA) but receives limited attention in current systems. This work proposes a knowledge-enhanced graph neural network (KGNN) for reasoning over multiple paragraphs with entities. KGNN utilizes relational facts from a knowledge graph to construct an entity graph, explicitly capturing entity relatedness. Experimental results on the HotpotQA dataset demonstrate KGNN outperforms baseline methods in both distractor and full wiki settings. Further analysis indicates KGNN is effective and robust with an increasing number of retrieved paragraphs.

1 Introduction

Open-domain question answering (OpenQA) aims to answer questions using large-scale knowledge sources like unlabelled corpora. The field has gained traction with the development of large datasets such as Quasar, SearchQA, and TriviaQA, leading to numerous promising OpenQA models.

However, many existing OpenQA datasets and models primarily focus on reasoning within a single paragraph or single-hop reasoning across paragraphs. The HotpotQA dataset was introduced to address multi-paragraph reasoning challenges. Multi-paragraph reasoning is a significant and practical problem for advancing OpenQA towards greater intelligence. Current OpenQA systems typically handle multiple paragraphs in one of two ways:
1. Treating each paragraph independently, hindering cross-paragraph reasoning.
2. Concatenating all paragraphs into a single long text, which is computationally expensive in terms of time and memory.

To facilitate multi-paragraph reasoning, we propose a knowledge-enhanced graph neural network (KGNN). KGNN first constructs an entity graph using all named entities from the paragraphs, incorporating co-reference edges for entities appearing across different paragraphs. Subsequently, to explicitly capture entity relatedness, KGNN leverages relational facts from a knowledge graph (KG) to build a relational entity graph. This involves adding relation edges between entities that have a defined relationship in the KG. We hypothesize that reasoning information can be effectively captured through propagation over this relational entity graph. For instance, in Figure 1, to answer a question about the entity "Wildest Dreams," two types of one-hop reasoning are required: recognizing that "Wildest Dreams" appears in multiple paragraphs and utilizing the relational fact (Wildest Dreams, lyrics by, Max Martin and Shellback).

Our primary contribution is a novel reasoning module that integrates knowledge. Experiments show that reasoning over entities significantly improves our model's performance compared to all baseline models on the HotpotQA dataset. Our analysis further demonstrates KGNN's robustness and strong capability in handling extensive text.

6 Related Work

6.1 Reading Comprehension

RC matches context and query. Multiple text RC datasets include MS MARCO and TriviaQA. These datasets combine document retrieval models with context-query matching models. Techniques for understanding multiple texts include connecting texts or coarse and fine reading. However, most RC questions require reasoning from a single sentence containing the answer (over 63.2% in TriviaQA, 86.2% in MS MARCO).

This motivates multi-hop QA. HotpotQA includes supervised evidence extraction. QAngaroo uses Wikipedia entity links; its differences from our focus are (1) no supervised evidence and (2) questions limited by knowledge base construction. MultiRC is an explainable multi-hop QA dataset with gold evidence sentences, but its evaluation script and leaderboard do not report evidence extraction scores, making comparison difficult. Unsupervised evidence extraction is important due to annotation cost. Wang et al. (2019) addressed unsupervised learning for explainable multi-hop QA but were limited to multiple-choice settings.

6.2 Recognizing Textual Entailment

RTE involves sentence matching. FEVER aims for verification and fact-checking on a large database, requiring document retrieval, evidence extraction, and answer prediction. Previous work used pipelined models for these subtasks. Our approach performs evidence extraction and answer prediction simultaneously, treating FEVER as an explainable multi-hop QA task.

**2 Task Definition**
We redefine explainable multi-hop QA to include the RC and RTE tasks.
**Def. 1. Explainable Multi-hop QA**
Input: Context C (multiple texts), Query Q (text)
Output: Answer Type AT (label), Answer String AS (text), Evidence E (multiple texts)

Context C is treated as one connected text in the model. If the connected C is too long (e.g., over 2000 words), it is truncated. Query Q is the query. The model answers Q with an answer type AT or an answer string AS. Answer Type AT is selected from answer candidates (e.g., ‘Yes’). Answer candidates depend on the task setting. Answer String AS exists only if there are not enough answer candidates to answer Q. Answer string AS is a short span in C. Evidence E consists of sentences in C and is required to answer Q.

For RC, we tackle HotpotQA. In HotpotQA, answer candidates are ‘Yes’, ‘No’, and ‘Span’. Answer string AS exists if and only if answer type AT is ‘Span’. C consists of ten Wikipedia paragraphs. Evidence E consists of two or more sentences in C.

For RTE, we tackle FEVER. In FEVER, answer candidates are ‘Supports’, ‘Refutes’, and ‘Not Enough Info’. Answer string AS does not exist. C is the Wikipedia database. Evidence E consists of sentences in C.

**3 Proposed Method**
This section explains the overall model architecture, which contains our model as a module, and then the details of our QFE.

**3.1 Model Architecture**
Except for the evidence layer, our model is the same as the baseline (Clark and Gardner, 2018) used in HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018). Figure 2 shows the model architecture. The input of the model is context C and query Q. The model has the following layers:

*   **Word Embedding Layer**: Encodes C and Q as sequences of word vectors. A word vector is the concatenation of a pre-trained word embedding and a character-based embedding obtained using a CNN (Kim, 2014). The outputs are C1 ∈ Rlw×dw, Q1 ∈Rmw×dw, where lw is the length (in words) of C, mw is the length of Q, and dw is the size of the word vector.
*   **Context Layer**: Encodes C1, Q1 as contextual vectors C2 ∈Rlw×2dc, Q2 ∈Rmw×2dc by using a bi-directional RNN (Bi-RNN), where dc is the output size of a uni-directional RNN.
*   **Matching Layer**: Encodes C2, Q2 as matching vectors C3 ∈Rlw×dc by using bi-directional attention (Seo et al., 2017), a Bi-RNN, and self-attention (Wang et al., 2017).
*   **Evidence Layer**: First encodes C3 as [→C4; ←−C4] ∈Rlw×2dc by a Bi-RNN. Let j1(i) be the index of the first word of the i-th sentence in C and j2(i) be the index of the last word. We define the vector of the i-th sentence as:
    xi = [−−−→c4,j2(i); ←−−−c4,j1(i)] ∈R2dc.
    Here, X ∈Rls×2dc is the sentence-level context vectors, where ls is the number of sentences of C.
    QFE, described later, receives sentence-level context vectors X ∈Rls×2dc and contextual query vectors Q2 ∈Rmw×2dc as Y. QFE outputs the probability distribution that the i-th sentence is the evidence:
    Pr(i) = QFE(X, Y = Q2). (1)
    Then, the evidence layer concatenates the word-level vectors and the sentence-level vectors:
    c5,j = [c3,j; xi(j)] ∈R3dc,
    where the j-th word in C is included in the i(j)-th sentence in C.
*   **Answer Layer**: Predicts the answer type AT and the answer string AS from C5. The layer has stacked Bi-RNNs. The output of each Bi-RNN is mapped to a probability distribution by a fully connected layer and the softmax function.
    For RC, the layer has three stacked Bi-RNNs. Each probability indicates the start of the answer string, ˆAS1 ∈Rlw, the end of the answer string ˆAS2 ∈Rlw, and the answer type, ˆAT ∈R3. For RTE, the layer has one Bi-RNN. The probability indicates the answer type.

**Loss Function:**
Our model uses multi-task learning with a loss function L = LA+LE, where LA is the loss of the answer and LE is the loss of the evidence. The answer loss LA is the sum of the cross-entropy losses for all probability distributions obtained by the answer layer. The evidence loss LE is defined in subsection 3.3.

**3.2 Query Focused Extractor**
Query Focused Extractor (QFE) is shown as the red box in Figure 2. QFE is an extension of the extractive summarization model of Chen and Bansal.

Summarization uses an encoder-decoder architecture (Cheng and Lapata, 2016; Nallapati et al., 2017; Narayan et al., 2018). Sentence-level extractive summarization is used for content selection in abstractive summarization (Chen and Bansal, 2018). This model extracts sentences in order of importance and edits them. This model has been extended for evidence extraction, considering evidence must be extracted in order of importance, not original order as in conventional models.

**Conclusion**

The main contributions of this study are:
1. The QFE model, based on a summarization model for explainable multi-hop QA.
2. The dependency between evidence and question coverage achieved through the summarization model.
3. State-of-the-art performance in evidence extraction for both RC and RTE tasks.

For RC, the QFE architecture, a simple replacement of the baseline, achieved state-of-the-art performance. The ablation study confirmed that replacing the evidence extraction model with QFE improves performance. The adaptive termination contributes to exact matching and precision scores in evidence extraction. The difficulty of questions for QFE depends on the number of required evidence sentences. This study is the first to base its experimental discussion on HotpotQA.

For RTE, the QFE architecture achieved a higher evidence extraction score and a comparable label prediction score compared to competing models. This study is the first to present a joint approach for RC and FEVER.

Evaluation metrics: Prediction of AT, AS, and E were evaluated using official HotpotQA metrics. Exact Match (EM) and F1 scores were used for both answer and evidence. Answer evaluation used classification accuracy of AT. If AT was 'Span', word-level matching of AS was also measured. For evidence, partial match was evaluated by sentence IDs, not word-level partial matches. Joint EM and Joint F1 (Yang et al., 2018) were used for metrics on both answer and evidence.

4.3 Results
Does our model achieve state-of-the-art performance?
In the distractor setting (Table 2), QFE achieved the best evidence extraction score among compared models. It also showed comparable answer selection performance, resulting in state-of-the-art performance on Joint EM and F1 metrics, which are the primary metrics for the dataset. QFE outperformed the baseline model across all metrics. Despite not using pre-trained language models like BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) for encoding, it surpassed methods that did, such as DFGN + BERT and BERT Plus. Specifically, the evidence EM score improved by +37.5 points against the baseline and +5.4 points against GRN.

In the fullwiki setting (Table 3), QFE outperformed the baseline in all metrics. However, it was outperformed by Cognitive Graph (Ding et al., 2019), an unpublished model at submission time. HotpotQA exhibits a dataset shift problem (Quionero-Candela et al., 2009), where the distribution of gold evidence sentences and answerability differs between training (distractor setting) and test (fullwiki setting) phases. In the fullwiki setting, questions may have fewer than two gold evidence sentences or be unanswerable. Our current QA and QFE models do not address this dataset shift; future work will focus on it.

Does QFE contribute to performance?
Ablation study results are shown in Table 4. QFE performed best among the compared models. While the primary difference between our overall model and the baseline is the evidence extraction model, answer scores also improved. QFE also outperformed the model using only RNN extraction without glimpse.

QFE defines the terminal condition as reaching the EOE sentence, termed adaptive termination. This adaptive termination contributed to QFE's performance. Compared to a baseline extracting the two sentences with the highest scores (as two is the most frequent number of evidence sentences), QFE achieved better performance.

The Query Focused Extractor (QFE), shown in Figure 2, is an extension of the extractive summarization model by Chen and Bansal (2018), adapted for query-focused settings. While Chen and Bansal used an attention mechanism to extract sentences covering important information from a source document, QFE extracts sentences from context C with attention on query Q, ensuring the evidence covers information relevant to Q. Figure 3 provides an overview of QFE.

QFE takes sentence-level context vectors $X \in \mathbb{R}^{l_s \times 2d_c}$ and contextual query vectors $Y \in \mathbb{R}^{m_w \times 2d_c}$ as input. A "timestep" refers to an operation that extracts a sentence. QFE updates the RNN state ($z_t \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$) as follows:
$z_t = \text{RNN}(z_{t-1}, x_{e_t}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$,
where $e_t \in \{1, \dots, l_s\}$ is the index of the sentence extracted at step $t$, and $E_t = \{e_1, \dots, e_t\}$ is the set of sentences extracted up to step $t$.

QFE extracts the $i$-th sentence based on the probability distribution (Figure 3, light blue box):
$\text{Pr}(i; E_{t-1}) = \text{softmax}_i(u_t^i)$
$u_t^i = \begin{cases} v_p^\top \tanh(W_{p1}x_i + W_{p2}g_t + W_{p3}z_t) & (i \notin E_{t-1}) \\ -\infty & (\text{otherwise}) \end{cases}$
The sentence extracted is $e_t = \text{argmax}_i \text{Pr}(i; E_{t-1})$.

$g_t$ is a query vector representing importance at step $t$, defined as a glimpse vector (Vinyals et al., 2016) (Figure 3, green box):
$g_t = \sum_{j} \alpha_t^j W_{g1} y_j \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$
$\alpha_t = \text{softmax}(a_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{m_w}$
$a_t^j = v_g^\top \tanh(W_{g1} y_j + W_{g2} z_t)$.

The initial RNN state is obtained from a fully connected layer and max pooling over $X$. All parameters $W_\cdot \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c \times 2d_c}$ and $v_\cdot \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$ are trainable.

### Training Phase

During training, teacher-forcing is used to define the loss function. The evidence loss $L_E$ is the negative log-likelihood, regularized by a coverage mechanism (See et al., 2017):
$L_E = -\sum_{t=1}^{|E|} \log \left( \max_{i \in E \setminus E_{t-1}} \text{Pr}(i; E_{t-1}) \right) + \sum_{i} \min(c_{t_i}, \alpha_{t_i})$.
The maximum operation in the first term selects the sentence with the highest probability, implying QFE extracts sentences in predicted importance order. The loss function ignores the order of evidence sentences as there is no ground truth order for extraction. The coverage vector $c_t$ is defined as $c_t = \sum_{\tau=1}^{t-1} \alpha_\tau$.

To learn the termination condition for extraction, a dummy "End Of Extraction" (EOE) sentence is added to the sentence set. When the EOE sentence is extracted, QFE terminates. The EOE sentence vector $x_{\text{EOE}} \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$ is a trainable parameter, independent of the samples. The model is trained to extract the EOE sentence after all evidence.

### Test Phase

In the test phase, QFE terminates extraction upon reaching the EOE sentence. The predicted evidence $\hat{E}$ is defined as:
$\hat{E} = \text{argmin}_{\hat{E}} \left( -\frac{1}{|\hat{E}|} \sum_{t} \log \max_{i \notin \hat{E}_{t-1}} \text{Pr}(i; \hat{E}_{t-1}) \right)$,
where $\hat{E}_t$ is the predicted evidence up to step $t$. QFE employs beam search to find $\hat{E}$.

### Experiments on RC

#### HotpotQA Dataset

In HotpotQA, queries $Q$ are created by crowd workers, requiring reasoning over two Wikipedia paragraphs for answers. Answer types (AT) include ‘Yes’, ‘No’, and ‘Span’. The answer string $AS$, if it exists, is a span within the two paragraphs. The context $C$ consists of ten paragraphs and has two settings:

1.  **Distractor Setting:** $C$ includes the two gold paragraphs used to create $Q$ and eight paragraphs retrieved from Wikipedia using TF-IDF with $Q$. Table 1 shows statistics for this setting.
2.  **Fullwiki Setting:** All ten paragraphs in $C$ are retrieved. $C$ may not contain the two gold paragraphs, in which case $AS$ and $E$ cannot be extracted, preventing perfect oracle model accuracy. The training data for the fullwiki setting is identical to the distractor setting.

#### Experimental Setup

**Comparison Models:** Our baseline model is similar to Yang et al. (2018), with the following differences: We use Equation (1), whereas their model uses $\text{Pr}(i) = \text{sigmoid}(w^\top x_i + b)$, where $w \in \mathbb{R}^{2d_c}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$ are trainable parameters. Their evidence loss $L_E$ sums binary cross-entropy for each sentence being evidence. In the test phase, sentences with probabilities above a threshold are selected. A threshold of 0.4 was chosen for the highest F1 score on the development set. Other implementation details are consistent with Yang et al. (2018) and are elaborated in Appendix A.1.

topic: Depth perception tasks focus on estimating the distance of objects from a single image or sequence, which is crucial for applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and 3D scene understanding. What is the better method for depth perception tasks: UniDepthV2 or UniDepth?

paper1.title: UniDepthV2: Universal Monocular Metric Depth Estimation Made Simpler
paper1.abstract:
Accurate monocular metric depth estimation
                        (MMDE) is crucial to solving downstream tasks in 3D perception and modeling. However, the remarkable accuracy of
                        recent MMDE methods is confined to their training domains.
                        These methods fail to generalize to unseen domains even in the
                        presence of moderate domain gaps, which hinders their practical
                        applicability. We propose a new model, UniDepthV2, capable
                        of reconstructing metric 3D scenes from solely single images
                        across domains. Departing from the existing MMDE paradigm,
                        UniDepthV2 directly predicts metric 3D points from the input
                        image at inference time without any additional information, striving for a universal and flexible MMDE solution. In particular,
                        UniDepthV2 implements a self-promptable camera module predicting a dense camera representation to condition depth features.
                        Our model exploits a pseudo-spherical output representation,
                        which disentangles the camera and depth representations. In
                        addition, we propose a geometric invariance loss that promotes
                        the invariance of camera-prompted depth features. UniDepthV2
                        improves its predecessor UniDepth model via a new edge-guided
                        loss which enhances the localization and sharpness of edges
                        in the metric depth outputs, a revisited, simplified and more
                        efficient architectural design, and an additional uncertainty-level
                        output which enables downstream tasks requiring confidence.
                        Thorough evaluations on ten depth datasets in a zero-shot
                        regime consistently demonstrate the superior performance and
                        generalization of UniDepthV2. Code and models are available at:
                        github.com/lpiccinelli-eth/UniDepth.

Fine-tuning performance serves as an indicator of a model’s ability to specialize to specific downstream tasks and domains. UniDepthV2 effectively adapts to new domains and outperforms methods that were pre-trained on large, diverse datasets before fine-tuning on NYU or KITTI, such as [16], [29], [33]. This is particularly evident in the outdoor setting (KITTI), as shown in Table IV.

Our training strategy incorporates variable image aspect ratios and resolutions within the same distributed batch. Combined with camera conditioning and invariance learning, this approach enhances the model’s robustness to changes in input image shape. Figure 4 quantifies this effect: the y-axis represents normalized metric accuracy (δ1 scaled by the method’s maximum value), while the x-axis varies the image shape. The normalization ensures a consistent scale across models. UniDepthV2 is almost invariant to image shape, demonstrating that it can effectively trade off resolution for speed without sacrificing accuracy, as clearly illustrated in Figure 4.

C. Ablation Studies
The importance of each new component introduced in UniDepthV2 in Sec. III is evaluated by ablating the method in Tables V, VI, and VII. All ablations exploit the predicted camera representation, if not stated otherwise. Table V evaluates the impact of various architectural modifications compared to UniDepth [17], analyzing their effects on both performance and efficiency. Table VI assesses the importance of the proposed loss function (Sec. III-D) and examines the effect of applying the geometric invariance loss originally introduced in UniDepth [17] (Sec. III-C) in different spaces. The rationale behind our design choices is to maintain simplicity while maximizing effectiveness. Confidence:
The confidence measure (Sec. III-E) is evaluated on three zero-shot datasets in Fig. 5. The y-axis is normalized RMSE (RMSE divided by per-dataset RMSE at x=0), and the x-axis is confidence quantile. Evaluation includes pixels with confidence exceeding the threshold for each quantile. A reliable confidence estimate should negatively correlate with error, meaning higher-confidence regions should have lower RMSE. Fig. 5 validates this negative correlation for UniDepthV2's predicted confidence, demonstrating its reliability.

V. CONCLUSION
UniDepthV2 is introduced as a universal monocular metric depth estimation model that generalizes across diverse domains without requiring camera parameters at test time. Improvements in model architecture and training objective losses lead to state-of-the-art performance with enhanced computational efficiency. Extensive zero-shot and fine-tuning evaluations confirm this. The training strategy allows for a flexible trade-off between inference speed and detail preservation via variable input resolutions at test time while maintaining global scale consistency.

Architecture Modifications (UniDepth to UniDepthV2):
1.  **SHE + Sine**: Replaced Spherical Harmonics (SH)-based encoding with standard Sine encoding. Minimal performance difference observed.
2.  **- Attention**: Removed attention mechanism due to high computational cost. Resulted in a significant performance drop (-4.3% for δ1) but more than 2x efficiency improvement.
3.  **+ ResNet Blocks**: Replaced MLP-based decoder with ResNet blocks (3x3 convolutions) to leverage spatial structure. Minimal impact on efficiency.
4.  **+ Multi-resol.**: Integrated multi-resolution feature fusion from encoder to decoder (FPN-style). Achieved similar performance to original UniDepth with one-third of computation.

- `✓` LEG−SSI, `Z` OLcon: Significant improvements: +4.7% δ1, +1.8% FA. ρA also improved, suggesting a less noisy training process.

- V2: Proposed UniDepthV2.
- Cond: Presence of camera-prompting mechanism.

- `V1, ✓ Cond`: Original UniDepth with camera conditioning.

Lcon Output Space:
- Investigated applying the consistency loss (Lcon) directly in the output space (Z) versus within camera-conditioned features at each scale (D|E).
- Minimal differences were observed between applying the loss directly in the output space (Z).

Prompting is fundamental to avoid mode collapse in scene scale and to alleviate the depth module from predicting depth from scratch, as scale is modeled by camera output. The internal representation of the camera module is based on pinhole parameterization: focal length (fx, fy) and principal point (cx, cy). These four intrinsics are projected to scalar values: ∆fx, ∆fy, ∆cx, ∆cy. They represent multiplicative residuals to a pinhole camera initialization, H/2 for y-components and W/2 for x-components, leading to fx = ∆fxW/2, fy = ∆fyH/2, cx = ∆cxW/2, cy = ∆cyH/2, ensuring invariance towards input image sizes.

A backprojection operation based on intrinsic parameters is applied to each pixel coordinate to produce corresponding rays. Normalized rays represent vectors on a unit sphere. Azimuth and elevation are extracted from backprojected rays, creating a "dense" angular camera representation. This representation undergoes Sine encoding to produce embeddings E. These embeddings are passed to the depth module as a prompt, acting as a conditioning factor via cross-attention between projected encoder feature maps {Fi}4i=1, with Fi ∈Rh×w×C and (h, w) = (H/14, W/14), and camera embeddings E. Camera-prompted depth features Fi|E ∈Rh×w×C are defined as:
F_i|E = MLP(CA(Fi, E))
where CA is a cross-attention block and MLP is a MultiLayer Perceptron with one 4C-channel hidden layer.

C. Geometric Invariance Loss
Spatial locations from the same scene captured by different cameras should correspond when the depth module is conditioned on the specific camera. A geometric invariance loss enforces the consistency of camera-prompted depth features of the same scene from different sensors, specifically on features extracted from identical 3D locations.

For each image, N distinct geometrical augmentations {Ti}N i=1 are performed (N=2 in experiments). This involves sampling a rescaling factor r ∼ 2U[−2,2] and a relative translation t ∼ U[−0.1,0.1], then cropping to a randomly selected input shape. This simulates sampling a pair of images from the same scene and extrinsic parameters, captured by different cameras.

Let Ci and Zi describe the predicted camera representation and camera-aware depth output corresponding to augmentation Ti. Camera representations differ for diverse geometric augmentations (Ci ̸= Cj if Ti ̸= Tj). The geometric invariance loss is expressed as:
L_con(Z1, Z2) = ||T2 ∘ T⁻¹1 (Z1) - sg(Z2)||₁
where Zi is the depth output after being conditioned by camera prompt Ei, decoded, and sg(·) is the stop-gradient detach operation. Z2 is used as pseudo ground truth (GT). The bidirectional loss is computed as:
1/2(Lcon(Z1, Z2) + Lcon(Z2, Z1)).
The geometric invariance loss must be applied to camera-aware components, such as the output depth map, to avoid enforcing consistency across features with purposefully different camera information.

D. Edge-Guided Normalized Loss
Modern depth estimation methods must balance global scene understanding with local geometric precision. UniDepth excels at the former but lacks accuracy in local, fine-grained details. UniDepthV2 introduces the Edge-Guided Scale-Shift Invariant Loss (LEG−SSI) to enhance local precision. This loss is computed over image patches extracted from regions where the RGB spatial gradient ranks in the top 5%-quantile, capturing high-contrast areas with potential depth discontinuities. Patch sizes are randomly sampled between 4% and 8% of the input image’s smallest dimension. By focusing on these salient regions, the model learns to distinguish genuine geometric discontinuities from misleading high-frequency textures that do not correspond to actual depth changes. This approach discourages errors caused by structured patterns like checkerboard textures or repetitive details on flat surfaces that can falsely suggest depth variations.

UniDepthV2 is implemented in PyTorch and CUDA.
Training uses the AdamW optimizer (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999) with an initial learning rate of 5 × 10−5.
The learning rate is divided by 10 for backbone weights every experiment.
Weight decay is set to 0.1.
Cosine Annealing is used as the learning rate and weight decay scheduler, reducing to one-tenth starting from 30% of training.
Training runs for 300k optimization iterations with a batch size of 128.
Training time is 6 days on 16 NVIDIA 4090 with half precision.
Dataset sampling uses a weighted sampler, with dataset weights equal to their number of scenes.
Augmentations include geometric (random resizing, cropping, translation) and photometric (brightness, gamma, saturation, hue shift).
Image ratio is randomly sampled per batch between 2:1 and 1:2.
The ViT backbone is initialized with weights from DINO-pre-trained models.
Ablations use 100k training steps with a ViT-S backbone and the same training pipeline.
Evaluation is performed on eight zero-shot validation sets, covering indoor and outdoor scenes.
UniDepthV2 outperforms baselines, including methods requiring ground-truth camera parameters.
UniDepthV2 shows consistent improvement (0.5% to 18.1%) over the second-best method in the FA metric.
UniDepthV2 outperforms UniDepth in most cases, except for the ρA metric on IBims-1, DDAD, and NuScenes.
The camera parameter estimation (ρA) shows marginal improvements, suggesting a need for additional camera-only training.
Fine-tuning is performed on NYU and KITTI datasets.

paper2.title: UniDepth: Universal Monocular Metric Depth Estimation
paper2.abstract:
Accurate monocular metric depth estimation (MMDE)
                        is crucial to solving downstream tasks in 3D perception
                        and modeling. However, the remarkable accuracy of recent
                        MMDE methods is confined to their training domains. These
                        methods fail to generalize to unseen domains even in the presence of moderate domain gaps, which hinders their practical
                        applicability. We propose a new model, UniDepth, capable
                        of reconstructing metric 3D scenes from solely single images
                        across domains. Departing from the existing MMDE methods, UniDepth directly predicts metric 3D points from the
                        input image at inference time without any additional information, striving for a universal and flexible MMDE solution.
                        In particular, UniDepth implements a self-promptable camera module predicting dense camera representation to condition depth features. Our model exploits a pseudo-spherical
                        output representation, which disentangles camera and depth
                        representations. In addition, we propose a geometric invariance loss that promotes the invariance of camera-prompted
                        depth features. Thorough evaluations on ten datasets in a
                        zero-shot regime consistently demonstrate the superior performance of UniDepth, even when compared with methods
                        directly trained on the testing domains. Code and models
                        are available at: github.com/lpiccinelli-eth/unidepth.

B. Ablations
B.1. Ablations with ViT backbone
Ablations with ViT backbone are provided in Table 9. Trends are consistent with the convolutional backbone. Ablated components contribute similarly between ViT-L [12] and ConvNext-L [33] backbones.
Utilizing a ViT backbone shows larger variability for out-of-domain results and a stronger effect of pseudo-spherical representation. The increased susceptibility of scene depth scale to domain shift is related to backbone comparison in Table 1. Convolutional architectures exhibit superior resilience to scale-related domain shifts, while showing relative disadvantage in handling appearance-related domain shifts. SIlog consistently favors ViT over convolutional methods, emphasizing the latter’s diminished performance in appearance domain shifts. However, scale-dependent metrics do not consistently favor ViT, indicating that the constrained receptive field of convolutional methods yields higher robustness to domain shifts associated with scale.

Refraining from relying on the camera constrains the model’s capacity to recover a multimodal distribution for out-of-domain samples. The lack of a (bootstrapped) prior prevents the depth module from serving as a corrective mechanism based on an initial scale estimation and imposes an unnecessary computational burden, i.e., recovering the depth values from scratch. This limitation is underscored by the marked variability observed for test sets strongly out-of-distribution, such as KITTI, when comparing the utilization or absence of camera information (rows 2 and 3, respectively). In particular, Full achieves 95.2% in δ1 in KITTI, while “– Camera” obtains 58.9% for the same test set, despite a mere 2% difference between the two versions on nuScenes and DDAD.

Optimization and Output Representation. All ablations employ the same loss LλMSE, but across different output spaces. In row 4, a Cartesian output space is used instead of a pseudo-spherical from Sec. 3.1, which results in substantially inferior performance due to the respective intertwined formulation of camera and depth output spaces. The Baseline (row 8) also employs a Cartesian representation, but the negative impact of this choice is less pronounced in this model because of the absence of a camera module. More specifically, the decoder of Baseline is not conditioned on inaccurate prior camera and scale information as in row 4. Moreover, row 9 corresponds to Baseline with pseudo-spherical representation. Comparison between row 8 and row 9 shows that when predicting directly the 3D outputs, the choice of the output representation is still relevant in defining a better internal representation and optimization. Row 5 demonstrates the positive impact of the geometric invariance loss. This loss contributes to enhanced in-domain and out-of-domain performance by promoting the invariance of depth features to appearance variations owing to different camera intrinsics. Furthermore, stopping the gradient from propagating from the Camera Module to the Encoder (row 7), as described in Sec. 3.4, proves particularly beneficial in avoiding scale and camera overfitting in zero-shot testing, and stabilizes the training. The more stable training is obtained by limiting the dominant effect that camera supervision has on the gradient of the Encoder weights compared to depth supervision.

Camera Representation. In row 6, the model incorporates a sparse camera representation, specifically the pinhole camera model with (fx, fy, cx, cy), leading to sparse camera prompting and scalar supervision; the camera module still predicts the residual components as outlined in Sec. 3.2. This approach hurts generalization, as evidenced by ARelC in the out-of-domain evaluation, despite the slight improvement in in-domain ARelC. We speculate that the four prompts convey less robust information to the depth module than their dense counterpart, resulting in inferior performance for depth metrics compared to Full for both in- and out-of-domain.

UniDepth exploits an angular pseudo-spherical representation (θ, ϕ, zlog). An alternative representation uses the bearing vector (rx, ry, rz) and log-depth (zlog), where (rx, ry, rz) ∈ S2. Bearing vectors are obtained by unprojecting image coordinates using the pinhole camera model. The output tuple is (rx, ry, rz, zlog), and the loss LλMSE is applied with λrx = λry = λrz = 1 and λz = 0.15. Rays and angles have a direct relationship: θ = arctan(rx/rz) and ϕ = arccos(ry). Table 10 compares the effectiveness of this alternative representation to the one in Section 3. The difference is marginal and often within the uncertainty range, indicating similarity. The primary difference is in output space dimensionality; bearing vectors span R3, constrained to the unit-sphere manifold by L2 normalization.

Algorithm 1: GT depth boundaries refining.
procedure BOUNDARYREFINE(Zlog)
  L = Laplacian(Zlog, k = 5)
  M = I[L10% ≤ L ≤ L90%]
  M = (M ⊖eye3) ⊕eye3
  M = MedianBlur(M, k = 3)
  Z = exp(Zlog) · M
  return Z

KITTI Eigen-split uses corrected and accumulated GT depth maps, with 45 images with inaccurate GT discarded from the original 697.

Diode indoor ground-truth correction: Diode [50] ground-truth depth has inaccuracies at boundaries, presenting low, non-zero depth values. These artifacts affect validation results. Algorithm 1 detects boundary artifacts and masks depth in corresponding neighborhoods.

Features are interpolated to a common shape (h, w) = (H/16, W/16).
Two independent projections are utilized for feature maps F ∈Rh×w×C×B, where B corresponds to four scales and C=512.
Class tokens ∈RC×B are fed to the Camera Module only.

Camera Module:
Camera parameters are initialized with four class tokens from the Encoder.
Flattened and stacked feature maps from the encoder are detached and used as keys and values in one cross-attention layer.
Queries correspond to the four camera parameters.
Output is processed by a MultiLayer Perceptron (MLP) with one hidden layer of dimension 2048 and GELU activation.
Cross-attention and MLP have a residual connection.
Four tokens are processed with two additional self-attention layers, projected to dimension one, and exponentiated.
Camera parameters are obtained as fx = ∆fxW/2, fy = ∆fyH/2, cx = ∆cxW/2, cy = ∆cyH/2.
Dense camera representation C is obtained by backprojecting with predicted camera parameters: (rx, ry, rz) = K−1[u, v, 1]T.
Azimuth and elevation angles, θ and ϕ, are calculated as in Sec. B.
Angular representation is embedded through Laplace Spherical Harmonics Embedding (SHE) leading to 81 channels, resulting in E ∈Rh×w×81.

Depth Module:
Depth latents are initialized as the average of features F along the B dimension.
Latents are conditioned on the original feature tensor F via one cross-attention layer where two projections of F are keys and values, and L are queries.
One MLP is applied, similar to the Camera Module.
Depth features are conditioned on camera prompts E with one additional cross-attention layer, where keys and values are two projections of camera embeddings E, and one MLP is used.
Features are decoded in three consecutive stages.
Stage 1: Three self-attention layers with E as positional encoding. Processed with one ConvNext layer, upsampled by a factor of two, channels halved.
Stage 2: Two self-attention layers. MLP hidden dimension halved from 2048. Upsampled by a factor of two, channels halved.
Stage 3: One self-attention layer. MLP hidden dimension halved from previous stage. Upsampled by a factor of two, channels halved.
Each stage's output is projected to dimension one.
Three output maps are interpolated to a common shape (H/2, W/2) and pixel-wise averaged.
Final log-depth output Zlog is obtained by upsampling to the input shape (H, W).
Final depth is element-wise exponentiation of Zlog.

Encoder: Effectiveness shown with convolutional and transformer-based encoders (ConvNext [33], ViT [12]). Feature maps extracted at each layer; feature map for a scale is the pixel-wise average. For ConvNext, class tokens are average pooled feature maps. Last 3 layers (pooling, fully connected, softmax) are removed from classification backbones. **4.3. Ablation Study**

The importance of each component in UniDepth (Sec. 3) is evaluated by ablating the method in Table 5. All ablations use the predicted camera representation, unless stated otherwise. The Oracle model operates with known camera information during training and testing, similar to [21, 59]. The Baseline is a straightforward encoder-decoder implementation with a (x,y,z) output. Baseline++ uses the proposed pseudo-spherical representation. Module architectures are consistent. The In-Domain column shows testing on validation splits of training domains; Out-of-Domain corresponds to zero-shot testing (Sec. 4.1). In-Domain results are more homogeneous than Out-of-Domain, which is noisier but more informative for gauging downstream and in-the-wild performance.

**Architecture:** The Oracle model shows more robust scale-dependent performance in zero-shot testing compared to the Full model, indicating the task's inherent demand. The Baseline model, lacking external information and proper internal/output design, yields inferior results for both In-Domain and Out-of-Domain scenarios in depth and 3D reconstruction metrics.

**Camera Module:** Table 5, row 3, shows the Camera Module's substantial effect on scale-invariant and scale-dependent metrics for in- and out-of-domain testing. This disparity arises from the model's lack of prior scale knowledge, hindering optimal use of the diverse training set. Predicting only depth, not full 3D output, aids convergence during training, as seen when compared to methods predicting 3D without camera information (rows 8 and 9) or with intertwined optimization (row 4).

topic: Depth perception tasks focus on estimating the distance of objects from a single image or sequence, which is crucial for applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and 3D scene understanding. What is the better method for depth perception tasks: UniDepthV2 or DCDepth?

paper1.title: UniDepthV2: Universal Monocular Metric Depth Estimation Made Simpler
paper1.abstract:
Accurate monocular metric depth estimation
                        (MMDE) is crucial to solving downstream tasks in 3D perception and modeling. However, the remarkable accuracy of
                        recent MMDE methods is confined to their training domains.
                        These methods fail to generalize to unseen domains even in the
                        presence of moderate domain gaps, which hinders their practical
                        applicability. We propose a new model, UniDepthV2, capable
                        of reconstructing metric 3D scenes from solely single images
                        across domains. Departing from the existing MMDE paradigm,
                        UniDepthV2 directly predicts metric 3D points from the input
                        image at inference time without any additional information, striving for a universal and flexible MMDE solution. In particular,
                        UniDepthV2 implements a self-promptable camera module predicting a dense camera representation to condition depth features.
                        Our model exploits a pseudo-spherical output representation,
                        which disentangles the camera and depth representations. In
                        addition, we propose a geometric invariance loss that promotes
                        the invariance of camera-prompted depth features. UniDepthV2
                        improves its predecessor UniDepth model via a new edge-guided
                        loss which enhances the localization and sharpness of edges
                        in the metric depth outputs, a revisited, simplified and more
                        efficient architectural design, and an additional uncertainty-level
                        output which enables downstream tasks requiring confidence.
                        Thorough evaluations on ten depth datasets in a zero-shot
                        regime consistently demonstrate the superior performance and
                        generalization of UniDepthV2. Code and models are available at:
                        github.com/lpiccinelli-eth/UniDepth.
