Fine-tuning performance serves as an indicator of a model’s ability to specialize to specific downstream tasks and domains. UniDepthV2 effectively adapts to new domains and outperforms methods that were pre-trained on large, diverse datasets before fine-tuning on NYU or KITTI, such as [16], [29], [33]. This is particularly evident in the outdoor setting (KITTI), as shown in Table IV.

Our training strategy incorporates variable image aspect ratios and resolutions within the same distributed batch. Combined with camera conditioning and invariance learning, this approach enhances the model’s robustness to changes in input image shape. Figure 4 quantifies this effect: the y-axis represents normalized metric accuracy (δ1 scaled by the method’s maximum value), while the x-axis varies the image shape. The normalization ensures a consistent scale across models. UniDepthV2 is almost invariant to image shape, demonstrating that it can effectively trade off resolution for speed without sacrificing accuracy, as clearly illustrated in Figure 4.

V. CONCLUSION
UniDepthV2 is introduced as a universal monocular metric depth estimation model that generalizes across diverse domains without requiring camera parameters at test time. Improvements in model architecture and training objective losses lead to state-of-the-art performance with enhanced computational efficiency. Extensive zero-shot and fine-tuning evaluations confirm this. The training strategy allows for a flexible trade-off between inference speed and detail preservation via variable input resolutions at test time while maintaining global scale consistency.

Prompting is fundamental to avoid mode collapse in scene scale and to alleviate the depth module from predicting depth from scratch, as scale is modeled by camera output. The internal representation of the camera module is based on pinhole parameterization: focal length (fx, fy) and principal point (cx, cy). These four intrinsics are projected to scalar values: ∆fx, ∆fy, ∆cx, ∆cy. They represent multiplicative residuals to a pinhole camera initialization, H/2 for y-components and W/2 for x-components, leading to fx = ∆fxW/2, fy = ∆fyH/2, cx = ∆cxW/2, cy = ∆cyH/2, ensuring invariance towards input image sizes.

A backprojection operation based on intrinsic parameters is applied to each pixel coordinate to produce corresponding rays. Normalized rays represent vectors on a unit sphere. Azimuth and elevation are extracted from backprojected rays, creating a "dense" angular camera representation. This representation undergoes Sine encoding to produce embeddings E. These embeddings are passed to the depth module as a prompt, acting as a conditioning factor via cross-attention between projected encoder feature maps {Fi}4i=1, with Fi ∈Rh×w×C and (h, w) = (H/14, W/14), and camera embeddings E. Camera-prompted depth features Fi|E ∈Rh×w×C are defined as:
F_i|E = MLP(CA(Fi, E))
where CA is a cross-attention block and MLP is a MultiLayer Perceptron with one 4C-channel hidden layer.

C. Geometric Invariance Loss
Spatial locations from the same scene captured by different cameras should correspond when the depth module is conditioned on the specific camera. A geometric invariance loss enforces the consistency of camera-prompted depth features of the same scene from different sensors, specifically on features extracted from identical 3D locations.

For each image, N distinct geometrical augmentations {Ti}N i=1 are performed (N=2 in experiments). This involves sampling a rescaling factor r ∼ 2U[−2,2] and a relative translation t ∼ U[−0.1,0.1], then cropping to a randomly selected input shape. This simulates sampling a pair of images from the same scene and extrinsic parameters, captured by different cameras.

Let Ci and Zi describe the predicted camera representation and camera-aware depth output corresponding to augmentation Ti. Camera representations differ for diverse geometric augmentations (Ci ̸= Cj if Ti ̸= Tj). The geometric invariance loss is expressed as:
L_con(Z1, Z2) = ||T2 ∘ T⁻¹1 (Z1) - sg(Z2)||₁
where Zi is the depth output after being conditioned by camera prompt Ei, decoded, and sg(·) is the stop-gradient detach operation. Z2 is used as pseudo ground truth (GT). The bidirectional loss is computed as:
1/2(Lcon(Z1, Z2) + Lcon(Z2, Z1)).
The geometric invariance loss must be applied to camera-aware components, such as the output depth map, to avoid enforcing consistency across features with purposefully different camera information.

D. Edge-Guided Normalized Loss
Modern depth estimation methods must balance global scene understanding with local geometric precision. UniDepth excels at the former but lacks accuracy in local, fine-grained details. UniDepthV2 introduces the Edge-Guided Scale-Shift Invariant Loss (LEG−SSI) to enhance local precision. This loss is computed over image patches extracted from regions where the RGB spatial gradient ranks in the top 5%-quantile, capturing high-contrast areas with potential depth discontinuities. Patch sizes are randomly sampled between 4% and 8% of the input image’s smallest dimension. By focusing on these salient regions, the model learns to distinguish genuine geometric discontinuities from misleading high-frequency textures that do not correspond to actual depth changes. This approach discourages errors caused by structured patterns like checkerboard textures or repetitive details on flat surfaces that can falsely suggest depth variations.

UniDepthV2 is implemented in PyTorch and CUDA.
Training uses the AdamW optimizer (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999) with an initial learning rate of 5 × 10−5.
The learning rate is divided by 10 for backbone weights every experiment.
Weight decay is set to 0.1.
Cosine Annealing is used as the learning rate and weight decay scheduler, reducing to one-tenth starting from 30% of training.
Training runs for 300k optimization iterations with a batch size of 128.
Training time is 6 days on 16 NVIDIA 4090 with half precision.
Dataset sampling uses a weighted sampler, with dataset weights equal to their number of scenes.
Augmentations include geometric (random resizing, cropping, translation) and photometric (brightness, gamma, saturation, hue shift).
Image ratio is randomly sampled per batch between 2:1 and 1:2.
The ViT backbone is initialized with weights from DINO-pre-trained models.
Ablations use 100k training steps with a ViT-S backbone and the same training pipeline.
Evaluation is performed on eight zero-shot validation sets, covering indoor and outdoor scenes.
UniDepthV2 outperforms baselines, including methods requiring ground-truth camera parameters.
UniDepthV2 shows consistent improvement (0.5% to 18.1%) over the second-best method in the FA metric.
UniDepthV2 outperforms UniDepth in most cases, except for the ρA metric on IBims-1, DDAD, and NuScenes.

Fine-tuning is performed on NYU and KITTI datasets.

paper2.title: DCDepth: Progressive Monocular Depth Estimation in Discrete Cosine Domain
paper2.abstract:
In this paper, we introduce DCDepth, a novel framework for the long-standing
                        monocular depth estimation task. Moving beyond conventional pixel-wise depth
                        estimation in the spatial domain, our approach estimates the frequency coefficients
                        of depth patches after transforming them into the discrete cosine domain. This
                        unique formulation allows for the modeling of local depth correlations within each
                        patch. Crucially, the frequency transformation segregates the depth information
                        into various frequency components, with low-frequency components encapsulating
                        the core scene structure and high-frequency components detailing the finer aspects.
                        This decomposition forms the basis of our progressive strategy, which begins with
                        the prediction of low-frequency components to establish a global scene context,
                        followed by successive refinement of local details through the prediction of higherfrequency components. We conduct comprehensive experiments on NYU-DepthV2, TOFDC, and KITTI datasets, and demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance
                        of DCDepth. Code is available at https://github.com/w2kun/DCDepth.

Limitation and Broader Impact:
Our method uses differentiable inverse DCT to transform predicted spectrum back to spatial domain, allowing end-to-end training by minimizing the difference between spatial-domain estimation and ground truth. However, sparse ground truth may lead to inefficient frequency estimation supervision. Two regularization terms were proposed to prevent incorrect optimization, but the method is more effective with dense supervision. Future work will explore more effective training strategies for sparse depth ground truth.

Monocular depth estimation is crucial for interpreting 3D scenes from 2D images, with applications in autonomous driving, robotics, and 3D modeling. Our method is poised to positively impact these fields by advancing their capabilities. Given the fundamental nature of monocular depth estimation, our work is not anticipated to have a significant negative societal impact.

Conclusion:
DCDepth, a novel framework for MDE, progressively estimates patch-wise depth in the frequency domain and recovers spatial-domain depth via inverse DCT. This formulation models local depth correlations and uses a global-to-local scheme for accurate depth estimation. Leveraging DCT's energy compaction property, DCDepth balances accuracy and inference speed, making it suitable for practical applications.

Missing values in depth ground truth can inadequately supervise frequency-domain predictions. To mitigate this, two regularization terms are introduced. Frequency regularization loss enforces sparsity of high-frequency coefficients:
Lf = ∑(ϵu+v −1) · |fu,v|
where fu,v is the frequency coefficient indexed by (u, v), and ϵ = 1.2. A smoothness term promotes the smoothness of D̂:
Ls = |∂x D̂| · e−|∂xIt| + |∂y D̂| · e−|∂yIt|
where ∂x and ∂y are image gradients along horizontal and vertical axes, respectively, and |·| denotes the absolute value. The final loss is a weighted sum of these three terms.

Experiment
This section evaluates DCDepth through a comparative analysis with established methodologies. Datasets and evaluation metrics are delineated, followed by implementation specifics. Ablation studies demonstrate the efficacy of proposed modules.

Dataset and Evaluation Metric
Dataset
The method is evaluated on three datasets covering diverse indoor and outdoor scenes.
1. NYU-Depth-V2 [36]: Indoor environments, RGB-D images from Microsoft Kinect. Scenes include bedrooms, offices, classrooms. Resolution: 640 × 480. Data split: 24231 training, 654 test images (following BTS [17]).
2. TOFDC [52]: Collected using a mobile phone with a Time-of-Flight (ToF) camera. Subjects: flowers, human figures, toys. Diverse scenes and lighting. 10,000 training, 560 testing samples. Resolution: 512 × 384.
3. KITTI [13]: Outdoor dataset, RGB images with sparse depth maps from a car-mounted laser scanner. Resolution: 1216 × 352. Splits used: Eigen split [11] (23158 training, 697 test) and official split (42949 training, 500 test).

Metrics
Established metrics are used for comprehensive evaluation, consistent with prior works [58, 3, 34]. Key metrics include: relative absolute error (Abs Rel), relative squared error (Sq Rel), root mean squared error (RMSE), absolute logarithmic error (log10), root mean squared logarithmic error (RMSE log), inverse root mean squared error (iRMSE), and threshold accuracy (δ < 1.25, δ < 1.25², and δ < 1.25³). Appendix provides details.

Implementation Detail
DCDepth is implemented using the Pytorch library [25]. Training uses a batch size of 8 on four NVIDIA RTX-4090 GPUs with data-distributed parallel computing.

**Progressive Estimation in Discrete Cosine Domain**
Estimating depth from a single image is challenging, especially for scenes with intricate geometry. A progressive method based on 2D DCT is proposed to estimate scene depth from a global to local perspective.
Input image is I ∈ R<sup>3×H×W</sup>.
The proposed method, Ψ(·), predicts frequency coefficients C ∈ R<sup>S<sup>2</sup>×H<sub>S</sub>×W<sub>S</sub></sup> for non-overlapping depth patches P ∈ R<sup>S×S</sup>, where S=8.
These coefficients are transformed back to the spatial domain ˆD ∈ R<sup>H×W</sup> using inverse 2D DCT:
ˆD = T<sup>−1</sup>(Ψ(I)) (4)
Separating low- and high-frequency components in a depth map divides the scene into overall structures with gradual depth changes and local details with sharp depth transitions. This enables breaking down the MDE task into multiple prediction stages, from simpler to more complex.
Initially, the DC coefficient C<sub>0</sub> is predicted, establishing a foundational depth context.
Subsequently, AC coefficients {C<sub>i</sub>}<sub>i=1</sub><sup>S<sup>2</sup>−1</sup> are iteratively estimated in ascending frequency order.
During inverse transformation to spatial domain, unpredicted coefficients are padded with zeros.
In iterative step k, higher-frequency components are predicted, and preceding frequency predictions are refined:
C<sub>k</sub> = C<sub>k−1</sub> + ∆C<sub>k</sub> (5)
by estimating a correction term ∆C<sub>k</sub>.
To reduce iterations for estimating all S<sup>2</sup> coefficients, the energy compaction property of DCT is utilized. The frequency spectrum C is partitioned into subgroups along the subdiagonal, yielding 2S−1 subgroups {g<sub>i</sub>}<sub>i=0</sub><sup>2S−2</sup>. Merging high-frequency subgroups further streamlines the process.
This grouping strategy ensures lower-frequency groups have fewer components requiring more prediction steps, while higher-frequency groups have more components requiring fewer steps.
Intermediate depth maps are shown in Fig. 2.

**DCDepth Architecture**
The DCDepth framework comprises four components: an image encoder, a Pyramid Feature Fusion (PFF) module, a decoder, and a Progressive Prediction Head (PPH).
The image encoder extracts image features F = {F<sub>0</sub>, F<sub>1</sub>, F<sub>2</sub>, F<sub>3</sub>} at resolutions 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, and 1/32 of the input image size. Shallow features contain texture details; deep features hold global and semantic information.
The PFF module, Γ(·), amalgamates these features, yielding an integrated representation F′ = Γ(F).
The decoder, D(·), uses three neural CRF modules and two PixelShuffle modules. It processes and upscales F′ to ˆF = D(F′), achieving 1/8 of the original resolution.
The PPH performs estimations at the same resolution as ˆF.
It down-samples F<sub>0</sub> to half its resolution using DCT-based downsampling.
This down-sampled feature is concatenated with ˆF, forming the initial hidden state for progressive estimation.

DCDepth is implemented using Pytorch and trained with a batch size of 8 on four NVIDIA RTX-4090 GPUs using data-distributed parallel computing.

The PPH performs estimations at the same resolution as $\hat{F}$. It begins by down-sampling $F_0$ to half its resolution using DCT-based downsampling. This down-sampled feature is concatenated with $\hat{F}$, forming the initial hidden state for progressive estimation.

**Pyramid Feature Fusion Module**
The PFF aims to leverage multi-scale image features for enriched representations conducive to scene understanding. Feature aggregation requires proficient downsampling to mitigate information loss. A novel DCT-based downsampling strategy minimizes this loss. For a feature map $F \in R^{C \times H \times W}$ downsampled by a factor of $R$, $F$ is partitioned into patches $P \in R^{C \times R^2 \times \frac{H}{R} \times \frac{W}{R}}$. Each channel of $P$ is transformed into the frequency domain using Eq. 2. The DCT's energy compaction property condenses key information into dominant frequency components. This enables reducing channels from $C \times R^2$ to $C \times \frac{R^2}{r}$ with a reduction rate of $r$ via 1x1 convolutions with groups set to $C$. The squeezed feature maps are consolidated through a 1x1 convolution, a 5x5 depth-wise convolution, generating an output with $C'$ channels and reduced spatial resolution.

**Progressive Prediction Head**
The PPH incorporates two encoders: $E_s(\cdot)$ for spatial-domain inputs and $E_f(\cdot)$ for frequency-domain inputs. The spatial encoder, with three convolutional layers (stride 2), convolves and downsamples the spatial-domain input $\hat{D}$, producing a feature map at 1/8 the original resolution. The $E_f(\cdot)$ architecture is detailed. For frequency input $C \in R^{L \times H \times W}$, where $L$ is the number of valid frequency components, these are split into $L$ chunks of shape $1 \times H \times W$. Each chunk is processed through three convolutional layers with Swish activation to extract features of dimensions $C \times H \times W$ per frequency component. Given variability in $L$ across iterative steps, a cross-attention mechanism merges information from frequency components. A learnable aggregation token of dimensions $1 \times C$ compiles information from individual frequency components at each pixel location, yielding feature outputs of shape $C \times H \times W$ and compressing dimension $L$. The PPH operates iteratively, using a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), $G(\cdot, \cdot)$, to encode historical estimation states:
$H_i = G(E_s(\hat{D}_{i-1}), E_f(C_{i-1}))$
prior to iterative step $i$. The hidden state $H$ is projected to the coefficient output by a Pyramid Pooling Module (PPM) to aggregate global context, followed by a linear projection.

**Loss Function**
The scaled scale-invariant loss [17, 3] calibrates model depth estimations $\hat{D}_i$ at each iterative step $i$ against ground truth depth map $D$. The loss function is formulated as:
$L_d = \alpha \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{N} \beta^{N-i} \left( \frac{1}{M} \sum d_i^2 - \frac{\lambda}{M^2} (\sum d_i)^2 \right)$
where $d = \hat{D}_i - D$, $N$ is the number of iterative steps, and $M$ is the number of valid depth values. We set $\alpha = 10$, $\beta = 0.8$, and $\lambda = 0.85$ across experiments.

topic: Depth perception tasks focus on estimating the distance of objects from a single image or sequence, which is crucial for applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and 3D scene understanding. What is the better method for depth perception tasks: UniDepthV2 or DiffusionDepth-I?

paper1.title: UniDepthV2: Universal Monocular Metric Depth Estimation Made Simpler
paper1.abstract:
Accurate monocular metric depth estimation
                        (MMDE) is crucial to solving downstream tasks in 3D perception and modeling. However, the remarkable accuracy of
                        recent MMDE methods is confined to their training domains.
                        These methods fail to generalize to unseen domains even in the
                        presence of moderate domain gaps, which hinders their practical
                        applicability. We propose a new model, UniDepthV2, capable
                        of reconstructing metric 3D scenes from solely single images
                        across domains. Departing from the existing MMDE paradigm,
                        UniDepthV2 directly predicts metric 3D points from the input
                        image at inference time without any additional information, striving for a universal and flexible MMDE solution. In particular,
                        UniDepthV2 implements a self-promptable camera module predicting a dense camera representation to condition depth features.
                        Our model exploits a pseudo-spherical output representation,
                        which disentangles the camera and depth representations. In
                        addition, we propose a geometric invariance loss that promotes
                        the invariance of camera-prompted depth features. UniDepthV2
                        improves its predecessor UniDepth model via a new edge-guided
                        loss which enhances the localization and sharpness of edges
                        in the metric depth outputs, a revisited, simplified and more
                        efficient architectural design, and an additional uncertainty-level
                        output which enables downstream tasks requiring confidence.
                        Thorough evaluations on ten depth datasets in a zero-shot
                        regime consistently demonstrate the superior performance and
                        generalization of UniDepthV2. Code and models are available at:
                        github.com/lpiccinelli-eth/UniDepth.

UniDepthV2 effectively adapts to new domains and outperforms methods that were pre-trained on large, diverse datasets before fine-tuning on NYU or KITTI, such as [16], [29], [33]. This is particularly evident in the outdoor setting (KITTI), as shown in Table IV.

Our training strategy incorporates variable image aspect ratios and resolutions within the same distributed batch. Combined with camera conditioning and invariance learning, this approach enhances the model’s robustness to changes in input image shape. Figure 4 quantifies this effect: the y-axis represents normalized metric accuracy (δ1 scaled by the method’s maximum value), while the x-axis varies the image shape. The normalization ensures a consistent scale across models. UniDepthV2 is almost invariant to image shape, demonstrating that it can effectively trade off resolution for speed without sacrificing accuracy, as clearly illustrated in Figure 4.

All ablations exploit the predicted camera representation, if not stated otherwise. V. CONCLUSION
UniDepthV2 is introduced as a universal monocular metric depth estimation model that generalizes across diverse domains without requiring camera parameters at test time. Improvements in model architecture and training objective losses lead to state-of-the-art performance with enhanced computational efficiency. Extensive zero-shot and fine-tuning evaluations confirm this. The training strategy allows for a flexible trade-off between inference speed and detail preservation via variable input resolutions at test time while maintaining global scale consistency.

Prompting is fundamental to avoid mode collapse in scene scale and to alleviate the depth module from predicting depth from scratch, as scale is modeled by camera output. The internal representation of the camera module is based on pinhole parameterization: focal length (fx, fy) and principal point (cx, cy). These four intrinsics are projected to scalar values: ∆fx, ∆fy, ∆cx, ∆cy. They represent multiplicative residuals to a pinhole camera initialization, H/2 for y-components and W/2 for x-components, leading to fx = ∆fxW/2, fy = ∆fyH/2, cx = ∆cxW/2, cy = ∆cyH/2, ensuring invariance towards input image sizes.

A backprojection operation based on intrinsic parameters is applied to each pixel coordinate to produce corresponding rays. Normalized rays represent vectors on a unit sphere. Azimuth and elevation are extracted from backprojected rays, creating a "dense" angular camera representation. This representation undergoes Sine encoding to produce embeddings E. These embeddings are passed to the depth module as a prompt, acting as a conditioning factor via cross-attention between projected encoder feature maps {Fi}4i=1, with Fi ∈Rh×w×C and (h, w) = (H/14, W/14), and camera embeddings E. Camera-prompted depth features Fi|E ∈Rh×w×C are defined as:
F_i|E = MLP(CA(Fi, E))
where CA is a cross-attention block and MLP is a MultiLayer Perceptron with one 4C-channel hidden layer.

C. Geometric Invariance Loss
Spatial locations from the same scene captured by different cameras should correspond when the depth module is conditioned on the specific camera. A geometric invariance loss enforces the consistency of camera-prompted depth features of the same scene from different sensors, specifically on features extracted from identical 3D locations.

For each image, N distinct geometrical augmentations {Ti}N i=1 are performed (N=2 in experiments). This involves sampling a rescaling factor r ∼ 2U[−2,2] and a relative translation t ∼ U[−0.1,0.1], then cropping to a randomly selected input shape. This simulates sampling a pair of images from the same scene and extrinsic parameters, captured by different cameras.

Let Ci and Zi describe the predicted camera representation and camera-aware depth output corresponding to augmentation Ti. Camera representations differ for diverse geometric augmentations (Ci ̸= Cj if Ti ̸= Tj). The geometric invariance loss is expressed as:
L_con(Z1, Z2) = ||T2 ∘ T⁻¹1 (Z1) - sg(Z2)||₁
where Zi is the depth output after being conditioned by camera prompt Ei, decoded, and sg(·) is the stop-gradient detach operation. Z2 is used as pseudo ground truth (GT). The bidirectional loss is computed as:
1/2(Lcon(Z1, Z2) + Lcon(Z2, Z1)).
The geometric invariance loss must be applied to camera-aware components, such as the output depth map, to avoid enforcing consistency across features with purposefully different camera information.

D. Edge-Guided Normalized Loss
Modern depth estimation methods must balance global scene understanding with local geometric precision. UniDepth excels at the former but lacks accuracy in local, fine-grained details. UniDepthV2 introduces the Edge-Guided Scale-Shift Invariant Loss (LEG−SSI) to enhance local precision. This loss is computed over image patches extracted from regions where the RGB spatial gradient ranks in the top 5%-quantile, capturing high-contrast areas with potential depth discontinuities. Patch sizes are randomly sampled between 4% and 8% of the input image’s smallest dimension. By focusing on these salient regions, the model learns to distinguish genuine geometric discontinuities from misleading high-frequency textures that do not correspond to actual depth changes. This approach discourages errors caused by structured patterns like checkerboard textures or repetitive details on flat surfaces that can falsely suggest depth variations.

paper2.title: DiffusionDepth: Diffusion Denoising Approach for Monocular Depth Estimation
paper2.abstract:
Monocular depth estimation is a challenging task that
                        predicts the pixel-wise depth from a single 2D image. Current methods typically model this problem as a regression
                        or classification task. We propose DiffusionDepth, a new
                        approach that reformulates monocular depth estimation as
                        a denoising diffusion process. It learns an iterative denoising process to ‘denoise’ random depth distribution into a
                        depth map with the guidance of monocular visual conditions. The process is performed in the latent space encoded by a dedicated depth encoder and decoder. Instead
                        of diffusing ground truth (GT) depth, the model learns to reverse the process of diffusing the refined depth of itself into
                        random depth distribution. This self-diffusion formulation
                        overcomes the difficulty of applying generative models to
                        sparse GT depth scenarios. The proposed approach benefits
                        this task by refining depth estimation step by step, which is
                        superior for generating accurate and highly detailed depth
                        maps. Experimental results on KITTI and NYU-Depth-V2
                        datasets suggest that a simple yet efficient diffusion approach could reach state-of-the-art performance in both indoor and outdoor scenarios with acceptable inference time.
                        Codes are available through link.

**Qualitative Study of Denoising Process:**
*   Provides an intuitive understanding of how the denoising process refines depth maps.

4.2. Ablation Study
Qualitative Study of Denoising Process
The denoising process visualizes depth prediction refinement step by step in Fig. 6. Initially (t < 10), shapes and edges are initialized from a random depth distribution. The guided denoising model then refines depth values and corrects distance relations iteratively, resembling recognizing scene shapes before considering inter-object depth relations using visual clues. The process is faster in complex outdoor scenarios (KITTI). Beyond 15 steps, competitive results on KITTI are achieved, despite slightly lower intermediate results.

Denoising Inference
An ablation study on inference steps investigates different settings to reveal properties. Lower inference steps reduce GPU memory consumption and increase inference speed. Two settings are considered: 1) train with 1000 diffusion steps and 20 inference steps, then change inference steps; 2) train with different inference steps. Experiments on NYU-Depth-V2 (Tab. 4) show that directly changing inference steps after training leads to significant performance drops, unlike diffusion for detection boxes. This is attributed to depth map denoising being closer to a generative task. However, training with desired inference settings accelerates inference with minimal performance degradation.

Figure 7 shows inference speed on KITTI with an RTX 3090 GPU. DiffusionDepth reaches 14 FPS (ResNet) and 5 FPS (Swin Backbones) with 20 inference steps, suitable for practical use, with potential for further acceleration.

Experiments also showed its ability to utilize visual depth conditions like Bins as denoising guidance, achieving competitive performance. Detailed hyperparameters and visualization results are available in the Appendix.

**5. Conclusion**
This paper reformulates monocular depth estimation as a diffusion-denoising approach. The iterative refinement of the depth latent enables DiffusionDepth to generate accurate and highly detailed depth maps. Experimental results indicate state-of-the-art performance and verify the feasibility of applying diffusion-denoising models to 3D perception tasks. A detailed ablation study provides insights for future work.

Diffusion-Depth achieves state-of-the-art performance on the NYU-Depth-V2 dataset. BinsFormer and DepthFormer are selected for comparison, as URCDC-depth and VA-Depth are not open-sourced. Visual comparison is reported in Fig. 8.

**Illustration of the Denoising Process.**
Visualization results on KITTI illustrate the diffusion process in Fig. 10 and Fig. 9. The denoising process begins with initializing the upper and lower bounds of the predictable area (t=2, t=5). A black area at the upper part of the depth map corresponds to the end of the road or sky with very large depth values, not predicted by the model. Subsequent steps (t=8, t=10) refine shapes and structure. The denoising model gradually adjusts the depth map to match accurate distance correlations and real depth values, sharpening object shapes.

More visualization results on NYU-Depth-V2 illustrate the diffusion process in Fig. 11. Unlike KITTI, the dense GT depth in NYU-Depth-V2 shows no unpredictable areas. Subsequent steps (t<10) refine shapes and structure. The denoising model adjusts the depth map to match accurate distance correlations and real depth values, handling edge extreme depth variances better than previous baselines and sharpening object shapes.

Visual condition c is an aggregated feature map with lower resolution, exhibiting a strong local relation to the depth latent xt to be denoised. A local projection layer upsamples c to match the shape of xt (H/2 × W/2 × d) while preserving local feature relationships. The projected condition is fused with xt via element-wise summation through a CNN block and a self-attention layer. The fused depth latent is processed by a standard BottleNeck CNN layer and channel-wise attention with a residual connection. The denoising output xt-1 is computed using DDIM inference with a predefined diffusion schedule.

**Diffusion-Denoising Process**

The diffusion process q(xt|x0) and denoising process pθ(xt-1|xt, c) are defined. Trainable parameters include the conditioned denoising model µθ(xt, t, c) and visual feature extractors. Training minimizes the LD loss between diffusion results and denoising predictions:

Lddim = ∥xt−1 −µθ(xt, t, c)∥² (4)

The diffusion result xt-1 is calculated via the diffusion process, supervising the depth latent at each step after refinement by reversing the diffusion process.

**Depth Latent Space**

Diffusion processes are performed in an encoded latent depth space, similar to latent diffusion. The refined depth latent x0 (H/2 × W/2 × d) is transferred to depth estimation de (H × W × 1) by a depth decoder consisting of sequential 1x1 convolution, 3x3 de-convolution, 3x3 convolution, and Sigmoid activation.

de = 1/sig(x0).clamp(η) - 1 (5)

where η is the max output range, set to 1e6. A BottleNeck CNN block (d channels, 1x1 kernel) encodes GT depth ˆde into latent depth ˆx0. The decoder and encoder are trained end-to-end by minimizing a pixel-wise depth loss:

Lpixel = (1/T) Σ δ²i + λ (Σ δi)² (6)

where δi = ˆde − de is the pixel-wise depth error on valid pixels, λ is 0.85, and T is the total number of valid pixels. Supervision is also applied to latent spaces using L2 loss between encoded GT latent ˆx0 and depth latent x0, with a valid mask:

Llatent = ∥x0 −ˆx0∥² (7)

The overall loss function is a weighted sum:

L = λ₁Lddim + λ₂Lpixel + λ₃Lpixel (8)

**Self-Diffusion**

To address the problem of sparse ground truth (GT) depth, particularly in outdoor scenarios (e.g., KITTI dataset with 3.75-5% density), DiffusionDepth introduces a self-diffusion process. Instead of directly diffusing on sparse GT depth in latent space, noise is gradually added to the refined depth latent x0 from the current denoising output. Augmentations like random crop, jitter, and flip allow the model to organize the entire depth map, improving visual quality. For indoor scenarios with dense GT values, diffusion on either refined or GT depth is feasible.

Experiments are conducted on outdoor and indoor scenarios. The KITTI dataset, captured outdoors with a depth range of 0-100m, has image resolution around 1216x352 pixels and sparse GT depth (3.75% to 5% density). topic: Depth perception tasks focus on estimating the distance of objects from a single image or sequence, which is crucial for applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and 3D scene understanding. What is the better method for depth perception tasks: UniDepthV2 or PixelFormer?

paper1.title: UniDepthV2: Universal Monocular Metric Depth Estimation Made Simpler
paper1.abstract:
Accurate monocular metric depth estimation
                        (MMDE) is crucial to solving downstream tasks in 3D perception and modeling. However, the remarkable accuracy of
                        recent MMDE methods is confined to their training domains.
                        These methods fail to generalize to unseen domains even in the
                        presence of moderate domain gaps, which hinders their practical
                        applicability. We propose a new model, UniDepthV2, capable
                        of reconstructing metric 3D scenes from solely single images
                        across domains. Departing from the existing MMDE paradigm,
                        UniDepthV2 directly predicts metric 3D points from the input
                        image at inference time without any additional information, striving for a universal and flexible MMDE solution. In particular,
                        UniDepthV2 implements a self-promptable camera module predicting a dense camera representation to condition depth features.
                        Our model exploits a pseudo-spherical output representation,
                        which disentangles the camera and depth representations. In
                        addition, we propose a geometric invariance loss that promotes
                        the invariance of camera-prompted depth features. UniDepthV2
                        improves its predecessor UniDepth model via a new edge-guided
                        loss which enhances the localization and sharpness of edges
                        in the metric depth outputs, a revisited, simplified and more
                        efficient architectural design, and an additional uncertainty-level
                        output which enables downstream tasks requiring confidence.
                        Thorough evaluations on ten depth datasets in a zero-shot
                        regime consistently demonstrate the superior performance and
                        generalization of UniDepthV2. Code and models are available at:

Fine-tuning performance serves as an indicator of a model’s ability to specialize to specific downstream tasks and domains. UniDepthV2 effectively adapts to new domains and outperforms methods that were pre-trained on large, diverse datasets before fine-tuning on NYU or KITTI, such as [16], [29], [33]. This is particularly evident in the outdoor setting (KITTI), as shown in Table IV.

Our training strategy incorporates variable image aspect ratios and resolutions within the same distributed batch. Combined with camera conditioning and invariance learning, this approach enhances the model’s robustness to changes in input image shape. Figure 4 quantifies this effect: the y-axis represents normalized metric accuracy (δ1 scaled by the method’s maximum value), while the x-axis varies the image shape. The normalization ensures a consistent scale across models. UniDepthV2 is almost invariant to image shape, demonstrating that it can effectively trade off resolution for speed without sacrificing accuracy, as clearly illustrated in Figure 4.

V. CONCLUSION
UniDepthV2 is introduced as a universal monocular metric depth estimation model that generalizes across diverse domains without requiring camera parameters at test time. Improvements in model architecture and training objective losses lead to state-of-the-art performance with enhanced computational efficiency. Extensive zero-shot and fine-tuning evaluations confirm this. The training strategy allows for a flexible trade-off between inference speed and detail preservation via variable input resolutions at test time while maintaining global scale consistency.

Prompting is fundamental to avoid mode collapse in scene scale and to alleviate the depth module from predicting depth from scratch, as scale is modeled by camera output. The internal representation of the camera module is based on pinhole parameterization: focal length (fx, fy) and principal point (cx, cy). These four intrinsics are projected to scalar values: ∆fx, ∆fy, ∆cx, ∆cy. They represent multiplicative residuals to a pinhole camera initialization, H/2 for y-components and W/2 for x-components, leading to fx = ∆fxW/2, fy = ∆fyH/2, cx = ∆cxW/2, cy = ∆cyH/2, ensuring invariance towards input image sizes.

A backprojection operation based on intrinsic parameters is applied to each pixel coordinate to produce corresponding rays. Normalized rays represent vectors on a unit sphere. Azimuth and elevation are extracted from backprojected rays, creating a "dense" angular camera representation. This representation undergoes Sine encoding to produce embeddings E. These embeddings are passed to the depth module as a prompt, acting as a conditioning factor via cross-attention between projected encoder feature maps {Fi}4i=1, with Fi ∈Rh×w×C and (h, w) = (H/14, W/14), and camera embeddings E. Camera-prompted depth features Fi|E ∈Rh×w×C are defined as:
F_i|E = MLP(CA(Fi, E))
where CA is a cross-attention block and MLP is a MultiLayer Perceptron with one 4C-channel hidden layer.

C. Geometric Invariance Loss
Spatial locations from the same scene captured by different cameras should correspond when the depth module is conditioned on the specific camera. A geometric invariance loss enforces the consistency of camera-prompted depth features of the same scene from different sensors, specifically on features extracted from identical 3D locations.

For each image, N distinct geometrical augmentations {Ti}N i=1 are performed (N=2 in experiments). This involves sampling a rescaling factor r ∼ 2U[−2,2] and a relative translation t ∼ U[−0.1,0.1], then cropping to a randomly selected input shape. This simulates sampling a pair of images from the same scene and extrinsic parameters, captured by different cameras.

Let Ci and Zi describe the predicted camera representation and camera-aware depth output corresponding to augmentation Ti. Camera representations differ for diverse geometric augmentations (Ci ̸= Cj if Ti ̸= Tj). The geometric invariance loss is expressed as:
L_con(Z1, Z2) = ||T2 ∘ T⁻¹1 (Z1) - sg(Z2)||₁
where Zi is the depth output after being conditioned by camera prompt Ei, decoded, and sg(·) is the stop-gradient detach operation. Z2 is used as pseudo ground truth (GT). The bidirectional loss is computed as:
1/2(Lcon(Z1, Z2) + Lcon(Z2, Z1)).
The geometric invariance loss must be applied to camera-aware components, such as the output depth map, to avoid enforcing consistency across features with purposefully different camera information.

D. Edge-Guided Normalized Loss
Modern depth estimation methods must balance global scene understanding with local geometric precision. UniDepth excels at the former but lacks accuracy in local, fine-grained details. UniDepthV2 introduces the Edge-Guided Scale-Shift Invariant Loss (LEG−SSI) to enhance local precision. This loss is computed over image patches extracted from regions where the RGB spatial gradient ranks in the top 5%-quantile, capturing high-contrast areas with potential depth discontinuities. Patch sizes are randomly sampled between 4% and 8% of the input image’s smallest dimension. By focusing on these salient regions, the model learns to distinguish genuine geometric discontinuities from misleading high-frequency textures that do not correspond to actual depth changes. This approach discourages errors caused by structured patterns like checkerboard textures or repetitive details on flat surfaces that can falsely suggest depth variations.

UniDepthV2 is implemented in PyTorch and CUDA.
Training uses the AdamW optimizer (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999) with an initial learning rate of 5 × 10−5.
The learning rate is divided by 10 for backbone weights every experiment.
Weight decay is set to 0.1.
Cosine Annealing is used as the learning rate and weight decay scheduler, reducing to one-tenth starting from 30% of training.
Training runs for 300k optimization iterations with a batch size of 128.
Training time is 6 days on 16 NVIDIA 4090 with half precision.
Dataset sampling uses a weighted sampler, with dataset weights equal to their number of scenes.
Augmentations include geometric (random resizing, cropping, translation) and photometric (brightness, gamma, saturation, hue shift).
Image ratio is randomly sampled per batch between 2:1 and 1:2.
The ViT backbone is initialized with weights from DINO-pre-trained models.
Ablations use 100k training steps with a ViT-S backbone and the same training pipeline.
Evaluation is performed on eight zero-shot validation sets, covering indoor and outdoor scenes.
UniDepthV2 outperforms baselines, including methods requiring ground-truth camera parameters.
UniDepthV2 shows consistent improvement (0.5% to 18.1%) over the second-best method in the FA metric.
UniDepthV2 outperforms UniDepth in most cases, except for the ρA metric on IBims-1, DDAD, and NuScenes.

paper2.title: Attention Attention Everywhere: Monocular Depth Prediction with Skip Attention
paper2.abstract:
Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) aims to predict
                        pixel-wise depth given a single RGB image. For both, the
                        convolutional as well as the recent attention-based models,
                        encoder-decoder-based architectures have been found to be
                        useful due to the simultaneous requirement of global context and pixel-level resolution. Typically, a skip connection module is used to fuse the encoder and decoder features, which comprises of feature map concatenation followed by a convolution operation. Inspired by the demonstrated benefits of attention in a multitude of computer vision problems, we propose an attention-based fusion of encoder and decoder features. We pose MDE as a pixel query
                        refinement problem, where coarsest-level encoder features
                        are used to initialize pixel-level queries, which are then
                        refined to higher resolutions by the proposed Skip Attention Module (SAM). We formulate the prediction problem
                        as ordinal regression over the bin centers that discretize
                        the continuous depth range and introduce a Bin Center
                        Predictor (BCP) module that predicts bins at the coarsest
                        level using pixel queries. Apart from the benefit of image
                        adaptive depth binning, the proposed design helps learn
                        improved depth embedding in initial pixel queries via direct supervision from the ground truth. Extensive experiments on the two canonical datasets, NYUV2 and KITTI,
                        show that our architecture outperforms the state-of-the-art
                        by 5.3% and 3.9%, respectively, along with an improved
                        generalization performance by 9.4% on the SUNRGBD
                        dataset. Code is available at https://github.com/
                        ashutosh1807/PixelFormer.git.

Effectiveness of embedding the depth information into the pixel queries: We experiment to showcase the usefulness of using the initial pixel queries to predict the bin centers. We compare our proposed design that predicts the bin centers using the initial pixel queries against using a vision transformer to predict the bin centers as in [1]. mViT-Last converts the feature map of the highest resolution (F shown in Fig. 2) into 16×16 patches and integrates the information in the first patch using multiple self-attention layers (L = 4). The first patch embedding is passed through MLP layers to predict the bin centers. Similarly, mViT-First predicts bin centers by passing the initial pixel queries to a ViT. We use patch size = 1 for mViT-First for a fair comparison.

Table 5 shows that both mVit-First and our approach outperform mVit-Last by 2.0% and 3.0%, respectively, in terms of Abs Rel, indicating that embedding depth information into the initial pixel queries via direct loss supervision helps predict better depth estimates. mVit-First does not give any further benefit to predicting bin centers since global information is already aggregated into the initial pixel queries via the PQI module.

Conclusion:
This work presents PixelFormer, a novel encoder-decoder strategy for Monocular Depth Estimation that poses the problem as a pixel query refinement problem. The global initial pixel queries predicted by the Pixel Query Initialiser module are refined to a higher resolution by querying the multiscale encoder features at various resolutions through the proposed Skip Attention Module. Unlike convolution-based skip connections, the module can fuse decoder features with long-range dependency, leading to more accurate depth labels. Our proposed Bin Center Prediction module helps constrain the network with depth information embedded into the initial pixel queries through direct loss supervision. Through extensive experiments, we showcase that PixelFormer improves state-of-the-art performance on the indoor dataset NYUV2 and outdoor dataset KITTI by 5.3% and 3.9%, respectively, along with an improved generalization performance by 9.4% on the indoor SUNRGBD dataset. In the future, we will try to apply our content adaptive fusion using SAM to other dense estimation tasks like semantic segmentation.

**3. Proposed Methodology**

**Problem Definition:** MDE is modeled as a classification-regression task. Given an input image $I$, the network predicts bin widths $b$ that discretize a continuous depth range into $n_{bins}$ intervals. Bins are predicted adaptively per image. The final $n_{bins}$-dimensional probability vector is treated as a weight vector. Depth $d_i$ at pixel $i$ is computed as a linear combination of probability scores and predicted per-image bin centers.

**Architecture Overview:** An input image $I$ is fed to a Swin Transformer, extracting feature maps at resolutions $\{1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32\}$ of $I$. These maps have a global receptive field. The $1/32$ scale feature map is input to the Pixel Query Initializer (PQI) module, which aggregates scene information using multi-scale global average pooling to initialize pixel queries. These queries are hierarchically refined with encoder feature maps using the Skip Attention Module (SAM) at various stages to predict per-pixel probability distributions over bin centers. Initialized pixel queries are also sent to the Bin Center Predictor (BCP). BCP adaptively predicts bin centers per image using global average pooling followed by MLP layers.

**Pixel Query Initializer (PQI):** PQI aggregates global scene information into each pixel-level embedding. The coarsest resolution feature map ($H/32 \times W/32 \times C_4$) is input. PQI uses pyramid spatial pooling (PSP) with adaptive global pooling at scales 1, 2, 3, and 6. Feature maps are upsampled to $1/32$ scale and concatenated. A convolution integrates global information, producing initial pixel queries $Q_I$ ($H/32 \times W/32 \times C$, where $C=512$).

**Bin Center Predictor (BCP):** Previous works used ViT to predict bin centers. Instead of decoding the feature map to high resolution, we use initial pixel queries to predict bin centers, which is more efficient and embeds depth information via direct ground truth supervision. BCP uses Global Average Pooling followed by an MLP layer to predict bin widths $b$ ($n_{bins}$ dimension). We use $n_{bins}=256$.
$b = MLP(GAP(Q))$ (1)
Bin centers are computed as:
$c^{(i)}(b_i) = d_{min} + \frac{(d_{max}-d_{min})}{\sum_{j=1}^{n_{bins}} b_j} b_i + \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} b_j$, for $i \in \{1, \dots, n_{bins}\}$ (2)

**Skip Attention Module (SAM) Overview:** For dense estimation, coarse semantic features and fine details are critical. We use a bottom-down approach, upsampling the lowest resolution feature map and injecting fine-level details from encoder feature maps using skip connections. Convolution operations typically use skip connections.

We employ a bottom-down approach, starting with the lowest resolution feature map, upsampling it, and injecting fine-level details from encoder feature maps at specific scales via skip connections. Unlike traditional convolution-based fusion, which uses static kernel weights, we utilize a Skip Attention Module (SAM). SAM fuses global-local features by computing self-similarity between pixel queries and encoder feature maps.

SAM Implementation:
Given a pixel query map $\hat{Q}_i$ and corresponding encoder features $E_i$ at scale $i$, a 3x3 convolution is applied to both $E_i$ and $\hat{Q}_i$ to equalize their channel dimensions. A query matrix $Q$ is derived from $\hat{Q}_i$, and key $K$ and value $V$ matrices are obtained from $E_i$ using MLPs for weights $W_q$, $W_k$, and $W_v$. To manage computational complexity, attention is restricted to a window, similar to Swin Transformer [19]. $Q$, $K$, and $V$ are divided into windows of size $W \times W$, with $W=7$. Let $Q_w$, $K_w$, and $V_w$ represent the query, key, and value within a window $w$. The output is computed as:

$Attention(Q, K, V) = Rearrange(Softmax(Q_w K_w^T + B)) V_w$

Here, $B$ is a learnable relative position bias matrix of size $w^2 \times w^2$, representing relative positional embeddings. The attention is calculated for each window, and the rearrange operation restores the windows to their original spatial positions.

For multi-depth embedding, each pixel query is divided into $H_i$ heads, and attention is applied per head. Per-pixel depth embeddings are aggregated using MLPs. Residual connections are added after attention and MLP layers for stable gradient flow.

Given $\hat{Q}_i$ and $E_i$ at level $i$:
$\bar{Q}_i = LayerNorm(\hat{Q}_i)$
$\bar{E}_i = LayerNorm(E_i)$
$Q = W_Q \bar{Q}_i$, $K = W_K \bar{E}_i$, $V = W_V \bar{E}_i$
$\hat{Q}_{i-1} = MultiheadAttention(Q, K, V) + \hat{Q}_i$
$\hat{Q}_{i-1} = MLP(\hat{Q}_{i-1}) + \hat{Q}_{i-1}$
$\hat{Q}_{i-1} = MLP(\hat{Q}_{i-1}) + \hat{Q}_i + E_i$

Channel dimensions $D_1, D_2, D_3, D_4 = \{128, 256, 512, 1024\}$ are used for convolutional kernels applied before attention-based fusion at stage $i$. The number of attention heads $H_1, H_2, H_3, H_4 = \{4, 8, 16, 32\}$ at level $i$. Refer to Fig. 2 for details.

Decoder Architecture:
The decoder starts with an initial pixel query $\hat{Q}_I$ from the PQI module. $\hat{Q}_I$ is upsampled by a factor of two using Pixel Shuffle [26] and input to the SAM module with encoder feature $E_4$. Initial pixel queries are refined to finer resolutions by attending to multi-scale encoder features through the SAM module. For a pixel query at level $\hat{Q}_i$ and encoder feature $E_i$:

$\hat{Q}_i = SAM(Upsample(\hat{Q}_{i+1}, E_{i+1}))$ for $i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$.
Here, $\hat{Q}_4$ is equivalent to $\hat{Q}_I$. A convolution is applied to $\hat{Q}_0$ to produce the final depth embedding $F$ of size $H/32 \times W/32 \times nbins$. A pixel-wise softmax is then applied to obtain per-bin probability distribution $p_{bins}$:

$p_{bins} = Softmax(Conv(\hat{Q}_0))$ (3)

The final depth is predicted as a linear combination of bin centers weighted by their probabilities:

$d_i = \sum_{k=1}^{n_{bins}} c(b_k) p_{ik}$ (4)

where $d_i$ is the predicted depth at pixel $i$, $c(b_k)$ is the $k$-th bin center, $n_{bins}$ is the number of bins, and $p_{ik}$ is the probability for bin center $k$ at pixel $i$.

Training Loss:
We use a scaled Scale-Invariant Loss (SILog) [3] for supervision. Given ground truth depth ($d_i^*$) and predicted depth ($d_i$) at pixel $i$, the logarithmic distance is calculated as: $g_i = \log(\hat{d}_i) - \log(d_i^*)$. The SILog loss is:

$L_{SILog} = \alpha \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i} g_i^2 - \lambda \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i} g_i\right)^2}$ (5)

Here, $n$ is the number of pixels with available ground truth. We set $\lambda = 0.85$ and $\alpha = 10$ for all experiments, following [1].

Datasets and Evaluation:
NYU Depth V2: NYUV2 [27] is an indoor dataset comprising 120K RGB and depth pairs of size 480x640, captured from 464 indoor scenes.

Pixel Query Initialiser Module. Pixel queries are refined by a SAM module to finer scales.
Recent MDE techniques [1] formulate the problem as classification-regression. Depth is predicted by a linear combination of bin centers discretized over the depth range. Bin centers are predicted adaptively per image, allowing the network to concentrate on depth range regions more likely to occur in the scene of the input image.
A vision transformer aggregates global information from the output of another encoder-decoder-based transformer model to generate bin centers. Posing MDE as a pixel query refinement problem starting from the coarsest resolution, a lightweight Bin Center Module (BCP) predicts bin centers based on initial pixel queries. This is more efficient than decoding features and then attending again in current SOTA [1]. The proposed design embeds depth information into initial pixel queries via direct ground truth supervision.

Contributions:
1. A novel strategy for predicting depth using a single image by viewing it as a pixel query refinement problem.
2. A Skip Attention Module (SAM) using a window-based cross-attention module to refine pixel queries from decoder feature maps for cross-attending to higher resolution encoder features.
3. A Bin Center Predictor (BCP) Module that estimates bin centers adaptively per image using global information from coarsest-level feature maps. This provides direct supervision to initial pixel queries from ground truth depth, leading to better query embedding.
4. Combination of novel design elements in an encoder-decoder framework comprised of a vision transformer backbone.

The proposed architecture, PixelFormer, achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on indoor NYUV2 and outdoor KITTI datasets, improving current SOTA by 5.3% (absolute relative error) and 3.9% (square relative error). PixelFormer improves generalization performance by 9.4% over SOTA on the SUNRGBD dataset (absolute relative error).

2. Related Works

CNN based MDE Techniques:
Eigen et al. [3] first utilized CNN to predict depth from a single image by integrating global and local information.
Song et al. [28] proposed a Laplacian pyramid-based model.
CLIFFNet [30] uses a multi-scale convolutional fusion architecture for high-quality depth prediction.
Yin et al. [33] introduced a geometric constraint named virtual normal.
Naderi et al. [20] proposed similarity between RGB image and corresponding depth map at geometric edges to regularize predicted depth.
Lee et al. [17] enforce a model to learn scene structural information by learning relationships between nearby image patches.
Patil et al. [23] exploit coplanar pixels to improve predicted depth.

Transformer based MDE Models:
Recent works use Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to improve CNN receptive field in lower layers.
Ranftl et al. [24] uses a CNN to extract feature maps at 1/16 resolution, passed to a vision transformer for global information aggregation.
Bhat et al. [1] uses a CNN-based encoder-decoder backbone and a ViT model to predict adaptive bins and pixel-level depths.
NeWCRFs [34] uses Swin Transformer backbone [19] with CRFs at multiple scales.

MDE as Classification Vs Regression Task:
Modeling MDE as a regression problem leads to suboptimal solutions and convergence issues.
Huan et al. [4] first introduced depth prediction as a classification-regression problem solved by a CNN-based classification network, predicting depth as a linear combination of bin centers.
Bhat et al. [1] proposed predicting bin centers adaptively per image using a ViT transformer on top of a transformer-based encoder-decoder backbone.
This work proposes a single encoder-decoder backbone with a lightweight BCP module to predict bin centers using coarsest resolution encoder feature maps.

Skip Connections:
Skip connections were introduced by UNet [25] to forward high-resolution information from encoder to decoder via feature fusion.
However, naive fusion of early encoder and late decoder information is hindered by their semantic gap [35].
MultiResUnet [12] replaces simplistic skip connections with residual blocks to alleviate the semantic gap.
Attention U-Net [21] suppresses irrelevant regions while highlighting salient features for a specific task before feature fusion.
SANet [31] uses attention to complete point clouds at the decoder stage by injecting information.

paper1.title: UniDepthV2: Universal Monocular Metric Depth Estimation Made Simpler
paper1.abstract:
Accurate monocular metric depth estimation
                        (MMDE) is crucial to solving downstream tasks in 3D perception and modeling. However, the remarkable accuracy of
                        recent MMDE methods is confined to their training domains.
                        These methods fail to generalize to unseen domains even in the
                        presence of moderate domain gaps, which hinders their practical
                        applicability. We propose a new model, UniDepthV2, capable
                        of reconstructing metric 3D scenes from solely single images
                        across domains. Departing from the existing MMDE paradigm,
                        UniDepthV2 directly predicts metric 3D points from the input
                        image at inference time without any additional information, striving for a universal and flexible MMDE solution. In particular,
                        UniDepthV2 implements a self-promptable camera module predicting a dense camera representation to condition depth features.
                        Our model exploits a pseudo-spherical output representation,
                        which disentangles the camera and depth representations. In
                        addition, we propose a geometric invariance loss that promotes
                        the invariance of camera-prompted depth features. UniDepthV2
                        improves its predecessor UniDepth model via a new edge-guided
                        loss which enhances the localization and sharpness of edges
                        in the metric depth outputs, a revisited, simplified and more
                        efficient architectural design, and an additional uncertainty-level
                        output which enables downstream tasks requiring confidence.
                        Thorough evaluations on ten depth datasets in a zero-shot
                        regime consistently demonstrate the superior performance and
                        generalization of UniDepthV2. Code and models are available at:
                        github.com/lpiccinelli-eth/UniDepth.

Fine-tuning performance serves as an indicator of a model’s ability to specialize to specific downstream tasks and domains. UniDepthV2 effectively adapts to new domains and outperforms methods that were pre-trained on large, diverse datasets before fine-tuning on NYU or KITTI, such as [16], [29], [33]. This is particularly evident in the outdoor setting (KITTI), as shown in Table IV.

Our training strategy incorporates variable image aspect ratios and resolutions within the same distributed batch. Combined with camera conditioning and invariance learning, this approach enhances the model’s robustness to changes in input image shape. Figure 4 quantifies this effect: the y-axis represents normalized metric accuracy (δ1 scaled by the method’s maximum value), while the x-axis varies the image shape. The normalization ensures a consistent scale across models. UniDepthV2 is almost invariant to image shape, demonstrating that it can effectively trade off resolution for speed without sacrificing accuracy, as clearly illustrated in Figure 4.

V. CONCLUSION
UniDepthV2 is introduced as a universal monocular metric depth estimation model that generalizes across diverse domains without requiring camera parameters at test time. Improvements in model architecture and training objective losses lead to state-of-the-art performance with enhanced computational efficiency. Extensive zero-shot and fine-tuning evaluations confirm this. The training strategy allows for a flexible trade-off between inference speed and detail preservation via variable input resolutions at test time while maintaining global scale consistency.

Prompting is fundamental to avoid mode collapse in scene scale and to alleviate the depth module from predicting depth from scratch, as scale is modeled by camera output. The internal representation of the camera module is based on pinhole parameterization: focal length (fx, fy) and principal point (cx, cy). These four intrinsics are projected to scalar values: ∆fx, ∆fy, ∆cx, ∆cy. They represent multiplicative residuals to a pinhole camera initialization, H/2 for y-components and W/2 for x-components, leading to fx = ∆fxW/2, fy = ∆fyH/2, cx = ∆cxW/2, cy = ∆cyH/2, ensuring invariance towards input image sizes.

A backprojection operation based on intrinsic parameters is applied to each pixel coordinate to produce corresponding rays. Normalized rays represent vectors on a unit sphere. Azimuth and elevation are extracted from backprojected rays, creating a "dense" angular camera representation. This representation undergoes Sine encoding to produce embeddings E. These embeddings are passed to the depth module as a prompt, acting as a conditioning factor via cross-attention between projected encoder feature maps {Fi}4i=1, with Fi ∈Rh×w×C and (h, w) = (H/14, W/14), and camera embeddings E. Camera-prompted depth features Fi|E ∈Rh×w×C are defined as:
F_i|E = MLP(CA(Fi, E))
where CA is a cross-attention block and MLP is a MultiLayer Perceptron with one 4C-channel hidden layer.

C. Geometric Invariance Loss
Spatial locations from the same scene captured by different cameras should correspond when the depth module is conditioned on the specific camera. A geometric invariance loss enforces the consistency of camera-prompted depth features of the same scene from different sensors, specifically on features extracted from identical 3D locations.

For each image, N distinct geometrical augmentations {Ti}N i=1 are performed (N=2 in experiments). This involves sampling a rescaling factor r ∼ 2U[−2,2] and a relative translation t ∼ U[−0.1,0.1], then cropping to a randomly selected input shape. This simulates sampling a pair of images from the same scene and extrinsic parameters, captured by different cameras.

Let Ci and Zi describe the predicted camera representation and camera-aware depth output corresponding to augmentation Ti. Camera representations differ for diverse geometric augmentations (Ci ̸= Cj if Ti ̸= Tj). The geometric invariance loss is expressed as:
L_con(Z1, Z2) = ||T2 ∘ T⁻¹1 (Z1) - sg(Z2)||₁
where Zi is the depth output after being conditioned by camera prompt Ei, decoded, and sg(·) is the stop-gradient detach operation. Z2 is used as pseudo ground truth (GT). The bidirectional loss is computed as:
1/2(Lcon(Z1, Z2) + Lcon(Z2, Z1)).
The geometric invariance loss must be applied to camera-aware components, such as the output depth map, to avoid enforcing consistency across features with purposefully different camera information.

D. Edge-Guided Normalized Loss
Modern depth estimation methods must balance global scene understanding with local geometric precision. UniDepth excels at the former but lacks accuracy in local, fine-grained details. UniDepthV2 introduces the Edge-Guided Scale-Shift Invariant Loss (LEG−SSI) to enhance local precision. This loss is computed over image patches extracted from regions where the RGB spatial gradient ranks in the top 5%-quantile, capturing high-contrast areas with potential depth discontinuities. Patch sizes are randomly sampled between 4% and 8% of the input image’s smallest dimension. By focusing on these salient regions, the model learns to distinguish genuine geometric discontinuities from misleading high-frequency textures that do not correspond to actual depth changes. This approach discourages errors caused by structured patterns like checkerboard textures or repetitive details on flat surfaces that can falsely suggest depth variations.

UniDepthV2 is implemented in PyTorch and CUDA.
Training uses the AdamW optimizer (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999) with an initial learning rate of 5 × 10−5.
The learning rate is divided by 10 for backbone weights every experiment.
Weight decay is set to 0.1.
Cosine Annealing is used as the learning rate and weight decay scheduler, reducing to one-tenth starting from 30% of training.
Training runs for 300k optimization iterations with a batch size of 128.
Training time is 6 days on 16 NVIDIA 4090 with half precision.
Dataset sampling uses a weighted sampler, with dataset weights equal to their number of scenes.
Augmentations include geometric (random resizing, cropping, translation) and photometric (brightness, gamma, saturation, hue shift).
Image ratio is randomly sampled per batch between 2:1 and 1:2.
The ViT backbone is initialized with weights from DINO-pre-trained models.
Ablations use 100k training steps with a ViT-S backbone and the same training pipeline.
Evaluation is performed on eight zero-shot validation sets, covering indoor and outdoor scenes.
UniDepthV2 outperforms baselines, including methods requiring ground-truth camera parameters.
UniDepthV2 shows consistent improvement (0.5% to 18.1%) over the second-best method in the FA metric.
UniDepthV2 outperforms UniDepth in most cases, except for the ρA metric on IBims-1, DDAD, and NuScenes.
The camera parameter estimation (ρA) shows marginal improvements, suggesting a need for additional camera-only training.
Fine-tuning is performed on NYU and KITTI datasets.

paper2.title: SideRT: A Real-time Pure Transformer Architecture for Single Image Depth Estimation
paper2.abstract:
Since context modeling is critical for estimating
                        depth from a single image, researchers put tremendous effort into obtaining global context. Many
                        global manipulations are designed for traditional
                        CNN-based architectures to overcome the locality
                        of convolutions. Attention mechanisms or transformers originally designed for capturing longrange dependencies might be a better choice, but
                        usually complicates architectures and could lead
                        to a decrease in inference speed. In this work,
                        we propose a pure transformer architecture called
                        SideRT that can attain excellent predictions in realtime. In order to capture better global context,
                        Cross-Scale Attention (CSA) and Multi-Scale Refinement (MSR) modules are designed to work collaboratively to fuse features of different scales efficiently. CSA modules focus on fusing features
                        of high semantic similarities, while MSR modules aim to fuse features at corresponding positions. These two modules contain a few learnable
                        parameters without convolutions, based on which
                        a lightweight yet effective model is built. This architecture achieves state-of-the-art performances in
                        real-time (51.3 FPS) and becomes much faster with
                        a reasonable performance drop on a smaller backbone Swin-T (83.1 FPS). Furthermore, its performance surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by a
                        large margin, improving AbsRel metric 6.9% on
                        KITTI and 9.7% on NYU. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to show that transformerbased networks can attain state-of-the-art performance in real-time in the single image depth estimation field. Code will be made available soon.
methodology:
RMSE: $\sqrt{\frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{d\in D} ||d^* - d||^2}$
SqRel: $\frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{d\in D} \frac{||d^* - d||^2}{d^*}$

Conclusion
This paper introduces two efficient mechanisms for obtaining better global context. These techniques are used to build a lightweight pure transformer architecture with few learnable parameters and no convolutions. Our model demonstrates powerful context modeling capabilities, achieving state-of-the-art performance on two challenging datasets. This work shows that pure transformer architectures can balance accuracy and running time efficiency, providing insights for future research on real-time transformer architectures for practical applications.
