In this section, we present a general framework of our network and introduce three major components: cross-scale attention, multi-scale refinement, and multi-stage supervision.

3.1 Overview
Our SideRT network uses an encoder-decoder architecture for depth prediction from single images. Swin Transformers are employed as backbones. Input images are divided into 4x4 non-overlapping patches. Patches and relative positional embeddings are linearly projected and processed by shift window-based transformer blocks. Feature maps from all four stages are used in the decoder.

The decoder receives multi-scale feature maps from four stages:
(I) Stage 1: H/4 x W/4 x C
(II) Stage 2: H/8 x W/8 x 2C
(III) Stage 3: H/16 x W/16 x 4C
(IV) Stage 4: H/32 x W/32 x 8C
H and W represent input image height and width, and C is the number of channels from stage 1. The decoder fuses feature maps progressively from coarse to fine. It consists of two modules: cross-scale attention (CSA) and multi-scale refinement (MSR). CSA modules fuse feature maps based on semantic similarity to capture global context. MSR modules fuse feature maps based on spatial correspondence. Fusion is done in a coarse-to-fine manner to produce the final prediction, matching the input image resolution.

3.2 Cross-Scale Attention
The CSA module has two parts: a linear layer to project features to the same channel count and an attention-based fusion for merging adjacent scale feature maps based on semantic similarity. Input feature maps are F1 (shallower stage) and F2 (deeper stage), with dimensions C1xH1xW1 and C2xH2xW2, respectively. After linear projection L(·), the fusion is:
F12 = L(F1) + softmax(L(F1) × L(F2)) × L(F2)
The linear layer projects F1 from C1×H1×W1 to C×(H1×W1), and F2 from C2×H2×W2 to C×(H2×W2). Unlike traditional CNNs where global context weakens in the decoder, CSA naturally captures global context dependency between adjacent scales by calculating attention scores softmax(L(F1) × L(F2)) across the entire feature map. This global context includes semantic and depth information.

3.3 Multi-Scale Refinement
Multiple MSR modules work collaboratively in a top-down pyramid. A coarser-resolution feature map from a higher MSR pyramid level and a finer-resolution feature map from a lower CSA pyramid level are input to an MSR module. The MSR module outputs a refined feature map using a low-level semantic, accurately localized feature map from the CSA pyramid. This output and the next finer-resolution feature map from the CSA pyramid are fed into the subsequent MSR module until the final feature map is generated. The refinement process is iterated from coarse to fine.

Each MSR module comprises three parts: bilinear interpolation to upsample the coarser feature map, element-wise addition with the finer feature map from the CSA pyramid, and two MLP layers to reduce aliasing effects and generate a depth map at each scale. The last two MSR modules are appended to generate.

SideRT: A Real-time Pure Transformer Architecture for Single Image Depth Estimation

Abstract
Context modeling is critical for estimating depth from a single image. Researchers have focused on obtaining global context. Attention mechanisms or transformers, designed for capturing long-range dependencies, might be suitable but often complicate architectures and decrease inference speed.

This work proposes SideRT, a pure transformer architecture for real-time single image depth estimation. To capture better global context, Cross-Scale Attention (CSA) and Multi-Scale Refinement (MSR) modules work collaboratively to efficiently fuse features of different scales. CSA modules fuse features with high semantic similarity, while MSR modules fuse features at corresponding positions. These modules contain few learnable parameters without convolutions, enabling a lightweight yet effective model.

SideRT achieves state-of-the-art performance in real-time (51.3 FPS) and is faster with a smaller backbone (Swin-T, 83.1 FPS) with a reasonable performance drop. Its performance surpasses previous state-of-the-art by a large margin, improving AbsRel by 6.9% on KITTI and 9.7% on NYU. This is the first work demonstrating transformer-based networks achieving state-of-the-art real-time performance in single image depth estimation. Code will be made available.

1 Introduction
Single image depth estimation (SIDE) is crucial for extracting 3D geometry, with applications in automatic driving, robotics navigation, and augmented reality. The main difficulty of SIDE is the lack of multiple views to establish geometric relationships, requiring 3D geometric clues to be derived from a single image.

Figure 1: Inference speed versus AbsRel performance on the KITTI test set. SideRT models achieve better accuracy than state-of-the-art methods at a much faster speed.

To address this ill-posed problem, extracting global context is paramount, relying heavily on deep neural networks. CNN-based architectures once dominated SIDE but, due to the locality of convolution, global context was primarily obtained near the bottleneck in low-resolution feature maps, leading to the loss of essential 3D structural clues like local details. To obtain high-resolution global context, the SIDE field has trended towards enlarging receptive fields using large backbones, feature pyramids, spatial pyramid pooling, and atrous convolutions.

Another approach to extract global context leverages the long-range dependency modeling capability of attention mechanisms. Attention modules compute responses by estimating matching scores to all positions and gathering corresponding embeddings, guaranteeing a global receptive field. Transformers, initially designed for natural language processing and using attention as a core component, are increasingly applied in computer vision. Their powerful ability to establish long-range dependencies has pushed state-of-the-art performance forward when integrated into fully convolutional architectures.

However, attention mechanisms are typically time- and memory-consuming, compromising inference speed. While efficient implementations exist, similar efforts are rare in the SIDE field.

This paper explores achieving state-of-the-art performance in real-time using transformers and attention mechanisms. We introduce the SIDE Real-time Transformer (SideRT), based on an encoder-decoder architecture.

This paper addresses state-of-the-art real-time performance with transformers and attention mechanisms in the Single Image Depth Estimation (SIDE) field. We introduce the SIDE Real-time Transformer (SideRT), an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder uses Swin transformers. The decoder features a novel Cross-Scale Attention (CSA) mechanism and a Multi-Scale Refinement (MSR) module. Both CSA and MSR are global operations that work together.

In CSA, finer-resolution features are augmented by coarser-resolution features using attention scores based on semantic similarity. In MSR, coarser-resolution features are merged into spatially corresponding finer-resolution features. These modules use few learnable parameters, fusing multi-scale feature maps with minimal computational overhead.

Based on CSA and MSR, a lightweight decoder progressively performs hierarchical depth optimization for coarse-to-fine prediction. Multi-Stage Supervision (MSS) is applied at each stage to facilitate training.

SideRT outperforms previous state-of-the-art models at 51.3 FPS, improving AbsRel on KITTI from 0.058 to 0.054 and on NYU from 0.103 to 0.093. Using a smaller backbone (Swin-T), SideRT achieves 0.060 AbsRel on KITTI at 83.1 FPS and 0.124 AbsRel on NYU at 84.4 FPS. This is the first demonstration of transformer-based networks achieving state-of-the-art real-time performance in SIDE.

**Related Work**

SIDE is a practical computer vision task for 3D scene understanding. Due to the inherent ambiguity of 3D mapping from a single view, SIDE is an ill-posed problem. Deep learning has significantly advanced the field.

**CNN-based:** Eigen et al. (2014) first introduced CNNs to SIDE. Subsequent research employed more powerful networks like ResNet and DenseNet to improve global context understanding and depth inference reliability. Techniques such as atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP), spatial pyramid pooling, and feature pyramids were used to enlarge receptive fields (Lee et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2018; Song et al., 2021).

**Attention-based:** Attention mechanisms establish pixel-wise associations, addressing long-range dependency issues crucial for contextual knowledge extraction in SIDE. Lee et al. (2021) used attention for feature learning on patches to enhance prediction accuracy. Xu et al. (2021) designed channel and spatial attention modules to improve high-level context and low-level spatial features. Huynh et al. (2020) explored self-attention to establish pixel associations as depth priors. Aich et al. (2021) and Hao et al. (2018) applied attention for multi-level feature fusion. Jiao et al. (2018) developed an attention-driven loss to improve depth prediction quality over long ranges.

**Transformer-based:** Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017), initially for NLP, are deep neural networks leveraging self-attention. Their strong representation capabilities led to applications in SIDE. Yang et al. (2021) introduced ViT architectures (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) to compensate for convolutional locality. Ranftl et al. (2021) found ViT encoders more effective than convolutional ones for SIDE. Bhat et al. (2021) used ViT for global scene information processing and adaptive depth range division.

This work differs by exploring a fully non-convolutional architecture, proving state-of-the-art performance is achievable without convolutions. It also demonstrates real-time capability even with heavy backbones like Swin-L.

**Method**

This section details our network's general framework and its three main components: Cross-Scale Attention (CSA), Multi-Scale Refinement (MSR), and Multi-Stage Supervision (MSS). Figure 2 illustrates the SideRT architecture.

paper2.title: Transformers in Self-Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation with Unknown Camera Intrinsics
paper2.abstract:
The advent of autonomous driving and advanced driver assistance systems necessitates continuous developments in computer vision for 3D scene understanding. Self-supervised monocular depth estimation, a method
                        for pixel-wise distance estimation of objects from a single camera without the use of ground truth labels, is
                        an important task in 3D scene understanding. However, existing methods for this task are limited to convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures. In contrast with CNNs that use localized linear operations
                        and lose feature resolution across the layers, vision transformers process at constant resolution with a global
                        receptive field at every stage. While recent works have compared transformers against their CNN counterparts for tasks such as image classification, no study exists that investigates the impact of using transformers
                        for self-supervised monocular depth estimation. Here, we first demonstrate how to adapt vision transformers for self-supervised monocular depth estimation. Thereafter, we compare the transformer and CNN-based
                        architectures for their performance on KITTI depth prediction benchmarks, as well as their robustness to
                        natural corruptions and adversarial attacks, including when the camera intrinsics are unknown. Our study
                        demonstrates how transformer-based architecture, though lower in run-time efficiency, achieves comparable
                        performance while being more robust and generalizable.
methodology:
• Fusion block channels reduced to 96 from 256 in DPT.
• Four Head modules predict depth at 4 scales.
• Head modules use 2 convolutions instead of 3 (no performance difference found).
• Refer to Table 2 for Head module architecture details.

Table 2: Head module architecture details.
Layers:
- 32 3x3 Convolutions, stride=1, padding=1
- ReLU
- Bilinear Interpolation to upsample by 2
- 32 Pointwise Convolutions
- Sigmoid

3.1.2 Ego-Motion Network
• Encoder: DeiT-Base (Touvron et al., 2021) adapted.
• Input: Two images concatenated along the channel dimension. Embedding layer repeated accordingly.
• Reassemble module passes transformer tokens to the decoder. Refer to Table 1 for module structure.
• Decoder: Adapted from Monodepth2 (Godard et al., 2019).
• MT-SfMLearner: Resulting architecture when both depth and ego-motion networks use transformers.

3.2 Appearance-based Losses
• Adopted appearance-based losses and auto-masking from CNN-based Monodepth2 (Godard et al., 2019).
• Photometric reprojection loss: Pixel-wise ℓ1 distance and Structural Similarity (SSIM) between real and synthesized target images.
• Multi-scale edge-aware smoothness loss on depth predictions.
• Auto-masking disregards temporally stationary pixels in image triplets.
• Texture-copy artifacts reduced by upscaling depths (predicted at 4 scales) from intermediate decoder layers to input resolution.

3.3 Intrinsics
• Accurate camera intrinsics (K matrix) are essential for self-supervised depth estimation.
• Intrinsics can vary within a dataset or be unknown for crowdsourced datasets.
• Introduced an intrinsics estimation module by modifying the ego-motion network.
• Ego-motion network learns focal length, principal point, translation, and rotation.
• A convolutional path in the ego-motion decoder learns intrinsics.
• Decoder features before activation from the penultimate layer pass through global average pooling.
• Two branches of pointwise convolutions reduce channels from 256 to 2:
    - One branch uses softplus activation for focal lengths (always positive).
    - The other branch has no activation for principal point estimation.
• Ego-motion decoder is the same for convolutional and transformer architectures.
• Intrinsics estimation method is modularly usable with both architectures.
• Figure 1 shows MT-SfMLearner with learned intrinsics.

4 RESULTS
• Comparative analysis between MT-SfMLearner and existing CNN-based methods.
• Contrastive study on depth and ego-motion network architectures: impact on accuracy, robustness (natural corruptions, adversarial attacks), and efficiency (computational, energy).
• Analysis of intrinsics predictions: correctness, run-time efficiency, and impact on depth estimation accuracy and robustness.

4.1 Implementation Details
4.1.1 Dataset
• Results reported on Eigen Split (Eigen et al., 2014) of KITTI (Geiger et al., 2013) dataset.
• Static frames removed as per (Zhou et al., 2017).
• Split: 39,810 training, 4424 validation, 697 test images.
• Per-image scaled dense depth prediction without post-processing (Godard et al., 2019).

4.1.2 Training Settings
• Implemented in PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019).
• Trained on Tesla V100 GPU for 20 epochs.
• Resolution: 640 × 192 with batch-size 12.
• MT-SfMLearner also trained at resolutions 416 × 128 (batch-size 12) and 1024 × 320 (batch-size 2).

Since self-supervised monocular depth estimation networks concurrently train an ego-motion network, we investigate the impact of each network's architecture on depth estimation. We consider both Convolutional (C) and Transformer (T) networks for depth and ego-motion estimation. The resulting four combinations are (C, C), (C, T), (T, C), and (T, T), ordered by increasing influence of transformers on depth estimation. To compare our transformer-based method fairly with convolutional networks, Monodepth2 with a ResNet-101 encoder is used. All four combinations are trained thrice for an image size of 640×192, assuming known ground-truth camera intrinsics.

### Performance

The best performance on i.i.d. for the four combinations is reported in Table 5, with depth predictions visualized in Figure 2. The i.i.d. test set is the same as in Section 4.2.

We observe that the combination of transformer-based depth and ego-motion networks, MT-SfMLearner, performs best under two error metrics and two accuracy metrics. The remaining combinations perform comparably.

Figure 2: Disparity maps on KITTI for qualitative comparison of all four architecture combinations of depth and ego-motion networks. Example areas where the global receptive field of transformer is advantageous are highlighted in green. Example areas where local receptive field of CNNs is advantageous are highlighted in white.

Transformers provide more uniform estimates for larger objects like vehicles, vegetation, and buildings. They are also less affected by reflections from windows, likely due to larger receptive fields leading to more globally coherent predictions. Convolutional networks produce sharper boundaries and perform better on thinner objects like traffic signs and poles, likely due to their inherent inductive bias for spatial locality.

### Robustness

While the combinations perform comparably on the i.i.d. dataset, they may differ in robustness and generalizability. We study the impact of natural corruptions and adversarial attacks on depth performance using:

*   **Natural corruptions:** Following Hendrycks and Dietterich (2019) and Michaelis et al. (2019), 15 corrupted versions of the KITTI i.i.d. test set are generated at severity level 5. These fall under 4 categories: noise (Gaussian, shot, impulse), blur (defocus, glass, motion, zoom), weather (snow, frost, fog, brightness), and digital (contrast, elastic, pixelate, JPEG).
*   **Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) adversarial:** (The text cuts off here, but implies PGD adversarial attacks were also considered.)

Natural corruptions (severity 5) included:

- Gradients calculated with respect to training loss.
- Perturbation accumulated over min(ε + 4, ⌈1.25·ε⌉) iterations with a step-size of 1 (Kurakin et al., 2016).
- For KITTI sequence edges, appearance-based loss only for feasible image pairs.

Symmetrically flipped adversarial examples:
- Inspired by Wong et al. (2020).
- Fool networks into predicting flipped estimates.
- Used gradients of RMSE loss with targets as horizontal and vertical flips of i.i.d. predictions.
- Attack strength ε ∈ {1.0, 2.0, 4.0}.

Both architectures run depth and intrinsics estimation in real-time with an inference speed > 30 fps. The transformer-based method consumes higher energy and is computationally more demanding than its convolutional counterpart.

Conclusion:
This work investigates the impact of transformer architecture on SfM-inspired self-supervised monocular depth estimation. The transformer-based method MT-SfMLearner performs comparably against contemporary convolutional methods on the KITTI depth prediction benchmark. CNNs provide local spatial bias, while transformers predict uniform and coherent depths. Transformers in the depth network result in higher robustness to natural corruptions. Transformers in both depth and ego-motion networks result in higher robustness to adversarial attacks. These conclusions hold even when focal length and principal point are learned. However, transformers are computationally more demanding and have lower energy efficiency. This work assists in evaluating the trade-off between performance, robustness, and efficiency for selecting the suitable architecture.

topic: Depth perception tasks focus on estimating the distance of objects from a single image or sequence, which is crucial for applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and 3D scene understanding. What is the better method for depth perception tasks: SideRT or DiPE?

paper1.title: SideRT: A Real-time Pure Transformer Architecture for Single Image Depth Estimation
paper1.abstract:
Since context modeling is critical for estimating
                        depth from a single image, researchers put tremendous effort into obtaining global context. Many
                        global manipulations are designed for traditional
                        CNN-based architectures to overcome the locality
                        of convolutions. Attention mechanisms or transformers originally designed for capturing longrange dependencies might be a better choice, but
                        usually complicates architectures and could lead
                        to a decrease in inference speed. In this work,
                        we propose a pure transformer architecture called
                        SideRT that can attain excellent predictions in realtime. In order to capture better global context,
                        Cross-Scale Attention (CSA) and Multi-Scale Refinement (MSR) modules are designed to work collaboratively to fuse features of different scales efficiently. CSA modules focus on fusing features
                        of high semantic similarities, while MSR modules aim to fuse features at corresponding positions. These two modules contain a few learnable
                        parameters without convolutions, based on which
                        a lightweight yet effective model is built. This architecture achieves state-of-the-art performances in
                        real-time (51.3 FPS) and becomes much faster with
                        a reasonable performance drop on a smaller backbone Swin-T (83.1 FPS). Furthermore, its performance surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by a
                        large margin, improving AbsRel metric 6.9% on
                        KITTI and 9.7% on NYU. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to show that transformerbased networks can attain state-of-the-art performance in real-time in the single image depth estimation field. Code will be made available soon.

Cross-scale Attention (CSA): Evaluated by removing CSA modules (Row 4 and 5 in Table 4). CSA module improves performance with small computational overhead (+0.8M Params) and small decrease in speed (-12.0 FPS). Row 1-2 in Table 4 show CSA module significantly improves depth prediction from Swin-T encoder. CSA module enlarges the receptive field of the encoder. Swin-T+CSA achieves similar performance to VNL [Yin et al., 2019] and outperforms some metrics of DORN [Fu et al., 2018].

Multi-stage Supervision (MSS): Training pure transformer architecture is more difficult than CNN-based counterpart.

MSR modules use upsampling to fuse features with corresponding spatial positions. Each MSR module consists of an element-wise addition between the upsampled feature map from the MSR pyramid and a finer-resolution feature map from the CSA pyramid, followed by two MLP layers to reduce aliasing effects and generate a depth map at each scale. The last two MSR modules generate the final result at input resolution and do not receive outputs from CSA modules. MLP layers facilitate global information flow.

Multi-Stage Supervision (MSS) is proposed to ease training. Each scale is supervised by a loss calculated between the prediction and corresponding ground truth. Multi-stage losses are then weighted and summed.

To address the imbalance of dense depth data at close areas and sparse data at distances, the square root loss function is adopted. This loss calculates the difference of predicted depth and ground truth in log space.

$L(y, y^*) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N_V} \sum_{i \in V} d_i^2 - \lambda (\frac{1}{N_V} \sum_{i \in V} d_i)^2}$
where $d_i = \log y_i - \log y^*_i$.
$y$ is the predicted depth map, $y^*$ is the ground truth depth map, $V$ is the set of valid pixels, $N_V$ is the total number of valid pixels, and $\lambda$ is set to 0.85.

SideRT is applied to KITTI and NYU datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods at faster speeds.

Multi-stage Supervision. Training pure transformer architectures is more difficult than CNN-based ones [Tolstikhin et al., 2021; Dosovitskiy et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021]. Multi-stage supervision (MSS) results in smoother training loss curves and easier model convergence. MSS significantly improves all metrics, accelerating training and enhancing the performance of pure transformer architectures.
Multi-scale Refinement. Multi-scale refinement (MSR) modules boost performance by collaboratively augmenting encoder feature maps with channel similarity attention (CSA) modules. CSA merges features with high similarity globally, while MSR fuses features at similar positions across different pyramid levels.
Inference Speed. The lightweight decoder has 1.1 million parameters, while the backbone contains most of the parameters. Adding the proposed decoder decreases the AbsRel metric by 74.9% with only a 20.4% decrease in inference speed.

After adding CSA, reference pixels show a stronger response from a larger scope. CSA modules yield higher responses from pixels with similar categories and depths, beneficial for depth prediction tasks.

Conclusion
This paper introduces two efficient mechanisms for obtaining better global context. These techniques are used to build a lightweight pure transformer architecture with few learnable parameters and no convolutions. Our model demonstrates powerful context modeling capabilities, achieving state-of-the-art performance on two challenging datasets. This work shows that pure transformer architectures can balance accuracy and running time efficiency, providing insights for future research on real-time transformer architectures for practical applications.

In this section, we present a general framework of our network and introduce three major components: cross-scale attention, multi-scale refinement, and multi-stage supervision.

3.1 Overview
Our SideRT network uses an encoder-decoder architecture for depth prediction from single images. Swin Transformers are employed as backbones. Input images are divided into 4x4 non-overlapping patches. Patches and relative positional embeddings are linearly projected and processed by shift window-based transformer blocks. Feature maps from all four stages are used in the decoder.

The decoder receives multi-scale feature maps from four stages:
(I) Stage 1: H/4 x W/4 x C
(II) Stage 2: H/8 x W/8 x 2C
(III) Stage 3: H/16 x W/16 x 4C
(IV) Stage 4: H/32 x W/32 x 8C
H and W represent input image height and width, and C is the number of channels from stage 1. The decoder fuses feature maps progressively from coarse to fine. It consists of two modules: cross-scale attention (CSA) and multi-scale refinement (MSR). CSA modules fuse feature maps based on semantic similarity to capture global context. MSR modules fuse feature maps based on spatial correspondence. Fusion is done in a coarse-to-fine manner to produce the final prediction, matching the input image resolution.

3.2 Cross-Scale Attention
The CSA module has two parts: a linear layer to project features to the same channel count and an attention-based fusion for merging adjacent scale feature maps based on semantic similarity. Input feature maps are F1 (shallower stage) and F2 (deeper stage), with dimensions C1xH1xW1 and C2xH2xW2, respectively. After linear projection L(·), the fusion is:
F12 = L(F1) + softmax(L(F1) × L(F2)) × L(F2)
The linear layer projects F1 from C1×H1×W1 to C×(H1×W1), and F2 from C2×H2×W2 to C×(H2×W2). Unlike traditional CNNs where global context weakens in the decoder, CSA naturally captures global context dependency between adjacent scales by calculating attention scores softmax(L(F1) × L(F2)) across the entire feature map. This global context includes semantic and depth information.

3.3 Multi-Scale Refinement
Multiple MSR modules work collaboratively in a top-down pyramid. A coarser-resolution feature map from a higher MSR pyramid level and a finer-resolution feature map from a lower CSA pyramid level are input to an MSR module. The MSR module outputs a refined feature map using a low-level semantic, accurately localized feature map from the CSA pyramid. This output and the next finer-resolution feature map from the CSA pyramid are fed into the subsequent MSR module until the final feature map is generated. The refinement process is iterated from coarse to fine.

Each MSR module comprises three parts: bilinear interpolation to upsample the coarser feature map, element-wise addition with the finer feature map from the CSA pyramid, and two MLP layers to reduce aliasing effects and generate a depth map at each scale. The last two MSR modules are appended to generate.

SideRT: A Real-time Pure Transformer Architecture for Single Image Depth Estimation

Abstract
Context modeling is critical for estimating depth from a single image. Researchers have focused on obtaining global context. Attention mechanisms or transformers, designed for capturing long-range dependencies, might be suitable but often complicate architectures and decrease inference speed.

This work proposes SideRT, a pure transformer architecture for real-time single image depth estimation. To capture better global context, Cross-Scale Attention (CSA) and Multi-Scale Refinement (MSR) modules work collaboratively to efficiently fuse features of different scales. CSA modules fuse features with high semantic similarity, while MSR modules fuse features at corresponding positions. These modules contain few learnable parameters without convolutions, enabling a lightweight yet effective model.

SideRT achieves state-of-the-art performance in real-time (51.3 FPS) and is faster with a smaller backbone (Swin-T, 83.1 FPS) with a reasonable performance drop. Its performance surpasses previous state-of-the-art by a large margin, improving AbsRel by 6.9% on KITTI and 9.7% on NYU. This is the first work demonstrating transformer-based networks achieving state-of-the-art real-time performance in single image depth estimation. Code will be made available.

1 Introduction
Single image depth estimation (SIDE) is crucial for extracting 3D geometry, with applications in automatic driving, robotics navigation, and augmented reality. The main difficulty of SIDE is the lack of multiple views to establish geometric relationships, requiring 3D geometric clues to be derived from a single image.

Figure 1: Inference speed versus AbsRel performance on the KITTI test set. SideRT models achieve better accuracy than state-of-the-art methods at a much faster speed.

To address this ill-posed problem, extracting global context is paramount, relying heavily on deep neural networks. CNN-based architectures once dominated SIDE but, due to the locality of convolution, global context was primarily obtained near the bottleneck in low-resolution feature maps, leading to the loss of essential 3D structural clues like local details. To obtain high-resolution global context, the SIDE field has trended towards enlarging receptive fields using large backbones, feature pyramids, spatial pyramid pooling, and atrous convolutions.

Another approach to extract global context leverages the long-range dependency modeling capability of attention mechanisms. Attention modules compute responses by estimating matching scores to all positions and gathering corresponding embeddings, guaranteeing a global receptive field. Transformers, initially designed for natural language processing and using attention as a core component, are increasingly applied in computer vision. Their powerful ability to establish long-range dependencies has pushed state-of-the-art performance forward when integrated into fully convolutional architectures.

However, attention mechanisms are typically time- and memory-consuming, compromising inference speed. While efficient implementations exist, similar efforts are rare in the SIDE field.

This paper explores achieving state-of-the-art performance in real-time using transformers and attention mechanisms. We introduce the SIDE Real-time Transformer (SideRT), based on an encoder-decoder architecture.

This paper addresses state-of-the-art real-time performance with transformers and attention mechanisms in the Single Image Depth Estimation (SIDE) field. We introduce the SIDE Real-time Transformer (SideRT), an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder uses Swin transformers. The decoder features a novel Cross-Scale Attention (CSA) mechanism and a Multi-Scale Refinement (MSR) module. Both CSA and MSR are global operations that work together.

In CSA, finer-resolution features are augmented by coarser-resolution features using attention scores based on semantic similarity. In MSR, coarser-resolution features are merged into spatially corresponding finer-resolution features. These modules use few learnable parameters, fusing multi-scale feature maps with minimal computational overhead.

Based on CSA and MSR, a lightweight decoder progressively performs hierarchical depth optimization for coarse-to-fine prediction. Multi-Stage Supervision (MSS) is applied at each stage to facilitate training.

SideRT outperforms previous state-of-the-art models at 51.3 FPS, improving AbsRel on KITTI from 0.058 to 0.054 and on NYU from 0.103 to 0.093. Using a smaller backbone (Swin-T), SideRT achieves 0.060 AbsRel on KITTI at 83.1 FPS and 0.124 AbsRel on NYU at 84.4 FPS. This is the first demonstration of transformer-based networks achieving state-of-the-art real-time performance in SIDE.

**Related Work**

SIDE is a practical computer vision task for 3D scene understanding. Due to the inherent ambiguity of 3D mapping from a single view, SIDE is an ill-posed problem. Deep learning has significantly advanced the field.

**CNN-based:** Eigen et al. (2014) first introduced CNNs to SIDE. Subsequent research employed more powerful networks like ResNet and DenseNet to improve global context understanding and depth inference reliability. Techniques such as atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP), spatial pyramid pooling, and feature pyramids were used to enlarge receptive fields (Lee et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2018; Song et al., 2021).

**Attention-based:** Attention mechanisms establish pixel-wise associations, addressing long-range dependency issues crucial for contextual knowledge extraction in SIDE. Lee et al. (2021) used attention for feature learning on patches to enhance prediction accuracy. Xu et al. (2021) designed channel and spatial attention modules to improve high-level context and low-level spatial features. Huynh et al. (2020) explored self-attention to establish pixel associations as depth priors. Aich et al. (2021) and Hao et al. (2018) applied attention for multi-level feature fusion. Jiao et al. (2018) developed an attention-driven loss to improve depth prediction quality over long ranges.

**Transformer-based:** Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017), initially for NLP, are deep neural networks leveraging self-attention. Their strong representation capabilities led to applications in SIDE. Yang et al. (2021) introduced ViT architectures (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) to compensate for convolutional locality. Ranftl et al. (2021) found ViT encoders more effective than convolutional ones for SIDE. Bhat et al. (2021) used ViT for global scene information processing and adaptive depth range division.

This work differs by exploring a fully non-convolutional architecture, proving state-of-the-art performance is achievable without convolutions. It also demonstrates real-time capability even with heavy backbones like Swin-L.

**Method**

This section details our network's general framework and its three main components: Cross-Scale Attention (CSA), Multi-Scale Refinement (MSR), and Multi-Stage Supervision (MSS). Figure 2 illustrates the SideRT architecture.

paper2.title: DiPE: Deeper into Photometric Errors for Unsupervised Learning of Depth and Ego-motion from Monocular Videos
paper2.abstract:
Unsupervised learning of depth and ego-motion
                        from unlabelled monocular videos has recently drawn great
                        attention, which avoids the use of expensive ground truth in the
                        supervised one. It achieves this by using the photometric errors
                        between the target view and the synthesized views from its adjacent source views as the loss. Despite significant progress, the
                        learning still suffers from occlusion and scene dynamics. This
                        paper shows that carefully manipulating photometric errors
                        can tackle these difficulties better. The primary improvement
                        is achieved by a statistical technique that can mask out the
                        invisible or nonstationary pixels in the photometric error map
                        and thus prevents misleading the networks. With this outlier
                        masking approach, the depth of objects moving in the opposite
                        direction to the camera can be estimated more accurately.
                        To the best of our knowledge, such scenarios have not been
                        seriously considered in the previous works, even though they
                        pose a higher risk in applications like autonomous driving.
                        We also propose an efficient weighted multi-scale scheme to
                        reduce the artifacts in the predicted depth maps. Extensive
                        experiments on the KITTI dataset show the effectiveness of
                        the proposed approaches. The overall system achieves state-oftheart performance on both depth and ego-motion estimation.

Careful processing of photometric errors in unsupervised learning of depth and ego-motion from monocular videos addresses occlusion and scene dynamics.

Outlier masking fails to mask objects with speeds close to the camera, as they are estimated to maximum depth, and photometric errors can fall within the inlier region. Monodepth2's auto-masking handles such cases. The proposed outlier masking collaborates with Monodepth2's minimum reprojection for more accurate foreground object boundaries.

The auto-masking excludes pixels with photometric errors larger than the direct photometric error between target and source views. Minimum reprojection retains pixels with the minimum photometric error across all source views. Masks for photometric error map PE(It, Is→t) are denoted as $M^s_p$, $M^s_a$, and $M^s_{mr}$.

$M^s_a = \text{PE}(I_t, I_{s→t}) < \text{PE}(I_t, I_s)$ (10)

where $P_s$ denotes PE(It, Is→t). $\eta$ and $\lambda$ are weights for the two types of losses, and $e$ is a weighting factor for edge-aware smoothness loss across scales.

Implementation Details:
Approaches are based on Monodepth2. Depth CNN is a fully convolutional encoder-decoder network with 640×192 resolution. Pose CNN is a standard CNN with a fully connected layer for 6-DoF relative camera motion. Both networks use ResNet18 pretrained on ImageNet as backbone. For depth estimation, only nearby 2 frames (S = {t−1, t+1}) and pair-input Pose are used. For ego-motion estimation, all-input Pose CNN is experimented with nearby 4 frames (S = {t −2, t −1, t + 1, t + 2}) and 2 frames (S = {t −1, t + 1}).

Hyper-parameters: $\eta = 1$, $\lambda = 0.001$, $e = 0.5$. Weighting factor f for multi-scale scheme is 0.25. DiPE is trained for 20 epochs using Adam. DiPE uses a batch size of 16, taking 9 hours on a single Titan Xp. Initial learning rate is $10^{−4}$, divided by 5 after 15 and 18 epochs. Outlier masking reduces training errors; decreasing learning rate helps DiPE converge better. Monodepth2 uses approximated intrinsic parameters. Calibrated intrinsic parameters are used for every training sample, with principal point flipped during horizontal flips.

KITTI Eigen Split:
Standard Eigen split of KITTI dataset is adopted for monocular depth estimation. A subset of the training set containing no static frames is used for training (39,810 samples). Validation set has 4,424 samples, and test set has 697 samples. Approximately one-tenth (432) of the validation set is used for validation per epoch. Predicted depth maps are aligned to ground truth by multiplying the median value ratio. Conventional metrics and cropping region from [5] are used, with a standard depth cap of 80m. Error metrics include absolute relative error.

Our outlier masking method is proposed for oncoming moving objects. This technique can help minimum reprojection recover a more accurate boundary for foreground objects in predicted depth maps.

**III. METHODOLOGY**

**A. Preliminaries**

The monocular unsupervised learning scheme is shown in Fig. 2. A training sample contains the target frame $I_t$ at time $t$ and source frames $I_s$ at nearby times, $s \in S$. Conventionally, $S = \{t−1, t+1\}$ or $S = \{t−2, t−1, t+1, t+2\}$. Given the shared intrinsic matrix $K$, the synthesis from source view $s$ to target view $t$ is expressed as:

$I_{s→t} = I_s⟨proj(D_t, T_{t→s}, K)⟩$
(1)

The differentiable bilinear sampling operator is [27].
proj() projects pixel pt in the target image to point ps in the source image:
ps ≃KTt→sD(pt)K−1pt (2)
where pt and ps are homogeneous coordinates.

Photometric error is computed using a combination of L1 and SSIM:
PE(Ia, Ib) = 0.85(1 − SSIM(Ia, Ib)) + 0.15∥Ia − Ib∥₁ (3)

An edge-aware smoothness term is also applied:
Les = mean(|∂xd∗t|e−|∂xIt| + |∂yd∗t|e−|∂yIt|) (4)
where d∗t = dt/dt is the mean-normalized inverse depth from [28] to discourage depth shrinking.
Both losses are applied at 4 scales to avoid gradient locality.

B. Outlier Masking
Adverse factors like occlusion and scene dynamics can damage image reconstruction. Pixels in the photometric error map can be invalid and misleading during training. Most pixels are visible and stationary, while occluded and moving pixels produce more significant photometric errors. Outlier masking is based on this observation.
The outlier mask is determined by the statistical information of photometric errors.
The mean and standard deviation of pixel photometric errors from all source images are computed for each training sample:
µ = mean{PE(It, Is→t)|s ∈ S} (5)
σ = std{PE(It, Is→t)|s ∈ S} (6)
An outlier mask for the photometric error map PE(It, Is→t) is computed:
M_ol = µ − lσ < PE(It, Is→t) < µ + uσ (7)
where l and u are lower and upper thresholds.
The mask excludes possible occluded or moving regions.
Setting u = 0.5 is effective; a higher value fails to mask moving objects, and a lower value masks out stationary objects.
Setting l = 1 masks pixels with very small photometric errors, typically from homogeneous regions and less valuable for training.
This selection of u and l retains principal photometric errors for optimization, as shown in Fig. 3.

C. Weighted Multi-Scale Scheme
To avoid local minima caused by the bilinear sampler's gradient locality [27], unsupervised learning models predict 4-scale depth maps and compute multi-scale photometric losses. However, this can lead to "holes" in low-texture regions and texture-copy artifacts.
Monodepth2 [4] uses a full-resolution multi-scale scheme by upsampling depth maps to full resolution, warping full-resolution images, and computing losses at full resolution.
This full-resolution scheme increases computation and GPU memory.
To reduce training overhead, a weighted multi-scale scheme is proposed to devalue low-resolution photometric losses.
A scale factor f < 1 is defined to compute the weight for scale r:
w_r = f^r (8)
where r ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}.

D. Integrated Objective Function
While outlier masking excludes most irregular pixels, it has limitations. Pixels moving out of the image boundary are not masked. These "out-of-box" pixels can be masked by retaining only pixels reprojected inside the source image box [29].
Outlier masking also fails to mask objects with speeds very close to the camera, as these objects are often estimated similarly.

Outlier masking technique excludes occluded and moving regions, especially oncoming objects, by observing larger photometric errors in these areas. Visible background typically dominates scenes, with invisible or moving pixels showing inconsistencies that hinder optimization. A weighted multi-scale scheme complements outlier masking for better depth maps.

Experimental validation on the KITTI dataset proves the effectiveness of the outlier masking and weighted multi-scale contributions. Combined with a baseline model and other masking practices, this forms DiPE, an unsupervised monocular depth and ego-motion estimation system.

Recent advancements in unsupervised monocular depth estimation (MDE) utilize deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Some methods directly regress ground truth depth, while others combine deep learning with graphical models or treat MDE as a classification problem. Models trained on datasets with ground truth depth often lack generalization to real-world scenarios.

Unsupervised learning schemes leverage stereo images or adjacent monocular video frames to create supervisory signals, typically using photometric differences between a view and its synthesis. Synthesis is computed from an additional view using estimated depth and pose. Stereo videos have been exploited for training to utilize both spatial and temporal cues. Monocular videos, being more generalized and available, are the focus of this paper.

SfM-Learner, an early method using monocular videos, employs an additional Pose CNN to estimate relative motion for view synthesis. However, photometric consistency is often compromised by occlusion and moving objects. Subsequent methods to improve this framework fall into categories like masking photometric errors, joint learning with optical flow, and modeling object motion. Masking strategies, such as explainability masks and uncertainty maps, may require extra networks. Joint learning with optical flow necessitates new networks for flow estimation. Object motion modeling requires modules for segmentation and motion estimation.

In contrast, overlap and blank masks, geometrically derived from image warping, offer a lightweight approach to occlusion. Monodepth2 uses minimum reprojection, taking the minimum photometric errors from all source views as a masking technique for occlusion. Monodepth2 also employs auto-masking for objects moving at speeds similar to the camera. While effective, this simple strategy has not addressed oncoming moving objects. The proposed outlier masking method addresses this issue, and further enhances minimum reprojection for more accurate results.

DiPE: Deeper into Photometric Errors for Unsupervised Learning of Depth and Ego-motion from Monocular Videos

Unsupervised learning of depth and ego-motion from unlabelled monocular videos avoids the use of expensive ground truth. It uses photometric errors between target and synthesized adjacent views as the loss. Learning suffers from occlusion and scene dynamics. This paper shows manipulating photometric errors can tackle these difficulties. An improvement is a statistical technique that masks invisible or non-stationary pixels in the photometric error map, preventing misleading networks. This outlier masking approach improves depth estimation of objects moving opposite to the camera. Such scenarios have not been seriously considered, posing a risk in autonomous driving. An efficient weighted multi-scale scheme reduces artifacts in predicted depth maps. Extensive experiments on the KITTI dataset show effectiveness. The system achieves state-of-the-art performance on depth and ego-motion estimation.

Depth and ego-motion estimation is core to SLAM. Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) is flexible for applications like autonomous mobile robotics and AR/VR. Tracking 6-DoF motion for moving cameras is critical. Traditional supervised methods require expensive ground truth, limiting generalization. Unsupervised learning from monocular videos offers a more generalizable solution.

Unsupervised learning models typically contain two networks: one for predicting the depth map of the target view, and another for motion between target and adjacent views. Network outputs allow target view reconstruction from adjacent source views via image warping. The resulting photometric loss serves as the supervisory signal. However, image reconstruction is disrupted by between-view occlusion and scene dynamics, harming network learning due to incorrect supervision.

Figure 1 illustrates the detriment of occlusion and dynamics. (a) Occlusion: point P visible in Ct but occluded in Ct+1. To achieve photometric consistency, P is estimated with shorter depth, blurring foreground objects. (b) Co-directional motion: if point M moves forward like camera C, it's likely estimated with farther depth, producing ‘dark holes’. (c) Contra-directional motion: when point M moves backward opposite to camera C, it's estimated with shorter depth.

The theory of minimizing between-view reconstruction errors affecting depth estimation of occluded regions and moving objects is illustrated in Figure 1. Many methods address occlusion and dynamics with considerable improvement. For example, ‘dark holes’ from co-directionally moving objects are tackled in recent works [2], [3], [4]. However, latest models significantly underestimate depth for contra-directionally moving objects. Inaccuracy of such objects has not been reported, which can cause issues in applications like autonomous driving, where underrated oncoming car distances could lead to unnecessary braking or avoidance.

Multi-Stage Supervision (MSS) is proposed to ease training. Each scale is supervised by a loss calculated between the prediction and corresponding ground truth. Multi-stage losses are then weighted and summed.

Conclusion
This paper introduces two efficient mechanisms for obtaining better global context. These techniques are used to build a lightweight pure transformer architecture with few learnable parameters and no convolutions. Our model demonstrates powerful context modeling capabilities, achieving state-of-the-art performance on two challenging datasets. This work shows that pure transformer architectures can balance accuracy and running time efficiency, providing insights for future research on real-time transformer architectures for practical applications.

In this section, we present a general framework of our network and introduce three major components: cross-scale attention, multi-scale refinement, and multi-stage supervision.

3.1 Overview
Our SideRT network uses an encoder-decoder architecture for depth prediction from single images. Swin Transformers are employed as backbones. Input images are divided into 4x4 non-overlapping patches. Patches and relative positional embeddings are linearly projected and processed by shift window-based transformer blocks. Feature maps from all four stages are used in the decoder.

The decoder receives multi-scale feature maps from four stages:
(I) Stage 1: H/4 x W/4 x C
(II) Stage 2: H/8 x W/8 x 2C
(III) Stage 3: H/16 x W/16 x 4C
(IV) Stage 4: H/32 x W/32 x 8C
H and W represent input image height and width, and C is the number of channels from stage 1. The decoder fuses feature maps progressively from coarse to fine. It consists of two modules: cross-scale attention (CSA) and multi-scale refinement (MSR). CSA modules fuse feature maps based on semantic similarity to capture global context. MSR modules fuse feature maps based on spatial correspondence. Fusion is done in a coarse-to-fine manner to produce the final prediction, matching the input image resolution.

3.2 Cross-Scale Attention
The CSA module has two parts: a linear layer to project features to the same channel count and an attention-based fusion for merging adjacent scale feature maps based on semantic similarity. Input feature maps are F1 (shallower stage) and F2 (deeper stage), with dimensions C1xH1xW1 and C2xH2xW2, respectively. After linear projection L(·), the fusion is:
F12 = L(F1) + softmax(L(F1) × L(F2)) × L(F2)
The linear layer projects F1 from C1×H1×W1 to C×(H1×W1), and F2 from C2×H2×W2 to C×(H2×W2). Unlike traditional CNNs where global context weakens in the decoder, CSA naturally captures global context dependency between adjacent scales by calculating attention scores softmax(L(F1) × L(F2)) across the entire feature map. This global context includes semantic and depth information.

3.3 Multi-Scale Refinement
Multiple MSR modules work collaboratively in a top-down pyramid. A coarser-resolution feature map from a higher MSR pyramid level and a finer-resolution feature map from a lower CSA pyramid level are input to an MSR module. The MSR module outputs a refined feature map using a low-level semantic, accurately localized feature map from the CSA pyramid. This output and the next finer-resolution feature map from the CSA pyramid are fed into the subsequent MSR module until the final feature map is generated. The refinement process is iterated from coarse to fine.

Each MSR module comprises three parts: bilinear interpolation to upsample the coarser feature map, element-wise addition with the finer feature map from the CSA pyramid, and two MLP layers to reduce aliasing effects and generate a depth map at each scale. The last two MSR modules are appended to generate.

SideRT: A Real-time Pure Transformer Architecture for Single Image Depth Estimation

Abstract
Context modeling is critical for estimating depth from a single image. Researchers have focused on obtaining global context. Attention mechanisms or transformers, designed for capturing long-range dependencies, might be suitable but often complicate architectures and decrease inference speed.

This work proposes SideRT, a pure transformer architecture for real-time single image depth estimation. To capture better global context, Cross-Scale Attention (CSA) and Multi-Scale Refinement (MSR) modules work collaboratively to efficiently fuse features of different scales. CSA modules fuse features with high semantic similarity, while MSR modules fuse features at corresponding positions. These modules contain few learnable parameters without convolutions, enabling a lightweight yet effective model.

SideRT achieves state-of-the-art performance in real-time (51.3 FPS) and is faster with a smaller backbone (Swin-T, 83.1 FPS) with a reasonable performance drop. Its performance surpasses previous state-of-the-art by a large margin, improving AbsRel by 6.9% on KITTI and 9.7% on NYU. This is the first work demonstrating transformer-based networks achieving state-of-the-art real-time performance in single image depth estimation. Code will be made available.

1 Introduction
Single image depth estimation (SIDE) is crucial for extracting 3D geometry, with applications in automatic driving, robotics navigation, and augmented reality. The main difficulty of SIDE is the lack of multiple views to establish geometric relationships, requiring 3D geometric clues to be derived from a single image.

Figure 1: Inference speed versus AbsRel performance on the KITTI test set. SideRT models achieve better accuracy than state-of-the-art methods at a much faster speed.

To address this ill-posed problem, extracting global context is paramount, relying heavily on deep neural networks. CNN-based architectures once dominated SIDE but, due to the locality of convolution, global context was primarily obtained near the bottleneck in low-resolution feature maps, leading to the loss of essential 3D structural clues like local details. To obtain high-resolution global context, the SIDE field has trended towards enlarging receptive fields using large backbones, feature pyramids, spatial pyramid pooling, and atrous convolutions.

Another approach to extract global context leverages the long-range dependency modeling capability of attention mechanisms. Attention modules compute responses by estimating matching scores to all positions and gathering corresponding embeddings, guaranteeing a global receptive field. Transformers, initially designed for natural language processing and using attention as a core component, are increasingly applied in computer vision. Their powerful ability to establish long-range dependencies has pushed state-of-the-art performance forward when integrated into fully convolutional architectures.

However, attention mechanisms are typically time- and memory-consuming, compromising inference speed. While efficient implementations exist, similar efforts are rare in the SIDE field.

This paper explores achieving state-of-the-art performance in real-time using transformers and attention mechanisms. We introduce the SIDE Real-time Transformer (SideRT), based on an encoder-decoder architecture.

This paper addresses state-of-the-art real-time performance with transformers and attention mechanisms in the Single Image Depth Estimation (SIDE) field. We introduce the SIDE Real-time Transformer (SideRT), an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder uses Swin transformers. The decoder features a novel Cross-Scale Attention (CSA) mechanism and a Multi-Scale Refinement (MSR) module. Both CSA and MSR are global operations that work together.

In CSA, finer-resolution features are augmented by coarser-resolution features using attention scores based on semantic similarity. In MSR, coarser-resolution features are merged into spatially corresponding finer-resolution features. These modules use few learnable parameters, fusing multi-scale feature maps with minimal computational overhead.

Based on CSA and MSR, a lightweight decoder progressively performs hierarchical depth optimization for coarse-to-fine prediction. Multi-Stage Supervision (MSS) is applied at each stage to facilitate training.

SideRT outperforms previous state-of-the-art models at 51.3 FPS, improving AbsRel on KITTI from 0.058 to 0.054 and on NYU from 0.103 to 0.093. Using a smaller backbone (Swin-T), SideRT achieves 0.060 AbsRel on KITTI at 83.1 FPS and 0.124 AbsRel on NYU at 84.4 FPS. This is the first demonstration of transformer-based networks achieving state-of-the-art real-time performance in SIDE.

**Related Work**

SIDE is a practical computer vision task for 3D scene understanding. Due to the inherent ambiguity of 3D mapping from a single view, SIDE is an ill-posed problem. Deep learning has significantly advanced the field.

**CNN-based:** Eigen et al. (2014) first introduced CNNs to SIDE. Subsequent research employed more powerful networks like ResNet and DenseNet to improve global context understanding and depth inference reliability. Techniques such as atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP), spatial pyramid pooling, and feature pyramids were used to enlarge receptive fields (Lee et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2018; Song et al., 2021).

**Attention-based:** Attention mechanisms establish pixel-wise associations, addressing long-range dependency issues crucial for contextual knowledge extraction in SIDE. Lee et al. (2021) used attention for feature learning on patches to enhance prediction accuracy. Xu et al. (2021) designed channel and spatial attention modules to improve high-level context and low-level spatial features. Huynh et al. (2020) explored self-attention to establish pixel associations as depth priors. Aich et al. (2021) and Hao et al. (2018) applied attention for multi-level feature fusion. Jiao et al. (2018) developed an attention-driven loss to improve depth prediction quality over long ranges.

**Transformer-based:** Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017), initially for NLP, are deep neural networks leveraging self-attention. Their strong representation capabilities led to applications in SIDE. Yang et al. (2021) introduced ViT architectures (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) to compensate for convolutional locality. Ranftl et al. (2021) found ViT encoders more effective than convolutional ones for SIDE. Bhat et al. (2021) used ViT for global scene information processing and adaptive depth range division.

This work differs by exploring a fully non-convolutional architecture, proving state-of-the-art performance is achievable without convolutions. It also demonstrates real-time capability even with heavy backbones like Swin-L.

paper2.title: Self-Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation: Solving the Dynamic Object Problem by Semantic Guidance
paper2.abstract:
Self-supervised monocular depth estimation presents a powerful method to obtain 3D scene information from single camera images, which is trainable on arbitrary image sequences without requiring depth labels, e.g., from a LiDAR sensor. 
                        In this work we present a new self-supervised semantically-guided depth estimation (SGDepth) method to deal with moving dynamic-class (DC) objects, such as moving cars and pedestrians, which violate the static-world assumptions typically made during training of such models. 
                        Specifically, we propose (i) mutually beneficial cross-domain training of (supervised) semantic segmentation and self-supervised depth estimation with task-specific network heads, (ii) a semantic masking scheme providing guidance to prevent moving DC objects from contaminating the photometric loss, and (iii) a detection method for frames with non-moving DC objects, from which the depth of DC objects can be learned. 
                        We demonstrate the performance of our method on several benchmarks, in particular on the Eigen split, where we exceed all baselines without test-time refinement.
methodology:
The final loss is a combination of photometric losses (9) and (3), smoothness loss (4), and cross-entropy loss (5):
$J^{t}_{total} = J^{t}_{ce} + \beta J^{t}_{sm} + \begin{cases} J^{t}_{phm}, & \Lambda^t < \theta_\Lambda \\ J^{t}_{ph}, & \text{else} \end{cases}$

$J^{t}_{ph}$, $J^{t}_{phm}$, and $J^{t}_{sm}$ are computed only on training images for depth estimation. $J^{t}_{ce}$ is computed only in the segmentation domain. Segmentation and depth losses are not weighted against each other in this equation; weighting occurs during the backward pass guided by (6).

**Experimental Setup**

**Network Topology:** The topology is based on an encoder-decoder architecture with skip connections. An ImageNet pretrained ResNet18 encoder is used for comparability with existing work. The depth head has a sigmoid output $\sigma_{t,i}$, converted to a depth map by $\frac{1}{a\sigma_{t,i}+b}$, with $a$ and $b$ constraining depth values to the range [0.1, 100]. The segmentation decoder uses the same architecture as the depth decoder, with the last layer having $S$ feature maps whose elements are converted to class probabilities by a softmax function. The pose network's architecture is the same as in [20].

**Training Aspects:** For depth estimation training, all images are resized to 640×192 (128×416 and 384×1280 are also evaluated). For semantic segmentation, images are randomly cropped to the same resolution. Zero-mean normalization is applied to RGB images for the ResNet encoder. Input images are augmented with horizontal flipping, random brightness (±0.2), contrast (±0.2), saturation (±0.2), and hue (±0.1). Photometric losses (3, 9) are calculated on images without color augmentations. Loss is computed on four scales, similar to [20].

Gradient scaling from (6) is applied at all connections between encoder and decoder with an optimal scale factor of $\lambda = 0.1$. The fraction $\epsilon$ of images for which photometric loss is not masked according to (9) is set to 0 after 30 epochs and increases linearly to only use loss (3) in the last epoch. This encourages learning from frames with non-moving DC objects after they are removed from the loss. DC object classes $S_{DC}$ include all human and vehicle categories [9].

Models are trained for 40 epochs using the Adam optimizer with batch sizes of 12 for single-task and 6 for multi-task models. Batches from task-specific datasets are concatenated, passed through the encoder, then disconnected for respective decoders. The learning rate is set to $10^{-4}$ and reduced to $10^{-5}$ after 30 epochs. Training only depth estimation with the [20] architecture is termed "SGDepth only depth". Joint training of semantic segmentation and depth estimation is termed "SGDepth full".

**Datasets:** One dataset is used for semantic segmentation training, and another for self-supervised depth estimation training. Cityscapes dataset [9] is used for semantic segmentation. Different subsets of the KITTI dataset [17] are used for depth estimation training. Depth estimation results are compared by training and evaluating on the Eigen split [12] of KITTI, removing static scenes from the training subset as in [71]. The single image depth prediction Benchmark split from KITTI [56] is also used for training and evaluation. For joint depth and segmentation prediction, the KITTI split defined by [18] is used, with its test set being the official training set of KITTI Stereo 2015 dataset [40]. Training image counts may deviate slightly from original definitions due to the need for preceding and succeeding images for depth estimation training. Data subset sizes are in Table 4.

**Evaluation Metrics:** Depth estimation is evaluated using four error metrics: absolute relative error (Abs Rel), squared relative error (Sq Rel), root mean squared error (RMSE), and logarithmic root mean squared error (RMSE log), as defined in [12] and computed as in [38, 71].

Depth Error Metrics (Eigen and KITTI splits):
  - Abs Rel:  $$ \frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i \in I} \frac{|d_i - \hat{d}_i|}{d_i} $$

  - Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU):  $$ mIoU = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s \in S} \frac{TP_s}{TP_s + FP_s + FN_s} $$
  - $S$: set of all classes in Cityscapes.
  - $TP_s$: true positive predictions for class $s$.
  - $FP_s$: false positive predictions for class $s$.
  - $FN_s$: false negative predictions for class $s$.
  - Depth metrics are computed image-wise and then averaged.
  - For mIoU, TP, FP, and FN are summed over all images in the test set before calculating mIoU.

Evaluation Section B:
  - Provides additional examples comparing SGDepth with baselines and SGDepth (depth only).
  - All models trained and tested on Eigen splits [12] of KITTI dataset [17].

Depth Comparison to Baselines (Section B.1):
  - SGDepth predictions are sharpened at object boundaries, especially for small objects like traffic lights and signs.
  - This sharpening is attributed to the joint training of depth estimation and semantic segmentation, allowing the encoder to better learn object boundaries which guide depth estimation.
  - The sharpening effect might be underestimated by numerical evaluation because ground truth depth labels often do not cover the entire image (e.g., upper regions where signs/lights are).
  - SGDepth also allows for better learned depth of DC objects.

Two decoder heads are used, one for depth and one for segmentation. The segmentation decoder is trained in a source domain supervised by $y_{t,s}$ using (5). The depth decoder is trained in a target domain under self-supervision according to (3) and (4). For mini-batches containing data from both domains, gradients from separate decoders propagate into the shared encoder. Instead of scaling loss functions, gradients are scaled upon reaching the encoder. Let $g_{depth}$ and $g_{seg}$ be gradients from the two decoders. The total gradient $g_{total}$ propagated to the encoder is:
$$g_{total} = (1 − \lambda) g_{depth} + \lambda g_{seg}$$ (6)

Moving DC objects can contaminate the photometric error. This occurs when projected views are invalid, leading to unfavorable contributions to the photometric loss. To address this, regions with potentially moving DC objects are masked by calculating a DC object mask $\mu_t$ (8) from segmentation masks.

Moving DC objects contaminate the photometric error. To mask out DC objects in the current frame $x_t$ and wrongfully projected DC objects in projected frames $x'_{t→t}$, projected semantic masks $m'_{t→t}$ are calculated. Nearest-neighbor sampling is applied, replacing bilinear sampling for $x'_{t→t,i}$ with the value of the closest pixel in $m'_{t}$. The projected semantic mask is calculated as:
$$m'_{t→t} = \text{near}(m'_{t}, u_{t→t'}, u'_{t})$$ (7)

Defining DC object classes $S_{DC} \subset S$, the DC object mask $\mu_t \in \{0, 1\}^{H \times W}$ is defined by its pixel elements:
$$\mu_{t,i} = \begin{cases} 1, & m_{t,i} \notin S_{DC} \land m'_{t→t,i} \notin S_{DC} \text{ for all } t' \in T' \\ 0, & \text{else} \end{cases}$$ (8)
The mask has 0 at pixels belonging to a DC object in any of the three frames, and 1 otherwise. Using the DC object mask $\mu_t$, a semantically-masked photometric loss adapting (3) is defined:
$$J_{phm}^t = \mu_t \odot \min_{t' \in T'} \left( \frac{\alpha}{2}(1 - \text{SSIM}(x_t, x'_{t→t})) + (1 - \alpha)|x_t - x'_{t→t}| \right)$$ (9)
This loss only considers non-DC pixels. The mask from auto-masking [20,23,24] is also considered but omitted in (3) and (9) for simplicity.

**Self-Supervised Depth Estimation With Semantic Guidance**

**Detecting Non-Moving DC Objects:** Instead of excluding DC objects completely, they are learned from only when not in motion. A measure is needed to determine if a DC object is in motion. If a DC object has been observed in motion, the warped semantic mask in the target image $m'_{t→t}$ has low consistency with the semantic mask $m_t$ in the target image. The intersection over union for dynamic object classes between $m'_{t→t}$ and $m_t$ is measured by:
$$\Lambda_{t,t'} = \frac{\sum_{i \in I} \kappa_{t,t',i}}{\sum_{i \in I} \nu_{t,t',i}}, \text{with}$$
$$\kappa_{t,t',i} = \begin{cases} 1, & m_{t,i} \in S_{DC} \land m'_{t→t,i} \in S_{DC} \\ 0, & \text{else} \end{cases}$$
$$\nu_{t,t',i} = \begin{cases} 1, & m_{t,i} \in S_{DC} \lor m'_{t→t,i} \in S_{DC} \\ 0, & \text{else} \end{cases}$$ (10)
The indicator $\Lambda_{t,t'} \in [0, 1]$ signals perfect alignment and no moving DC objects if it equals 1, and a high share of moving DC objects if it equals 0. If two frames at times $t' \in T' = \{t−1, t+1\}$ are considered, the mean value $\Lambda_t$ of all $\Lambda_{t,t'}$ is taken. A threshold $\theta_\Lambda \in [0, 1]$ is defined, above which an image is considered static.

**Learning from Non-Moving DC Objects:** Given a measure indicating whether an image is static or dynamic after each epoch, $\Lambda_t$ is calculated for each image. The threshold $\theta_\Lambda$ is chosen such that a fraction $\epsilon \in [0, 1]$ of images are trained without the semantically-masked photometric loss. The final loss is a combination of the photometric losses (9) and (3), the smoothness loss (4), and the cross-entropy loss (5):
$$J_{total}^t = J_{ce}^t + \beta J_{sm}^t + \begin{cases} J_{phm}^t, & \Lambda_t < \theta_\Lambda \\ J_{ph}^t, & \text{else} \end{cases}$$ (11)
Where $J_{ph}^t, J_{phm}^t,$ and $J_{sm}^t$ are components of the total loss.

5.2 Ablation Studies
Table 3 shows results on the Kitti split, starting from baselines and adding contributions to the full method. Training depth and segmentation together in a multi-task fashion improves depth estimation. Multi-task prediction is during training; evaluation can be done separately. Gradient scaling improves depth and particularly semantic segmentation. Masking out DC objects initially decreases performance as the network has no objective for their depth. Introducing a threshold θΛ learns DC object depth from a fraction ϵ of images with non-moving DC objects. Scheduling ϵ starts with best samples and then includes more "noisy" samples. topic: Depth perception tasks focus on estimating the distance of objects from a single image or sequence, which is crucial for applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and 3D scene understanding. What is the better method for depth perception tasks: SideRT or packnSFMHR_RVC?

paper1.title: SideRT: A Real-time Pure Transformer Architecture for Single Image Depth Estimation
paper1.abstract:
Since context modeling is critical for estimating
                        depth from a single image, researchers put tremendous effort into obtaining global context. Many
                        global manipulations are designed for traditional
                        CNN-based architectures to overcome the locality
                        of convolutions. Attention mechanisms or transformers originally designed for capturing longrange dependencies might be a better choice, but
                        usually complicates architectures and could lead
                        to a decrease in inference speed. In this work,
                        we propose a pure transformer architecture called
                        SideRT that can attain excellent predictions in realtime. In order to capture better global context,
                        Cross-Scale Attention (CSA) and Multi-Scale Refinement (MSR) modules are designed to work collaboratively to fuse features of different scales efficiently. CSA modules focus on fusing features
                        of high semantic similarities, while MSR modules aim to fuse features at corresponding positions. These two modules contain a few learnable
                        parameters without convolutions, based on which
                        a lightweight yet effective model is built. This architecture achieves state-of-the-art performances in
                        real-time (51.3 FPS) and becomes much faster with
                        a reasonable performance drop on a smaller backbone Swin-T (83.1 FPS). Furthermore, its performance surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by a
                        large margin, improving AbsRel metric 6.9% on
                        KITTI and 9.7% on NYU. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to show that transformerbased networks can attain state-of-the-art performance in real-time in the single image depth estimation field. Code will be made available soon.

4.2 Benchmark Datasets
KITTI and NYU datasets used for performance evaluation.
KITTI [Geiger et al., 2013]: Road environment acquired in autonomous driving scene. Image resolution: 1242x375 pixels. Split strategy from [Eigen et al., 2014]. Test set: 697 images from 29 scenes. Training set: 23488 images from 32 scenes. Maximum prediction depth: 80 meters.
NYU dataset [Silberman et al., 2012]: 120K images from Microsoft Kinect camera, including 464 indoor scenes. Resolution: 640x480. Train/test split from [Eigen et al., 2014]. Training: 249 scenarios. Testing: 654 images from 215 scenarios. Depth map center-cropped to 561x427 for evaluation.

4.3 Comparison with State-of-the-art
Metrics from [Eigen et al., 2014] used for monocular depth estimation performance evaluation. Formulations in Table 3.
Comparison with state-of-the-art methods on KITTI and NYU datasets. Method achieves best performance on all metrics.
KITTI dataset: AbsRel decreased by 6.9%, SqRel decreased by 8.9% compared to previous state-of-the-art.
NYU dataset: AbsRel decreased by 9.7%, RMSE decreased by 8.0% compared to previous state-of-the-art.
Small models (SideRT(Swin-T), SideRT(Swin-S)) outperform many state-of-the-art methods on KITTI and NYU.
Heavy backbone (Swin-L, ~200 million parameters) does not slow down inference and shows similar speed to smaller models (SideRT(Swin-B), SideRT(Swin-S)).
Achieved real-time prediction at 51.3 FPS while surpassing state-of-the-art.

Cross-scale Attention (CSA): Evaluated by removing CSA modules (Row 4 and 5 in Table 4). CSA module improves performance with small computational overhead (+0.8M Params) and small decrease in speed (-12.0 FPS). Row 1-2 in Table 4 show CSA module significantly improves depth prediction from Swin-T encoder. CSA module enlarges the receptive field of the encoder. Swin-T+CSA achieves similar performance to VNL [Yin et al., 2019] and outperforms some metrics of DORN [Fu et al., 2018].

Multi-stage Supervision (MSS): Training pure transformer architecture is more difficult than CNN-based counterpart.

MSR modules use upsampling to fuse features with corresponding spatial positions. Each MSR module consists of an element-wise addition between the upsampled feature map from the MSR pyramid and a finer-resolution feature map from the CSA pyramid, followed by two MLP layers to reduce aliasing effects and generate a depth map at each scale. The last two MSR modules generate the final result at input resolution and do not receive outputs from CSA modules. MLP layers facilitate global information flow.

Multi-Stage Supervision (MSS) is proposed to ease training. Each scale is supervised by a loss calculated between the prediction and corresponding ground truth. Multi-stage losses are then weighted and summed.

To address the imbalance of dense depth data at close areas and sparse data at distances, the square root loss function is adopted. This loss calculates the difference of predicted depth and ground truth in log space.

$L(y, y^*) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N_V} \sum_{i \in V} d_i^2 - \lambda (\frac{1}{N_V} \sum_{i \in V} d_i)^2}$
where $d_i = \log y_i - \log y^*_i$.
$y$ is the predicted depth map, $y^*$ is the ground truth depth map, $V$ is the set of valid pixels, $N_V$ is the total number of valid pixels, and $\lambda$ is set to 0.85.

SideRT is applied to KITTI and NYU datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods at faster speeds.

- Model implemented in PyTorch.
- Swin transformers pretrained on ImageNet used as encoders.
- Trained from scratch for 160 epochs with batch size 6.

- Training performed on 8 NVIDIA A100 SXM GPUs.

Conclusion
This paper introduces two efficient mechanisms for obtaining better global context. These techniques are used to build a lightweight pure transformer architecture with few learnable parameters and no convolutions. Our model demonstrates powerful context modeling capabilities, achieving state-of-the-art performance on two challenging datasets. This work shows that pure transformer architectures can balance accuracy and running time efficiency, providing insights for future research on real-time transformer architectures for practical applications.
