where d∗t = dt/dt is the mean-normalized inverse depth from [28] to discourage depth shrinking.
Both losses are applied at 4 scales to avoid gradient locality.

B. Outlier Masking
Adverse factors like occlusion and scene dynamics can damage image reconstruction. Pixels in the photometric error map can be invalid and misleading during training. Most pixels are visible and stationary, while occluded and moving pixels produce more significant photometric errors. Outlier masking is based on this observation.
The outlier mask is determined by the statistical information of photometric errors.
The mean and standard deviation of pixel photometric errors from all source images are computed for each training sample:
µ = mean{PE(It, Is→t)|s ∈ S} (5)
σ = std{PE(It, Is→t)|s ∈ S} (6)
An outlier mask for the photometric error map PE(It, Is→t) is computed:
M_ol = µ − lσ < PE(It, Is→t) < µ + uσ (7)
where l and u are lower and upper thresholds.
The mask excludes possible occluded or moving regions.
Setting u = 0.5 is effective; a higher value fails to mask moving objects, and a lower value masks out stationary objects.
Setting l = 1 masks pixels with very small photometric errors, typically from homogeneous regions and less valuable for training.
This selection of u and l retains principal photometric errors for optimization, as shown in Fig. 3.

C. Weighted Multi-Scale Scheme
To avoid local minima caused by the bilinear sampler's gradient locality [27], unsupervised learning models predict 4-scale depth maps and compute multi-scale photometric losses. However, this can lead to "holes" in low-texture regions and texture-copy artifacts.
Monodepth2 [4] uses a full-resolution multi-scale scheme by upsampling depth maps to full resolution, warping full-resolution images, and computing losses at full resolution.
This full-resolution scheme increases computation and GPU memory.
To reduce training overhead, a weighted multi-scale scheme is proposed to devalue low-resolution photometric losses.
A scale factor f < 1 is defined to compute the weight for scale r:
w_r = f^r (8)
where r ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}.

D. Integrated Objective Function
While outlier masking excludes most irregular pixels, it has limitations. Pixels moving out of the image boundary are not masked. These "out-of-box" pixels can be masked by retaining only pixels reprojected inside the source image box [29].
Outlier masking also fails to mask objects with speeds very close to the camera, as these objects are often estimated similarly.

Outlier masking technique excludes occluded and moving regions, especially oncoming objects, by observing larger photometric errors in these areas. Visible background typically dominates scenes, with invisible or moving pixels showing inconsistencies that hinder optimization. A weighted multi-scale scheme complements outlier masking for better depth maps.

Experimental validation on the KITTI dataset proves the effectiveness of the outlier masking and weighted multi-scale contributions. Combined with a baseline model and other masking practices, this forms DiPE, an unsupervised monocular depth and ego-motion estimation system.

Recent advancements in unsupervised monocular depth estimation (MDE) utilize deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Some methods directly regress ground truth depth, while others combine deep learning with graphical models or treat MDE as a classification problem. Models trained on datasets with ground truth depth often lack generalization to real-world scenarios.

Unsupervised learning schemes leverage stereo images or adjacent monocular video frames to create supervisory signals, typically using photometric differences between a view and its synthesis. Synthesis is computed from an additional view using estimated depth and pose. Stereo videos have been exploited for training to utilize both spatial and temporal cues. Monocular videos, being more generalized and available, are the focus of this paper.

SfM-Learner, an early method using monocular videos, employs an additional Pose CNN to estimate relative motion for view synthesis. However, photometric consistency is often compromised by occlusion and moving objects. Subsequent methods to improve this framework fall into categories like masking photometric errors, joint learning with optical flow, and modeling object motion. Masking strategies, such as explainability masks and uncertainty maps, may require extra networks. Joint learning with optical flow necessitates new networks for flow estimation. Object motion modeling requires modules for segmentation and motion estimation.

In contrast, overlap and blank masks, geometrically derived from image warping, offer a lightweight approach to occlusion. Monodepth2 uses minimum reprojection, taking the minimum photometric errors from all source views as a masking technique for occlusion. Monodepth2 also employs auto-masking for objects moving at speeds similar to the camera. While effective, this simple strategy has not addressed oncoming moving objects. The proposed outlier masking method addresses this issue, and further enhances minimum reprojection for more accurate results.

DiPE: Deeper into Photometric Errors for Unsupervised Learning of Depth and Ego-motion from Monocular Videos

Unsupervised learning of depth and ego-motion from unlabelled monocular videos avoids the use of expensive ground truth. It uses photometric errors between target and synthesized adjacent views as the loss. Learning suffers from occlusion and scene dynamics. This paper shows manipulating photometric errors can tackle these difficulties. An improvement is a statistical technique that masks invisible or non-stationary pixels in the photometric error map, preventing misleading networks. This outlier masking approach improves depth estimation of objects moving opposite to the camera. Such scenarios have not been seriously considered, posing a risk in autonomous driving. An efficient weighted multi-scale scheme reduces artifacts in predicted depth maps. Extensive experiments on the KITTI dataset show effectiveness. The system achieves state-of-the-art performance on depth and ego-motion estimation.

Depth and ego-motion estimation is core to SLAM. Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) is flexible for applications like autonomous mobile robotics and AR/VR. Tracking 6-DoF motion for moving cameras is critical. Traditional supervised methods require expensive ground truth, limiting generalization. Unsupervised learning from monocular videos offers a more generalizable solution.

Unsupervised learning models typically contain two networks: one for predicting the depth map of the target view, and another for motion between target and adjacent views. Network outputs allow target view reconstruction from adjacent source views via image warping. The resulting photometric loss serves as the supervisory signal. However, image reconstruction is disrupted by between-view occlusion and scene dynamics, harming network learning due to incorrect supervision.

Figure 1 illustrates the detriment of occlusion and dynamics. (a) Occlusion: point P visible in Ct but occluded in Ct+1. To achieve photometric consistency, P is estimated with shorter depth, blurring foreground objects. (b) Co-directional motion: if point M moves forward like camera C, it's likely estimated with farther depth, producing ‘dark holes’. (c) Contra-directional motion: when point M moves backward opposite to camera C, it's estimated with shorter depth.

The theory of minimizing between-view reconstruction errors affecting depth estimation of occluded regions and moving objects is illustrated in Figure 1. Many methods address occlusion and dynamics with considerable improvement. For example, ‘dark holes’ from co-directionally moving objects are tackled in recent works [2], [3], [4]. However, latest models significantly underestimate depth for contra-directionally moving objects. Inaccuracy of such objects has not been reported, which can cause issues in applications like autonomous driving, where underrated oncoming car distances could lead to unnecessary braking or avoidance.

paper2.title: MultiDepth: Single-Image Depth Estimation via Multi-Task Regression and Classification
paper2.abstract:
We introduce MultiDepth, a novel training strategy and convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture that allows approaching
                        single-image depth estimation (SIDE) as a multi-task problem. SIDE is an important part of road scene understanding. It, thus,
                        plays a vital role in advanced driver assistance systems and autonomous vehicles. Best results for the SIDE task so far have been
                        achieved using deep CNNs. However, optimization of regression problems, such as estimating depth, is still a challenging task. For
                        the related tasks of image classification and semantic segmentation, numerous CNN-based methods with robust training behavior
                        have been proposed. Hence, in order to overcome the notorious instability and slow convergence of depth value regression during
                        training, MultiDepth makes use of depth interval classification as an auxiliary task. The auxiliary task can be disabled at test-time
                        to predict continuous depth values using the main regression branch more efficiently. We applied MultiDepth to road scenes and
                        present results on the KITTI depth prediction dataset. In experiments, we were able to show that end-to-end multi-task learning with
                        both, regression and classification, is able to considerably improve training and yield more accurate results.
methodology:
The output feature dimension from one to ncls. The decoder for the classification task closely resembles the structure of the regression branch. Keeping the task-specific branches shallow, and thus the ratio of shared vs. individual parameters high, encourages the learning of high-level features suitable for both tasks.

**Multi-Task Optimization**

Jointly training both tasks requires combining individual losses Ltask into a single multi-task objective Lmt for optimization. A naive approach is summing the losses: Lmt = Lreg + Lcls. However, the range and variance of values from Lreg and Lcls may differ significantly. Weighting with wreg and wcls, such that Lmt = wreg · Lreg + wcls · Lcls, allows for adjusting the contribution of each loss. Manually tuning these weights as hyperparameters is tedious and results in constant weights that may not adapt during training. Automatically optimizing dynamic parameters is a promising approach.

Existing methods weight tasks based on their homoscedastic uncertainty [23] or difficulty [17]. We adopt the former, introducing weighting parameters wreg = 0.5 · exp(−s²reg) and wcls = exp(−s²cls) with stask = loge(σ²task). While σtask represents actual task uncertainties, we optimize for stask due to numerical stability, following [23]. Minimizing Lmt = wreg · Lreg + wcls · Lcls favors the trivial solution wreg = wcls = 0. To prevent this, regularization terms rtask = 0.5 · stask are added to the weighted single-task losses, yielding our final multi-task loss:

Lmt = wreg · Lreg + rreg + wcls · Lcls + rcls. (3)

**Experiments**

We implemented a deep CNN and trained it on a large road scene understanding dataset to evaluate our approach.

**Network Implementation**

Since networks for SIDE and semantic segmentation share properties like feed-forward auto-encoder structures, architectures are often shared [28, 30]. Our auxiliary pixel-wise depth interval classification task is essentially a segmentation task. Therefore, well-performing deep CNN architectures for semantic segmentation are suitable as a basis.

PSPNet [51], with its pyramid pooling module, accumulates information from spatial context. The very deep ResNet-101 [20] backbone provides the capacity for learning rich representations. The network also features an encoder-decoder structure using pyramid pooling and dilated convolutions [5, 48] to preserve high-resolution feature maps. PSPNet achieves state-of-the-art results on various semantic segmentation datasets [51].

Matching our requirements, we re-implemented this architecture in PyTorch for our multi-task approach. An overview of our Multi-Depth network is shown in Figure 2. The auxiliary loss used in the original implementation by Zhao et al. [51] was not implemented.

Parameters are shared through the ResNet encoder, accounting for approximately 50% of total parameters. Sharing a majority of parameters enforces learning a common representation in the 2048-dimensional feature map, expected to contain high-level depth perception information. This representation is condensed for each task by task-specific pyramid pooling modules, subsequent blocks (convolution, batch normalization, ReLU, dropout), and final convolutional layers for reshaping. Skip connections are used, as in the original PSPNet, to retain spatial structure.

**Training and Validation Data**

Predicting depth with high robustness, redundancy, and accuracy is crucial for autonomous driving. As Multi-Depth is designed to meet these conditions, we chose to train.

MultiDepth introduces an auxiliary depth interval classification task to SIDE networks. Applied to SIDE in road scene understanding, extensive experiments show the benefits of posing SIDE as a multi-task problem with supervision from automatically derived ground-truth labels. The method outperforms single-task regression and classification baselines with 32 classes for the auxiliary classification branch and learned weighting. MultiDepth achieved an SILog of 16.05 on the anonymous KITTI depth prediction test set [45, 14], demonstrating good overall results from the training strategy.

Increasing the number of classes improves training stability and performance, with ncls ≥ 4 yielding minor improvements. Using more classes than necessary does not significantly degrade results but produces a secondary output with lower quantization errors. Models with 4 ≤ ncls ≤ 64 achieved nearly identical results; ncls = 32 was selected for best convergence.

Learned weights improve training over equally weighted or manually tuned tasks. Learned weights consistently outperformed manual tuning, demonstrating effectiveness and saving computation time despite adding few parameters.

Log-normalization of depth values: Scaling to the relevant range (minimum to maximum depth in the dataset) improved results compared to scaling from 0–256 m. The relevant range may differ for other applications.

Patch size: Training on larger patches (256 × 256 px) outperformed smaller ones, yielding the best results in the experiments. This configuration was submitted to the KITTI depth prediction benchmark.

Final training results: The model with the highest validation score was selected for submission. Table 1 shows performance comparisons. All MultiDepth configurations significantly outperformed single-task baselines.

A common and robust representation for both tasks is learned during training by sharing a major part of the network weights. The encoder part, expected to learn a rich representation of input data, should be shared to encourage this behavior. The decoders, containing few layers, extract and reshape task-specific information from the shared encoded features. State-of-the-art architectures often use very deep classification networks as a backbone for deep feature extraction in the encoder, accounting for a vast majority of parameters.

**2.1 Efficient Optimization of Depth in Log-Space**

In autonomous driving, small errors in distance estimates for objects close to the camera can be fatal, while faraway objects require lower accuracy. This can be addressed by estimation in non-linear space. Modern CNN-based SIDE methods use sophisticated loss functions to incorporate such properties. The scale invariant logarithmic error (SILog) is commonly used for scoring depth estimation results:

$SILog(D, D^*) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i,j} (\log d_{i,j} - \log d^*_{i,j})^2 - \frac{1}{n^2} (\sum_{i,j} \log d_{i,j} - \log d^*_{i,j})^2$

This compares predicted depth maps $D^* = (d^*_{i,j})$ with $n$ depth values to the ground-truth $D$. Extensive loss functions yield superior results over basic ones like MSE, though MSE is computationally less expensive and faster. While not directly optimizing the final objective, MSE acts as a reasonable proxy.

To overcome limitations, computationally expensive operations are moved to the data pre-processing stage. Parallel pre-loading of batches allows direct objective optimization while maintaining speed and efficiency. Depth values $d$ in training data are transformed to normalized log-space during data loading. With globally defined boundaries $d_{min}$ and $d_{max}$, the transformed depth is:

$d_{log} = \frac{\log_e (d - d_{min} + 1)}{\log_e (d_{max} - d_{min} + 1)}$

**2.2 Regression of Depth Values**

Task-specific decoders can be added to extract information from encoder features. For the main task of regressing continuous depth values, the decoder predicts values in normalized log-space. Few network layers are expected to suffice for condensing and reshaping information, given the encoder's rich representation.

**2.3 Classification of Depth Intervals**

The auxiliary task of classifying discrete depth ranges requires corresponding target labels. A number of intervals, $n_{cls}$, is set to partition the continuous depth space. A low number of classes ensures stable convergence while preserving enough detail to support the regression branch. Unlike methods like Fu et al. [12] which report 80 intervals as optimal for ordinal regression, our approach uses classification merely to support the regression branch, prioritizing stable convergence and robust performance over high quantization errors. Following the concept of estimating non-linearly scaled depth values and existing approaches [12], intervals are uniformly distributed in normalized log-space.

Apart from different target labels and a change in output feature dimension to $n_{cls}$, the decoder for classification closely resembles the regression branch. Shallow task-specific branches maintain a high ratio of shared vs. individual parameters.

**Figure 2:** Network architecture for the MultiDepth approach, featuring a shared ResNet-101 encoder with dilated convolutions and task-specific decoders, including pyramid pooling for the main regression and auxiliary classification tasks. The multi-task loss is formed from contributing single-task losses using learned weighting terms representing task uncertainties.

Batch and patch sizes are coupled by GPU memory. Larger patches are favorable due to sparse ground-truth data. Larger batch sizes generally benefit optimization. A batch size of 32 with a patch size of 128x128 pixels offered the best trade-off. Adam [24] with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, and a weight decay λ = 0.0001 was used for optimization.

The learning rate α is a crucial hyperparameter. Following Smith [42], training was run for a few iterations with an increasing learning rate from minuscule to excessively high values to cover the full space of realistic α in 250 optimization steps. Repeating this with different starting α and exponential scheduler parameters yielded an α vs. Lmt diagram (Figure 4). Four intervals of α were observed: α < 10−6 resulted in Lmt stagnation; 10−6 < α < 10−3 showed Lmt decrease, the desired range; for α > 10−1, Lmt diverged. Learning rates in the second interval were deemed suitable. α = 10−4 was selected, close to the steepest descent of Lmt. A polynomial scheduler with γ = 0.9 was applied to decay α to zero over 5x10^5 training iterations (approximately 90 epochs). Epochs are not ideal for measuring progress due to random cropping.

Ablation studies evaluated the approach. Training was from scratch without pre-trained weights for the ResNet encoder. Networks were trained on a single NVIDIA GeForce 1080Ti GPU in approximately 5 days.

Baseline: Training the regression branch without the classification branch showed initial improvement, then divergence after 10^5 iterations, converging to an undesirable local minimum (Fu et al. [12]). Training a single-task classification model eliminated slow/unstable convergence issues, yielding better overall results.

MultiDepth approach: Adding an auxiliary classification branch to the regression network stabilized training, even with as few as two classes, similar to [32]. Increasing the number of classes further improved stability and performance.

Skip connections are used to retain spatial structure, as in the original PSPNet.

3.2 Training and Validation Data
Predicting depth with high robustness, redundancy, and accuracy is important for autonomous driving. The Multi-Depth method is trained and evaluated on road scene images from the KITTI dataset. This dataset provides ground-truth depth from sparse LiDAR point clouds. The training set has approximately 86,000 samples. Ground-truth depth is available for about 12% of pixels on average, with some samples having as little as 0.8%. Depth measurements show unequal spatial distribution, with a lack of data in the upper image parts. Training uses the full training set, and validation uses the "val_selection_cropped" set (1000 images). Final results are scored on the official KITTI depth prediction benchmark.

3.3 Data Augmentation and Scaling
Input images are randomly cropped to resolutions between 128x128 px and 256x256 px. Smaller patches lead to more images with insufficient ground-truth. Images are not scaled to exploit the fully-convolutional nature of the network during inference. Horizontal flipping is used as data augmentation, even for road scenes. Depth values are scaled using Equation (2) with dmin = 2 m and dmax = 125 m, following the training dataset's depth distribution. The lower bound is set tightly, and the upper bound is more generous. Class labels for the classification branch are derived by binning scaled depth values into equally spaced intervals in normalized log-space ([dcmin, dcmax]). Setting dcmin > dmin and dcmax < dmax simplifies the auxiliary task.

3.4 Training Procedure
Sparse MSE loss is used for the regression task, and sparse SoftMax cross-entropy loss for the classification task, due to sparse ground-truth. The multi-task loss is constructed using Equation (3). Weighting parameters for the multi-task loss (sreg, scls) are initialized to 1 and optimized with network parameters. Initialization of weighting parameters is robust. Batch and patch sizes are coupled due to GPU memory constraints. Larger patches are favored due to ground-truth sparsity.

paper1.title: DiPE: Deeper into Photometric Errors for Unsupervised Learning of Depth and Ego-motion from Monocular Videos
paper1.abstract:
Unsupervised learning of depth and ego-motion
                        from unlabelled monocular videos has recently drawn great
                        attention, which avoids the use of expensive ground truth in the
                        supervised one. It achieves this by using the photometric errors
                        between the target view and the synthesized views from its adjacent source views as the loss. Despite significant progress, the
                        learning still suffers from occlusion and scene dynamics. This
                        paper shows that carefully manipulating photometric errors
                        can tackle these difficulties better. The primary improvement
                        is achieved by a statistical technique that can mask out the
                        invisible or nonstationary pixels in the photometric error map
                        and thus prevents misleading the networks. With this outlier
                        masking approach, the depth of objects moving in the opposite
                        direction to the camera can be estimated more accurately.
                        To the best of our knowledge, such scenarios have not been
                        seriously considered in the previous works, even though they
                        pose a higher risk in applications like autonomous driving.
                        We also propose an efficient weighted multi-scale scheme to
                        reduce the artifacts in the predicted depth maps. Extensive
                        experiments on the KITTI dataset show the effectiveness of
                        the proposed approaches. The overall system achieves state-oftheart performance on both depth and ego-motion estimation.

Implementation Details:
Approaches are based on Monodepth2. Depth CNN is a fully convolutional encoder-decoder network with 640×192 resolution. Pose CNN is a standard CNN with a fully connected layer for 6-DoF relative camera motion. Both networks use ResNet18 pretrained on ImageNet as backbone. For depth estimation, only nearby 2 frames (S = {t−1, t+1}) and pair-input Pose are used. For ego-motion estimation, all-input Pose CNN is experimented with nearby 4 frames (S = {t −2, t −1, t + 1, t + 2}) and 2 frames (S = {t −1, t + 1}).

Hyper-parameters: $\eta = 1$, $\lambda = 0.001$, $e = 0.5$. Weighting factor f for multi-scale scheme is 0.25. DiPE is trained for 20 epochs using Adam. DiPE uses a batch size of 16, taking 9 hours on a single Titan Xp. Initial learning rate is $10^{−4}$, divided by 5 after 15 and 18 epochs. Outlier masking reduces training errors; decreasing learning rate helps DiPE converge better. Monodepth2 uses approximated intrinsic parameters. Calibrated intrinsic parameters are used for every training sample, with principal point flipped during horizontal flips.

KITTI Eigen Split:
Standard Eigen split of KITTI dataset is adopted for monocular depth estimation. A subset of the training set containing no static frames is used for training (39,810 samples). Validation set has 4,424 samples, and test set has 697 samples. Approximately one-tenth (432) of the validation set is used for validation per epoch. Predicted depth maps are aligned to ground truth by multiplying the median value ratio. Conventional metrics and cropping region from [5] are used, with a standard depth cap of 80m. Error metrics include absolute relative error.

Our outlier masking method is proposed for oncoming moving objects. This technique can help minimum reprojection recover a more accurate boundary for foreground objects in predicted depth maps.

**III. METHODOLOGY**

**A. Preliminaries**

The monocular unsupervised learning scheme is shown in Fig. 2. A training sample contains the target frame $I_t$ at time $t$ and source frames $I_s$ at nearby times, $s \in S$. Conventionally, $S = \{t−1, t+1\}$ or $S = \{t−2, t−1, t+1, t+2\}$. Given the shared intrinsic matrix $K$, the synthesis from source view $s$ to target view $t$ is expressed as:

$I_{s→t} = I_s⟨proj(D_t, T_{t→s}, K)⟩$
(1)

The differentiable bilinear sampling operator is [27].
proj() projects pixel pt in the target image to point ps in the source image:
ps ≃KTt→sD(pt)K−1pt (2)
where pt and ps are homogeneous coordinates.

Photometric error is computed using a combination of L1 and SSIM:
PE(Ia, Ib) = 0.85(1 − SSIM(Ia, Ib)) + 0.15∥Ia − Ib∥₁ (3)

An edge-aware smoothness term is also applied:
Les = mean(|∂xd∗t|e−|∂xIt| + |∂yd∗t|e−|∂yIt|) (4)
where d∗t = dt/dt is the mean-normalized inverse depth from [28] to discourage depth shrinking.
Both losses are applied at 4 scales to avoid gradient locality.

B. Outlier Masking
Adverse factors like occlusion and scene dynamics can damage image reconstruction. Pixels in the photometric error map can be invalid and misleading during training. Most pixels are visible and stationary, while occluded and moving pixels produce more significant photometric errors. Outlier masking is based on this observation.
The outlier mask is determined by the statistical information of photometric errors.
The mean and standard deviation of pixel photometric errors from all source images are computed for each training sample:
µ = mean{PE(It, Is→t)|s ∈ S} (5)
σ = std{PE(It, Is→t)|s ∈ S} (6)
An outlier mask for the photometric error map PE(It, Is→t) is computed:
M_ol = µ − lσ < PE(It, Is→t) < µ + uσ (7)
where l and u are lower and upper thresholds.
The mask excludes possible occluded or moving regions.
Setting u = 0.5 is effective; a higher value fails to mask moving objects, and a lower value masks out stationary objects.
Setting l = 1 masks pixels with very small photometric errors, typically from homogeneous regions and less valuable for training.
This selection of u and l retains principal photometric errors for optimization, as shown in Fig. 3.

C. Weighted Multi-Scale Scheme
To avoid local minima caused by the bilinear sampler's gradient locality [27], unsupervised learning models predict 4-scale depth maps and compute multi-scale photometric losses. However, this can lead to "holes" in low-texture regions and texture-copy artifacts.
Monodepth2 [4] uses a full-resolution multi-scale scheme by upsampling depth maps to full resolution, warping full-resolution images, and computing losses at full resolution.
This full-resolution scheme increases computation and GPU memory.
To reduce training overhead, a weighted multi-scale scheme is proposed to devalue low-resolution photometric losses.
A scale factor f < 1 is defined to compute the weight for scale r:
w_r = f^r (8)
where r ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}.

D. Integrated Objective Function
While outlier masking excludes most irregular pixels, it has limitations. Pixels moving out of the image boundary are not masked. These "out-of-box" pixels can be masked by retaining only pixels reprojected inside the source image box [29].
Outlier masking also fails to mask objects with speeds very close to the camera, as these objects are often estimated similarly.

Outlier masking technique excludes occluded and moving regions, especially oncoming objects, by observing larger photometric errors in these areas. Visible background typically dominates scenes, with invisible or moving pixels showing inconsistencies that hinder optimization. A weighted multi-scale scheme complements outlier masking for better depth maps.

Experimental validation on the KITTI dataset proves the effectiveness of the outlier masking and weighted multi-scale contributions. Combined with a baseline model and other masking practices, this forms DiPE, an unsupervised monocular depth and ego-motion estimation system.

Recent advancements in unsupervised monocular depth estimation (MDE) utilize deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Some methods directly regress ground truth depth, while others combine deep learning with graphical models or treat MDE as a classification problem. Models trained on datasets with ground truth depth often lack generalization to real-world scenarios.

Unsupervised learning schemes leverage stereo images or adjacent monocular video frames to create supervisory signals, typically using photometric differences between a view and its synthesis. Synthesis is computed from an additional view using estimated depth and pose. Stereo videos have been exploited for training to utilize both spatial and temporal cues. Monocular videos, being more generalized and available, are the focus of this paper.

SfM-Learner, an early method using monocular videos, employs an additional Pose CNN to estimate relative motion for view synthesis. However, photometric consistency is often compromised by occlusion and moving objects. Subsequent methods to improve this framework fall into categories like masking photometric errors, joint learning with optical flow, and modeling object motion. Masking strategies, such as explainability masks and uncertainty maps, may require extra networks. Joint learning with optical flow necessitates new networks for flow estimation. Object motion modeling requires modules for segmentation and motion estimation.

In contrast, overlap and blank masks, geometrically derived from image warping, offer a lightweight approach to occlusion. Monodepth2 uses minimum reprojection, taking the minimum photometric errors from all source views as a masking technique for occlusion. Monodepth2 also employs auto-masking for objects moving at speeds similar to the camera. While effective, this simple strategy has not addressed oncoming moving objects. The proposed outlier masking method addresses this issue, and further enhances minimum reprojection for more accurate results.

DiPE: Deeper into Photometric Errors for Unsupervised Learning of Depth and Ego-motion from Monocular Videos

Unsupervised learning of depth and ego-motion from unlabelled monocular videos avoids the use of expensive ground truth. It uses photometric errors between target and synthesized adjacent views as the loss. Learning suffers from occlusion and scene dynamics. This paper shows manipulating photometric errors can tackle these difficulties. An improvement is a statistical technique that masks invisible or non-stationary pixels in the photometric error map, preventing misleading networks. This outlier masking approach improves depth estimation of objects moving opposite to the camera. Such scenarios have not been seriously considered, posing a risk in autonomous driving. An efficient weighted multi-scale scheme reduces artifacts in predicted depth maps. Extensive experiments on the KITTI dataset show effectiveness. The system achieves state-of-the-art performance on depth and ego-motion estimation.

Depth and ego-motion estimation is core to SLAM. Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) is flexible for applications like autonomous mobile robotics and AR/VR. Tracking 6-DoF motion for moving cameras is critical. Traditional supervised methods require expensive ground truth, limiting generalization. Unsupervised learning from monocular videos offers a more generalizable solution.

Unsupervised learning models typically contain two networks: one for predicting the depth map of the target view, and another for motion between target and adjacent views. Network outputs allow target view reconstruction from adjacent source views via image warping. The resulting photometric loss serves as the supervisory signal. However, image reconstruction is disrupted by between-view occlusion and scene dynamics, harming network learning due to incorrect supervision.

Figure 1 illustrates the detriment of occlusion and dynamics. (a) Occlusion: point P visible in Ct but occluded in Ct+1. To achieve photometric consistency, P is estimated with shorter depth, blurring foreground objects. (b) Co-directional motion: if point M moves forward like camera C, it's likely estimated with farther depth, producing ‘dark holes’. (c) Contra-directional motion: when point M moves backward opposite to camera C, it's estimated with shorter depth.

The theory of minimizing between-view reconstruction errors affecting depth estimation of occluded regions and moving objects is illustrated in Figure 1. Many methods address occlusion and dynamics with considerable improvement. For example, ‘dark holes’ from co-directionally moving objects are tackled in recent works [2], [3], [4]. However, latest models significantly underestimate depth for contra-directionally moving objects. Inaccuracy of such objects has not been reported, which can cause issues in applications like autonomous driving, where underrated oncoming car distances could lead to unnecessary braking or avoidance.

paper2.title: Learn Stereo, Infer Mono: Siamese Networks for Self-Supervised, Monocular, Depth Estimation
paper2.abstract:
The field of self-supervised monocular depth estimation
                        has seen huge advancements in recent years. Most methods
                        assume stereo data is available during training but usually
                        under-utilize it and only treat it as a reference signal. We
                        propose a novel self-supervised approach which uses both
                        left and right images equally during training, but can still
                        be used with a single input image at test time, for monocular depth estimation. Our Siamese network architecture
                        consists of two, twin networks, each learns to predict a disparity map from a single image. At test time, however, only
                        one of these networks is used in order to infer depth. We
                        show state-of-the-art results on the standard KITTI Eigen
                        split benchmark as well as being the highest scoring selfsupervised method on the new KITTI single view benchmark. To demonstrate the ability of our method to generalize to new data sets, we further provide results on the
                        Make3D benchmark, which was not used during training.

**3.4. Post-processing**
Due to occlusions, the left side of the disparity map often lacks data. To address this, we use a post-processing method similar to Godard et al. [15]. At test time, given an image I, we also infer the depth of its horizontally mirrored image, m(I). The two disparity images are then blended using a weighting function.

**3.5. Discussion: Comparison with Godard et al. [15]**
Differences in our approach and Godard et al. [15] are significant.

**3.5.1 Similar loss, different components.**
Godard et al.'s loss averages predictions from two views, similar to ours. However, their predictions are not equivalent: both are produced from the left view, with the right view serving only as supervision (Figure 2). We provide inputs from both views simultaneously, treating them equally. This gives the network more input data, and each predicted disparity map is created independently from its corresponding image.

**Siamese Network ≠ Data Augmentation.** Our approach uses a Siamese network. In contrast, a single input network can be trained on the left image with the right image for supervision, and separately on flipped images with roles swapped [15]. This differs from our dual-input Siamese network approach.

First, using both images allows simultaneous backpropagation of information between branches, which is absent when training with a single view. Second, including both left and right images as input adds information otherwise unavailable due to occlusions and limited field-of-view.

Figure 3 compares the right disparity maps produced by Godard et al. and our method. Their disparity is blurry and lacks details and contours. This is likely due to uncertainty regarding the right image, creating asymmetry between dl and dr. Our prediction (bottom row) shows fine-grained left and right disparities. The left-right consistency of our loss relies on accurate predictions of both, compelling the network to predict the right disparity map as accurately as possible to minimize its loss.

**Why does flipping work? Can we just reverse the disparity directions?** Disparity directions can be reversed since dl = xl − xr and dr = xr − xl = −dl, where xl and xr are corresponding points in the left and right images.

However, this approach doesn't account for boundary effects (Figure 3). We expect left (right) disparity to include boundary artifacts on the left (right) due to missing data. Another limitation is that information differs between left and right images (Il ≠ Ir) due to different camera positions. We designed our network with a bias towards left images, but by exploiting symmetry and flipping right images, we assume the flipped distribution is the same (Il ∼ m(Ir)). This allows us to avoid bias and use the same network for both images.

**4. Results**
We evaluated our approach on standard monocular depth estimation benchmarks: KITTI Eigen split [13] and the KITTI single image depth prediction challenge [50]. To demonstrate generalization, we also provide results on the Make3D benchmark [43, 44]. Make3D has only 400 images, making training impossible. Our results were obtained without training on Make3D images, avoiding appearance biases present in KITTI.

**Implementation details.** Similar to previous work [15, 54], we first trained our model on the high-resolution Cityscapes dataset [7], then fine-tuned for 30 epochs on KITTI training images [13]. This maximizes training data and domain-shifts to KITTI. For optimization, we used the Adam optimizer [26] with β1 =

The approach can be applied to stereo pairs, allowing processing of both monocular and stereo views, similar to the human visual system. Future work will explore video and pose estimation. Integrating the post-processing step into network training for end-to-end learning is another technical matter. The approach requires relatively small networks, making it suitable for mobile platforms.

Data augmentation can flip both images and present them separately, but this prevents the network from seeing regions occluded in one view but visible in the other. These limitations are discussed in detail in Section 3.5.

Siamese networks require double the training time, but the net throughput is the same as a single network trained separately on both images, as two training images are processed in each step. Due to weight sharing, memory consumption is unaffected.

3.2. Network Architecture

The network architecture is based on DispNet [41], with modifications similar to those described by Godard et al. [15]. ResNet [20] and VGG [47] architecture variants are used. The network consists of an encoder-decoder pair with skip connections, allowing the network to overcome data loss during down-sampling while benefiting from a deep network.

The network produces multi-scale disparity maps: $d_1^{\text{view}}, \dots, d_4^{\text{view}}$ for the four scales, where 'view' represents either 'l' or 'r' for left/right images of a stereo pair. Lower-resolution disparity predictions are concatenated with the output of previous decoder layers and the corresponding encoder output via skip connections. These concatenated results are then fed into the next higher scale of the network [41]. A bilinear sampler, as used in [23], is employed to warp each disparity map and image onto its counterpart, enabling end-to-end back-propagation and learning.

3.3. Loss Function

A multi-scale loss is defined, related to one proposed by others [15]. The single-scale loss is defined as:
$L_s = \alpha_{im}(L_l^{im} + L_r^{im}) + \alpha_{tv}(L_l^{tv} + L_r^{tv}) + \alpha_{lr}(L_l^{lr} + L_r^{lr})$. (1)

The components of Eq. (1) average prediction errors from both left and right views. This differs from Garg et al. [11], who consider single-view predictions, and Godard et al. [15], who average two predictions that are not equivalent (see also Fig. 2).

The total loss is the sum over the four scales:
$L = \sum_{s=1}^{4} L_s$. (2)

Using only the loss defined for the highest resolution scale resulted in lower accuracy compared to combining multiple scales.

An additional modification to the loss, Eq. (2), compared to previous work [15] is the use of a total variation component instead of their disparity smoothness term, which improves disparity results. The terms in Eq. (1) are detailed below.

Image loss: Zhao et al. [56] showed that combining L1 loss with structural similarity (SSIM) loss [51] yields better results for image restoration. This loss function has been shown to be suitable for depth estimation [15, 54]. The original SSIM with a Gaussian kernel is used, which improves metric localization, unlike previous work [15] that used an average pooling version of SSIM.

SSIM is defined as:
$SSIM(x, y) = \frac{(2\mu_x\mu_y + c_1)(2\sigma_{xy} + c_2)}{(\mu_x^2 + \mu_y^2 + c_1)(\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + c_2)}$, (3)
where $x$ and $y$ are equal-sized windows in the two compared images. $\mu_x, \mu_y$ are the means, and $\sigma_x, \sigma_y$ are the variances of $x$ and $y$, respectively. $\sigma_{xy}$ is the covariance of $x$ and $y$. The image loss is measured as:
$L_l^{im} = \alpha \sum_{i,j} (1 - SSIM(I_l^{ij}, \hat{I}_l^{ij}))^2 + (1 - \alpha) ||I_l^{ij} - \hat{I}_l^{ij}||$. (4)

Left-right consistency loss: Adding a constraint on the left-right consistency of estimated disparity images improves results [15]. Since the task is self-supervised, any geometric property can be used as feedback. Left-right consistency is introduced to the loss as:
$L_l^{lr} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i,j} |d_l^{i,j} - d_r^{i,j} + d_l^{i,j}|$. (5)

Total variation loss: A total variation loss is used as a regularization term to promote smoothness of estimated disparity maps:
$L_{tv}(d) = \sum_{i,j} |d_{i+1,j} - d_{i,j}| + |d_{i,j+1} - d_{i,j}|$. (6)

Weighting this loss with the gradients of the original images, as suggested by [15], was found to emphasize disparity gradients in unnecessary places like windows and walls, which should have the same depth but different disparities in the weighted version.

3.4. Post-processing

Due to occlusions, the left side of the disparity map often lacks important data. A post-processing method based on the one suggested is employed to overcome this.

Our method is self-supervised, unlike other methods. It achieves comparable accuracy to supervised methods and outperforms supervised baselines on this benchmark. Our method is also faster than previous methods.

**Make3D Evaluation**
To test generalization, we evaluated our method on the Make3D dataset. A model trained only on Cityscapes data was used, as it has higher resolution and similar scenes. Central crops of images were taken to match Cityscapes aspect ratio.

The Make3D test set has 134 single-view RGB and depth image pairs. We use the C1 error measures, ignoring pixels with depth > 70 meters:
*   **Squared relative error (Sq Rel):** $\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i} \frac{(d_{gt}^i - d_p^i)^2}{d_{gt}^i}$
*   **Absolute relative error (Abs Rel):** $\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i} \frac{|d_{gt}^i - d_p^i|}{d_{gt}^i}$
*   **Root-mean squared error (RMSE):** $\sqrt{\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i} (d_{gt}^i - d_p^i)^2}$
*   **log10 error:** $\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i} |\log_{10}(d_{gt}^i) - \log_{10}(d_p^i)|$

In these measures, $d_{gt}^i$ is ground truth depth and $d_p^i$ is predicted depth. Results are reported in Table 3 with qualitative results in Figure 6.

Our method performs well on a different domain and scene, outperforming other self-supervised methods and achieving comparable results to some supervised methods.

**5. Conclusions**
We propose a self-supervised method for monocular depth estimation that trains on stereo image pairs but is applied to single images at test time. It requires no depth information or supervisory data during training. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results by effectively utilizing stereo input, specifically by symmetrically handling left and right images through mirroring the right image.

Technical contributions include a Siamese network with weight sharing, reducing model size by half and using only one branch at runtime for single-view input. We also defined a loss function that better represents our model's design.

An extension is applying our method to stereo settings, as there's nothing prohibiting it. This ability to process monocular and stereo views is similar to the human visual system.

Disparity map is used to inverse warp the right image and measure reconstruction loss. This approach is related to Godard et al. [15] but uses a Siamese network for better training data utilization. A detailed discussion of differences is in Sec. 3.5.

The method is also related to Kuznietsov et al. [30] who also use two networks. Differences include weight sharing in our two networks, reducing model size and enabling monocular test-time application. Kuznietsov et al. [30] use depth information as a semi-supervisory signal, whereas our method is completely self-supervised, using no depth information or other labels, yet achieving comparable results.

Some methods incorporate both depth and pose estimation [54, 57]. This work focuses solely on depth estimation and outperforms recent methods that combine both. Other self-supervised methods for depth extraction from monocular video [29, 38, 53] assume sequential data, which is not assumed here.

Siamese networks, first suggested by Bromley et al. [5], are used for tasks like metric learning [6] and recognition [27]. Some recent applications of Siamese networks to depth estimation [25, 37] were supervised and assumed stereo vision during training and testing.

**3. Our Approach**

Training uses pairs of rectified RGB images acquired in a controlled setup with a known camera baseline, enabling conversion from disparities to depth. This assumption of rectified stereo pairs is considered reasonable for large-scale datasets.

The aim is to learn mappings $\hat{d}_l = f(I_l)$ and $\hat{d}_r = f'(I_r)$, where $f()$ and $f'()$ are distinct functions. Inferring left and right disparity maps are different problems due to the relative camera positions. Training separate networks would prevent weight sharing and exploitation of problem symmetry.

An alternative method utilizes both images equivalently and symmetrically.

**3.1. Siamese Architecture with Mirroring**

To achieve equivalent and symmetric use of training data, the symmetry of the problem is exploited. Mirroring (horizontal flipping) of the right image $I_r$ creates $m(I_r)$, which can be treated as a left image. The function $f()$ can be applied to $m(I_r)$, and another mirroring is needed to obtain the right disparity. Thus, $f'(·) = m(f(m(·)))$. This architectural change leverages symmetry for training and inference.

Figure 2 illustrates the method's block diagram, comparing it to previous approaches. Garg et al. [11] and Godard et al. [15] use a single input image during training, with Garg et al. [11] using the right image solely as a supervisory signal. Our Siamese architecture takes both images simultaneously as input during training, treating both views equally. This saves memory and shares information between networks.

Previous methods [11, 15] under-utilize the right view, not feeding it as input to the encoder-decoder architecture. The right image is used only as a reference signal for the reconstructed image $\hat{I}_l(d_r) = \hat{I}_r$. Data augmentation can be used to flip both images and present them separately.

Figure 2 depicts system architectures:
*   **Left:** Garg et al. [11] uses the right image only as a supervisory signal.
*   **Center:** Godard et al. [15] favors the left image over the right image. Both use a single image as input during training.
*   **Right:** Our Siamese network trains on pairs of images, treating them equally via flipping the right image. The loss combines errors from two separate predictions, equally treating both views and their predictions. At test time, only the dashed-line area is used; other blocks are for training.

**Learn Stereo, Infer Mono: Siamese Networks for Self-Supervised, Monocular, Depth Estimation**

**Authors:** Matan Goldman¹, Tal Hassner²†, Shai Avidan¹
**Affiliations:** ¹Tel Aviv University, Israel, ²The Open University of Israel, Israel

**Abstract:**
This paper proposes a novel self-supervised approach for monocular depth estimation. Unlike existing methods that under-utilize stereo data during training, this approach uses both left and right images equally. At test time, it can infer depth from a single input image. The proposed Siamese network architecture consists of two twin networks, each predicting a disparity map from a single image. At test time, only one network is used for depth inference. This method achieves state-of-the-art results on the KITTI Eigen split benchmark and is the highest scoring self-supervised method on the new KITTI single view benchmark. Generalization to new datasets is demonstrated on the Make3D benchmark.

**1. Introduction:**
Single-view depth estimation is a crucial problem in computer vision with applications in autonomous driving, robotics, computational photography, and scene understanding. While humans can estimate depth from a single view using cues like motion parallax and perspective, it is an ill-posed problem.

Classical computer vision methods and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been applied to monocular depth estimation, but these are supervised and require extensive ground truth data, which is difficult to obtain.

Self-supervised approaches leverage intrinsic geometric properties to train monocular systems. These methods typically use both left and right images during training, but the second image serves only as a reference. Predicting both left and right disparity maps improves accuracy, but estimating the right disparity from the left image can lead to errors due to occlusions. This work fully utilizes both images for learning single-image disparity estimation.

This paper proposes a self-supervised approach that exploits the symmetry of the disparity problem for effective deep models. A key issue with existing methods is training a single network to predict both left and right disparity maps from one image, which is problematic due to occlusions. This approach addresses this by flipping images around the vertical axis for training. The network learns to predict a left disparity map, and right disparity maps are obtained by mirroring the right image, estimating disparity, and mirroring the result back.

A deep Siamese network predicts disparity maps from both the left image and the flipped right image. By mirroring the right image, predicting both left and right disparity maps becomes equivalent, allowing for training both Siamese networks with shared weights. This shared weighting reduces computational cost and enables single-image operation at test time.

paper1.title: Self-Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation: Solving the Dynamic Object Problem by Semantic Guidance
paper1.abstract:
Self-supervised monocular depth estimation presents a powerful method to obtain 3D scene information from single camera images, which is trainable on arbitrary image sequences without requiring depth labels, e.g., from a LiDAR sensor. 
                        In this work we present a new self-supervised semantically-guided depth estimation (SGDepth) method to deal with moving dynamic-class (DC) objects, such as moving cars and pedestrians, which violate the static-world assumptions typically made during training of such models. 
                        Specifically, we propose (i) mutually beneficial cross-domain training of (supervised) semantic segmentation and self-supervised depth estimation with task-specific network heads, (ii) a semantic masking scheme providing guidance to prevent moving DC objects from contaminating the photometric loss, and (iii) a detection method for frames with non-moving DC objects, from which the depth of DC objects can be learned. 
                        We demonstrate the performance of our method on several benchmarks, in particular on the Eigen split, where we exceed all baselines without test-time refinement.

The final loss is a combination of photometric losses (9) and (3), smoothness loss (4), and cross-entropy loss (5):
$J^{t}_{total} = J^{t}_{ce} + \beta J^{t}_{sm} + \begin{cases} J^{t}_{phm}, & \Lambda^t < \theta_\Lambda \\ J^{t}_{ph}, & \text{else} \end{cases}$

$J^{t}_{ph}$, $J^{t}_{phm}$, and $J^{t}_{sm}$ are computed only on training images for depth estimation. $J^{t}_{ce}$ is computed only in the segmentation domain. Segmentation and depth losses are not weighted against each other in this equation; weighting occurs during the backward pass guided by (6).

**Experimental Setup**

**Network Topology:** The topology is based on an encoder-decoder architecture with skip connections. An ImageNet pretrained ResNet18 encoder is used for comparability with existing work. The depth head has a sigmoid output $\sigma_{t,i}$, converted to a depth map by $\frac{1}{a\sigma_{t,i}+b}$, with $a$ and $b$ constraining depth values to the range [0.1, 100]. The segmentation decoder uses the same architecture as the depth decoder, with the last layer having $S$ feature maps whose elements are converted to class probabilities by a softmax function. The pose network's architecture is the same as in [20].

**Training Aspects:** For depth estimation training, all images are resized to 640×192 (128×416 and 384×1280 are also evaluated). For semantic segmentation, images are randomly cropped to the same resolution. Zero-mean normalization is applied to RGB images for the ResNet encoder. Input images are augmented with horizontal flipping, random brightness (±0.2), contrast (±0.2), saturation (±0.2), and hue (±0.1). Photometric losses (3, 9) are calculated on images without color augmentations. Loss is computed on four scales, similar to [20].

Gradient scaling from (6) is applied at all connections between encoder and decoder with an optimal scale factor of $\lambda = 0.1$. The fraction $\epsilon$ of images for which photometric loss is not masked according to (9) is set to 0 after 30 epochs and increases linearly to only use loss (3) in the last epoch. This encourages learning from frames with non-moving DC objects after they are removed from the loss. DC object classes $S_{DC}$ include all human and vehicle categories [9].

Models are trained for 40 epochs using the Adam optimizer with batch sizes of 12 for single-task and 6 for multi-task models. Batches from task-specific datasets are concatenated, passed through the encoder, then disconnected for respective decoders. The learning rate is set to $10^{-4}$ and reduced to $10^{-5}$ after 30 epochs. Training only depth estimation with the [20] architecture is termed "SGDepth only depth". Joint training of semantic segmentation and depth estimation is termed "SGDepth full".

**Datasets:** One dataset is used for semantic segmentation training, and another for self-supervised depth estimation training. Cityscapes dataset [9] is used for semantic segmentation. Different subsets of the KITTI dataset [17] are used for depth estimation training. Depth estimation results are compared by training and evaluating on the Eigen split [12] of KITTI, removing static scenes from the training subset as in [71]. The single image depth prediction Benchmark split from KITTI [56] is also used for training and evaluation. For joint depth and segmentation prediction, the KITTI split defined by [18] is used, with its test set being the official training set of KITTI Stereo 2015 dataset [40]. Training image counts may deviate slightly from original definitions due to the need for preceding and succeeding images for depth estimation training. Data subset sizes are in Table 4.

**Evaluation Metrics:** Depth estimation is evaluated using four error metrics: absolute relative error (Abs Rel), squared relative error (Sq Rel), root mean squared error (RMSE), and logarithmic root mean squared error (RMSE log), as defined in [12] and computed as in [38, 71].

Evaluation Metrics:

Depth Map Evaluation:
  - Evaluated using sparse ground truth (pixels with LiDAR measurement).
  - Median scaling applied to predicted depth maps before evaluation to compensate for global scale ambiguity.
  - Exception 1: On Eigen test split, a crop defined by [12] is applied.
  - Exception 2: On Benchmark test split, median scaling is not applied as depth labels are not freely available. Instead, the median of image-wise scale factors from the validation set is used as a global scale factor for test set predictions.
  - Metrics (12)-(21) are averaged over the respective test subset.

Depth Error Metrics (Eigen and KITTI splits):
  - Abs Rel:  $$ \frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i \in I} \frac{|d_i - \hat{d}_i|}{d_i} $$
  - Sq Rel:  $$ \frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i \in I} \frac{(d_i - \hat{d}_i)^2}{d_i} $$
  - RMSE:  $$ \sqrt{\frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i \in I} (d_i - \hat{d}_i)^2} $$
  - RMSE log:  $$ \sqrt{\frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i \in I} (\log d_i - \log \hat{d}_i)^2} $$
  - $I$: set of all pixels, $H$: height, $W$: width.

Depth Accuracy Metrics:
  - δ < 1.25:  $$ \frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i \in I} \max(\frac{d_i}{\hat{d}_i}, \frac{\hat{d}_i}{d_i}) < 1.25 $$
  - δ < 1.25²:  $$ \frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i \in I} \max(\frac{d_i}{\hat{d}_i}, \frac{\hat{d}_i}{d_i}) < 1.25^2 $$
  - δ < 1.25³:  $$ \frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i \in I} \max(\frac{d_i}{\hat{d}_i}, \frac{\hat{d}_i}{d_i}) < 1.25^3 $$
  - [·]: Iverson bracket (1 if true, 0 if false).

Additional Metrics (Benchmark split):
  - SILog:  $$ \frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i \in I} (\log d_i - \log \hat{d}_i)^2 - \left(\frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i \in I} (\log d_i - \log \hat{d}_i)\right)^2 $$
  - iRMSE:  $$ \sqrt{\frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i \in I} (\frac{1}{d_i} - \frac{1}{\hat{d}_i})^2} $$

Semantic Segmentation Evaluation:
  - Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU):  $$ mIoU = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s \in S} \frac{TP_s}{TP_s + FP_s + FN_s} $$
  - $S$: set of all classes in Cityscapes.
  - $TP_s$: true positive predictions for class $s$.
  - $FP_s$: false positive predictions for class $s$.
  - $FN_s$: false negative predictions for class $s$.
  - Depth metrics are computed image-wise and then averaged.
  - For mIoU, TP, FP, and FN are summed over all images in the test set before calculating mIoU.

Two decoder heads are used, one for depth and one for segmentation. The segmentation decoder is trained in a source domain supervised by $y_{t,s}$ using (5). The depth decoder is trained in a target domain under self-supervision according to (3) and (4). For mini-batches containing data from both domains, gradients from separate decoders propagate into the shared encoder. Instead of scaling loss functions, gradients are scaled upon reaching the encoder. Let $g_{depth}$ and $g_{seg}$ be gradients from the two decoders. The total gradient $g_{total}$ propagated to the encoder is:
$$g_{total} = (1 − \lambda) g_{depth} + \lambda g_{seg}$$ (6)

Moving DC objects can contaminate the photometric error. This occurs when projected views are invalid, leading to unfavorable contributions to the photometric loss. To address this, regions with potentially moving DC objects are masked by calculating a DC object mask $\mu_t$ (8) from segmentation masks.

Moving DC objects contaminate the photometric error. To mask out DC objects in the current frame $x_t$ and wrongfully projected DC objects in projected frames $x'_{t→t}$, projected semantic masks $m'_{t→t}$ are calculated. Nearest-neighbor sampling is applied, replacing bilinear sampling for $x'_{t→t,i}$ with the value of the closest pixel in $m'_{t}$. The projected semantic mask is calculated as:
$$m'_{t→t} = \text{near}(m'_{t}, u_{t→t'}, u'_{t})$$ (7)

Defining DC object classes $S_{DC} \subset S$, the DC object mask $\mu_t \in \{0, 1\}^{H \times W}$ is defined by its pixel elements:
$$\mu_{t,i} = \begin{cases} 1, & m_{t,i} \notin S_{DC} \land m'_{t→t,i} \notin S_{DC} \text{ for all } t' \in T' \\ 0, & \text{else} \end{cases}$$ (8)
The mask has 0 at pixels belonging to a DC object in any of the three frames, and 1 otherwise. Using the DC object mask $\mu_t$, a semantically-masked photometric loss adapting (3) is defined:
$$J_{phm}^t = \mu_t \odot \min_{t' \in T'} \left( \frac{\alpha}{2}(1 - \text{SSIM}(x_t, x'_{t→t})) + (1 - \alpha)|x_t - x'_{t→t}| \right)$$ (9)
This loss only considers non-DC pixels. The mask from auto-masking [20,23,24] is also considered but omitted in (3) and (9) for simplicity.

**Self-Supervised Depth Estimation With Semantic Guidance**

**Detecting Non-Moving DC Objects:** Instead of excluding DC objects completely, they are learned from only when not in motion. A measure is needed to determine if a DC object is in motion. If a DC object has been observed in motion, the warped semantic mask in the target image $m'_{t→t}$ has low consistency with the semantic mask $m_t$ in the target image. The intersection over union for dynamic object classes between $m'_{t→t}$ and $m_t$ is measured by:
$$\Lambda_{t,t'} = \frac{\sum_{i \in I} \kappa_{t,t',i}}{\sum_{i \in I} \nu_{t,t',i}}, \text{with}$$
$$\kappa_{t,t',i} = \begin{cases} 1, & m_{t,i} \in S_{DC} \land m'_{t→t,i} \in S_{DC} \\ 0, & \text{else} \end{cases}$$
$$\nu_{t,t',i} = \begin{cases} 1, & m_{t,i} \in S_{DC} \lor m'_{t→t,i} \in S_{DC} \\ 0, & \text{else} \end{cases}$$ (10)
The indicator $\Lambda_{t,t'} \in [0, 1]$ signals perfect alignment and no moving DC objects if it equals 1, and a high share of moving DC objects if it equals 0. If two frames at times $t' \in T' = \{t−1, t+1\}$ are considered, the mean value $\Lambda_t$ of all $\Lambda_{t,t'}$ is taken. A threshold $\theta_\Lambda \in [0, 1]$ is defined, above which an image is considered static.

**Learning from Non-Moving DC Objects:** Given a measure indicating whether an image is static or dynamic after each epoch, $\Lambda_t$ is calculated for each image. The threshold $\theta_\Lambda$ is chosen such that a fraction $\epsilon \in [0, 1]$ of images are trained without the semantically-masked photometric loss. The final loss is a combination of the photometric losses (9) and (3), the smoothness loss (4), and the cross-entropy loss (5):
$$J_{total}^t = J_{ce}^t + \beta J_{sm}^t + \begin{cases} J_{phm}^t, & \Lambda_t < \theta_\Lambda \\ J_{ph}^t, & \text{else} \end{cases}$$ (11)
Where $J_{ph}^t, J_{phm}^t,$ and $J_{sm}^t$ are components of the total loss.

5.2 Ablation Studies
Table 3 shows results on the Kitti split, starting from baselines and adding contributions to the full method. Training depth and segmentation together in a multi-task fashion improves depth estimation. Multi-task prediction is during training; evaluation can be done separately. Gradient scaling improves depth and particularly semantic segmentation. Masking out DC objects initially decreases performance as the network has no objective for their depth. Introducing a threshold θΛ learns DC object depth from a fraction ϵ of images with non-moving DC objects. Scheduling ϵ starts with best samples and then includes more "noisy" samples. The final SGDepth model outperforms Liu et al. [35] mono approach in 6 out of 7 measures and Chen et al. [7] stereo approach in 5 out of 7 measures.

**Benefits of Multi-Task Training**

We compare our SGDepth method with baselines trained solely for depth estimation or semantic segmentation, using the KITTI splits defined in [18].

Joint training benefits depth estimation, as shown in Figure 8, which illustrates the semantic guidance's impact on individual images.
Semantic segmentation maps also improve compared to a baseline trained only on semantic segmentation (SGDepth only seg.) on the Cityscapes dataset.
This improvement on KITTI is likely because self-supervised depth estimation extracts features suitable for KITTI, bridging the domain shift from Cityscapes. Qualitative results support this claim.

paper2.title: 3D Packing for Self-Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation
paper2.abstract:
Although cameras are ubiquitous, robotic platforms typically rely on active sensors like LiDAR for direct 3D perception. In this work, we propose a novel self-supervised
                        monocular depth estimation method combining geometry
                        with a new deep network, PackNet, learned only from unlabeled monocular videos. Our architecture leverages novel
                        symmetrical packing and unpacking blocks to jointly learn
                        to compress and decompress detail-preserving representations using 3D convolutions. Although self-supervised, our
                        method outperforms other self, semi, and fully supervised
                        methods on the KITTI benchmark. The 3D inductive bias in
                        PackNet enables it to scale with input resolution and number of parameters without overfitting, generalizing better on
                        out-of-domain data such as the NuScenes dataset. Furthermore, it does not require large-scale supervised pretraining
                        on ImageNet and can run in real-time. Finally, we release
                        DDAD (Dense Depth for Automated Driving), a new urban
                        driving dataset with more challenging and accurate depth
                        evaluation, thanks to longer-range and denser ground-truth
                        depth generated from high-density LiDARs mounted on a
                        fleet of self-driving cars operating world-wide.

To study performance improvements of PackNet, an ablative analysis of architectural components is performed (Table 4). The base architecture, without packing and unpacking blocks, provides a strong baseline for monocular depth estimation. Introducing packing and unpacking boosts performance, particularly with more 3D convolutional filters, achieving state-of-the-art results with the architecture in Table 1.

ResNet architectures benefit from ImageNet pretraining due to their classification origins. However, pretrained ResNet architectures show performance degradation with longer training due to catastrophic forgetting and overfitting. PackNet achieves state-of-the-art results from random initialization and can be further improved by self-supervised pretraining on other datasets, effectively utilizing unlabeled information.

**5.7. Generalization Capability**

PackNet's generalization performance is investigated to confirm it learns transferable features rather than memorizing training data. Models trained on a combination of CityScapes and KITTI (CS+K) are evaluated on the NuScenes dataset [5] without fine-tuning. Table 5 shows PackNet generalizes better across diverse vehicles and countries (Germany for CS+K, USA + Singapore for NuScenes), outperforming standard architectures in all metrics without large-scale ImageNet pretraining.

**6. Conclusion**

PackNet, a novel convolutional network architecture for self-supervised monocular depth estimation, leverages symmetrical, detail-preserving packing and unpacking blocks to compress and decompress high-resolution visual information for fine-grained predictions. Trained solely on unlabeled monocular videos, PackNet surpasses existing self- and semi-supervised methods and is competitive with fully-supervised methods, operating in real-time. It generalizes better to different datasets and unseen environments without ImageNet pretraining, especially for longer depth ranges (up to 200m on DDAD dataset). By using weak velocity information during training, PackNet becomes scale-aware, producing metrically accurate depth maps from a single image.

$L(I_t, \hat{I}_t) = L_p(I_t, I_S) \odot M_p \odot M_t + \lambda_1 L_s(\hat{D}_t)$
$M_t$ is a binary mask that avoids computing the photometric loss on pixels without a valid mapping.
$\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication.
$\lambda_1$ enforces weighted depth regularization.
The overall loss in Equation 1 is averaged per-pixel, pyramid-scale, and image batch during training.

Appearance Matching Loss:
The pixel-level similarity between the target image $I_t$ and the synthesized target image $\hat{I}_t$ is estimated using Structural Similarity (SSIM) and an L1 pixel-wise loss.
$L_p(I_t, \hat{I}_t) = \alpha \frac{1 - SSIM(I_t, \hat{I}_t)}{2} + (1 - \alpha) \|I_t - \hat{I}_t\|$
To mitigate parallax errors, the minimum photometric loss per pixel for each source image in the context $I_S$ is calculated:
$L_p(I_t, I_S) = \min_{I_S} L_p(I_t, \hat{I}_t)$
This assumes the same pixel is not occluded or out-of-bounds in all context images.
Static pixels are masked out by removing those where the warped photometric loss $L_p(I_t, \hat{I}_t)$ is higher than their unwarped photometric loss $L_p(I_t, I_s)$, calculated using the original source image without view synthesis.
$M_p = \min_{I_S} L_p(I_t, I_s) > \min_{I_S} L_p(I_t, \hat{I}_t)$

Depth Smoothness Loss:
An edge-aware term is incorporated to regularize depth in texture-less regions.
$L_s(\hat{D}_t) = |\delta_x \hat{D}_t| e^{-|\delta_x I_t|} + |\delta_y \hat{D}_t| e^{-|\delta_y I_t|}$
The loss is weighted for each pyramid level and decays by a factor of 2 on down-sampling, starting with a weight of 1 for the 0th pyramid level.

Figure 2: PackNet-SfM: Scale-aware self-supervised monocular structure-from-motion architecture. PackNet is a novel depth network, optionally including weak velocity supervision for scale-aware depth and pose.

Scale-Aware SfM:
Monocular depth and ego-motion estimators predict scale-ambiguous values. The scene depth and camera ego-motion are estimated up to an unknown scale factor. The photometric loss is agnostic to metric depth. Existing self-supervised monocular approaches [6, 16, 18, 34] also suffer from this limitation and use LiDAR measurements at test-time.

Velocity Supervision Loss:
Instantaneous velocity measurements are incorporated into the self-supervised objective for metrically accurate and scale-aware monocular depth estimation.
An additional loss $L_v$ is imposed between the magnitude of the pose-translation component $\hat{t}$ and the measured instantaneous velocity $v$ multiplied by the time difference $\Delta T_{t \to s}$:
$L_v(\hat{t}_{t \to s}, v) = \|\hat{t}_{t \to s}\| - |v|\Delta T_{t \to s}$
The final scale-aware self-supervised objective loss $L_{scale}$ is:
$L_{scale}(I_t, \hat{I}_t, v) = L(I_t, \hat{I}_t) + \lambda_2 L_v(\hat{t}_{t \to s}, v)$
$\lambda_2$ balances the loss terms. This velocity loss allows the pose network to make metrically accurate predictions, leading the depth network to also learn metrically accurate estimates.

topic: Depth perception tasks focus on estimating the distance of objects from a single image or sequence, which is crucial for applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and 3D scene understanding. What is the better method for depth perception tasks: SGDepth or MultiDepth?

paper1.title: Self-Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation: Solving the Dynamic Object Problem by Semantic Guidance
paper1.abstract:
Self-supervised monocular depth estimation presents a powerful method to obtain 3D scene information from single camera images, which is trainable on arbitrary image sequences without requiring depth labels, e.g., from a LiDAR sensor. 
                        In this work we present a new self-supervised semantically-guided depth estimation (SGDepth) method to deal with moving dynamic-class (DC) objects, such as moving cars and pedestrians, which violate the static-world assumptions typically made during training of such models. 
                        Specifically, we propose (i) mutually beneficial cross-domain training of (supervised) semantic segmentation and self-supervised depth estimation with task-specific network heads, (ii) a semantic masking scheme providing guidance to prevent moving DC objects from contaminating the photometric loss, and (iii) a detection method for frames with non-moving DC objects, from which the depth of DC objects can be learned. 
                        We demonstrate the performance of our method on several benchmarks, in particular on the Eigen split, where we exceed all baselines without test-time refinement.
methodology:
The final loss is a combination of photometric losses (9) and (3), smoothness loss (4), and cross-entropy loss (5):
$J^{t}_{total} = J^{t}_{ce} + \beta J^{t}_{sm} + \begin{cases} J^{t}_{phm}, & \Lambda^t < \theta_\Lambda \\ J^{t}_{ph}, & \text{else} \end{cases}$

$J^{t}_{ph}$, $J^{t}_{phm}$, and $J^{t}_{sm}$ are computed only on training images for depth estimation. $J^{t}_{ce}$ is computed only in the segmentation domain. Segmentation and depth losses are not weighted against each other in this equation; weighting occurs during the backward pass guided by (6).

**Experimental Setup**

**Network Topology:** The topology is based on an encoder-decoder architecture with skip connections. An ImageNet pretrained ResNet18 encoder is used for comparability with existing work. The depth head has a sigmoid output $\sigma_{t,i}$, converted to a depth map by $\frac{1}{a\sigma_{t,i}+b}$, with $a$ and $b$ constraining depth values to the range [0.1, 100]. The segmentation decoder uses the same architecture as the depth decoder, with the last layer having $S$ feature maps whose elements are converted to class probabilities by a softmax function. The pose network's architecture is the same as in [20].

**Training Aspects:** For depth estimation training, all images are resized to 640×192 (128×416 and 384×1280 are also evaluated). For semantic segmentation, images are randomly cropped to the same resolution. Zero-mean normalization is applied to RGB images for the ResNet encoder. Input images are augmented with horizontal flipping, random brightness (±0.2), contrast (±0.2), saturation (±0.2), and hue (±0.1). Photometric losses (3, 9) are calculated on images without color augmentations. Loss is computed on four scales, similar to [20].

Gradient scaling from (6) is applied at all connections between encoder and decoder with an optimal scale factor of $\lambda = 0.1$. The fraction $\epsilon$ of images for which photometric loss is not masked according to (9) is set to 0 after 30 epochs and increases linearly to only use loss (3) in the last epoch. This encourages learning from frames with non-moving DC objects after they are removed from the loss. DC object classes $S_{DC}$ include all human and vehicle categories [9].

Models are trained for 40 epochs using the Adam optimizer with batch sizes of 12 for single-task and 6 for multi-task models. Batches from task-specific datasets are concatenated, passed through the encoder, then disconnected for respective decoders. The learning rate is set to $10^{-4}$ and reduced to $10^{-5}$ after 30 epochs. Training only depth estimation with the [20] architecture is termed "SGDepth only depth". Joint training of semantic segmentation and depth estimation is termed "SGDepth full".

**Datasets:** One dataset is used for semantic segmentation training, and another for self-supervised depth estimation training. Cityscapes dataset [9] is used for semantic segmentation. Different subsets of the KITTI dataset [17] are used for depth estimation training. Depth estimation results are compared by training and evaluating on the Eigen split [12] of KITTI, removing static scenes from the training subset as in [71]. The single image depth prediction Benchmark split from KITTI [56] is also used for training and evaluation. For joint depth and segmentation prediction, the KITTI split defined by [18] is used, with its test set being the official training set of KITTI Stereo 2015 dataset [40]. Training image counts may deviate slightly from original definitions due to the need for preceding and succeeding images for depth estimation training. Data subset sizes are in Table 4.

**Evaluation Metrics:** Depth estimation is evaluated using four error metrics: absolute relative error (Abs Rel), squared relative error (Sq Rel), root mean squared error (RMSE), and logarithmic root mean squared error (RMSE log), as defined in [12] and computed as in [38, 71].

  - Test: 697
