Visual embeddings ($v_i$) combine visual features from the decoder's pixel-decoding part ($D_{vis-lang}$) and features obtained via mask pooling from the encoder ($E_{vision, vis-lang}$). Instead of summing these, FC-CLIP constructs a geometric ensemble of logits by computing cosine similarity between individual visual features and ID class textual embeddings. These are termed in-vocabulary ($c_{i, \text{in}}$) and out-of-vocabulary ($c_{i, \text{out}}$) classifiers.

Final mask classification scores are given by:
$$
c_i(j) =
\begin{cases}
(c_{i, \text{in}}(j))^{(1-\alpha)} \cdot (c_{i, \text{out}}(j))^\alpha, & \text{if } j \in K \\
(c_{i, \text{in}}(j))^{(1-\beta)} \cdot (c_{i, \text{out}}(j))^\beta, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$
where $c_i(j)$ is the $j$-th element of $c_i$, $i=1, \dots, N$ (number of object queries), and $\alpha, \beta \in [0, 1]$ balance predictions between in- and out-of-vocabulary classifiers for ID and OOD prompting classes.

Experiments for VL4AD without OOD prompting varied $\alpha$ from 0.0 to 1.0. $\alpha=0.0$ uses only decoder-processed visual features, while $\alpha=1.0$ relies solely on raw features from the frozen vision encoder for CityScapes classes.

paper2.title: A Baseline for Detecting Misclassified and Out-of-Distribution Examples in Neural Networks
paper2.abstract:
We consider the two related problems of detecting if an example is misclassified or
                        out-of-distribution. We present a simple baseline that utilizes probabilities from
                        softmax distributions. Correctly classified examples tend to have greater maximum softmax probabilities than erroneously classified and out-of-distribution examples, allowing for their detection. We assess performance by defining several tasks in computer vision, natural language processing, and automatic speech
                        recognition, showing the effectiveness of this baseline across all. We then show
                        the baseline can sometimes be surpassed, demonstrating the room for future research on these underexplored detection tasks.

Mixing TIMIT audio with realistic noises from the Aurora-2 dataset (Hirsch & Pearce, 2000) with TIMIT audio volume at 100% and noise volume at 30% yields a mean SNR of approximately 5. Speakers remain audible but confuse the phone recognizer as prediction edit distance more than doubles. For further out-of-distribution examples, test examples from the THCHS-30 dataset (Wang & Zhang, 2015), a Chinese speech corpus, are used. Table 9 presents the results. When performing detection, softmax probabilities are computed while ignoring the blank symbol's logit. Without the blank symbol, softmax prediction probabilities allow differentiation between normal and abnormal distributions, enabling out-of-distribution detection.

4. ABNORMALITY DETECTION WITH AUXILIARY DECODERS

Softmax prediction probabilities enable abnormality detection. Other information may be more useful. Exploiting learned internal representations of neural networks, a normal classifier is trained with an appended auxiliary decoder that reconstructs the input (Figure 1). Auxiliary decoders can improve classification performance (Zhang et al., 2016). The decoder and scorer are trained jointly on in-distribution examples. Subsequently, blue layers in Figure 1 are frozen. Red layers are trained on clean and noised training examples. The sigmoid output of the red layers scores input normality. Noised examples are classified as abnormal, clean examples as normal, and the sigmoid is trained to output the input's class. This process results in a normal classifier, an auxiliary decoder, and an abnormality module. The gains from the abnormality module suggest research avenues for outperforming the baseline.

4.1. TIMIT

The abnormality module is tested on the TIMIT task with a different architecture, demonstrating how auxiliary components can significantly improve detection. The system is a three-layer, 1024-neuron wide classifier with an auxiliary decoder and abnormality module. This network takes 11 frames as input and predicts the phone of the center frame, with 26 features per frame. Weights are initialized according to (Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016c). The network trains for 20 epochs, and the abnormality module trains for two. The abnormality module is trained on clean examples and, as negative examples, TIMIT examples distorted with white noise, brown noise (spectral density proportional to 1/f²), or pink noise (spectral density proportional to 1/f) at various volumes.

Unlike previous experiments, THCHS-30 training examples are used instead of test set examples, as fully connected networks can evaluate the entire training set quickly. Fully connected deep neural networks are noise robust (Seltzer et al., 2013), yet the abnormality module can still detect out-of-distribution examples. This is remarkable given the network's frame classification error of 29.69% on the entire test (not core) dataset and an average classification error of 30.43% for distorted examples. This contrasts with bidirectional LSTMs, which showed a more pronounced performance decline. Softmax statistics alone did not provide useful out-of-distribution detection due to the slight classification degradation. In contrast, the abnormality module provided scores that allowed detection of different-but-similar examples, facilitating the determination of out-of-distribution status even when it does not significantly confuse the network.

4.2 MNIST
An MNIST classifier with three layers of width 256 is trained. An auxiliary decoder and abnormality module are used instead of relying solely on softmax statistics. For abnormal examples, training images are blurred, rotated, or have Gaussian noise added. Table 11 shows gains from the abnormality module, with consistent out-of-sample detection improvement compared to softmax prediction probabilities. The abnormality module further improves detection even for highly dissimilar examples.

8 Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2017

5 DISCUSSION AND FUTURE WORK
The abnormality module demonstrates that in some cases, representations of a network can outperform the baseline, suggesting various research directions. Promising future avenues include utilizing intra-class variance: if an example's distance to others of the same predicted class is abnormally high, it may be out-of-distribution (Giryes et al., 2015). Another approach is feeding a vector summarizing a layer’s activations into an RNN, with one vector per layer. The RNN could then identify abnormal activation patterns for out-of-distribution examples. Detections could also be made more fine-grained, distinguishing between known-unknown and unknown-unknown out-of-distribution examples. A different approach could involve outputting the probability of a correct detection, rather than just detecting correct classifications. These are potential ideas for improving error and out-of-distribution detection.

New detection methods should be tested on a variety of tasks and architectures. Recommended datasets include MNIST, CIFAR, IMDB, and tweets, as vision-only demonstrations may not transfer well to other architectures and datasets. Reporting AUPR and AUROC values is important, as is the underlying classifier's accuracy. An always-wrong classifier achieves maximum AUPR for error detection if error is the positive class. Future research need not use exact values from this paper for comparisons; instead, choosing a variety of datasets and architectures and comparing detection methods with a detector based on softmax prediction probabilities from classifiers is recommended for surpassing the baseline on this underexplored challenge.

6 CONCLUSION
A softmax prediction probability baseline for error and out-of-distribution detection across several architectures and numerous datasets was demonstrated. The abnormality module was then presented, providing superior scores for discriminating between normal and abnormal examples on tested cases. The abnormality module shows that the baseline can be surpassed in some cases, indicating room for future research. Researchers are encouraged to investigate architectures that make predictions considering abnormality estimates and to pursue more reliable detection methods.

Estimating model confidence is feasible using simple statistics derived from softmax distributions. These statistics effectively detect misclassified examples or those from different distributions across computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition tasks, establishing a strong baseline for error and out-of-distribution detection.

**Problem Formulation and Evaluation**

This paper addresses two problems:
1.  **Error and Success Prediction:** Predicting whether a trained classifier will err on or correctly classify a given test example.
2.  **In- and Out-of-Distribution Detection:** Predicting whether a test example originates from the same distribution as the training data or a different one.

A simple baseline is presented for these problems. Evaluation uses two metrics.

Comparing detectors is challenging due to potential class imbalance. A model might always predict the majority class, achieving high accuracy misleadingly. Threshold selection is necessary to balance false negatives (fn) and false positives (fp).

**Evaluation Metrics**

*   **Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC):** A threshold-independent metric. The ROC curve plots true positive rate (tpr = tp/(tp + fn)) against false positive rate (fpr = fp/(fp + tn)). AUROC represents the probability that a positive example has a higher detector score than a negative example. A random detector yields 50% AUROC, a perfect classifier 100%.

*   **Area Under the Precision-Recall curve (AUPR):** This metric is sometimes considered more informative than AUROC, especially when class base rates differ significantly. AUPR adjusts for differing positive and negative base rates. The PR curve plots precision (tp/(tp+fp)) against recall (tp/(tp + fn)). A baseline detector has an AUPR approximately equal to the precision; a perfect classifier has 100% AUPR. Since the base rate of the positive class influences AUPR, we specify which class is positive. AUPRs are reported with success/normal classes as positive, and then with error/abnormal classes as positive (by multiplying scores by -1). Treating error/abnormal classes as positive does not alter AUROC because P(S > E) = P(-E > -S).

Experiments begin in Section 3 with a baseline using the maximum probability from the softmax distribution. Section 4 describes a method using an auxiliary model component trained for input reconstruction.

**Softmax Prediction Probability as a Baseline**

This baseline uses the maximum probability from a softmax distribution to detect misclassified or out-of-distribution examples. For each example, the maximum softmax probability of the predicted class is computed. Areas under the PR and ROC curves are then derived from correctly and incorrectly classified test set examples to summarize the performance of a binary classifier using these maximum probabilities as scores.

paper1.title: VL4AD: Vision-Language Models Improve Pixel-wise Anomaly Detection
paper1.abstract:
Semantic segmentation networks have achieved significant
                        success under the assumption of independent and identically distributed
                        data. However, these networks often struggle to detect anomalies from
                        unknown semantic classes due to the limited set of visual concepts they
                        are typically trained on. To address this issue, anomaly segmentation
                        often involves fine-tuning on outlier samples, necessitating additional efforts for data collection, labeling, and model retraining. Seeking to avoid
                        this cumbersome work, we take a different approach and propose to incorporate vision-language (VL) encoders into existing anomaly detectors
                        to leverage the semantically broad VL pre-training for improved outlier
                        awareness. Additionally, we propose a new scoring function that enables
                        data- and training-free outlier supervision via textual prompts. The resulting VL4AD model, which includes max-logit prompt ensembling and
                        a class-merging strategy, achieves competitive performance on widely
                        used benchmark datasets, thereby demonstrating the potential of visionlanguage models for pixel-wise anomaly detection.
methodology:
An unusual pattern was identified where caravans are mistakenly classified as trucks due to their visual resemblance, resulting in low uncertainty values. This misclassification affects approximately 10% of predictions, significantly elevating the False Positive Rate (FPR). Introducing "caravan" as an Out-of-Distribution (OOD) prompt substantially alleviates this issue, reducing the FPR by a factor of 25 and improving the Average Precision (AP) by 10.4%. This improvement positions VL4AD as the second-best model in settings with outlier supervision, demonstrating the effectiveness and flexibility of OOD prompting.

For the obstacle track (RO21), VL4AD's performance is not as strong, potentially due to the small size of anomalies, which are difficult for the encoder to represent as it was originally trained on object-centered image-text pairs. Further details on this issue are available in Appendix 7.4.

## Ablation Study

An ablation study was conducted to validate the effectiveness of the model design, including pre-training, max-logit prompt ensembling, and class merging. An additional analysis of OOD prompting is provided in the following section.

For pre-training, the vision-only ConvNext-L model pre-trained on ImageNet-22K was utilized with the standard Mask2Former decoder. The same training protocol (COCO-CityScapes) was used for the vision-language variant. Training the model on CityScapes for 90K iterations from scratch did not yield significant benefits over the current setup. Experiments were conducted with both unfrozen and frozen encoders.

For max-logit ensembling, a baseline using only one concept per semantic class was compared. The results of these ablations are presented in Table 2, showing pixel-level metrics on RA19 and FS LaF, as well as mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) as a generalization score on CityScapes.

For vision-only models, the unfrozen variant showed the best CityScapes classification performance across all setups. However, both variants exhibited low AP on OOD datasets, indicating a lack of OOD awareness. With vision-language pre-training, the model surpassed vision-only models in every metric except for FPR on RA19, supporting the hypothesis that vision-language models are generally more OOD-aware.

Class merging reduced the FPR on RA19 by almost a factor of three (to 15.3%) and on FS LaF by a factor of two (to 4.2%), demonstrating its effectiveness in addressing high uncertainty between in-distribution (ID) classes. Max-logit prompt ensembling slightly improved mIoU on CityScapes by 0.8%. On anomaly detection in RA19, it significantly improved AP by 13.8%, attributed to better alignment between ID visual and text embeddings. Combining all three methods achieved the best performance without outlier supervision, validating the model's design.

7.3 Class Merging
To improve OOD detection performance, especially with numerous ID classes, textual prompts of related ID classes are concatenated as alternative concepts within superclasses during testing. The 19 semantic classes are grouped into eight superclasses, three superclasses, and a single superclass. The eight superclasses include the seven CityScapes abstract superclasses plus a standalone class for car. For the three superclasses, classes are grouped into static objects/background, moving objects, and humans. Grouping details are in Tab. 8 and Tab. 9.

Reducing the number of superclasses from 19 to 8 and then to 3 results in monotonic improvement in average precision (AP) and false positive rate (FPR) on RA19 and FS LaF datasets. FPR on both datasets decreases by over 50%. When all semantic classes merge into a single superclass, only one term remains in Eq. 1, causing the softmax function to output a probability of 1.0. The sigmoid function is used instead, but its saturation tendency is speculated to be why the three superclasses setup outperforms the single superclass setup on RA19.

Additional experiments involve randomly merging 19 semantic classes into three superclasses, repeated 100 times for three models trained with different random seeds. FPR on RA19 and FS LaF is determined and illustrated in Fig. 6. This compares random merging to structured merging based on semantic similarities. Any class merging generally results in a lower mean FPR than no merging. Structured merging consistently outperforms both random merging and no merging. The main experiments utilize structured merging with three superclasses.

7.4 Issues for Small-Size Obstacles Detection
VL4AD performs strongly on anomaly tracks (RA21 of SMIYC, RoadAnomaly19, FishyScapes Lost and Found) but less so on obstacle tracks (RO21 of SMIYC). This is attributed to smaller anomalous objects in obstacle tracks and the characteristics of frozen CLIP encoders pre-trained on object-centered text-image pairs. Geometric image-based data augmentations or extracting visual features from earlier layers may mitigate this. Visualizations from the SMIYC obstacle track validation set (Fig. 7) show weak differences in uncertainty scores between obstacles and the road, especially for distant obstacles. Cropping the obstacle area and feeding it to the network significantly enhances this contrast without substantially increasing false positive pixels. RbA shows good contrast but introduces more false positives with cropped input.

7.5 Further Visualizations for the SMIYC Anomaly Track and FishyScapes Lost and Found
Further visualizations from the anomaly track (RA21) of SMIYC are presented.

4.4 Impact of OOD Prompting

We observed the benefits of OOD prompts on RA19 and SMIYC RA21 datasets. This is attributed to the use of multiple OOD concepts. We investigate the effects of individual prompts. For a given OOD concept, we split RA19 into two subsets: frames showing the concept (known unknowns) and frames showing other OOD concepts but not the selected one (unknown unknowns). We measure performance on the whole dataset and both subsets, with and without OOD prompting.

AP and FPR on known unknowns subsets are generally better than without OOD prompting. This indicates our model retains open-vocabulary capabilities and can reject OOD objects using our scoring function. For unknown-unknowns subsets, AP and FPR show fluctuations around 1% when applying different prompts, which are not statistically significant. OOD prompts positively affect OOD detection on known unknowns while having a negligible impact on unknown unknowns. This is expected as OOD prompts trigger higher ID class uncertainty only when corresponding OOD objects appear.

We also experiment with using OOD class names from RbA's outlier supervision dataset as OOD prompts. Some RbA classes overlap with RA19 instances (e.g., cow, zebra, bear), explaining why RbA prompts perform similarly to other used prompts. These results highlight the flexibility and effectiveness of OOD prompting.

4.5 Efficiency and Trade-Off Analysis

VL4AD includes an additional text encoder, which might raise concerns about runtime efficiency. However, textual embeddings from the CLIP text encoder are kept after determining ID semantic classes and OOD prompts, avoiding further text encoder forward passes at test time. VL4AD is approximately 5% slower than vision-only ConvNext with Mask2Former on an NVIDIA A100. This slight difference is likely due to VL4AD's cosine similarities with text embeddings including more parameters than the linear layers in vision-only Mask2Former.

We analyze the trade-off between anomaly detection and ID pixel identification. Applying uncertainty thresholds used for RA19 and FS LaF to CityScapes predictions assesses how many pixels are correctly classified as ID. The "void" class in CityScapes is excluded. At a recall of 0.9 on RA19, approximately 2% of CityScapes pixels are incorrectly identified as OOD. With OOD prompting, this figure reduces to approximately 0.5%, demonstrating its effectiveness. Both variants perform similarly on FS LaF.

On RA19, approximately 2% of CityScapes pixels are incorrectly identified as OOD. With OOD prompting, this reduces to approximately 0.5%, demonstrating its effectiveness. On FS LaF, both variants misclassify 3% of CityScapes pixels at a recall of 0.9 using OOD prompts from RA19.

Fig. 5 shows the ID pixel retention rate on CityScapes as a function of OOD recall for RA19/FS LaF. VL4AD achieves a recall of 0.9 on both RA19 and FS LaF, correctly identifying at least 97% of CityScapes pixels as ID. OOD prompting further enhances the ID retention rate on RA19.

Limitations: VL4AD is constrained by CLIP's vision encoder, particularly for small obstacles, impacting its pixel-level performance on RO21. Enhancing CLIP's local representation for dense prediction is a future direction. VL4AD uses a concept dictionary and fixed prompt templates. Experiments with learnable prompts did not improve performance, possibly due to overfitting to limited CityScapes classes. Developing training strategies for learnable prompts in limited-class pixel-wise anomaly detection remains a challenge.

Conclusion: This work presents an approach for pixel-wise anomaly detection, leveraging vision-language models for broader OOD knowledge compared to vision-only methods that often rely on outlier supervision. The proposed method uses max-logit prompt ensembling to align ID textual and visual embeddings, class merging to reduce uncertainty on edge pixels, and a new scoring function for data- and training-free outlier supervision via textual prompts. Evaluated on RA19, FS LaF, and SMIYC, VL4AD is competitive with vision-only models but does not require additional data or retraining. The strategy of max-logit prompt ensembling, class merging, and OOD prompting significantly improves performance and demonstrates the capability of vision-language models for pixel-level anomaly detection.

Visual embeddings ($v_i$) combine visual features from the decoder's pixel-decoding part ($D_{vis-lang}$) and features obtained via mask pooling from the encoder ($E_{vision, vis-lang}$). Instead of summing these, FC-CLIP constructs a geometric ensemble of logits by computing cosine similarity between individual visual features and ID class textual embeddings. These are termed in-vocabulary ($c_{i, \text{in}}$) and out-of-vocabulary ($c_{i, \text{out}}$) classifiers.

Final mask classification scores are given by:
$$
c_i(j) =
\begin{cases}
(c_{i, \text{in}}(j))^{(1-\alpha)} \cdot (c_{i, \text{out}}(j))^\alpha, & \text{if } j \in K \\
(c_{i, \text{in}}(j))^{(1-\beta)} \cdot (c_{i, \text{out}}(j))^\beta, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$
where $c_i(j)$ is the $j$-th element of $c_i$, $i=1, \dots, N$ (number of object queries), and $\alpha, \beta \in [0, 1]$ balance predictions between in- and out-of-vocabulary classifiers for ID and OOD prompting classes.

Experiments for VL4AD without OOD prompting varied $\alpha$ from 0.0 to 1.0. $\alpha=0.0$ uses only decoder-processed visual features, while $\alpha=1.0$ relies solely on raw features from the frozen vision encoder for CityScapes classes.

Table 5 shows AP remains high across RA19 and FS LaF datasets, outperforming the vision-only variant. FPR on RA19 varies significantly. $\alpha=0.0$ leads to overfitting to CityScapes. $\alpha=1.0$ prevents effective learning from CityScapes, resulting in high FPR. $\alpha=0.4$ and $\alpha=0.6$ show the best balance for OOD detection. Improved performance with OOD prompting is observed at $\alpha=0.4$. Hyperparameters used are $\alpha=0.4$ and $\beta=0.8$.

To mitigate overfitting, random cropping (1.1 ratio) is applied to input images. Textual prompts are constructed by combining prompt templates and alternative concepts. Eight variants of each prompt are created using 1% dropout on transformer-based text encoder attention and feed-forward layers before training. During inference, dropout is disabled, and normalized mean textual embeddings are calculated with respect to prompt templates for each alternative concept.

The model is initially trained on COCO-panoptic for 50 epochs (batch size 16, learning rate $10^{-4}$), then fine-tuned on CityScapes for 10K iterations (batch size 8, learning rate $2.5 \times 10^{-5}$). The learning rate of the encoder is reduced for the unfrozen vision-only variant.

Simplified setup: three ID classes (human, car, truck) and two OOD classes (animal, caravan).
ID input: Model correctly predicts class with and without OOD prompts.
Far-OOD input: Model works well in both cases; OOD prompts reduce weight on incorrect ID classes.
Near-OOD input: OOD class introduction is crucial to avoid erroneous ID classification.
OOD input definition: All ID class probabilities (negative uncertainties) are below the decision threshold.

Experimental Setup:
Datasets: SMIYC test set, RoadAnomaly19 (RA19), Fishy-Scapes Lost and Found (FS LaF) validation set.
ID objects: CityScapes categories.
OOD objects: All other object types.
SMIYC test set tracks: Road Anomaly (RA21), Road Obstacle (RO21) (smaller anomalous objects).
Pixel-level evaluation metrics: Average precision (AP), false positive rate (FPR) at 95% true positive rate.
SMIYC component-level metrics: Adjusted IoU over ground truth segments (sIoU gt), positive predicted value (PPV), mean F1.

Hyperparameters:
Default: Values specified in [52].
Encoder: ConvNeXt-L variant [34] from OpenCLIP [25], pre-trained on LAION-2B [44]. Frozen.
Decoder: Trained on COCO panoptic [30] as in [52] for initialisation.
Fine-tuning: CityScapes dataset, 10K iterations, learning rate 2.5 x 10^-5, reductions at 85% and 95% duration.
Max-logit ensembling: Conceptual dictionary from [16, 50, 52] with modifications.
OOD prompting: OOD class names from RA21 for RA21/RO21 evaluations, RA19 class names for RA19/FS LaF assessments. Class names are standard metadata.
Training details: Appendix 7.1 (hyperparameters), 7.2 (prompt descriptions), 7.3 (class-merging strategies).
Comparison: VL4AD with OOD prompting vs. outlier exposure methods (which use OOD image datasets; VL4AD uses only textual names).
Evaluation: Three random seeds, mean performance with two standard deviations.

Pixel-wise Evaluation:
RA19: VL4AD surpasses RbA [38] and UNO [12] (with/without outlier supervision). OOD prompting: +3.3% AP, -0.6 FPR (no further training/data prep).
FS LaF: VL4AD FPR superior to UNO [12] (without outlier supervision); UNO has marginally higher AP. OOD prompt gain on RA19 does not extend to FS LaF (prompts tailored for RA19). VL4AD is second among methods with outlier supervision. Other models do not use class merging.
Comparison with FC-CLIP [52] on FS LaF and RA19: VL4AD significantly stronger.

SMIYC anomaly track (RA21):
Component-level (sIoU gt, PPV, mean F1): VL4AD competitive with/without outlier supervision.
Pixel-level: VL4AD without OOD prompting has exceptionally high FPR.
Reason: Caravans mistakenly classified as trucks due to visual resemblance, assigning low uncertainty. Affects ~10% of predictions.

paper2.title: A Simple Unified Framework for Detecting Out-of-Distribution Samples and Adversarial Attacks
paper2.abstract:
Detecting test samples drawn sufficiently far away from the training distribution
                        statistically or adversarially is a fundamental requirement for deploying a good
                        classifier in many real-world machine learning applications. However, deep neural networks with the softmax classifier are known to produce highly overconfident
                        posterior distributions even for such abnormal samples. In this paper, we propose
                        a simple yet effective method for detecting any abnormal samples, which is applicable to any pre-trained softmax neural classifier. We obtain the class conditional
                        Gaussian distributions with respect to (low- and upper-level) features of the deep
                        models under Gaussian discriminant analysis, which result in a confidence score
                        based on the Mahalanobis distance. While most prior methods have been evaluated for detecting either out-of-distribution or adversarial samples, but not both,
                        the proposed method achieves the state-of-the-art performances for both cases in
                        our experiments. Moreover, we found that our proposed method is more robust
                        in harsh cases, e.g., when the training dataset has noisy labels or small number of
                        samples. Finally, we show that the proposed method enjoys broader usage by applying it to class-incremental learning: whenever out-of-distribution samples are
                        detected, our classification rule can incorporate new classes well without further
                        training deep models.
methodology:
A confidence score M(x) is computed on a test sample x. If M(x) is above a threshold, it is classified as positive (in-distribution). The Euclidean distance, using only empirical class means, is used for comparison. ResNet is trained on CIFAR-10. Tiny-ImageNet is used as an out-of-distribution dataset. The Mahalanobis distance-based metric outperforms the Euclidean and maximum softmax score methods.

Calibration Techniques:
Input pre-processing involves adding controlled noise to test samples. For each test sample x, a pre-processed sample bx is calculated:
bx = x + εsign(▽xM(x)) = x − εsign(▽x(f(x) − bµbc)⊤bΣ−1(f(x) − bµbc))
Here, ε is the noise magnitude, and bc is the index of the closest class. The confidence score is then measured using bx. This noise is generated to increase the confidence score, not for adversarial attacks. This perturbation can better separate in- and out-of-distribution samples. Similar input pre-processing in [21] aims to increase the softmax score of the predicted label. Our method differs as the noise is generated to increase the proposed metric.

Algorithm 2: Updating Mahalanobis distance-based classifier for class-incremental learning.
Input: Samples from a new class {xi : ∀i = 1 . . . NC+1}, means and covariances of observed classes {bµc : ∀c = 1 . . . C}, bΣ
1. Compute the new class mean: bµC+1 ← 1/NC+1 * Σ_i f(xi)
2. Compute the covariance of the new class: bΣC+1 ← 1/NC+1 * Σ_i (f(xi) − bµC+1)(f(xi) − bµC+1)⊤
3. Update the shared covariance: bΣ ← (C/(C+1)) * bΣ + (1/(C+1)) * bΣC+1
Output: Means and covariances of all classes {bµc : ∀c = 1 . . . C + 1}, bΣ

Feature ensemble: To enhance performance, confidence scores from low-level features, in addition to final features, are measured and combined. For training data, ℓ-th hidden features fℓ(x) are extracted, and their empirical class means bµℓ,c and tied covariances bΣℓ are computed. For each test sample x, the confidence score from the ℓ-th layer is measured using formula (2). This method can improve calibration by extracting more input-specific information from low-level features. The area under ROC (AUROC) curves for a threshold-based detector using confidence scores from different basic blocks of DenseNet trained on CIFAR-10 are measured. Similar trends are observed on ResNet. Performance on various OOD samples (SVHN, LSUN, TinyImageNet, and adversarial samples from DeepFool) is shown in Figure 2. Intermediate feature dimensions are reduced using average pooling. Confidence scores from low-level features often provide better calibration than final features (e.g., for LSUN, TinyImageNet, and DeepFool). A feature ensemble method is designed to further improve performance. Confidence scores from all layers are extracted and integrated by weighted averaging: Σℓ αℓMℓ(x), where Mℓ(·) is the confidence score at the ℓ-th layer and αℓ is its weight. Weights are chosen by training a logistic regression detector on validation samples. This weighted averaging of confidence scores can prevent performance degradation if some layer scores are ineffective; their trained weights would be near zero.

Class-incremental learning using Mahalanobis distance-based score: The Mahalanobis distance-based confidence score can be used in class-incremental learning. A classifier pre-trained on base classes is updated with new classes and samples. This is challenging due to catastrophic forgetting and limited memory. Existing methods often involve generative models or data sampling, which can be computationally expensive. Based on the proposed confidence score, a simple classification method is developed without complex training. It assumes the classifier is well-trained.

Detection performance using ResNet trained on CIFAR-10 with SVHN as OOD.
Our method incrementally applied shows stepwise improvement.
Our method significantly outperforms the baseline without feature ensembles and input pre-processing.
This indicates our method effectively characterizes OOD samples compared to the posterior distribution.
Feature ensembles and input pre-processing further improve detection performance over ODIN.

Datasets:
- CIFAR-10: 50,000 training images, 10,000 test images, 10 classes.

- SVHN: 73,257 training images, 26,032 test images, 10 digits. (Extra dataset not used for training).
- TinyImageNet: 10,000 test images, 200 classes. Downsampled to 32x32.
- LSUN: 10,000 test images, 10 scenes. Downsampled to 32x32.

Tested Methods:
- Baseline [13]: Confidence score is max y P(y|x).
- ODIN [21]:
    - Temperature scaling: P(y = by|x; T) = exp(f_by(x)/T) / sum_y exp(f_y(x)/T), where T > 0.
    - Pre-processing: x' = x - epsilon_odin * sign(-▽x log P_theta(y = by|x; T)).
    - Classification: max y P_theta(y|x'; T). Classified as positive if score > delta.
    - epsilon_odin choices: {0, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.0014, 0.002, 0.0024, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2}.
    - T choices: {1, 10, 100, 1000}.

Hyperparameters for our method:
- Magnitude of noise.
- Layer indexes for feature ensemble.
- Confidence scores extracted from the end of each dense (or residual) block of DenseNet (or ResNet).
- Feature maps reduced by average pooling: F x H x W -> F x 1.
- Magnitude of noise choices: {0, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.0014, 0.002, 0.0024, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2}.

Performance Metrics:
- True Negative Rate (TNR) at 95% True Positive Rate (TPR).
- Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC).
- Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPR). AUPR-IN (in-distribution positive), AUPR-OUT (out-of-distribution positive).
- Detection Accuracy: 1 - min_delta [ P_in(q(x) <= delta) * P(x is from Pin) + P_out(q(x) > delta) * P(x is from Pout) ], assuming P(x is from Pin) = P(x is from Pout).
- AUROC, AUPR, and detection accuracy are threshold-independent.

Experimental setups in detecting adversarial samples:

- Basic Iterative Method (BIM) [16].
- DeepFool [26].
- Carlini-Wagner (CW) [3].

LID outperforms in detecting complex attacks like BIM, DeepFool, and CW. Our method surpasses LID in most cases. Our method also outperforms LID in detecting OOD samples in all tested cases.

**3.3 Class-Incremental Learning**

**Setup:**
*   ResNet-34 is trained for CIFAR-100 and downsampled ImageNet classification.
*   A classifier is pre-trained on base classes; new classes are incrementally added.
*   **Scenario 1:** Half of CIFAR-100 classes are base, the rest are new.
*   **Scenario 2:** All CIFAR-100 classes are base, 100 ImageNet classes are new.
*   All scenarios are tested five times and averaged. Class splits are randomly generated per trial.
*   **Comparison Methods:**
    *   Softmax classifier (fine-tuned for new classes, only softmax layer updated for near-zero cost training).
    *   Euclidean classifier (accommodates new classes by computing class mean).
*   **Memory Management (Softmax Classifier):** Follows Rebuffi & Kolesnikov [29]. A small number of old class samples are kept in memory. Memory size matches that for Mahalanobis distance-based classifier (sum of learned classes and hidden feature dimension, 512 in experiments).
*   **Evaluation:**
    *   Base-new class accuracy curve adjusted by a bias to new class scores (similar to [18]).
    *   Area Under Curve (AUC) measured to provide an imbalanced measure of performance.

**Comparison with Other Classifiers:**
*   Figure 4 compares incremental learning performance (AUC) in two scenarios.
*   Each sub-figure shows AUC vs. number of learned classes (left) and base-new class accuracy curve after last new class addition (right).
*   Mahalanobis distance-based classifier (ours) significantly outperforms other methods, especially as the number of new classes increases.
*   A crossing is observed in the right figure of Figure 4(b) in small regimes due to catastrophic forgetting.
*   **AUC Performance:**
    *   Our method: 40.0% (22.1%)
    *   Softmax classifier: 32.7% (15.6%)
    *   Euclidean distance classifier: 32.9% (17.1%)
    *   (First experiment (Second experiment) results)
*   Similar trends observed when CIFAR-100 classes are base and CIFAR-10 classes are new (reported in supplementary material).
*   Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our confidence score compared to others.

**4 Conclusion**
*   Propose a simple yet effective method for detecting abnormal test samples (out-of-distribution and adversarial).
*   Core idea: Induce a generative classifier under LDA assumption and define a new confidence score.
*   With calibration techniques (input pre-processing, feature ensemble), the method performs strongly across tasks: OOD detection, adversarial attack detection, and class-incremental learning.
*   Method is more robust to hyperparameter choices and extreme scenarios (noisy labels, small datasets).
*   Approach has potential for broader application.

C
More experimental results
C.1
Robustness of our method in detecting adversarial samples
To verify robustness, we measured detection performance by training ResNet on CIFAR-10 with varying numbers of training data and random labels. Our method (blue bar) outperforms LID (green bar) across all experiments (Figure 5).
C.2
Class-incremental learning
Figure 6 compares AUCs when CIFAR-100 is pre-trained and CIFAR-10 serves as new classes. Our Mahalanobis distance-based classifier significantly outperforms others as the number of new classes increases. With all new classes added, our method achieves an AUC of 47.7%, compared to 41.0% for the softmax classifier and 43.0% for the Euclidean distance classifier.
C.3
Experimental results on joint confidence loss
The proposed detector using a softmax neural classifier trained with standard cross-entropy loss typically outperforms the ODIN detector, which uses a softmax classifier trained with confidence loss [19]. The latter involves jointly training a generator and classifier to calibrate the posterior distribution. Our detector further improves performance when used with a model trained by confidence loss, indicating our method enhances any pre-trained softmax neural classifier.

Figure 7: Performances of baseline [13], ODIN [21], and Mahalanobis (ours) detectors under various training losses for in-distribution CIFAR-10 and SVHN, and out-of-distribution SVHN, TinyImageNet, and LSUN.
C.4
Comparison with ODIN

Table 5: Distinguishing in- and out-of-distribution test set data for image classification. Hyper-parameters are tuned using in- and out-of-distribution validation sets. All values are percentages; best results are bolded.

The proposed method is robust to hyperparameter choices and extreme scenarios like noisy labels or small datasets. It has potential applications in active learning, ensemble learning, and few-shot learning.

paper1.title: On Advantages of Mask-level Recognition for Outlier-aware Segmentation
paper1.abstract:
Most dense recognition approaches bring a separate decision in each particular pixel. These approaches deliver
                        competitive performance in usual closed-set setups. However, important applications in the wild typically require
                        strong performance in presence of outliers. We show that
                        this demanding setup greatly benefit from mask-level predictions, even in the case of non-finetuned baseline models.
                        Moreover, we propose an alternative formulation of dense
                        recognition uncertainty that effectively reduces false positive responses at semantic borders. The proposed formulation produces a further improvement over a very strong
                        baseline and sets the new state of the art in outlier-aware
                        semantic segmentation with and without training on negative data. Our contributions also lead to performance improvement in a recent panoptic setup. In-depth experiments
                        confirm that our approach succeeds due to implicit aggregation of pixel-level cues into mask-level predictions.

**6. Conclusion**
Robust performance in the presence of outliers is crucial for scene understanding applications. Previous dense prediction approaches often fail due to their reliance on pixel-level OOD detection, neglecting correlations between neighboring pixels. This work addresses this by shifting OOD detection from pixels to regions, leveraging mask-level predictions to aggregate pixel-level evidence and increase the statistical power of anomaly scores. Performing OOD detection before ensembling decisions over masks further boosts performance. Injecting negative data into void content and extending mask-based models for panoptic inference in the presence of outliers further enhance results. Experiments demonstrate that mask-level outlier detection significantly outperforms pixel-level counterparts and achieves state-of-the-art AP performance among methods that do not train on real negative data. It also improves upon the previous state of the art in outlier-aware panoptic segmentation.

4.2. Outlier-aware panoptic segmentation on MS COCO

Mask-level outlier detection can be applied for panoptic segmentation. We consider the hardest setup from a recent related work [29] that relabels 20% of thing classes from COCO as void pixels during training. These classes include dining table, banana, bicycle, cake, sink, cat, keyboard, and bear. During inference, the model must classify all pixels from these classes into the dedicated anomalous thing class.

Outlier-aware performance is measured by standard metrics PQ, SQ, and RQ. Our models use a ResNet-50 backbone, consistent with previous work [29].

Mask-level training encourages all masks to avoid void pixels. Our anomaly detectors are sensitive to the resulting lack of mask assignment. Therefore, our supervision intensity is very similar to void-suppression [29]. Our inference recovers the dense anomaly map by thresholding the mask-level anomaly score. The threshold is validated for 95% TPR in outlier detection on a held-out validation image. Each anomalous pixel is assigned to its preferred mask, and instances are formed by keeping all masks with more than 200 pixels.

Table 4 compares our method to several approaches from the EOPSN paper [29]. We outperform all previous work despite significantly less supervision. Our method can easily accommodate anomalous stuff classes.

Figure 6 shows qualitative results on three scenes from COCO val. The rows display: input image, ground truth, two results from [29], and our results. The qualitative results illustrate improvements of our method over previous state of the art in outlier-aware panoptic segmentation.

3.3. Detecting outliers in mask-level predictions
A method recovering dense anomaly scores as mask-level uncertainty of the strongest mask is considered first. Using max-softmax as the uncertainty measure, the score is formulated as:
$s_{AHM}^{ood}(x)[r, c] = -\max_{k=1...K} p_{\argmax_m i[r,c]}(Y=k|x)$. (5)
AHM stands for Anomaly score of Hard-assigned Masks. This approach ignores the uncertainty of the dominant mask assignment, which is suboptimal. Combining uncertainties of pixel-level mask assignment and mask-level recognition is pursued.

Closed-set semantic segmentation scores (3) are considered, quantifying their uncertainty using an arbitrary anomaly detector. With the max-logit detector [26], the score is:
$s_{AEM}^{ood}(x)[r, c] = -\max_{k=1...K} \sum_i m_i[r, c] \cdot p_i(Y=k|x)$. (6)
Closed-set semantic scores are viewed as ensembled outputs of per-mask classifiers, with mask assignments as weights. This score is denoted as Anomaly of Ensembled Mask-wide predictions (AEM).

Anomaly detector is applied directly to mask-level classification scores. Evidence in each pixel is aggregated according to its mask assignments $m$. This is interpreted as an Ensemble over Anomaly scores of Mask-wide predictions (EAM). This approach has intuitive appeal due to its direct relation to mask-level uncertainty. Quantifying mask-level uncertainty by maximum per-class probability yields a lower bound of the AEM score (6):
$s_{EAM}^{ood}(x)[r, c] = \sum_i m_i[r, c] \cdot (-\max_{k=1...K} p_i(Y=k|x)) \leq -\max_{k=1...K} \sum_i m_i[r, c] \cdot p_i(Y=k|x)$ (7)
Fig. 2 (right) illustrates EAM score computation from M2F outputs.

The difference between these approaches is expected to be most visible at semantic borders, where adjacent masks often lower pixel assignment confidence. In such situations, EAM correctly outputs a lower anomaly score than AEM. Fig. 4 illustrates EAM and AEM scoring differences on two scenes from Fishyscapes L&F. Similar behavior is observed in most image pixels, but EAM clearly outputs lower anomaly scores on semantic boundaries, reducing false positive detections in inlier pixels at these locations.

Figure 4. Pixel-level vs. mask-level OOD detection. Mask-level OOD detection alleviates false positives at semantic borders.

3.4. Performance enhancement with negative data
Training with negative data is an important component in outlier detection [5, 12, 23, 28, 57] for addressing feature collapse. For dense prediction, this typically involves pasting negative data over inlier training images [3, 21], requiring an additional loss term in negative pixels [12, 28, 42]. The proposed approach requires no changes in the model or loss function.

Negative pixels are set to the void class ground truth, instructing masks to avoid them. This is reasonable as void pixels do not belong to any class of interest. This training increases void content variety and penalizes masks that claim void pixels. Standard dense classifiers [14, 50] cannot be trained with negatives labeled as void due to the standard per-pixel cross-entropy loss not being computed in void pixels. This pasting procedure is specific for mask-level recognition.

Figure 5 shows a training example with input image crop and corresponding ground truth binary labels. None of the ground truth labels include pasted negative pixels. Experiments show this supervision generalizes to outlier detection in real-world images.

Experiments explore the advantages of mask-level recognition in outlier-aware semantic segmentation.

The resulting models set the new state of the art in outlier-aware segmentation on two tracks from the Segment Me If You Can (SMIYC) benchmark and adapted MS COCO.

2. Related work
The related work considers models for mask-level recognition tasks (Sec. 2.1) and segmentation in presence of outliers (Sec. 2.2).

2.1. Recognition of free-form regions
Early approaches to mask-wide recognition relied on class-agnostic bottom-up proposals. They aggregated handcrafted [9] or convolutional [19, 25, 51] features along proposed regions and made mask-wide decisions by classifying pooled representations. Mask-RCNN extends this approach by sharing features across proposal detection and mask-wide classification, as well as by end-to-end training of all parameters. PointRend proposes to back-propagate the loss only through selected low-uncertainty predictions [33]. This allows increasing Mask-RCNN resolution from 28×28 to 224×224 with negligible impact on training footprint. MaskFormer precludes dependence on bottom-up proposals by directly assigning pixels to masks that span arbitrary image regions [17]. Its key component is a hypernetwork [24] that produces weights for two 1×1 convolutions that convert pixel-level embeddings into mask assignment scores and subsequently into semantic maps. This is the first architecture to deliver competitive experimental performance on semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and panoptic segmentation. Mask2Former [16] further improves the mask hypernetwork by introducing a special attention layer that promotes progressive focusing onto foreground pixels for a particular mask. Our work explores Mask2Former performance in the context of outlier-aware segmentation and outlier-aware panoptic segmentation.

2.2. Segmentation in presence of outliers
Recognition in the wild involves test regions beyond the training taxonomy. Adequate models should reject decisions in such pixels [54]. This can be done by restricting the shape of the decision boundary [1, 55] or by complementing the classifier with an anomaly detector [27, 38]. The decision boundary can be restricted by thresholding distance from learned class centers in the embedding space [10, 55]. This can be further improved by employing a stronger classifier [58]. However, many of these approaches fail if unknown samples map to the same features as samples from known classes, an occurrence known as feature collapse [45].

Early approaches for extending discriminative predictions with OOD detection have been based on prediction confidence [27], input perturbations [38], density estimation [48], and Bayesian uncertainty [47]. Semantic anomalies [53] are noted as especially hard to detect [32, 48, 56]. Generating synthetic anomalies in tandem with the discriminative task is a promising approach [13, 22, 35, 63]. Further empirical improvements have been achieved by mimicking anomalies with negative training data [28, 42]. However, this may lead to over-optimistic performance estimates due to possible overlap with test anomalies.

Outlier detection is especially interesting in dense prediction due to applications in robust scene understanding [7, 11, 62]. However, straightforward adaptations of image-wide approaches experience two failure modes: they often fail to accurately localize anomalies in front of inlier backgrounds [3], and they are prone to false positives in inlier pixels with high entropy predictions at semantic borders [52]. Therefore, much work proposes custom designs to alleviate these problems.

Partially anomalous images can be accounted for by learning on mixed-content images [3, 5, 23, 57]. Correlation between neighboring pixels can be addressed by aggregating evidence through meta-classification [52] or input preprocessing [38]. Real training data can be avoided by fitting generative heads to pre-trained [7] or jointly trained [29, 37] features. Another line of work trains on synthetic negatives corresponding to adversarial noise [2] or samples of a jointly trained generative model [21]. Finally, some approaches detect the discrepancy between the input and the resynthesized scene [5, 41, 59, 60].

Our work formulates outlier detection according to mask-wide predictions. Unlike meta-classification approaches [12, 52], our method requires only one learning episode and does not require neg

Abstract
Transformer-based architectures and large language models (LLMs) have advanced road scene perception accuracy. However, current road scene segmentation approaches are trained on closed-set data, limiting detection of out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Road anomaly detection methods exist but rely on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection, facing two issues: (1) inadequate consideration of anomalous region objectiveness, leading to incomplete segmentation when anomalies resemble known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, causing detection of anomalies irrelevant to autonomous driving. This paper proposes a novel framework, Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness (SOTA), for autonomous driving. SOTA enhances objectiveness segmentation with a Semantic Fusion Block (SFB) and filters irrelevant anomalies using a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA). Evaluations on Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and RoadAnomaly datasets show SOTA consistently improves OOD detection performance and achieves robust segmentation.

Task-aware Aggregation Module:
1. Identifies road class from semantic segmentation output.
2. Generates a binary road mask.
3. Refines mask using a 15x15 convolutional kernel filled with ones, applied iteratively 15 times.
4. Each iteration involves padded convolution followed by thresholding at 0 to maintain binary format.
5. Results in an expanded road prompt $y_t$ capturing uncertain boundary regions.

Projection and Alignment Module:
Projection Module:
1. Lightweight learnable convolutional sub-network.
2. Transforms raw OoD confidence map into an intermediate semantic representation.
3. Input: 1x256x256 single-channel.
4. Processed through two 2x2 convolutional layers with stride 2.
5. Spatial resolution reduced to 64x64.
6. Channel dimension expanded to 16.
7. Each layer followed by LayerNorm and GELU activation.
8. Output feature map shape: 16x64x64.

Alignment Module:
1. Aligns intermediate semantic features with image encoder's representation.
2. Applies a final 1x1 convolutional layer.
3. Maps 16-channel feature map to a 256-dimensional embedding.
4. Preserves spatial structure.
5. Output tensor shape: 256x64x64.
6. Used for downstream fusion with image features.

1. Training dataset preparation uses Outlier Exposure (OE) strategy.
2. Cityscapes dataset used as inlier background (2,975 training images).

paper1.title: On Advantages of Mask-level Recognition for Outlier-aware Segmentation
paper1.abstract:
Most dense recognition approaches bring a separate decision in each particular pixel. These approaches deliver
                        competitive performance in usual closed-set setups. However, important applications in the wild typically require
                        strong performance in presence of outliers. We show that
                        this demanding setup greatly benefit from mask-level predictions, even in the case of non-finetuned baseline models.
                        Moreover, we propose an alternative formulation of dense
                        recognition uncertainty that effectively reduces false positive responses at semantic borders. The proposed formulation produces a further improvement over a very strong
                        baseline and sets the new state of the art in outlier-aware
                        semantic segmentation with and without training on negative data. Our contributions also lead to performance improvement in a recent panoptic setup. In-depth experiments
                        confirm that our approach succeeds due to implicit aggregation of pixel-level cues into mask-level predictions.

**6. Conclusion**
Robust performance in the presence of outliers is crucial for scene understanding applications. Previous dense prediction approaches often fail due to their reliance on pixel-level OOD detection, neglecting correlations between neighboring pixels. This work addresses this by shifting OOD detection from pixels to regions, leveraging mask-level predictions to aggregate pixel-level evidence and increase the statistical power of anomaly scores. Performing OOD detection before ensembling decisions over masks further boosts performance. Injecting negative data into void content and extending mask-based models for panoptic inference in the presence of outliers further enhance results. Experiments demonstrate that mask-level outlier detection significantly outperforms pixel-level counterparts and achieves state-of-the-art AP performance among methods that do not train on real negative data. It also improves upon the previous state of the art in outlier-aware panoptic segmentation.

4.2. Outlier-aware panoptic segmentation on MS COCO

Mask-level outlier detection can be applied for panoptic segmentation. We consider the hardest setup from a recent related work [29] that relabels 20% of thing classes from COCO as void pixels during training. These classes include dining table, banana, bicycle, cake, sink, cat, keyboard, and bear. During inference, the model must classify all pixels from these classes into the dedicated anomalous thing class.

Outlier-aware performance is measured by standard metrics PQ, SQ, and RQ. Our models use a ResNet-50 backbone, consistent with previous work [29].

Mask-level training encourages all masks to avoid void pixels. Our anomaly detectors are sensitive to the resulting lack of mask assignment. Therefore, our supervision intensity is very similar to void-suppression [29]. Our inference recovers the dense anomaly map by thresholding the mask-level anomaly score. The threshold is validated for 95% TPR in outlier detection on a held-out validation image. Each anomalous pixel is assigned to its preferred mask, and instances are formed by keeping all masks with more than 200 pixels.

Table 4 compares our method to several approaches from the EOPSN paper [29]. We outperform all previous work despite significantly less supervision. Our method can easily accommodate anomalous stuff classes.

3.3. Detecting outliers in mask-level predictions
A method recovering dense anomaly scores as mask-level uncertainty of the strongest mask is considered first. Using max-softmax as the uncertainty measure, the score is formulated as:
$s_{AHM}^{ood}(x)[r, c] = -\max_{k=1...K} p_{\argmax_m i[r,c]}(Y=k|x)$. (5)
AHM stands for Anomaly score of Hard-assigned Masks. This approach ignores the uncertainty of the dominant mask assignment, which is suboptimal. Combining uncertainties of pixel-level mask assignment and mask-level recognition is pursued.

Closed-set semantic segmentation scores (3) are considered, quantifying their uncertainty using an arbitrary anomaly detector. With the max-logit detector [26], the score is:
$s_{AEM}^{ood}(x)[r, c] = -\max_{k=1...K} \sum_i m_i[r, c] \cdot p_i(Y=k|x)$. (6)
Closed-set semantic scores are viewed as ensembled outputs of per-mask classifiers, with mask assignments as weights. This score is denoted as Anomaly of Ensembled Mask-wide predictions (AEM).

Anomaly detector is applied directly to mask-level classification scores. Evidence in each pixel is aggregated according to its mask assignments $m$. This is interpreted as an Ensemble over Anomaly scores of Mask-wide predictions (EAM). This approach has intuitive appeal due to its direct relation to mask-level uncertainty. Quantifying mask-level uncertainty by maximum per-class probability yields a lower bound of the AEM score (6):
$s_{EAM}^{ood}(x)[r, c] = \sum_i m_i[r, c] \cdot (-\max_{k=1...K} p_i(Y=k|x)) \leq -\max_{k=1...K} \sum_i m_i[r, c] \cdot p_i(Y=k|x)$ (7)
Fig. 2 (right) illustrates EAM score computation from M2F outputs.

The difference between these approaches is expected to be most visible at semantic borders, where adjacent masks often lower pixel assignment confidence. In such situations, EAM correctly outputs a lower anomaly score than AEM. Fig. 4 illustrates EAM and AEM scoring differences on two scenes from Fishyscapes L&F. Similar behavior is observed in most image pixels, but EAM clearly outputs lower anomaly scores on semantic boundaries, reducing false positive detections in inlier pixels at these locations.

Figure 4. Pixel-level vs. mask-level OOD detection. Mask-level OOD detection alleviates false positives at semantic borders.

3.4. Performance enhancement with negative data
Training with negative data is an important component in outlier detection [5, 12, 23, 28, 57] for addressing feature collapse. For dense prediction, this typically involves pasting negative data over inlier training images [3, 21], requiring an additional loss term in negative pixels [12, 28, 42]. The proposed approach requires no changes in the model or loss function.

Negative pixels are set to the void class ground truth, instructing masks to avoid them. This is reasonable as void pixels do not belong to any class of interest. This training increases void content variety and penalizes masks that claim void pixels. Standard dense classifiers [14, 50] cannot be trained with negatives labeled as void due to the standard per-pixel cross-entropy loss not being computed in void pixels. This pasting procedure is specific for mask-level recognition.

Figure 5 shows a training example with input image crop and corresponding ground truth binary labels. None of the ground truth labels include pasted negative pixels. Experiments show this supervision generalizes to outlier detection in real-world images.

Experiments explore the advantages of mask-level recognition in outlier-aware semantic segmentation.

2. Related work
The related work considers models for mask-level recognition tasks (Sec. 2.1) and segmentation in presence of outliers (Sec. 2.2).

2.1. Recognition of free-form regions
Early approaches to mask-wide recognition relied on class-agnostic bottom-up proposals. They aggregated handcrafted [9] or convolutional [19, 25, 51] features along proposed regions and made mask-wide decisions by classifying pooled representations. Mask-RCNN extends this approach by sharing features across proposal detection and mask-wide classification, as well as by end-to-end training of all parameters. PointRend proposes to back-propagate the loss only through selected low-uncertainty predictions [33]. This allows increasing Mask-RCNN resolution from 28×28 to 224×224 with negligible impact on training footprint. MaskFormer precludes dependence on bottom-up proposals by directly assigning pixels to masks that span arbitrary image regions [17]. Its key component is a hypernetwork [24] that produces weights for two 1×1 convolutions that convert pixel-level embeddings into mask assignment scores and subsequently into semantic maps. This is the first architecture to deliver competitive experimental performance on semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and panoptic segmentation. Mask2Former [16] further improves the mask hypernetwork by introducing a special attention layer that promotes progressive focusing onto foreground pixels for a particular mask. Our work explores Mask2Former performance in the context of outlier-aware segmentation and outlier-aware panoptic segmentation.

2.2. Segmentation in presence of outliers
Recognition in the wild involves test regions beyond the training taxonomy. Adequate models should reject decisions in such pixels [54]. This can be done by restricting the shape of the decision boundary [1, 55] or by complementing the classifier with an anomaly detector [27, 38]. The decision boundary can be restricted by thresholding distance from learned class centers in the embedding space [10, 55]. This can be further improved by employing a stronger classifier [58]. However, many of these approaches fail if unknown samples map to the same features as samples from known classes, an occurrence known as feature collapse [45].

Early approaches for extending discriminative predictions with OOD detection have been based on prediction confidence [27], input perturbations [38], density estimation [48], and Bayesian uncertainty [47]. Semantic anomalies [53] are noted as especially hard to detect [32, 48, 56]. Generating synthetic anomalies in tandem with the discriminative task is a promising approach [13, 22, 35, 63]. Further empirical improvements have been achieved by mimicking anomalies with negative training data [28, 42]. However, this may lead to over-optimistic performance estimates due to possible overlap with test anomalies.

Outlier detection is especially interesting in dense prediction due to applications in robust scene understanding [7, 11, 62]. However, straightforward adaptations of image-wide approaches experience two failure modes: they often fail to accurately localize anomalies in front of inlier backgrounds [3], and they are prone to false positives in inlier pixels with high entropy predictions at semantic borders [52]. Therefore, much work proposes custom designs to alleviate these problems.

Partially anomalous images can be accounted for by learning on mixed-content images [3, 5, 23, 57]. Correlation between neighboring pixels can be addressed by aggregating evidence through meta-classification [52] or input preprocessing [38]. Real training data can be avoided by fitting generative heads to pre-trained [7] or jointly trained [29, 37] features. Another line of work trains on synthetic negatives corresponding to adversarial noise [2] or samples of a jointly trained generative model [21]. Finally, some approaches detect the discrepancy between the input and the resynthesized scene [5, 41, 59, 60].

Our work formulates outlier detection according to mask-wide predictions. Unlike meta-classification approaches [12, 52], our method requires only one learning episode and does not require neg

paper2.title: Maskomaly:Zero-Shot Mask Anomaly Segmentation
paper2.abstract:
We present a simple and practical framework for anomaly segmentation called Maskomaly.
                        It builds upon mask-based standard semantic segmentation networks by adding a simple
                        inference-time post-processing step which leverages the raw mask outputs of such networks.
                        Maskomaly does not require additional training and only adds a small computational overhead
                        to inference. Most importantly, it does not require anomalous data at training. We show top
                        results for our method on SMIYC, RoadAnomaly, and StreetHazards. On the most central
                        benchmark, SMIYC1
                        , Maskomaly outperforms all directly comparable approaches. Further,
                        we introduce a novel metric that benefits the development of robust anomaly segmentation

To avoid overconfident predictions, we scale the output by the uncertainty of the dominant mask, resulting in a softer assignment:

`oreject[i,j] = min_{n ∈ I} (1 - m_n[i,j] * max_{1 ≤ l ≤ C} p_n[l])` (1)

Other methods assign high outlier scores at the boundaries of two inlier classes. By computing the pairwise intersection of inlier class masks after thresholding them at `Tb`, we identify these areas and assign them an outlier score `εb`.

**Anomalous Masks**

Despite the simplicity of the rejection-based approach, domain shifts can cause failures. Similar to [26], on FishyScapes LaF [4], over 50% of outlier pixels belong to an inlier mask, suggesting sub-optimal performance of `oreject`.

**Algorithm 1 Maskomaly, Hyperparameters = {Tmask, Tb, εb, λ}**

1: function MASKOMALY(M, P, A, I)
2:   for 1 ≤ n ≤ N do  ▷ Add inlier masks to I
3:     if (argmax_{1 ≤ l ≤ C+1} p_n[l]) ≠ C+1 ∧ (max_{1 ≤ l ≤ C+1} p_n[l]) ≥ Tmask then
4:       I ← I ∪ {n}
5:   for i, j ∈ H × W do  ▷ Reject inlier pixels
6:     `oreject[i,j]` ← min_{n ∈ I} (1 - m_n[i,j] · max_{1 ≤ l ≤ C} p_n[l])
7:   for {k, n} ⊆ I do  ▷ Reject borders
8:     b ← (m_k > Tb) ⊙ (m_n > Tb)
9:     b ← min(1 - b + εb, 1)
10:    `oreject` ← min(`oreject`, b)
11:  for i, j ∈ H × W do  ▷ Accept anomalous predictions
12:    `oaccept[i,j]` ← max_{n ∈ A} (m_n[i,j] · p_n[C+1])
13: return λ · `oreject` + (1 - λ) · `oaccept`  ▷ Interpolate reject and accept scores

We analyze the behavior of each mask individually. A query is considered specialized for class `c` if it predicts class `c` with probability 1−ε in over `Tquery` of cases. On a test set of Cityscapes [13] with `Tquery`=0.9 and ε=0.1, we found such specialized queries.

The challenge in finding void-class queries is differentiating between coherent void-class masks and noise. This is done by computing the average IoU of each mask with anomalies on a validation set and extracting queries with an average IoU larger than threshold `TIoU`. With this set of masks `A`, we compute a prediction that accepts predictions from masks associated with anomalies:

`oaccept[i,j] = max_{n ∈ A} (m_n[i,j] · p_n[C+1])` (2)

Maskomaly combines modules from Sec. 3.1 and 3.2.

**Maximal Detection Margin**

Chan et al. [7] argue for metrics beyond Average Precision, FPR95, and AuROC. Fig. 3 illustrates the issue with Average Precision; while Max. Entropy achieves a high AP, it assigns high scores to non-anomalous regions. Practical anomaly detection requires a threshold that effectively separates data. Our contribution is a new metric for anomaly detection that encourages more robust methods.

Maximal Detection Margin (MDM) requires a threshold `Tmargin` and a metric `d` measuring the difference between a binary ground-truth map `B` and a soft prediction `A` thresholded at multiple levels. MDM is the length of the largest interval in which all thresholds achieve at least `Tmargin` regarding metric `d`, normalized to [0,1]:

`MDM_{Tmargin}^{d}(A,B) = max_{0 ≤ x < y ≤ 1} (y - x) · 1{∀z ∈ [x,y] : d(A > z, B) > Tmargin}` (3)

Anomaly Segmentation aims to predict a dense map of outlier probabilities for a given image.
Methods average over multiple predictions [4, 44]. Other methods estimate uncertainty by computing the dissimilarity between the input and a resynthesized image [14, 39, 48], conditioned on semantic segmentation.
A recent work [1] trains a network to predict errors of a frozen semantic segmentation network, attacking it with FGSM [21] to stimulate failure.
GMMSeg [37] uses GMMs to capture class-conditional densities and train dense representations discriminatively.
Methods that train on auxiliary data include:
- Pebal [47]: Jointly optimizes pixel-wise anomaly abstention learning and energy-based models.
- DenseHybrid [25]: Utilizes discriminative and generative modeling simultaneously.
- Max. Entropy [8]: Learns to predict high entropy at anomalous regions and uses a meta-classifier to reduce false positives.

Mask-Based Approaches:
Outputs of mask-based segmentation networks are leveraged in [29] to detect anomaly bounding boxes using uncertainty in instance predictions.
[5] predicts anomaly presence based on the count of instance proposals.
In contrast, our method predicts a dense anomaly map for an image, assigning a continuous score to each pixel.
[19] segments anomalies by rejecting regions with known objects.

Figure 2: Maskomaly computes anomaly segmentation by combining two separate predictions.
Module Y uses class distribution P to identify inlier masks, constructing a prediction with low values within inlier masks or their borders.
Module X constructs a second prediction by assigning high probability to pixels in masks found to predict anomalies on a validation set (denoted by A).
The final prediction interpolates these two initial predictions with parameter λ.

Our method does not train one binary classifier per semantic class but uses a single semantic segmentation model. Rejecting known regions is one part; we also utilize "anomalous" masks as positive predictions.
Concurrent work [26] uses Mask2Former for anomaly segmentation, combining a score with a standard detector [32].
Another work [43] introduces a new metric for outlier detection training.
Our work contributes a complete post-processing method, does not use auxiliary data, and views masks as cohesive units.

Method
Given C semantic inlier classes, the goal is to receive an RGB image (H×W×3) and output a dense anomaly segmentation o=[0,1]H×W, assigning high values to anomalous regions and low values to inliers. Anomalies are objects not fitting into any of the C classes.
Our method utilizes intermediary outputs of any mask-based segmentation networks, specifically a set of soft-masks M={m1,...,mN} and probability vectors P={p1,...,pN}, where N is the number of masks and C+1 is the void class label.
A pixel [i,j] belongs to mask mk if k=argmax1≤n≤Nmn[i,j].
A mask mk belongs to an inlier class if argmax1≤l≤C+1pk[l]̸=C+1.
We use Mask2Former [12] with a Swin-L backbone trained on Cityscapes [13] as a high-performing mask-based segmentation network, but our method is not restricted to it.

Masks as Binary Classifiers
The segmentation network outputs class probabilities and mask scores. For C known classes, we expect at least one mask. Interpreting each mask as a binary classifier, a mask mi has a set of coordinates sTmask

paper1.title: On Advantages of Mask-level Recognition for Outlier-aware Segmentation
paper1.abstract:
Most dense recognition approaches bring a separate decision in each particular pixel. These approaches deliver
                        competitive performance in usual closed-set setups. However, important applications in the wild typically require
                        strong performance in presence of outliers. We show that
                        this demanding setup greatly benefit from mask-level predictions, even in the case of non-finetuned baseline models.
                        Moreover, we propose an alternative formulation of dense
                        recognition uncertainty that effectively reduces false positive responses at semantic borders. The proposed formulation produces a further improvement over a very strong
                        baseline and sets the new state of the art in outlier-aware
                        semantic segmentation with and without training on negative data. Our contributions also lead to performance improvement in a recent panoptic setup. In-depth experiments
                        confirm that our approach succeeds due to implicit aggregation of pixel-level cues into mask-level predictions.

**6. Conclusion**
Robust performance in the presence of outliers is crucial for scene understanding applications. Previous dense prediction approaches often fail due to their reliance on pixel-level OOD detection, neglecting correlations between neighboring pixels. This work addresses this by shifting OOD detection from pixels to regions, leveraging mask-level predictions to aggregate pixel-level evidence and increase the statistical power of anomaly scores. Performing OOD detection before ensembling decisions over masks further boosts performance. Injecting negative data into void content and extending mask-based models for panoptic inference in the presence of outliers further enhance results. Experiments demonstrate that mask-level outlier detection significantly outperforms pixel-level counterparts and achieves state-of-the-art AP performance among methods that do not train on real negative data. It also improves upon the previous state of the art in outlier-aware panoptic segmentation.

4.2. Outlier-aware panoptic segmentation on MS COCO

Mask-level outlier detection can be applied for panoptic segmentation. We consider the hardest setup from a recent related work [29] that relabels 20% of thing classes from COCO as void pixels during training. These classes include dining table, banana, bicycle, cake, sink, cat, keyboard, and bear. During inference, the model must classify all pixels from these classes into the dedicated anomalous thing class.

Outlier-aware performance is measured by standard metrics PQ, SQ, and RQ. Our models use a ResNet-50 backbone, consistent with previous work [29].

Mask-level training encourages all masks to avoid void pixels. Our anomaly detectors are sensitive to the resulting lack of mask assignment. Therefore, our supervision intensity is very similar to void-suppression [29]. Our inference recovers the dense anomaly map by thresholding the mask-level anomaly score. The threshold is validated for 95% TPR in outlier detection on a held-out validation image. Each anomalous pixel is assigned to its preferred mask, and instances are formed by keeping all masks with more than 200 pixels.

3.3. Detecting outliers in mask-level predictions
A method recovering dense anomaly scores as mask-level uncertainty of the strongest mask is considered first. Using max-softmax as the uncertainty measure, the score is formulated as:
$s_{AHM}^{ood}(x)[r, c] = -\max_{k=1...K} p_{\argmax_m i[r,c]}(Y=k|x)$. (5)
AHM stands for Anomaly score of Hard-assigned Masks. This approach ignores the uncertainty of the dominant mask assignment, which is suboptimal. Combining uncertainties of pixel-level mask assignment and mask-level recognition is pursued.

Closed-set semantic segmentation scores (3) are considered, quantifying their uncertainty using an arbitrary anomaly detector. With the max-logit detector [26], the score is:
$s_{AEM}^{ood}(x)[r, c] = -\max_{k=1...K} \sum_i m_i[r, c] \cdot p_i(Y=k|x)$. (6)
Closed-set semantic scores are viewed as ensembled outputs of per-mask classifiers, with mask assignments as weights. This score is denoted as Anomaly of Ensembled Mask-wide predictions (AEM).

Anomaly detector is applied directly to mask-level classification scores. Evidence in each pixel is aggregated according to its mask assignments $m$. This is interpreted as an Ensemble over Anomaly scores of Mask-wide predictions (EAM). This approach has intuitive appeal due to its direct relation to mask-level uncertainty. Quantifying mask-level uncertainty by maximum per-class probability yields a lower bound of the AEM score (6):
$s_{EAM}^{ood}(x)[r, c] = \sum_i m_i[r, c] \cdot (-\max_{k=1...K} p_i(Y=k|x)) \leq -\max_{k=1...K} \sum_i m_i[r, c] \cdot p_i(Y=k|x)$ (7)
Fig. 2 (right) illustrates EAM score computation from M2F outputs.

The difference between these approaches is expected to be most visible at semantic borders, where adjacent masks often lower pixel assignment confidence. In such situations, EAM correctly outputs a lower anomaly score than AEM. Fig. 4 illustrates EAM and AEM scoring differences on two scenes from Fishyscapes L&F. Similar behavior is observed in most image pixels, but EAM clearly outputs lower anomaly scores on semantic boundaries, reducing false positive detections in inlier pixels at these locations.
