Combining the proposed EAM outlier detector with negative supervision attains competitive results in outlier-aware semantic and panoptic segmentation. Further improvements can be obtained by combining the proposed approach with negative supervision. The resulting models set the new state of the art in outlier-aware segmentation on two tracks from the Segment Me If You Can (SMIYC) benchmark and adapted MS COCO.

2. Related work
The related work considers models for mask-level recognition tasks (Sec. 2.1) and segmentation in presence of outliers (Sec. 2.2).

2.1. Recognition of free-form regions
Early approaches to mask-wide recognition relied on class-agnostic bottom-up proposals. They aggregated handcrafted [9] or convolutional [19, 25, 51] features along proposed regions and made mask-wide decisions by classifying pooled representations. Mask-RCNN extends this approach by sharing features across proposal detection and mask-wide classification, as well as by end-to-end training of all parameters. PointRend proposes to back-propagate the loss only through selected low-uncertainty predictions [33]. This allows increasing Mask-RCNN resolution from 28×28 to 224×224 with negligible impact on training footprint. MaskFormer precludes dependence on bottom-up proposals by directly assigning pixels to masks that span arbitrary image regions [17]. Its key component is a hypernetwork [24] that produces weights for two 1×1 convolutions that convert pixel-level embeddings into mask assignment scores and subsequently into semantic maps. This is the first architecture to deliver competitive experimental performance on semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and panoptic segmentation. Mask2Former [16] further improves the mask hypernetwork by introducing a special attention layer that promotes progressive focusing onto foreground pixels for a particular mask. Our work explores Mask2Former performance in the context of outlier-aware segmentation and outlier-aware panoptic segmentation.

2.2. Segmentation in presence of outliers
Recognition in the wild involves test regions beyond the training taxonomy. Adequate models should reject decisions in such pixels [54]. This can be done by restricting the shape of the decision boundary [1, 55] or by complementing the classifier with an anomaly detector [27, 38]. The decision boundary can be restricted by thresholding distance from learned class centers in the embedding space [10, 55]. This can be further improved by employing a stronger classifier [58]. However, many of these approaches fail if unknown samples map to the same features as samples from known classes, an occurrence known as feature collapse [45].

Early approaches for extending discriminative predictions with OOD detection have been based on prediction confidence [27], input perturbations [38], density estimation [48], and Bayesian uncertainty [47]. Semantic anomalies [53] are noted as especially hard to detect [32, 48, 56]. Generating synthetic anomalies in tandem with the discriminative task is a promising approach [13, 22, 35, 63]. Further empirical improvements have been achieved by mimicking anomalies with negative training data [28, 42]. However, this may lead to over-optimistic performance estimates due to possible overlap with test anomalies.

Outlier detection is especially interesting in dense prediction due to applications in robust scene understanding [7, 11, 62]. However, straightforward adaptations of image-wide approaches experience two failure modes: they often fail to accurately localize anomalies in front of inlier backgrounds [3], and they are prone to false positives in inlier pixels with high entropy predictions at semantic borders [52]. Therefore, much work proposes custom designs to alleviate these problems.

Partially anomalous images can be accounted for by learning on mixed-content images [3, 5, 23, 57]. Correlation between neighboring pixels can be addressed by aggregating evidence through meta-classification [52] or input preprocessing [38]. Real training data can be avoided by fitting generative heads to pre-trained [7] or jointly trained [29, 37] features. Another line of work trains on synthetic negatives corresponding to adversarial noise [2] or samples of a jointly trained generative model [21]. Finally, some approaches detect the discrepancy between the input and the resynthesized scene [5, 41, 59, 60].

Our work formulates outlier detection according to mask-wide predictions. Unlike meta-classification approaches [12, 52], our method requires only one learning episode and does not require neg

paper2.title: A Simple Unified Framework for Detecting Out-of-Distribution Samples and Adversarial Attacks
paper2.abstract:
Detecting test samples drawn sufficiently far away from the training distribution
                        statistically or adversarially is a fundamental requirement for deploying a good
                        classifier in many real-world machine learning applications. However, deep neural networks with the softmax classifier are known to produce highly overconfident
                        posterior distributions even for such abnormal samples. In this paper, we propose
                        a simple yet effective method for detecting any abnormal samples, which is applicable to any pre-trained softmax neural classifier. We obtain the class conditional
                        Gaussian distributions with respect to (low- and upper-level) features of the deep
                        models under Gaussian discriminant analysis, which result in a confidence score
                        based on the Mahalanobis distance. While most prior methods have been evaluated for detecting either out-of-distribution or adversarial samples, but not both,
                        the proposed method achieves the state-of-the-art performances for both cases in
                        our experiments. Moreover, we found that our proposed method is more robust
                        in harsh cases, e.g., when the training dataset has noisy labels or small number of
                        samples. Finally, we show that the proposed method enjoys broader usage by applying it to class-incremental learning: whenever out-of-distribution samples are
                        detected, our classification rule can incorporate new classes well without further
                        training deep models.
methodology:
A confidence score M(x) is computed on a test sample x. If M(x) is above a threshold, it is classified as positive (in-distribution). The Euclidean distance, using only empirical class means, is used for comparison. ResNet is trained on CIFAR-10. Tiny-ImageNet is used as an out-of-distribution dataset. The Mahalanobis distance-based metric outperforms the Euclidean and maximum softmax score methods.

Calibration Techniques:
Input pre-processing involves adding controlled noise to test samples. For each test sample x, a pre-processed sample bx is calculated:
bx = x + εsign(▽xM(x)) = x − εsign(▽x(f(x) − bµbc)⊤bΣ−1(f(x) − bµbc))
Here, ε is the noise magnitude, and bc is the index of the closest class. The confidence score is then measured using bx. This noise is generated to increase the confidence score, not for adversarial attacks. This perturbation can better separate in- and out-of-distribution samples. Similar input pre-processing in [21] aims to increase the softmax score of the predicted label. Our method differs as the noise is generated to increase the proposed metric.

Algorithm 2: Updating Mahalanobis distance-based classifier for class-incremental learning.
Input: Samples from a new class {xi : ∀i = 1 . . . NC+1}, means and covariances of observed classes {bµc : ∀c = 1 . . . C}, bΣ
1. Compute the new class mean: bµC+1 ← 1/NC+1 * Σ_i f(xi)
2. Compute the covariance of the new class: bΣC+1 ← 1/NC+1 * Σ_i (f(xi) − bµC+1)(f(xi) − bµC+1)⊤
3. Update the shared covariance: bΣ ← (C/(C+1)) * bΣ + (1/(C+1)) * bΣC+1
Output: Means and covariances of all classes {bµc : ∀c = 1 . . . C + 1}, bΣ

Feature ensemble: To enhance performance, confidence scores from low-level features, in addition to final features, are measured and combined. For training data, ℓ-th hidden features fℓ(x) are extracted, and their empirical class means bµℓ,c and tied covariances bΣℓ are computed. For each test sample x, the confidence score from the ℓ-th layer is measured using formula (2). This method can improve calibration by extracting more input-specific information from low-level features. The area under ROC (AUROC) curves for a threshold-based detector using confidence scores from different basic blocks of DenseNet trained on CIFAR-10 are measured. Similar trends are observed on ResNet. Performance on various OOD samples (SVHN, LSUN, TinyImageNet, and adversarial samples from DeepFool) is shown in Figure 2. Intermediate feature dimensions are reduced using average pooling. Confidence scores from low-level features often provide better calibration than final features (e.g., for LSUN, TinyImageNet, and DeepFool). A feature ensemble method is designed to further improve performance. Confidence scores from all layers are extracted and integrated by weighted averaging: Σℓ αℓMℓ(x), where Mℓ(·) is the confidence score at the ℓ-th layer and αℓ is its weight. Weights are chosen by training a logistic regression detector on validation samples. This weighted averaging of confidence scores can prevent performance degradation if some layer scores are ineffective; their trained weights would be near zero.

Class-incremental learning using Mahalanobis distance-based score: The Mahalanobis distance-based confidence score can be used in class-incremental learning. A classifier pre-trained on base classes is updated with new classes and samples. This is challenging due to catastrophic forgetting and limited memory. Existing methods often involve generative models or data sampling, which can be computationally expensive. Based on the proposed confidence score, a simple classification method is developed without complex training. It assumes the classifier is well-trained.

**3.3 Class-Incremental Learning**

**Setup:**
*   ResNet-34 is trained for CIFAR-100 and downsampled ImageNet classification.
*   A classifier is pre-trained on base classes; new classes are incrementally added.
*   **Scenario 1:** Half of CIFAR-100 classes are base, the rest are new.
*   **Scenario 2:** All CIFAR-100 classes are base, 100 ImageNet classes are new.
*   All scenarios are tested five times and averaged. Class splits are randomly generated per trial.
*   **Comparison Methods:**
    *   Softmax classifier (fine-tuned for new classes, only softmax layer updated for near-zero cost training).
    *   Euclidean classifier (accommodates new classes by computing class mean).
*   **Memory Management (Softmax Classifier):** Follows Rebuffi & Kolesnikov [29]. A small number of old class samples are kept in memory. Memory size matches that for Mahalanobis distance-based classifier (sum of learned classes and hidden feature dimension, 512 in experiments).
*   **Evaluation:**
    *   Base-new class accuracy curve adjusted by a bias to new class scores (similar to [18]).
    *   Area Under Curve (AUC) measured to provide an imbalanced measure of performance.

**Comparison with Other Classifiers:**
*   Figure 4 compares incremental learning performance (AUC) in two scenarios.
*   Each sub-figure shows AUC vs. number of learned classes (left) and base-new class accuracy curve after last new class addition (right).
*   Mahalanobis distance-based classifier (ours) significantly outperforms other methods, especially as the number of new classes increases.
*   A crossing is observed in the right figure of Figure 4(b) in small regimes due to catastrophic forgetting.
*   **AUC Performance:**
    *   Our method: 40.0% (22.1%)
    *   Softmax classifier: 32.7% (15.6%)
    *   Euclidean distance classifier: 32.9% (17.1%)
    *   (First experiment (Second experiment) results)
*   Similar trends observed when CIFAR-100 classes are base and CIFAR-10 classes are new (reported in supplementary material).
*   Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our confidence score compared to others.

**4 Conclusion**
*   Propose a simple yet effective method for detecting abnormal test samples (out-of-distribution and adversarial).
*   Core idea: Induce a generative classifier under LDA assumption and define a new confidence score.
*   With calibration techniques (input pre-processing, feature ensemble), the method performs strongly across tasks: OOD detection, adversarial attack detection, and class-incremental learning.
*   Method is more robust to hyperparameter choices and extreme scenarios (noisy labels, small datasets).
*   Approach has potential for broader application.

C
More experimental results
C.1
Robustness of our method in detecting adversarial samples
To verify robustness, we measured detection performance by training ResNet on CIFAR-10 with varying numbers of training data and random labels. Our method (blue bar) outperforms LID (green bar) across all experiments (Figure 5).
C.2
Class-incremental learning
Figure 6 compares AUCs when CIFAR-100 is pre-trained and CIFAR-10 serves as new classes. Our Mahalanobis distance-based classifier significantly outperforms others as the number of new classes increases. With all new classes added, our method achieves an AUC of 47.7%, compared to 41.0% for the softmax classifier and 43.0% for the Euclidean distance classifier.
C.3
Experimental results on joint confidence loss
The proposed detector using a softmax neural classifier trained with standard cross-entropy loss typically outperforms the ODIN detector, which uses a softmax classifier trained with confidence loss [19]. Our detector further improves performance when used with a model trained by confidence loss, indicating our method enhances any pre-trained softmax neural classifier.

paper1.abstract:
With the emergence of transformer-based architectures and large
                        language models (LLMs), the accuracy of road scene perception has
                        substantially advanced. Nonetheless, current road scene segmentation approaches are predominantly trained on closed-set data,
                        resulting in insufficient detection capabilities for out-of-distribution
                        (OOD) objects. To overcome this limitation, road anomaly detection
                        methods have been proposed. However, existing methods primarily depend on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection
                        techniques, facing two critical issues: (1) inadequate consideration of the objectiveness attributes of anomalous regions, causing incomplete segmentation when anomalous objects share similarities
                        with known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, leading to the detection of anomalies irrelevant
                        to autonomous driving tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel
                        framework termed Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness
                        (SOTA) for autonomous driving scenes. Specifically, SOTA enhances
                        the segmentation of objectiveness through a Semantic Fusion Block
                        (SFB) and filters anomalies irrelevant to road navigation tasks using
                        a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA).
                        Extensive empirical evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets, including Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and
                        RoadAnomaly, demonstrate that the proposed SOTA consistently
                        improves OOD detection performance across diverse detectors,
                        achieving robust and accurate segmentation outcomes.

Pixel-level Results. As summarized in Table 6, our method significantly outperforms the baseline RbA [35] and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets. Similarly, on RO-21, our method yields an 8.00% improvement in PPV and a 9.55% increase in F1*. In contrast, SOTA delivers more accurate and comprehensive segmentation of OOD objects while effectively suppressing extraneous pixel predictions beyond the road area. Abstract
Transformer-based architectures and large language models (LLMs) have advanced road scene perception accuracy. However, current road scene segmentation approaches are trained on closed-set data, limiting detection of out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Road anomaly detection methods exist but rely on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection, facing two issues: (1) inadequate consideration of anomalous region objectiveness, leading to incomplete segmentation when anomalies resemble known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, causing detection of anomalies irrelevant to autonomous driving. This paper proposes a novel framework, Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness (SOTA), for autonomous driving. SOTA enhances objectiveness segmentation with a Semantic Fusion Block (SFB) and filters irrelevant anomalies using a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA). Evaluations on Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and RoadAnomaly datasets show SOTA consistently improves OOD detection performance and achieves robust segmentation.

Task-aware Aggregation Module:
1. Identifies road class from semantic segmentation output.
2. Generates a binary road mask.
3. Refines mask using a 15x15 convolutional kernel filled with ones, applied iteratively 15 times.
4. Each iteration involves padded convolution followed by thresholding at 0 to maintain binary format.
5. Results in an expanded road prompt $y_t$ capturing uncertain boundary regions.

Projection and Alignment Module:
Projection Module:
1. Lightweight learnable convolutional sub-network.
2. Transforms raw OoD confidence map into an intermediate semantic representation.
3. Input: 1x256x256 single-channel.
4. Processed through two 2x2 convolutional layers with stride 2.
5. Spatial resolution reduced to 64x64.
6. Channel dimension expanded to 16.
7. Each layer followed by LayerNorm and GELU activation.
8. Output feature map shape: 16x64x64.

Alignment Module:
1. Aligns intermediate semantic features with image encoder's representation.
2. Applies a final 1x1 convolutional layer.
3. Maps 16-channel feature map to a 256-dimensional embedding.
4. Preserves spatial structure.
5. Output tensor shape: 256x64x64.
6. Used for downstream fusion with image features.

Outlier Exposure:
1. Training dataset preparation uses Outlier Exposure (OE) strategy.
2. Cityscapes dataset used as inlier background (2,975 training images).
3. Objects selected from COCO dataset as OoD objects (excluding categories overlapping with Cityscapes).
4. COCO objects pasted onto Cityscapes images with 0.9 probability per image to simulate anomaly scenarios.
5. RbA framework [35] applied to composite images to compute anomaly scores and semantic logits.

paper2.title: Maskomaly:Zero-Shot Mask Anomaly Segmentation
paper2.abstract:
We present a simple and practical framework for anomaly segmentation called Maskomaly.
                        It builds upon mask-based standard semantic segmentation networks by adding a simple
                        inference-time post-processing step which leverages the raw mask outputs of such networks.
                        Maskomaly does not require additional training and only adds a small computational overhead
                        to inference. Most importantly, it does not require anomalous data at training. We show top
                        results for our method on SMIYC, RoadAnomaly, and StreetHazards. On the most central
                        benchmark, SMIYC1
                        , Maskomaly outperforms all directly comparable approaches. Further,
                        we introduce a novel metric that benefits the development of robust anomaly segmentation
                        methods and demonstrate its informativeness on RoadAnomaly.

Ablations
Individual Components:
The influence of individual algorithm parts is evaluated by removing them one at a time. A straightforward baseline leveraging Mask2Former outputs is included.
This baseline computes basline[i,j] based on the maximum value among Nmn[i,j] and the class index of the maximum value.

Datasets:

RoadAnomaly [39]: 60 images, 30 of which are also in SMIYC’s test set. Internet-sourced street scenes with anomalies.

Metrics:
Average Precision (AP)

Hyperparameters:
Semantic segmentation Mask2Former model [12] with Swin-L [41] backbone, trained on CityScapes [13].
SMIYC [7] validation set used for all experiments.
Method is not sensitive to hyperparameter values due to robust Mask2Former predictions.
RoadAnomaly [39]: >85% of masks assigned to a class with confidence ≥0.9, suggesting Tmask ≤0.9 is suitable.
93% of pixels in soft mask membership maps have a score ≤0.1; from the remaining, 80% have a score ≥0.9, indicating Tb ≥0.1 is good for separating "border" from "core" pixels.
λ choice based on most likely prior (non-anomalies) for symmetry, thus λ >0.5 optimizes for AP.
Experimental settings: λ = 0.6, TIoU = 0.25, Tmask = 0.3, Tb = 0.1, εb = 0.001, Tquery=0.9.
Initialization of I includes queries influenced by ambiguous ground labeling [13], indexed by IoU with street predictions on SMIYC [7] validation set.

To avoid overconfident predictions, we scale the output by the uncertainty of the dominant mask, resulting in a softer assignment:

`oreject[i,j] = min_{n ∈ I} (1 - m_n[i,j] * max_{1 ≤ l ≤ C} p_n[l])` (1)

Other methods assign high outlier scores at the boundaries of two inlier classes. By computing the pairwise intersection of inlier class masks after thresholding them at `Tb`, we identify these areas and assign them an outlier score `εb`.

**Anomalous Masks**

Despite the simplicity of the rejection-based approach, domain shifts can cause failures. Similar to [26], on FishyScapes LaF [4], over 50% of outlier pixels belong to an inlier mask, suggesting sub-optimal performance of `oreject`.

**Algorithm 1 Maskomaly, Hyperparameters = {Tmask, Tb, εb, λ}**

1: function MASKOMALY(M, P, A, I)
2:   for 1 ≤ n ≤ N do  ▷ Add inlier masks to I
3:     if (argmax_{1 ≤ l ≤ C+1} p_n[l]) ≠ C+1 ∧ (max_{1 ≤ l ≤ C+1} p_n[l]) ≥ Tmask then
4:       I ← I ∪ {n}
5:   for i, j ∈ H × W do  ▷ Reject inlier pixels
6:     `oreject[i,j]` ← min_{n ∈ I} (1 - m_n[i,j] · max_{1 ≤ l ≤ C} p_n[l])
7:   for {k, n} ⊆ I do  ▷ Reject borders
8:     b ← (m_k > Tb) ⊙ (m_n > Tb)
9:     b ← min(1 - b + εb, 1)
10:    `oreject` ← min(`oreject`, b)
11:  for i, j ∈ H × W do  ▷ Accept anomalous predictions
12:    `oaccept[i,j]` ← max_{n ∈ A} (m_n[i,j] · p_n[C+1])
13: return λ · `oreject` + (1 - λ) · `oaccept`  ▷ Interpolate reject and accept scores

We analyze the behavior of each mask individually. A query is considered specialized for class `c` if it predicts class `c` with probability 1−ε in over `Tquery` of cases. On a test set of Cityscapes [13] with `Tquery`=0.9 and ε=0.1, we found such specialized queries.

The challenge in finding void-class queries is differentiating between coherent void-class masks and noise. This is done by computing the average IoU of each mask with anomalies on a validation set and extracting queries with an average IoU larger than threshold `TIoU`. With this set of masks `A`, we compute a prediction that accepts predictions from masks associated with anomalies:

`oaccept[i,j] = max_{n ∈ A} (m_n[i,j] · p_n[C+1])` (2)

Maskomaly combines modules from Sec. 3.1 and 3.2.

**Maximal Detection Margin**

Chan et al. [7] argue for metrics beyond Average Precision, FPR95, and AuROC. Fig. 3 illustrates the issue with Average Precision; while Max. Entropy achieves a high AP, it assigns high scores to non-anomalous regions. Practical anomaly detection requires a threshold that effectively separates data. Our contribution is a new metric for anomaly detection that encourages more robust methods.

Maximal Detection Margin (MDM) requires a threshold `Tmargin` and a metric `d` measuring the difference between a binary ground-truth map `B` and a soft prediction `A` thresholded at multiple levels. MDM is the length of the largest interval in which all thresholds achieve at least `Tmargin` regarding metric `d`, normalized to [0,1]:

`MDM_{Tmargin}^{d}(A,B) = max_{0 ≤ x < y ≤ 1} (y - x) · 1{∀z ∈ [x,y] : d(A > z, B) > Tmargin}` (3)

**Experimental Setup**

*   **FishyScapes [4] Static:** Dataset based on inserting objects from Pascal VOC [16] into Cityscapes [13] images. Includes 1000 test images and 30 validation images.

A baseline leverages Mask2Former outputs:
$obaseline[i,j]=

\max_{1 \leq n \leq N} m_{n}[i,j], & \text{if } \underset{1 \leq l \leq C+1}{\operatorname{argmax}} m_{n}[i,j][l]=C+1 \\
1 - \max_{1 \leq n \leq N} m_{n}[i,j], & \text{otherwise.}

This baseline checks each pixel individually for belonging to an anomalous mask. It assigns the probability of belonging to class C+1 or one minus the probability of belonging to its predicted inlier class.

Table 4 shows the performance of ablated models and the baseline (Id 1) on the RoadAnomaly dataset and SMIYC test set. All ablated methods outperform the baseline. Individual components perform better than PEBAL [47] or DenseHybrid [25] without outlier supervision. Rejecting border regions significantly reduces FPR95. Combining rejection and acceptance yields the largest improvement, indicating component complementarity. The mask-based approach allows acting on masks as a coherent component. Initializing I with masks that predict the ambiguous ground class [13] significantly gains AP and reduces FPR95, leading to the complete Maskomaly method (Id 6). This initialization has a high impact on RoadAnomaly [39] as anomalies are located on streets or ground.

Fig. 5 shows a complete performance image. Individual components exhibit less smooth curves than methods like Max Entropy, due to considering masks at a component level and potentially activating entire regions with slight threshold increases. Maskomaly (Id 6) has a smoother curve and its graph lies above all individual component combinations (Id 2-5). Handling borders (Id 4) in addition to rejecting areas (Id 3) only shows separation in the higher recall range, where the borderless version slightly loses.

Method:
To demonstrate the algorithm's impact decoupled from its backbone, it is compared to state-of-the-art methods paired with Mask2Former [12]. Three other methods are built around mask-based segmentation outputs. For comparison against fine-tuned Mask2Former methods, see Nayal et al. [43]. Table 5 presents results of EAM [26], RbA [43], M2A [45], and our method on the SMIYC test set. Our method performs best among those not resorting to auxiliary data. Although EAM and RbA benefit from training with anomalous data, our method keeps pace in AP and FPR95, as well as PPV. Our method is only 1.1% behind the current best method in AP.

Anomaly Segmentation aims to predict a dense map of outlier probabilities for a given image.
Methods average over multiple predictions [4, 44]. Other methods estimate uncertainty by computing the dissimilarity between the input and a resynthesized image [14, 39, 48], conditioned on semantic segmentation.
A recent work [1] trains a network to predict errors of a frozen semantic segmentation network, attacking it with FGSM [21] to stimulate failure.
GMMSeg [37] uses GMMs to capture class-conditional densities and train dense representations discriminatively.
Methods that train on auxiliary data include:
- Pebal [47]: Jointly optimizes pixel-wise anomaly abstention learning and energy-based models.
- DenseHybrid [25]: Utilizes discriminative and generative modeling simultaneously.
- Max. Entropy [8]: Learns to predict high entropy at anomalous regions and uses a meta-classifier to reduce false positives.

Mask-Based Approaches:
Outputs of mask-based segmentation networks are leveraged in [29] to detect anomaly bounding boxes using uncertainty in instance predictions.
[5] predicts anomaly presence based on the count of instance proposals.
In contrast, our method predicts a dense anomaly map for an image, assigning a continuous score to each pixel.
[19] segments anomalies by rejecting regions with known objects.

Figure 2: Maskomaly computes anomaly segmentation by combining two separate predictions.
Module Y uses class distribution P to identify inlier masks, constructing a prediction with low values within inlier masks or their borders.
Module X constructs a second prediction by assigning high probability to pixels in masks found to predict anomalies on a validation set (denoted by A).
The final prediction interpolates these two initial predictions with parameter λ.

Our method does not train one binary classifier per semantic class but uses a single semantic segmentation model. Rejecting known regions is one part; we also utilize "anomalous" masks as positive predictions.
Concurrent work [26] uses Mask2Former for anomaly segmentation, combining a score with a standard detector [32].
Another work [43] introduces a new metric for outlier detection training.
Our work contributes a complete post-processing method, does not use auxiliary data, and views masks as cohesive units.

Method
Given C semantic inlier classes, the goal is to receive an RGB image (H×W×3) and output a dense anomaly segmentation o=[0,1]H×W, assigning high values to anomalous regions and low values to inliers. Anomalies are objects not fitting into any of the C classes.
Our method utilizes intermediary outputs of any mask-based segmentation networks, specifically a set of soft-masks M={m1,...,mN} and probability vectors P={p1,...,pN}, where N is the number of masks and C+1 is the void class label.
A pixel [i,j] belongs to mask mk if k=argmax1≤n≤Nmn[i,j].
A mask mk belongs to an inlier class if argmax1≤l≤C+1pk[l]̸=C+1.
We use Mask2Former [12] with a Swin-L backbone trained on Cityscapes [13] as a high-performing mask-based segmentation network, but our method is not restricted to it.

Masks as Binary Classifiers
The segmentation network outputs class probabilities and mask scores. For C known classes, we expect at least one mask. Interpreting each mask as a binary classifier, a mask mi has a set of coordinates sTmask

topic: Image segmentation anomaly detection aims to identify and segment unusual or unexpected regions in images, supporting safety-critical applications in medical imaging, manufacturing, and autonomous systems. What is the better method for image segmentation anomaly detection tasks: SOTA-RbA or ObsNet?

paper1.title: Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-awareness Unknown Region for Autonomous Driving
paper1.abstract:
With the emergence of transformer-based architectures and large
                        language models (LLMs), the accuracy of road scene perception has
                        substantially advanced. Nonetheless, current road scene segmentation approaches are predominantly trained on closed-set data,
                        resulting in insufficient detection capabilities for out-of-distribution
                        (OOD) objects. To overcome this limitation, road anomaly detection
                        methods have been proposed. However, existing methods primarily depend on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection
                        techniques, facing two critical issues: (1) inadequate consideration of the objectiveness attributes of anomalous regions, causing incomplete segmentation when anomalous objects share similarities
                        with known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, leading to the detection of anomalies irrelevant
                        to autonomous driving tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel
                        framework termed Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness
                        (SOTA) for autonomous driving scenes. Specifically, SOTA enhances
                        the segmentation of objectiveness through a Semantic Fusion Block
                        (SFB) and filters anomalies irrelevant to road navigation tasks using
                        a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA).
                        Extensive empirical evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets, including Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and
                        RoadAnomaly, demonstrate that the proposed SOTA consistently
                        improves OOD detection performance across diverse detectors,
                        achieving robust and accurate segmentation outcomes.
methodology:
demonstrates superior segmentation quality by providing more complete and accurate identification of OOD objects while effectively reducing redundant pixel predictions beyond the road region.

4.2 Main Results
Pixel-level Results. As summarized in Table 6, our method significantly outperforms the baseline RbA [35] and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets. While RPL+CoroCL [28] achieves slightly better AuROC and FPR on the Fishyscapes Lost&Found dataset, SOTA improves the AuPRC by a significant margin of 5.5% compared to RPL+CoroCL. Furthermore, SOTA consistently outperforms RPL+CoroCL across all other datasets.

Component-level Results. Table 2 presents the component-level evaluation on the SMIYC RA-21 and SMIYC RO-21 benchmarks. Compared to RbA, our method achieves substantial improvements on RA-21, including a 5.58% increase in sIoU, an 18.31% boost in PPV, and a 14.67% gain in F1*. Similarly, on RO-21, our method yields an 8.00% improvement in PPV and a 9.55% increase in F1*. While Mask2Anomaly achieves a higher performance on RO-21, our approach surpasses it on RA-21, achieving a 0.88% improvement in sIoU and a 12.87% increase in F1*. Moreover, while ContMAV achieves higher PPV and F1* scores on RA-21, it does not report results on RO-21, whereas our approach consistently enhances performance across both datasets.

Qualitative Results. Figure 3 presents a visual comparison of anomaly segmentation results produced by three representative methods: RPL [28], RbA [35], and our proposed method SOTA. In the figure, the first column shows the original input images, while the subsequent columns display the corresponding anomaly maps of various approaches. It can be observed that RPL tends to generate diffused predictions with substantial false positives, particularly along object boundaries and in areas outside the road region. Although RbA improves upon RPL by offering sharper delineation, it still suffers from incomplete segmentation and residual noise. In contrast, SOTA delivers more accurate and comprehensive segmentation of OOD objects while effectively suppressing extraneous pixel predictions beyond the road area. These qualitative findings underscore the advantages of our approach, which unifies attribute-aware feature learning and scene-guided context modeling to achieve a superior balance between precise anomaly localization and noise reduction.

Abstract
Transformer-based architectures and large language models (LLMs) have advanced road scene perception accuracy. However, current road scene segmentation approaches are trained on closed-set data, limiting detection of out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Road anomaly detection methods exist but rely on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection, facing two issues: (1) inadequate consideration of anomalous region objectiveness, leading to incomplete segmentation when anomalies resemble known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, causing detection of anomalies irrelevant to autonomous driving. This paper proposes a novel framework, Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness (SOTA), for autonomous driving. SOTA enhances objectiveness segmentation with a Semantic Fusion Block (SFB) and filters irrelevant anomalies using a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA). Evaluations on Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and RoadAnomaly datasets show SOTA consistently improves OOD detection performance and achieves robust segmentation.

Task-aware Aggregation Module:
1. Identifies road class from semantic segmentation output.
2. Generates a binary road mask.
3. Refines mask using a 15x15 convolutional kernel filled with ones, applied iteratively 15 times.
4. Each iteration involves padded convolution followed by thresholding at 0 to maintain binary format.
5. Results in an expanded road prompt $y_t$ capturing uncertain boundary regions.

Projection and Alignment Module:
Projection Module:
1. Lightweight learnable convolutional sub-network.
2. Transforms raw OoD confidence map into an intermediate semantic representation.
3. Input: 1x256x256 single-channel.
4. Processed through two 2x2 convolutional layers with stride 2.
5. Spatial resolution reduced to 64x64.
6. Channel dimension expanded to 16.
7. Each layer followed by LayerNorm and GELU activation.
8. Output feature map shape: 16x64x64.

Alignment Module:
1. Aligns intermediate semantic features with image encoder's representation.
2. Applies a final 1x1 convolutional layer.
3. Maps 16-channel feature map to a 256-dimensional embedding.
4. Preserves spatial structure.
5. Output tensor shape: 256x64x64.
6. Used for downstream fusion with image features.

Outlier Exposure:
1. Training dataset preparation uses Outlier Exposure (OE) strategy.
2. Cityscapes dataset used as inlier background (2,975 training images).
3. Objects selected from COCO dataset as OoD objects (excluding categories overlapping with Cityscapes).
4. COCO objects pasted onto Cityscapes images with 0.9 probability per image to simulate anomaly scenarios.
5. RbA framework [35] applied to composite images to compute anomaly scores and semantic logits.

paper2.title: Triggering Failures: Out-Of-Distribution detection by learning from local adversarial attacks in Semantic Segmentation
paper2.abstract:
In this paper, we tackle the detection of out-of-distribution
                        (OOD) objects in semantic segmentation. By analyzing the
                        literature, we found that current methods are either accurate or fast but not both which limits their usability in real
                        world applications. To get the best of both aspects, we propose to mitigate the common shortcomings by following four
                        design principles: decoupling the OOD detection from the
                        segmentation task, observing the entire segmentation network instead of just its output, generating training data for
                        the OOD detector by leveraging blind spots in the segmentation network and focusing the generated data on localized
                        regions in the image to simulate OOD objects. Our main contribution is a new OOD detection architecture called ObsNet
                        associated with a dedicated training scheme based on Local
                        Adversarial Attacks (LAA). We validate the soundness of our
                        approach across numerous ablation studies. We also show it
                        obtains top performances both in speed and accuracy when
                        compared to ten recent methods of the literature on three
                        different datasets.
methodology:
MCDA: Data augmentation (geometric, color transformations) during inference. Uses entropy of 25 forward passes.
MC Dropout: Entropy of mean softmax prediction with dropout. Uses 50 forward passes.
Gaussian Perturbation Ensemble: Perturbs pre-trained network weights with a random Normal distribution, creating an ensemble centered around the pre-trained model.
ConﬁdNet: An observer network trained to predict the true class score. Uses online code, modifies data loader.
Temperature Scaling: Hyperparameters chosen for best calibration on validation set. Uses 1 minus the maximum of scaled prediction.
ODIN: Test-time adversarial attacks on the primary network. Hyperparameters Temp and ϵ chosen for best performance on validation set. Criterion is 1 minus the maximum prediction.
Deep ensemble: A small ensemble of 3 networks. Uses entropy of averaged forward passes.

Uncertainty maps show ObsNet produces stronger responses on OOD regions and highlights areas with wrong predictions (edges, small/far objects). Trade-off between accuracy and speed is excellent without compromise.

Conclusion: ObsNet, an observer network, addresses OOD detection in semantic segmentation by learning from triggered failures. Skip connections allow the observer to seek abnormal behavior within the main network. Local adversarial attacks trigger failures to train the observer network. This strategy combining an observer network with local adversarial attacks is fast, accurate, and detects unknown objects.

Implementation details & hyper-parameters
We use Pytorch3. Hyper-parameters are in Table 9. We train ObsNet with SGD, momentum, and weight decay for at most 50 epochs using early-stopping. ObsNet weights are initialized with those of the segmentation network. We use a scheduler to divide the learning rate by 2 at epoch 25 and epoch 45. We use the same data augmentation (Horizontal Flip and Random Crop) for training the segmentation network and ObsNet. We increase the weight of positive examples in the loss contribution (Pos Weight in Table 9).

Metrics for evaluating methods:
◦ fpr95tpr [32]: Measures the false positive rate when the true positive rate is 95%. Aim is to obtain the lowest possible false positive rate.
◦ Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AuRoc) [25]: Threshold-free metric corresponding to the probability that an example has a higher value than an uncertain one.
◦ Area under the Precision-Recall Curve (AuPR) [25]: Threshold-independent metric, less sensitive to unbalanced datasets than AuRoc.
◦ Adaptive Calibration Error (ACE) [47]: Adapts the range of each bin to focus more on the region where most predictions are made.
For all segmentation experiments, a Bayesian SegNet [2], [28] is used as the main network. ObsNet follows the same architecture as this SegNet. Ablation studies on architecture, hyperparameters, and training details are in the supplementary material.

Key requirements for a real-time safety OOD detector: accuracy, speed, easy training, and memory efficiency.
Our method addresses all requirements.
LAA is performed only at train time and mitigates imbalance in the training data for the observer.

Pseudo-ensemble approaches bypass training multiple networks, generating predictions from different random subsets of neurons or networks sampled from approximate weight distributions. They require multiple forward passes and/or storage of additional networks.
Our ObsNet is faster than ensembles, requiring the equivalent of two forward passes.

Deterministic networks that output predictive distributions trade predictive performance over computational efficiency, with results potentially matching MC Dropout for uncertainty estimation.

ODIN uses temperature scaling and small adversarial perturbations on the input at test-time for OOD detection. Lee et al. [31] extend this with a confidence score based on class-conditional Mahalanobis distance. These approaches work best with train OOD data for tuning but may not generalize. ODIN uses adversarial attacks at test time, which is not effective for structured output tasks due to per-pixel attack costs. Our method uses adversarial attacks during training as a proxy for OOD training samples, with no additional test-time cost.

Methods inspired by model calibration literature propose endowing the task network with an error prediction branch. Joint training is possible, but two-stage sequential training yields better stability and results. Our ObsNet uses an auxiliary network trained in two stages to learn from task network failure modes. While some methods focus on in-distribution errors, we address OOD detection without available training data. We generate failures for generalization to OOD detection by redesigning the training procedure and auxiliary network architecture, introducing Local Adversarial Attack (LAA).

Generic approaches:
- Maximum class probability from softmax prediction can be used for OOD detection.
- Temperature scaling is a post-hoc calibration strategy for softmax predictions using a validation set. Thresholding calibrated scores can detect OOD samples.
- Pre-training with adversarial attacked images can lead to better calibrated predictions and good OOD detection for image classification. These are considered baselines.

Proposed Method:
Our OOD semantic segmentation method is based on:
(i) Architecture: Decouple OOD detection from segmentation prediction for maximal accuracy in both tasks.
(ii) Training: Train an OOD detector without OOD data by generating training data with carefully designed adversarial attacks.

OOD detection without compromising predictive accuracy and computational time.
Four design principles:
(i) Architecture:
    (i.a) Decouple OOD detection from segmentation to alleviate trading accuracy for OOD robustness.
    (i.b) Observe the entire segmentation network, not just its output, to improve OOD detection accuracy.
(ii) Training:
    (ii.a) Generate additional training data for OOD detectors by leveraging segmentation network blind spots.
    (ii.b) Focus generated data on localized image regions to mimic OOD objects.

Proposed architecture: ObsNet
Associated training scheme: Local Adversarial Attacks (LAA)
ObsNet+LAA achieves top OOD detection performance on CamVid, StreetHazards, and BDD-Anomaly datasets.

Contributions:
- New OOD detection method for semantic segmentation based on four design principles.
- Implementation in ObsNet architecture with LAA training.
- Extensive ablation studies to empirically validate principles.
- Comparison to 10 diverse methods on three datasets, achieving top accuracy and speed.

Strengths:
- Compatible with any pre-trained segmentation network without alteration or fine-tuning.
- Fast inference requiring only one extra forward pass.
- High effectiveness, outperforming 10 diverse methods on three datasets.
- Requires pre-trained segmentation networks to allow adversarial attacks (common for deep neural networks).

Weaknesses:
- Observer network has memory/computation overhead comparable to the segmentation network, not ideal for real-time applications, but less than MC Dropout or deep ensemble methods.

Related work:
Outlier, novelty, anomaly, and OOD detection have been studied prior to deep learning.
Deep learning approaches include:
- Input reconstruction
- Predictive uncertainty
- Ensembles
- Adversarial attacks
- Using a void or background class
- Using a dataset

Anomaly detection by reconstruction in semantic segmentation:
- Training autoencoders or generative models on in-distribution data.
- OOD samples lead to erroneous reconstructions.
- Autoencoders under-perform on high-resolution urban images.
- Generative models require large data or complex pipelines.

Bayesian approaches and ensembles:
- Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) capture predictive uncertainty but scale poorly.

topic: Image segmentation anomaly detection aims to identify and segment unusual or unexpected regions in images, supporting safety-critical applications in medical imaging, manufacturing, and autonomous systems. What is the better method for image segmentation anomaly detection tasks: SOTA-RbA or RbA?

paper1.title: Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-awareness Unknown Region for Autonomous Driving
paper1.abstract:
With the emergence of transformer-based architectures and large
                        language models (LLMs), the accuracy of road scene perception has
                        substantially advanced. Nonetheless, current road scene segmentation approaches are predominantly trained on closed-set data,
                        resulting in insufficient detection capabilities for out-of-distribution
                        (OOD) objects. To overcome this limitation, road anomaly detection
                        methods have been proposed. However, existing methods primarily depend on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection
                        techniques, facing two critical issues: (1) inadequate consideration of the objectiveness attributes of anomalous regions, causing incomplete segmentation when anomalous objects share similarities
                        with known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, leading to the detection of anomalies irrelevant
                        to autonomous driving tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel
                        framework termed Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness
                        (SOTA) for autonomous driving scenes. Specifically, SOTA enhances
                        the segmentation of objectiveness through a Semantic Fusion Block
                        (SFB) and filters anomalies irrelevant to road navigation tasks using
                        a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA).
                        Extensive empirical evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets, including Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and
                        RoadAnomaly, demonstrate that the proposed SOTA consistently
                        improves OOD detection performance across diverse detectors,
                        achieving robust and accurate segmentation outcomes.

4.2 Main Results
Pixel-level Results. As summarized in Table 6, our method significantly outperforms the baseline RbA [35] and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets. While RPL+CoroCL [28] achieves slightly better AuROC and FPR on the Fishyscapes Lost&Found dataset, SOTA improves the AuPRC by a significant margin of 5.5% compared to RPL+CoroCL. Furthermore, SOTA consistently outperforms RPL+CoroCL across all other datasets.

Component-level Results. Table 2 presents the component-level evaluation on the SMIYC RA-21 and SMIYC RO-21 benchmarks. Compared to RbA, our method achieves substantial improvements on RA-21, including a 5.58% increase in sIoU, an 18.31% boost in PPV, and a 14.67% gain in F1*. Similarly, on RO-21, our method yields an 8.00% improvement in PPV and a 9.55% increase in F1*. While Mask2Anomaly achieves a higher performance on RO-21, our approach surpasses it on RA-21, achieving a 0.88% improvement in sIoU and a 12.87% increase in F1*. Moreover, while ContMAV achieves higher PPV and F1* scores on RA-21, it does not report results on RO-21, whereas our approach consistently enhances performance across both datasets.

Qualitative Results. Figure 3 presents a visual comparison of anomaly segmentation results produced by three representative methods: RPL [28], RbA [35], and our proposed method SOTA. In the figure, the first column shows the original input images, while the subsequent columns display the corresponding anomaly maps of various approaches. It can be observed that RPL tends to generate diffused predictions with substantial false positives, particularly along object boundaries and in areas outside the road region. Although RbA improves upon RPL by offering sharper delineation, it still suffers from incomplete segmentation and residual noise. In contrast, SOTA delivers more accurate and comprehensive segmentation of OOD objects while effectively suppressing extraneous pixel predictions beyond the road area. These qualitative findings underscore the advantages of our approach, which unifies attribute-aware feature learning and scene-guided context modeling to achieve a superior balance between precise anomaly localization and noise reduction.

Figure 4: SOTA Qualitative Ablation. Compared to the original outputs, SFB improves the segmentation completeness of OOD objects, while SG-PCA reduces false positives outside the road. When both modules are used together, we achieve the best results, simultaneously reducing false detections outside the road and enhancing the segmentation accuracy of OOD objects on the road.

4.3 Ablation Studies
SOTA Ablation Analysis. Table 3 presents an ablation study comparing different configurations of our proposed method SOTA. In configuration (a), no additional modules are applied, representing the baseline RbA output. In configuration (b), only the SG-PCA variant using the raw OOD prompt fusion (˜y) is applied, effectively using RbA’s anomaly score as the mask prompt input to SAM. Configuration (c) incorporates only the SFB along with mask decoder finetuning, thereby directly integrating the enhanced image features with the anomaly cues. In configuration (d), only the SG-PCA variant using the raw OOD prompt fusion (˜y) is applied with finetuning. Configuration (e) applies SG-PCA with both the raw OOD prompt fusion (˜y) and the road semantic prompt (y′t); here, the dual cues help refine the spatial context, yielding a distinct performance pattern. Configuration (f) employs SG-PCA with the combination of the raw OOD prompt and the road-related OOD prompt fusion (˜yt) with finetuning, demonstrating further improvement by incorporating contextual information that accounts for partial object extensions. In configuration (g), both SFB and SG-PCA (using ˜y and ˜yt) are integrated without finetuning the mask decoder, whereas configuration (h) activates both modules together with finetuning. Notably, configuration (h) achieves the highest performance, which yields a relative AuPRC gain and the lowest FPR on both Road-Anomaly and Fishyscapes Lost & Found. Abstract
Transformer-based architectures and large language models (LLMs) have advanced road scene perception accuracy. However, current road scene segmentation approaches are trained on closed-set data, limiting detection of out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Road anomaly detection methods exist but rely on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection, facing two issues: (1) inadequate consideration of anomalous region objectiveness, leading to incomplete segmentation when anomalies resemble known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, causing detection of anomalies irrelevant to autonomous driving. This paper proposes a novel framework, Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness (SOTA), for autonomous driving. SOTA enhances objectiveness segmentation with a Semantic Fusion Block (SFB) and filters irrelevant anomalies using a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA). Evaluations on Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and RoadAnomaly datasets show SOTA consistently improves OOD detection performance and achieves robust segmentation.

paper2.title: RbA: Segmenting Unknown Regions Rejected by All
paper2.abstract:
Standard semantic segmentation models owe their success
                        to curated datasets with a fixed set of semantic categories,
                        without contemplating the possibility of identifying unknown
                        objects from novel categories. Existing methods in outlier
                        detection suffer from a lack of smoothness and objectness
                        in their predictions, due to limitations of the per-pixel classification paradigm. Furthermore, additional training for
                        detecting outliers harms the performance of known classes.
                        In this paper, we explore another paradigm with region-level
                        classification to better segment unknown objects. We show
                        that the object queries in mask classification tend to behave
                        like one vs. all classifiers. Based on this finding, we propose
                        a novel outlier scoring function called RbA by defining the
                        event of being an outlier as being rejected by all known
                        classes. Our extensive experiments show that mask classification improves the performance of the existing outlier
                        detection methods, and the best results are achieved with
                        the proposed RbA. We also propose an objective to optimize
                        RbA using minimal outlier supervision. Further fine-tuning
                        with outliers improves the unknown performance, and unlike
                        previous methods, it does not degrade the inlier performance.

Crucially, RbA achieves this Out-of-Distribution (OoD) performance without degrading closed-set performance, unlike methods like PEBAL which cause a significant drop in mIoU. This demonstrates RbA's superior utilization of mask classification properties.

This indicates RbA's scoring function enhances performance irrespective of the backbone.

**5. Conclusion and Future Work**
This work explores using mask classification for unknown class segmentation. Object queries, acting as one-vs-all classifiers, independently reduce overconfidence in predicted scores, improving existing scoring-based methods like max logit and energy-based methods. We propose RbA, a novel outlier scoring function based on known class probabilities, treating mask classification results as multiple one-vs-all classifiers. We also introduce an objective to optimize RbA with limited outlier data, achieving significant performance gains without impacting closed-set performance. RbA eliminates uncertainty from inlier boundaries and ambiguous background regions, considerably reducing false positive rates. Furthermore, RbA preserves objectness and smoothness due to the region-level inductive biases learned by the mask classifier.

As this is an initial exploration of mask classification for unknown segmentation, its properties can be further investigated. The improved objectness preservation makes open-world incremental learning more feasible, with unknown masks serving as more reliable supervision. Current work is limited to static images; incorporating temporal or depth information could provide significant cues for detecting unknowns.

C. Details of Experiments

C.1. Specialization of Object Queries

Our method's foundation is the observation that object queries in mask classification exhibit independence. Each object query within a subset specializes in segmenting a specific class from the closed set. This behavior is predictable due to the bipartite matching between queries and ground truth class masks during training. We empirically verify this using the BDD100K dataset. For each object query, we count its high-confidence predictions for specific classes. Figure 8 illustrates the heatmap of counts for a Mask2Former model with 100 object queries, showing that a single object query predominantly predicts each closed-set class.

The main paper tests query independence using hard and soft masking, evaluating per-class IoU on Cityscapes. Figure 9 visually explains hard and soft masking.

Figure 9: Illustration of hard vs. soft masking of object queries. In hard masking, for predicting class k, object queries specialized for class k interact with image features while others are masked. In soft masking, all queries interact within the transformer decoder, but only the specialized query predicts class k afterwards.

C.2. Other Loss Functions

The main paper includes an ablation study comparing different loss functions against squared hinge loss. This section details the formulation and parameter settings for each loss function. Ωout denotes outlier pixels, and Ωin denotes inlier pixels.

Mean-Squared Error (MSE): We optimize RbA to approach α = 5 for outlier pixels.
$$LMSE = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} (R_bA(x) - \alpha)^2$$ (8)

L1: Similar to MSE, we optimize RbA with L1 loss, setting α to 5.
$$L_{L1} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} |R_bA(x) - \alpha|$$ (9)

Binary Cross Entropy (BCE): We treat outlier scoring as a per-pixel binary classification problem, with outliers as the positive class. RbA score serves as the logit for the positive class. Assuming y is the binary label (outlier/inlier) for pixel x, we optimize BCE loss:
$$L_{BCE} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} y \cdot \log(R_bA(x)) + (1 - y) \cdot \log(1 - R_bA(x))$$ (10)

KL Divergence: We use KL Divergence to minimize the distance between the predicted class distribution and a fixed distribution. For inlier pixels, we minimize distance to a Dirac delta function (correct class probability of 1.0). For outlier pixels, we minimize distance to a uniform distribution (maximum entropy). While not directly optimizing RbA, this loss helps estimate RbA's contribution by pushing predicted class probabilities toward ideal distributions for outliers and inliers.
Let Lp(x) be the class probability distribution for pixel x with ground truth label y. Let Pin(y) be a fixed probability distribution where class y has probability 1.0. Let U be a fixed uniform probability distribution. The loss function is defined as:
$$L_{in} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{in}} D_{KL}(L_p(x) \parallel P_{in}(y))$$
$$L_{out} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} D_{KL}(L_p(x) \parallel U)$$
$$L_{KL} = \frac{1}{2} (L_{in} + L_{out})$$ (11)

C.3. Other Methods with Mask2Former

To isolate the contribution of our scoring function RbA from the architecture, we present results for state-of-the-art methods PEBAL and DenseHybrid using the Mask2Former architecture. This section details this ablation experiment for each method. For fair comparison, both methods are trained by fine-tuning the same components as RbA: the MLP+Linear layers as shown in Figure 6.

Methods PEBAL [65] and DenseHybrid [25] were implemented using the Mask2Former architecture.

Ablation Experiment Details:
Both methods were fine-tuned using the same components as RbA (MLP+Linear layers) and the same outlier data supervision method.

PEBAL:
The optimized objective consists of three components:

1.  **Pixel-wise Anomaly Abstention Loss (PAL):**
    *   Loss function: $L_{PAL} = -\sum_{x \in \Omega} \log\left(\frac{L_{y(x)} + L_{K+1}(x)}{a(x)}\right)$
    *   $\Omega$: Set of all pixels in an image.
    *   $y \in \{1, \dots, K+1\}$: Ground truth class of pixel $x$.
    *   $K+1$: Class for outliers. In Mask2Former, $K+1$ is the "no object" class. This class is not dropped from region class probabilities $P$ during fine-tuning with the PEBAL objective.
    *   Abstention penalty term $a(x)$: $a(x) = (-E(x))^2$
    *   Free energy function $E(x)$: $E(x) = -\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(L_k(x))\right)$
    *   High penalty discourages abstention; low penalty encourages it.

2.  **Energy Term Optimization:**
    *   Loss function: $L_{energy} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{in}} \max(0, E(x) - \min)^2 + \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} \max(0, \text{mout} - E(x))^2$
    *   $\Omega_{in}$: Set of inlier pixels.
    *   $\Omega_{out}$: Set of outlier pixels.
    *   $\min$, $\text{mout}$: Hyper-parameters. Experimentally set to $\text{mout} = -2.5$ and $\min = -3.5$.

3.  **Regularization Term:**
    *   For smoothness and sparsity of the predicted energy map.
    *   Loss function: $L_{reg} = \sum_{x \in \Omega} \beta_1|E(x) - E(N(x))| + \beta_2|E(x)|$
    *   $N(x)$: Set of vertical and horizontal neighboring pixels of $x$.
    *   $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$: Hyper-parameters. Set to $\beta_1 = 3 \times 10^{-7}$ and $\beta_2 = 5 \times 10^{-5}$.

Full Objective:
*   $L_{PEBAL} = L_{PAL} + \beta L_{energy} + L_{reg}$
*   $\beta$: Weighted sum coefficient, set to $\beta = 0.1$.
*   Training: Started from the same checkpoint as RbA, optimized for 5K iterations with $L_{PEBAL}$. Other hyper-parameters were the same as RbA.

DenseHybrid:
*   An additional outlier prediction head $D(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times H \times W}$ was added to Mask2Former.
*   Outlier Prediction Head: $D(x) = \text{Conv}_{3 \times 3}(\text{ReLU}(\text{BatchNorm}(x)))$
    *   Takes the highest resolution feature map from the pixel decoder.
    *   Predicts a binary output for each pixel indicating outlier probability.

Objective Function:
*   $L_{DH} = \text{CE}(L(x_{in}), Y_{in}) + \beta_1 \text{CE}(D(x), Y_{out}) + \beta_2 L_o$
*   $\text{CE}$: Cross-entropy loss.
*   $x_{in} \in \Omega_{in}$: Set of inlier pixels.
*   $Y_{in}$: Ground truth for closed-set.
*   $Y_{out}$: Binary map where outlier pixels are 1.
*   $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$: Hyper-parameters. Experimentally set to $\beta_1 = 0.3$ and $\beta_2 = 0.03$.
*   $L_o$: $L_o = \frac{1}{|\Omega_{out}|} \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} \log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(L_k(x))\right) + \text{sg}[\text{mean}(L(x))]$
    *   $\text{sg}$: Stop gradient operation.
    *   $\text{mean}$: Mean of all elements in the input tensor.

We explore a region-level classification paradigm for object segmentation using mask-classification models like Mask2Former. These models predict regions and classify them, promoting spatial smoothness through region-level supervision. We investigate their properties for improved confidence value calibration, leveraging this to enhance existing Out-of-Distribution (OoD) detection methods that rely on predicted class scores.

Existing methods struggle with high false positive rates due to their inability to separate uncertainty sources, particularly on real-world datasets like Road Anomaly. Segmentation models often produce weak scores for inlier classes at boundaries, leading these regions to be misclassified as OoD. Our analysis of object queries in mask classification reveals their "one vs. all" classifier-like behavior. This observation inspires a novel outlier scoring function where a pixel is considered an outlier if rejected by all known classes, defined as a complementary event to being a known class. This scoring function mitigates irrelevant uncertainty sources, such as those at boundaries, significantly reducing false positive rates.

State-of-the-art OoD methods often use outlier data for supervision, which can improve unknown segmentation but degrades closed-set performance. Our goal is to identify unknowns without compromising inlier accuracy. We propose an objective to optimize our outlier scoring function with limited outlier data. Fine-tuning a small portion of the model with this objective, our method surpasses current state-of-the-art on datasets with high distribution shifts like Road Anomaly and SMIYC, without impacting closed-set performance.

Our contributions include:
* Studying the inherent uncertainty expression capabilities of mask classification models and using this to improve existing OoD segmentation methods.
* Proposing a novel outlier scoring function, based on the "one vs. all" behavior of object queries, which defines outliers as pixels not belonging to any known class. This function reduces uncertainty in ambiguous regions like semantic boundaries.
* Introducing a loss function that optimizes our scoring function using minimal outlier data, outperforming existing methods by fine-tuning only a small model portion and preserving closed-set performance.

**2. Related Work**
**Semantic Segmentation Paradigms:**
Since the advent of Fully Convolutional Networks (FCN), semantic segmentation has predominantly used per-pixel classification. This paradigm has been optimized through convolution, pooling operations, and multi-scale contextual information aggregation. More recent advancements involve transformer-based architectures and attention mechanisms.

Mask classification, prevalent in instance segmentation and object detection, allows pixels to belong to multiple proposals and detects a variable number of objects. Max-DeepLab uses mask classification for panoptic segmentation with auxiliary losses. While earlier attempts applied mask classification to semantic segmentation, they were surpassed by per-pixel methods until recently. MaskFormer variants employ mask classification.

Figure 3 illustrates the impact of masking object queries on per-class IoU in Cityscapes, comparing hard masking (no inter-query interaction) and soft masking (allowing interactions).

4.2 Main Results
Pixel-level Results. As summarized in Table 6, our method significantly outperforms the baseline RbA [35] and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets. While RPL+CoroCL [28] achieves slightly better AuROC and FPR on the Fishyscapes Lost&Found dataset, SOTA improves the AuPRC by a significant margin of 5.5% compared to RPL+CoroCL. Furthermore, SOTA consistently outperforms RPL+CoroCL across all other datasets.

Component-level Results. Table 2 presents the component-level evaluation on the SMIYC RA-21 and SMIYC RO-21 benchmarks. Compared to RbA, our method achieves substantial improvements on RA-21, including a 5.58% increase in sIoU, an 18.31% boost in PPV, and a 14.67% gain in F1*. Similarly, on RO-21, our method yields an 8.00% improvement in PPV and a 9.55% increase in F1*. While Mask2Anomaly achieves a higher performance on RO-21, our approach surpasses it on RA-21, achieving a 0.88% improvement in sIoU and a 12.87% increase in F1*. Moreover, while ContMAV achieves higher PPV and F1* scores on RA-21, it does not report results on RO-21, whereas our approach consistently enhances performance across both datasets.

Qualitative Results. Figure 3 presents a visual comparison of anomaly segmentation results produced by three representative methods: RPL [28], RbA [35], and our proposed method SOTA. In the figure, the first column shows the original input images, while the subsequent columns display the corresponding anomaly maps of various approaches. It can be observed that RPL tends to generate diffused predictions with substantial false positives, particularly along object boundaries and in areas outside the road region. Although RbA improves upon RPL by offering sharper delineation, it still suffers from incomplete segmentation and residual noise. In contrast, SOTA delivers more accurate and comprehensive segmentation of OOD objects while effectively suppressing extraneous pixel predictions beyond the road area. These qualitative findings underscore the advantages of our approach, which unifies attribute-aware feature learning and scene-guided context modeling to achieve a superior balance between precise anomaly localization and noise reduction.

When both modules are used together, we achieve the best results, simultaneously reducing false detections outside the road and enhancing the segmentation accuracy of OOD objects on the road.

Abstract
Transformer-based architectures and large language models (LLMs) have advanced road scene perception accuracy. However, current road scene segmentation approaches are trained on closed-set data, limiting detection of out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Road anomaly detection methods exist but rely on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection, facing two issues: (1) inadequate consideration of anomalous region objectiveness, leading to incomplete segmentation when anomalies resemble known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, causing detection of anomalies irrelevant to autonomous driving. This paper proposes a novel framework, Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness (SOTA), for autonomous driving. SOTA enhances objectiveness segmentation with a Semantic Fusion Block (SFB) and filters irrelevant anomalies using a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA). Evaluations on Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and RoadAnomaly datasets show SOTA consistently improves OOD detection performance and achieves robust segmentation.

Task-aware Aggregation Module:
1. Identifies road class from semantic segmentation output.
2. Generates a binary road mask.
3. Refines mask using a 15x15 convolutional kernel filled with ones, applied iteratively 15 times.
4. Each iteration involves padded convolution followed by thresholding at 0 to maintain binary format.
5. Results in an expanded road prompt $y_t$ capturing uncertain boundary regions.

Projection and Alignment Module:
Projection Module:
1. Lightweight learnable convolutional sub-network.
2. Transforms raw OoD confidence map into an intermediate semantic representation.
3. Input: 1x256x256 single-channel.
4. Processed through two 2x2 convolutional layers with stride 2.
5. Spatial resolution reduced to 64x64.
6. Channel dimension expanded to 16.
7. Each layer followed by LayerNorm and GELU activation.
8. Output feature map shape: 16x64x64.

Alignment Module:
1. Aligns intermediate semantic features with image encoder's representation.
2. Applies a final 1x1 convolutional layer.
3. Maps 16-channel feature map to a 256-dimensional embedding.
4. Preserves spatial structure.
5. Output tensor shape: 256x64x64.
6. Used for downstream fusion with image features.

Outlier Exposure:
1. Training dataset preparation uses Outlier Exposure (OE) strategy.
2. Cityscapes dataset used as inlier background (2,975 training images).
3. Objects selected from COCO dataset as OoD objects (excluding categories overlapping with Cityscapes).
4. COCO objects pasted onto Cityscapes images with 0.9 probability per image to simulate anomaly scenarios.
5. RbA framework [35] applied to composite images to compute anomaly scores and semantic logits.

paper2.title: DenseHybrid: Hybrid Anomaly Detection for Dense Open-set Recognition
paper2.abstract:
Anomaly detection can be conceived either through generative modelling of regular training data or by discriminating with respect to negative training data. These two approaches exhibit different
                        failure modes. Consequently, hybrid algorithms present an attractive research goal. Unfortunately, dense anomaly detection requires translational equivariance and very large input resolutions. These requirements
                        disqualify all previous hybrid approaches to the best of our knowledge.
                        We therefore design a novel hybrid algorithm based on reinterpreting
                        discriminative logits as a logarithm of the unnormalized joint distribution ˆp(x, y). Our model builds on a shared convolutional representation from which we recover three dense predictions: i) the closedset class posterior P(y|x), ii) the dataset posterior P(din|x), iii) unnormalized data likelihood ˆp(x). The latter two predictions are trained
                        both on the standard training data and on a generic negative dataset.
                        We blend these two predictions into a hybrid anomaly score which allows dense open-set recognition on large natural images. We carefully
                        design a custom loss for the data likelihood in order to avoid backpropagation through the untractable normalizing constant Z(θ). Experiments evaluate our contributions on standard dense anomaly detection benchmarks as well as in terms of open-mIoU - a novel metric for dense open-set performance. Our submissions achieve state-ofthe-art performance despite neglectable computational overhead over
                        the standard semantic segmentation baseline. Official implementation:
                        https://github.com/matejgrcic/DenseHybrid
methodology:
TPRA = TPA / (TPA + FNA)
open-IoUk = TPk / (TPk + FPk + FNk)
Closed-set classification
OOD detection
Dense open-set recognition
FPowk = Σ (FPi) for i ≠ k, i = 1 to K+1
FNowk = Σ (FNi) for i ≠ k, i = 1 to K+1
FNk = Σ (FNi) for i = 1 to K
FPk = Σ (FPi) for i = 1 to K
Fig. 5. The proposed open intersection over union (open-IoU) takes into account miss-classifications in anomalous pixels to accurately measure dense recognition performance in open world.
Measuring performance using the proposed open-IoU requires datasets with K+1 labels. Creating such taxonomy requires substantial resources. Currently, only StreetHazards [23] offers appropriate taxonomy for measuring open-IoU.
5 Experiments
We report dense anomaly detection and open-set recognition performance of the proposed DenseHybrid approach, and compare them with the state of the art. We also explore influence of distance, show computational requirements of the proposed module, and ablate the design choices.
5.1 Benchmarks and Datasets
We evaluate performance on standard benchmarks for dense anomaly detection. Fishyscapes [5] considers urban scenarios on a subset of LostAndFound [44] and on Cityscapes validation images with pasted anomalies (FS Static). SegmentMeIfYouCan (SMIYC) [9] moves away from anomaly injection. Instead, appropriate images are collected from the real world and grouped based on the anomaly size into AnomalyTrack (large) and ObstacleTrack (small). Additionally, the benchmark encapsulates all LostAndFound images. Unfortunately, both benchmarks only have binary labels which makes them insufficient for measuring the recognition performance as proposed in Sec. 4. StreetHazards [23] is a synthetic dataset created by CARLA virtual environment. The simulated environment enables smooth anomaly injection and low-cost label extraction. Consequently, the dataset contains K +1 labels which makes it suitable for measuring both anomaly detection and dense recognition.
5.2 Dense Anomaly Detection

**5.3 Dense Open-set Recognition**

**Implementation Details**

Standard segmentation networks are adapted for co-operation with the hybrid anomaly detector by appending an additional branch $g_\gamma$ (BN-ReLU-Conv1x1) that computes the discriminative anomaly output. Generative anomaly output is obtained by summing exponentiated logits. Recognition models are built based on dense classifiers and fine-tuned on mixed-content images with pasted negative instances from ADE20k. For SMIYC, LDN-121 [30] is fine-tuned for 10 epochs on images from Cityscapes [12], Vistas [42], and Wilddash2 [52]. For Fishyscapes, DeepLabV3+ with WideResNet38 [55] is fine-tuned for 10 epochs on Cityscapes. LDN-121 is trained on Street-Hazards for 120 epochs in a closed world, then the recognition model is fine-tuned on mixed-content images. Further details are provided in the supplement.

**Conclusion**

Discriminative and generative approaches to dense anomaly detection have different failure modes. This work proposes a synergy by fusing the data posterior and data likelihood derived from a standard discriminative model. The proposed hybrid setup relies on unnormalized distributions, avoiding the evaluation of intractable normalization constants during training and inference. The DenseHybrid architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard anomaly segmentation benchmarks and competitive dense recognition performance in the open world, measured by the novel open-mIoU score. Future work will focus on reducing the performance gap between closed-world and open-world recognition to improve autonomous driving safety.
