Hybrid Anomaly Detection for Dense Open-set Recognition

Related Work
Detecting samples deviating from training data generation is a long-standing problem [22], also known as anomaly detection or out-of-distribution (OOD) detection [24]. Early image-wide approaches used max-softmax probability [24], input perturbations [34], ensembling [31], or Bayesian uncertainty [40]. Improved performance was achieved through discriminative training against broad negative datasets [14, 25, 2, 37] or appropriately trained generative models [32, 21, 54].

Another research direction detects anomalies by estimating likelihood with a generative model. This revealed anomalies can have higher likelihood than inliers [41, 47, 53]. Group-wise anomaly detection [27] shows promise but has less practical importance. Generative models can be trained to assign low likelihood to negative data [25], potentially mitigating sub-optimal probability volume dispersion [38].

Image-wide anomaly detection methods are adaptable to dense prediction with varying success. Existing generative approaches do not provide dense likelihood estimates. Max-softmax and discriminative training with negative data are easily ported to dense prediction. Many dense anomaly detectors are trained on mixed-content images by pasting negatives (e.g., ImageNet, COCO, ADE20k) onto training images [2, 10, 4]. Discriminative anomaly detection can use a dedicated OOD head sharing features with the standard classification head. Shared features enhance OOD performance with negligible computational overhead compared to baseline semantic segmentation [2]. Recent work [10] promotes high softmax entropy in negative pixels.

Anomalies can be recognized in feature space [6]. However, this complicates detecting small objects due to subsampled features and feature collapse [38, 1]. Alternatively, anomaly detectors can use the dissimilarity between the input and a resynthesized image [36, 4, 50]. Resynthesis uses a generative model conditioned on predicted labels, but this is suitable only for uniform backgrounds like roads [36] and adds significant computational overhead, making it unsuitable for real-time applications.

Our dense anomaly detection approach combines discriminative detection and likelihood evaluation. Discriminative OOD detection was introduced in [2, 25, 14]. We improve it through synergy with likelihood testing. Dense likelihood evaluation was done by fitting a generative model to discriminative features [6]. However, their method is vulnerable to feature collapse [38, 1] due to two-phase training, and detecting small outliers is hindered by subsampling. Our method allows joint training with the standard dense prediction model and anomaly detection at full resolution.

We perform dense likelihood evaluation by reinterpreting logits as unnormalized joint likelihood [20]. However, method [20] is unsuitable for dense prediction due to the intractability of Langevin sampling at large resolutions. We reformulate their method to allow training on mixed-content images, which simplifies training by precluding backpropagation through the intractable normalizing constant Z(θ). To our knowledge, our design is the first approach for dense likelihood evaluation suitable for end-to-end training.

We build an open-set recognition model by thresholding our hybrid anomaly score and combining it with standard semantic segmentation predictions [7]. This model detects anomalies and recognizes inlier scenery simultaneously. Standard dense recognition metrics [16] do not account for accuracy on anomalous samples, as outlier pixels are recent additions to dense prediction benchmarks [52, 5, 9]. Previous work on discrimination with anomalous pixels focused more on algorithm robustness than recognition performance [52]. Thus, we propose a novel anomaly-aware performance metric called open-mIoU.

7.1 Limitations

Our method is termed hybrid because it optimizes two distinct training objectives:
i) dense discrimination between inliers and negatives, and ii) achieving a high likelihood for inliers and a low likelihood for negative data. While likelihood evaluation is a standard feature of generative models (excluding GANs) and might suggest sample generation capabilities, our formulation is not suitable for this purpose due to its handling of unnormalized distributions. This would necessitate MCMC sampling, which is infeasible at large resolutions with current techniques. Furthermore, even if sample generation were possible, the resulting approach would likely be too slow for real-time inference, as demonstrated by other image resynthesis methods.

7.2 Impact of Known Inliers on Anomaly Detection

Many real-world autonomous systems operate in environments with limited variability, such as warehouses or industrial plants. These environments typically exhibit perfectly aligned training and test distributions. Anomalous objects can still occur in such settings. We demonstrate that anomaly detection performance is significantly enhanced when known inlier instances from the test set are available. Table 7 illustrates this scenario using two DLv3+ segmentation networks. The first network was trained on the Cityscapes training set, while the second was trained on both the Cityscapes training and validation splits. Given that the Fishyscapes Static dataset is generated by overlaying negative objects onto Cityscapes validation images, we can assess anomaly detection performance with known inlier instances from the test set. The results show a drastic improvement in the average precision of anomaly detection, increasing from 60% to 89%. This indicates that the DenseHybrid anomaly detector is practical for scenarios with limited scene variety.

7.3 More Results

Table 8 presents the dense open-set recognition performance of generative and discriminative anomaly detectors on the StreetHazards dataset. The proposed hybrid anomaly score, calculated as the ratio of these two distributions, surpasses the performance of each individual component. Notably, the generative and discriminative outputs are trained using identical mixed-content images.

7.4 Implementation Details

Mixed-content training samples are created by pasting negative data onto inlier crops. Inlier crops are generated by jittering images within a range of [0.5, 2], applying random horizontal flips, and performing random square cropping to a size of 768. ADE20k instances are used as negative content. The negative images are resized to 768 pixels, and a random jittered crop of size 384 is extracted. Subsequently, two instances from the negative crop are pasted onto the inlier crop at random positions. For LDN-121, a batch size of 16 is used, along with the Adam optimizer and an initial learning rate of 10⁻⁵, which is decayed through a cosine schedule down to 10⁻⁷. The loss modulation hyper-parameter β is set to 0.03. For DLv3+, a batch size of 8 and inlier crops of 512 are used. The Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10⁻⁶ is employed, without decay. The loss modulation hyper-parameter β is set to 0.01.

In the case of Fishyscapes, DLv3+ with a WRN38 backbone, pre-trained by NVIDIA, is fine-tuned. However, due to hardware constraints, training from scratch to achieve the desired robustness for SMIYC was not feasible. Therefore, LDN-121 was chosen as an efficient alternative that can be trained on a single GPU. Utilizing the larger DLv3+ model would likely result in further improvements on SMIYC.

7.5 Visualizations

Figure 7 visualizes the anomaly detection performance of DenseHybrid on the SMIYC-AnomalyTrack and SMIYC-ObstacleTrack datasets. Anomalies detected by DenseHybrid are highlighted above the input images. The corresponding ground truth designates anomalies in orange, inlier pixels in white, and ignored pixels in black.

Fig. 7. Anomaly detection performance of DenseHybrid on SMIYC validation subsets.

We build our hybrid anomaly detector upon the discriminative dataset posterior P(din|x) and the generative data likelihood p(x). We express a novel hybrid anomaly score as log-ratio between P(dout|x) = 1 −P(din|x) and p(x):
$s(\mathbf{x}) := \ln \frac{P(d_{out}|\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x})} = \ln P(d_{out}|\mathbf{x}) - \ln \hat{p}(\mathbf{x}) + \ln Z \cong \ln P(d_{out}|\mathbf{x}) - \ln \hat{p}(\mathbf{x})$.

We can neglect Z since ranking performance is invariant to monotonic transformations. Other formulations of s(x) may also be effective, which is an interesting direction for future work.

Figure 3 illustrates the inference with the proposed open-set recognition setup. RGB input is fed to a hybrid dense model which produces pre-logit activations t and logits s. Then, we obtain the closed-set class posterior P(y|x) = softmax(s) and the unnormalized data likelihood ˆp(x). A distinct head g transforms pre-logits t into the dataset posterior P(dout|x). The anomaly score s(x) is a log-ratio between latter two distributions. The resulting anomaly map is thresholded and fused with the discriminative output into the final dense open-set recognition map.

The developed hybrid model aims at achieving a synergy between generative and discriminative modelling. However, the proposed hybrid interpretation requires specific training objectives. Dense class posteriors require a discriminative loss over the inlier data Din:
$L_{cls}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in D_{in}}[- \ln P(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})] = - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in D_{in}}[\mathbf{s}_y] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in D_{in}}[\ln \sum_i \exp{\mathbf{s}_i}]$.

The discriminative loss corresponds to the standard training in the closed world. We introduce the negative data Dout into the training procedure to ensure the desired behaviour of P(din|x) and p(x). Both distributions should yield low probability in negative pixels. We propose to train p(x) to maximize the likelihood in inliers and to minimize the likelihood in outliers. We derive the upper bound of the desired loss as follows:
$L_{\mathbf{x}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{in}}[- \ln p(\mathbf{x})] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{out}}[-\ln p(\mathbf{x})] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{in}}[- \ln \hat{p}(\mathbf{x})] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{out}}[-\ln \hat{p}(\mathbf{x})] = - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in D_{in}}[\mathbf{s}_y] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{out}}[\ln \sum_i\exp(\mathbf{s}_i)] \leq - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in D_{in}}[\mathbf{s}_y] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{out}}[\ln \sum_i\exp(\mathbf{s}_i)]$.

We eschew the backpropagation into the normalization constant Z, and derive the upper bound according to the following inequality:
$\ln \sum_i\exp{\mathbf{s}_i} \geq \max_i \mathbf{s}_i \geq \mathbf{s}_y$.

Proof of inequality (13) can be easily derived by recalling that log-sum-exp is a smooth upper bound of the max function. By comparing the standard classification loss (7) and the upper bound (12) we realize that minimizing the standard classification loss increases p(x) for inlier pixels. Indeed, minimizing the negative logarithm of softmax output increases the value of logit for the correct class.

4.2 Main Results
Pixel-level Results. As summarized in Table 6, our method significantly outperforms the baseline RbA [35] and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets. While RPL+CoroCL [28] achieves slightly better AuROC and FPR on the Fishyscapes Lost&Found dataset, SOTA improves the AuPRC by a significant margin of 5.5% compared to RPL+CoroCL. Furthermore, SOTA consistently outperforms RPL+CoroCL across all other datasets.

Component-level Results. Table 2 presents the component-level evaluation on the SMIYC RA-21 and SMIYC RO-21 benchmarks. Compared to RbA, our method achieves substantial improvements on RA-21, including a 5.58% increase in sIoU, an 18.31% boost in PPV, and a 14.67% gain in F1*. Similarly, on RO-21, our method yields an 8.00% improvement in PPV and a 9.55% increase in F1*. While Mask2Anomaly achieves a higher performance on RO-21, our approach surpasses it on RA-21, achieving a 0.88% improvement in sIoU and a 12.87% increase in F1*. Moreover, while ContMAV achieves higher PPV and F1* scores on RA-21, it does not report results on RO-21, whereas our approach consistently enhances performance across both datasets.

Qualitative Results. Figure 3 presents a visual comparison of anomaly segmentation results produced by three representative methods: RPL [28], RbA [35], and our proposed method SOTA. In the figure, the first column shows the original input images, while the subsequent columns display the corresponding anomaly maps of various approaches. It can be observed that RPL tends to generate diffused predictions with substantial false positives, particularly along object boundaries and in areas outside the road region. Although RbA improves upon RPL by offering sharper delineation, it still suffers from incomplete segmentation and residual noise. In contrast, SOTA delivers more accurate and comprehensive segmentation of OOD objects while effectively suppressing extraneous pixel predictions beyond the road area. These qualitative findings underscore the advantages of our approach, which unifies attribute-aware feature learning and scene-guided context modeling to achieve a superior balance between precise anomaly localization and noise reduction.

Figure 4: SOTA Qualitative Ablation. Compared to the original outputs, SFB improves the segmentation completeness of OOD objects, while SG-PCA reduces false positives outside the road. When both modules are used together, we achieve the best results, simultaneously reducing false detections outside the road and enhancing the segmentation accuracy of OOD objects on the road.

4.3 Ablation Studies
SOTA Ablation Analysis. Table 3 presents an ablation study comparing different configurations of our proposed method SOTA. In configuration (a), no additional modules are applied, representing the baseline RbA output. In configuration (b), only the SG-PCA variant using the raw OOD prompt fusion (˜y) is applied, effectively using RbA’s anomaly score as the mask prompt input to SAM. Configuration (c) incorporates only the SFB along with mask decoder finetuning, thereby directly integrating the enhanced image features with the anomaly cues. In configuration (d), only the SG-PCA variant using the raw OOD prompt fusion (˜y) is applied with finetuning. Configuration (e) applies SG-PCA with both the raw OOD prompt fusion (˜y) and the road semantic prompt (y′t); here, the dual cues help refine the spatial context, yielding a distinct performance pattern. Abstract
Transformer-based architectures and large language models (LLMs) have advanced road scene perception accuracy. However, current road scene segmentation approaches are trained on closed-set data, limiting detection of out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Road anomaly detection methods exist but rely on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection, facing two issues: (1) inadequate consideration of anomalous region objectiveness, leading to incomplete segmentation when anomalies resemble known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, causing detection of anomalies irrelevant to autonomous driving. This paper proposes a novel framework, Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness (SOTA), for autonomous driving. SOTA enhances objectiveness segmentation with a Semantic Fusion Block (SFB) and filters irrelevant anomalies using a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA). Evaluations on Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and RoadAnomaly datasets show SOTA consistently improves OOD detection performance and achieves robust segmentation.

Task-aware Aggregation Module:
1. Identifies road class from semantic segmentation output.
2. Generates a binary road mask.
3. Refines mask using a 15x15 convolutional kernel filled with ones, applied iteratively 15 times.
4. Each iteration involves padded convolution followed by thresholding at 0 to maintain binary format.
5. Results in an expanded road prompt $y_t$ capturing uncertain boundary regions.

Projection and Alignment Module:
Projection Module:
1. Lightweight learnable convolutional sub-network.
2. Transforms raw OoD confidence map into an intermediate semantic representation.
3. Input: 1x256x256 single-channel.
4. Processed through two 2x2 convolutional layers with stride 2.
5. Spatial resolution reduced to 64x64.
6. Channel dimension expanded to 16.
7. Each layer followed by LayerNorm and GELU activation.
8. Output feature map shape: 16x64x64.

Alignment Module:
1. Aligns intermediate semantic features with image encoder's representation.
2. Applies a final 1x1 convolutional layer.
3. Maps 16-channel feature map to a 256-dimensional embedding.
4. Preserves spatial structure.
5. Output tensor shape: 256x64x64.
6. Used for downstream fusion with image features.

Outlier Exposure:
1. Training dataset preparation uses Outlier Exposure (OE) strategy.
2. Cityscapes dataset used as inlier background (2,975 training images).
3. Objects selected from COCO dataset as OoD objects (excluding categories overlapping with Cityscapes).
4. COCO objects pasted onto Cityscapes images with 0.9 probability per image to simulate anomaly scenarios.
5. RbA framework [35] applied to composite images to compute anomaly scores and semantic logits.

paper2.title: Entropy Maximization and Meta Classification for Out-Of-Distribution Detection in Semantic Segmentation
paper2.abstract:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) for the semantic segmentation of images are usually trained to operate on a predefined closed set of object classes. This is in contrast to
                        the “open world” setting where DNNs are envisioned to be
                        deployed to. From a functional safety point of view, the ability to detect so-called “out-of-distribution” (OoD) samples,
                        i.e., objects outside of a DNN’s semantic space, is crucial
                        for many applications such as automated driving. A natural baseline approach to OoD detection is to threshold on
                        the pixel-wise softmax entropy. We present a two-step procedure that significantly improves that approach. Firstly,
                        we utilize samples from the COCO dataset as OoD proxy
                        and introduce a second training objective to maximize the
                        softmax entropy on these samples. Starting from pretrained
                        semantic segmentation networks we re-train a number of
                        DNNs on different in-distribution datasets and consistently
                        observe improved OoD detection performance when evaluating on completely disjoint OoD datasets. Secondly, we
                        perform a transparent post-processing step to discard false
                        positive OoD samples by so-called “meta classification.”
                        To this end, we apply linear models to a set of hand-crafted
                        metrics derived from the DNN’s softmax probabilities. In
                        our experiments we consistently observe a clear additional
                        gain in OoD detection performance, cutting down the number of detection errors by 52% when comparing the best
                        baseline with our results. We achieve this improvement sacrificing only marginally in original segmentation performance. Therefore, our method contributes to safer DNNs
                        with more reliable overall system performance.

Conclusion & Outlook:
A novel re-training approach for deep neural networks combines improved OoD detection with state-of-the-art semantic segmentation. This OoD training significantly enhances detection efficiency via softmax entropy thresholding, outperforming existing methods. Meta classifiers for entropy-based OoD object predictions, using lightweight logistic regressions, reliably classify OoD segments. The increased sensitivity from entropy maximization further enhances meta classifier efficiency. The combination of OoD training and meta classification can significantly improve safety-critical deep learning applications.

Future work includes applying OoD training for OoD object retrieval to assess their importance and the need for new concepts. Code is available at https://github.com/robin-chan/meta-ood.

After OoD training, the negative sample distribution is largely similar to the baseline. The median and upper quartile of negative entropy decrease to 0.1 and 0.2 respectively. The maximum negative entropy is 0.66. For positive samples, the distribution changes significantly with a large mass concentrated at very high entropy values. **C. Segment-wise Metrics for Meta Classifiers**

Meta classifiers are trained using hand-crafted metrics derived from softmax probabilities $f(x) \in (0, 1)^{|Z| \times |C|}$ and other information from deep convolutional neural networks. Let $\hat{Z}_{out}(x)$ be the set of pixel locations predicted as OoD in image $x$. An OoD segment/object prediction, $k \in \hat{K}(x) \subseteq P(\hat{Z}_{out}(x))$, is a connected component where entropy exceeds a given threshold. This differs from other segment-wise meta classification approaches that consider connected components with the same class label as segments.

Uncertainty per OoD segment $k$ is estimated by averaging pixel-wise scores for pixels $z \in k$. In addition to softmax probabilities $f_z(x)$, three pixel-wise dispersion measures are used:

1.  **Normalized Entropy:**
    $\bar{E}(f_z(x)) = -\frac{1}{|C|} \sum_{j \in C} f_{z_j}(x) \log(f_{z_j}(x))$

2.  **Variation Ratio:**
    $V(f_z(x)) = 1 - f_{z_{\hat{c}(z)}}(x)$

3.  **Probability Margin:**
    $M(f_z(x)) = V(f_z(x)) + \max_{j \in C \setminus \{\hat{c}(z)\}} f_{z_j}(x)$
    where $\hat{c}(z) := \arg \max_{j \in C} f_{z_j}(x)$ is the class label with the highest a posteriori probability.

Segment size $S(k) = |k|$ is used for averaging and as a direct meta classification input. Interior pixel locations $k_{in} = \{(h, w) \in k : [h \pm 1] \times [w \pm 1] \in k\}$ and boundary pixel locations $k_{bd} = k \setminus k_{in}$ are considered. Relative sizes of the boundary and interior are used as geometry features:
$\tilde{S} = S/S_{bd}$ and $\tilde{S}_{in} = S_{in}/S_{bd}$

Variances of pixel-wise scores are also considered, measuring deviation from the segment score mean, and significantly impact OoD detection meta classifiers.

The neighborhood of segment $k$ is defined as $k_{nb} = \{z' \in [h \pm 1] \times [w \pm 1] \subset |H| \times |W| : (h, w) \in k, z' \notin k\}$, where $Z = H \times W$ is the image. A metric for misplaced segments is:
$N(j|k) = \frac{1}{|k_{nb}|} \sum_{z \in k_{nb}} \mathbf{1}_{\{j=\hat{c}(z)\}} \forall j \in C$
This is the proportion of neighborhood pixels with class $j$ having the highest softmax score, relative to the neighborhood size.

The segment's geometric center is calculated as:
$C_h(k) = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{i=1}^{S} h_i$ and $C_w(k) = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{i=1}^{S} w_i$
where $z_i = (h_i, w_i) \in k$ for $i = 1, \dots, |k|$.

For each segment $k$, there are $m=83$ metrics in total (assuming $|C|=19$). This forms a structured dataset:
$\mu \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{|\cup_{x \in X} \hat{K}(x)| \times m} = \mathbb{R}^{|\cup_{x \in X} \hat{K}(x)| \times 83}$

Metrics considered:
*   Entropy
*   Baseline performance
*   Cityscapes void OoD training

6.2. Original Task Performance
To monitor that the baseline model does not unlearn its original task due to Out-of-Distribution (OoD) training, we evaluate the model’s performance on in-distribution data with OoD predictions at different entropy thresholds. The original task is the semantic segmentation of Cityscapes images, evaluated using the mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) metric. In addition to Cityscapes class predictions obtained via the standard maximum a posteriori (MAP) decision principle, we consider an extra OoD class prediction if the softmax entropy is above a given threshold $t$. We compute mIoU for the Cityscapes validation dataset, averaging only over the 19 Cityscapes class IoUs.

The state-of-the-art DeepLabv3+ model, serving as our baseline, achieves an mIoU score of 0.90 on the Cityscapes validation dataset without OoD predictions ($t = 1.0$). Retraining the CNN with entropy maximization on OoD inputs improves OoD-AUPRC scores, indicating better detection of OoD samples. This gain comes with a marginal drop in Cityscapes validation mIoU to 0.89. These mIoU scores remain nearly constant (deviations less than 1 percent point) for thresholds $t = 0.3, \dots, 1.0$. Generally, lower entropy thresholds result in more pixels predicted as OoD. At $t = 0.2$, a noticeable performance decrease is observed: 0.05 for the baseline and 0.03 for the retrained model. Further lowering the threshold leads to a more significant sacrifice of original performance. Therefore, we consider entropy thresholds of at least $t = 0.3$, as the performance loss appears acceptable given substantially improved OoD detection capability.

7. Segment-wise Evaluation
This section evaluates the meta-classification performance on LostAndFound. The main metrics for segment-wise evaluation are the numbers of False Positives (FPs) and False Negatives (FNs) with respect to an OoD object prediction. The F1-score ($F1 = \frac{2TP}{2TP + FP + FN}$) summarizes error rates. As removing FP OoD predictions should not significantly impact original performance, we also consider the miss rate of road pixels:
$$ \epsilon := 1 - \frac{|\hat{Z}_{in}(x) \cap Z_{in}(x)|}{|Z_{in}(x)|} - 1 $$
where $X$ is the dataset, $\hat{Z}_{in}$ are pixel locations predicted as in-distribution, and $Z_{in}$ are pixels annotated as in-distribution. $\epsilon$ measures the fraction of actual road pixels incorrectly identified.

We compute per-segment metrics for OoD object predictions in the LostAndFound test set and feed them into simple logistic regression meta-classification models. Segments are leave-one-out cross-validated for TP or FP classification. Least angle regression is used to analyze metrics most impactful on meta-classification. The analysis shows that after OoD training, the entropy metric $E(f(x))$ has the most impact.

Generally, higher entropy thresholds predict fewer OoD objects, consequently reducing data for linear models. This explains why meta-classifiers identify FPs more reliably at lower $t$. Abstract
Transformer-based architectures and large language models (LLMs) have advanced road scene perception accuracy. However, current road scene segmentation approaches are trained on closed-set data, limiting detection of out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Road anomaly detection methods exist but rely on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection, facing two issues: (1) inadequate consideration of anomalous region objectiveness, leading to incomplete segmentation when anomalies resemble known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, causing detection of anomalies irrelevant to autonomous driving. This paper proposes a novel framework, Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness (SOTA), for autonomous driving. SOTA enhances objectiveness segmentation with a Semantic Fusion Block (SFB) and filters irrelevant anomalies using a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA). Evaluations on Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and RoadAnomaly datasets show SOTA consistently improves OOD detection performance and achieves robust segmentation.

Task-aware Aggregation Module:
1. Identifies road class from semantic segmentation output.
2. Generates a binary road mask.
3. Refines mask using a 15x15 convolutional kernel filled with ones, applied iteratively 15 times.
4. Each iteration involves padded convolution followed by thresholding at 0 to maintain binary format.
5. Results in an expanded road prompt $y_t$ capturing uncertain boundary regions.

Projection and Alignment Module:
Projection Module:
1. Lightweight learnable convolutional sub-network.
2. Transforms raw OoD confidence map into an intermediate semantic representation.
3. Input: 1x256x256 single-channel.
4. Processed through two 2x2 convolutional layers with stride 2.
5. Spatial resolution reduced to 64x64.
6. Channel dimension expanded to 16.
7. Each layer followed by LayerNorm and GELU activation.
8. Output feature map shape: 16x64x64.

Alignment Module:
1. Aligns intermediate semantic features with image encoder's representation.
2. Applies a final 1x1 convolutional layer.
3. Maps 16-channel feature map to a 256-dimensional embedding.
4. Preserves spatial structure.
5. Output tensor shape: 256x64x64.
6. Used for downstream fusion with image features.

Outlier Exposure:
1. Training dataset preparation uses Outlier Exposure (OE) strategy.
2. Cityscapes dataset used as inlier background (2,975 training images).
3. Objects selected from COCO dataset as OoD objects (excluding categories overlapping with Cityscapes).
4. COCO objects pasted onto Cityscapes images with 0.9 probability per image to simulate anomaly scenarios.
5. RbA framework [35] applied to composite images to compute anomaly scores and semantic logits.

paper2.title: ATTA: Anomaly-aware Test-Time Adaptation for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Segmentation
paper2.abstract:
Recent advancements in dense out-of-distribution (OOD) detection have primarily
                        focused on scenarios where the training and testing datasets share a similar domain,
                        with the assumption that no domain shift exists between them. However, in realworld situations, domain shift often exits and significantly affects the accuracy of
                        existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection models. In this work, we propose a
                        dual-level OOD detection framework to handle domain shift and semantic shift
                        jointly. The first level distinguishes whether domain shift exists in the image by
                        leveraging global low-level features, while the second level identifies pixels with
                        semantic shift by utilizing dense high-level feature maps. In this way, we can
                        selectively adapt the model to unseen domains as well as enhance model’s capacity
                        in detecting novel classes. We validate the efficacy of our method on several OOD
                        segmentation benchmarks, including those with significant domain shifts and those
                        without, observing consistent performance improvements across various baseline
                        models. Code is available at https://github.com/gaozhitong/ATTA.
methodology:
Our method enhances PEBAL’s performance from 87% to 92% in AUC, 45% to 59% in AP, and reduces the FPR95 error from 44% to 33%. Compared to other methods, our method with PEBAL achieves new state-of-the-art performance across three datasets. Figure 3 provides qualitative results. Our ATTA approach improves OOD detection by mitigating domain-shift impact and encouraging model prediction confidence for inliers and outliers.

We submit our method with PEBAL [44] to SegmenMeIfYouCan [3] and Fishyscapes [1] online benchmarks. Our method consistently outperforms PEBAL [44]. Refer to Appendix D.3 and D.4 for details.

4.5 Ablation Study

We evaluate our model components on the Road Anomaly dataset using PEBAL [44] as baseline. We analyze the effectiveness of Selective Batch Normalization (SBN) and Anomaly-aware Self-Training (AST), and then examine each module's design.

Appendix E presents time and memory overhead, and additional ablation results.

5 Conclusion

This work proposes dense OOD detection under domain shift, highlighting limitations of existing methods in wild scenarios. We introduce a dual-level OOD detection framework to jointly handle domain and semantic shift, enabling selective adaptation to unseen domains and enhancing detection of novel classes. We validate our method on OOD segmentation benchmarks with and without significant domain shifts, demonstrating substantial performance gains, especially in cases with notable domain shifts.

ATTA can be further refined. Similar to other self-training methods, ATTA relies on a well-initialized model. While our adaptation method shows strong results on state-of-the-art models, improvement is less noticeable with weaker backbones. Test-time adaptation also adds computational time. Future research could focus on developing more efficient algorithms to reduce inference time. Our study introduces a more realistic setting for dense OOD detection under domain shift and aims to guide future work.

G.1 Specific Domain Shift in the Road Anomaly Dataset

The domain shift in the Road Anomaly dataset compared to Cityscapes includes adverse road conditions, diverse weather and lighting conditions, and various camera perspectives and conditions.

Adverse Road Conditions: Road Anomaly includes diverse rural locations with varied textures and colors due to different materials, wear, soil types, and vegetation, unlike the well-paved urban scenes in Cityscapes. Previous OOD detection methods often mistake these variations for anomalies, while our algorithm reduces such errors.

Weather and Lighting Variations: Road Anomaly includes snowy, rainy, foggy weather, and nighttime scenes, which affect surrounding areas and the sky, leading to more false positive errors in existing OOD detection models. Our method enhances adaptability to changes in weather and lighting.

Various Camera Conditions: Road Anomaly images can be captured from various angles and locations, such as alongside the road, differing from the typical road-centered perspective in Cityscapes. This variance can disrupt previously learned biases in road surface predictions.

**Constructing FS Static-C Dataset:**
The FS Static-C dataset was created by simulating domain shift through random smog, color shifting, and Gaussian blur. The fog function from Hendrycks and Dietterich [16] was incorporated. The ‘ColorJitter’ and ‘GaussianBlur’ transformations from the torchvision library were utilized. Each transformation was applied independently with a 50% probability. Random combinations of these transformations generated the final transformed images. This process created a diverse dataset encompassing various forms and levels of domain shift, enabling comprehensive evaluation and demonstration of robustness.

A Pseudo Code of ATTA
The pseudo code for Anomaly-aware Test-Time Adaptation (ATTA) is presented in Algorithm 1. Each test image xt utilizes a same pre-trained network parameter θ for initialization. The adaptation process consists of two stages: a domain-aware selective Batch Normalization (BN) updating stage and an online self-training stage based on an anomaly-aware entropy loss. The final output includes the inlier probability map and outlier score map for each test image.

Input: Test samples Dtest = {xt}T t=1, seen-class classifier fθ, unseen-class detector gθ with pretrained θ, number of iterations N, learning rate η, confidence thresholds τ1, τ2.
Output: Inlier probability maps {Ft}T t=1, outlier score maps {Gt}T t=1.

B More Implementation Details
Experimental Results of Previous OOD Methods: Experimental results for previous dense OOD detection methods are obtained by running pretrained model weights from official code repositories or as officially reported in original papers.

Implementation Details for Tent: For Tent [46], instructions from their original paper on segmentation tasks are followed. This includes considering affine transformation parameters in Batch Normalization layers as trainable parameters, using transductive batch normalization [36], and adopting episodic training. For fair comparison, the model is updated once per test image, Adam optimizer is used, and the learning rate is tuned on the FS Static-C dataset.

Implementation Details for GMM Modeling in Our Method: During Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) fitting, a peak-finding algorithm identifies the right-most peak in the OOD score distribution. This peak is used as the initial mean for the right GMM component before Expectation-Maximization (EM) optimization. This approach mitigates issues from multiple peaks in the inlier distribution, leveraging prior knowledge that the right-most peak likely represents outliers.

Details in Constructing FS Static-C Dataset: Domain shift in the FS Static-C dataset is simulated by introducing random smog, color shifting, and Gaussian noise, as described in Section 4.1.

4.2 Main Results
Pixel-level Results. As summarized in Table 6, our method significantly outperforms the baseline RbA [35] and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets. While RPL+CoroCL [28] achieves slightly better AuROC and FPR on the Fishyscapes Lost&Found dataset, SOTA improves the AuPRC by a significant margin of 5.5% compared to RPL+CoroCL. Furthermore, SOTA consistently outperforms RPL+CoroCL across all other datasets.

Component-level Results. Table 2 presents the component-level evaluation on the SMIYC RA-21 and SMIYC RO-21 benchmarks. Compared to RbA, our method achieves substantial improvements on RA-21, including a 5.58% increase in sIoU, an 18.31% boost in PPV, and a 14.67% gain in F1*. Similarly, on RO-21, our method yields an 8.00% improvement in PPV and a 9.55% increase in F1*. While Mask2Anomaly achieves a higher performance on RO-21, our approach surpasses it on RA-21, achieving a 0.88% improvement in sIoU and a 12.87% increase in F1*. Moreover, while ContMAV achieves higher PPV and F1* scores on RA-21, it does not report results on RO-21, whereas our approach consistently enhances performance across both datasets.

Qualitative Results. Figure 3 presents a visual comparison of anomaly segmentation results produced by three representative methods: RPL [28], RbA [35], and our proposed method SOTA. In the figure, the first column shows the original input images, while the subsequent columns display the corresponding anomaly maps of various approaches. It can be observed that RPL tends to generate diffused predictions with substantial false positives, particularly along object boundaries and in areas outside the road region. Although RbA improves upon RPL by offering sharper delineation, it still suffers from incomplete segmentation and residual noise. In contrast, SOTA delivers more accurate and comprehensive segmentation of OOD objects while effectively suppressing extraneous pixel predictions beyond the road area. These qualitative findings underscore the advantages of our approach, which unifies attribute-aware feature learning and scene-guided context modeling to achieve a superior balance between precise anomaly localization and noise reduction.

Abstract
Transformer-based architectures and large language models (LLMs) have advanced road scene perception accuracy. However, current road scene segmentation approaches are trained on closed-set data, limiting detection of out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Road anomaly detection methods exist but rely on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection, facing two issues: (1) inadequate consideration of anomalous region objectiveness, leading to incomplete segmentation when anomalies resemble known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, causing detection of anomalies irrelevant to autonomous driving. This paper proposes a novel framework, Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness (SOTA), for autonomous driving. SOTA enhances objectiveness segmentation with a Semantic Fusion Block (SFB) and filters irrelevant anomalies using a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA). Evaluations on Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and RoadAnomaly datasets show SOTA consistently improves OOD detection performance and achieves robust segmentation.

Task-aware Aggregation Module:
1. Identifies road class from semantic segmentation output.
2. Generates a binary road mask.

Projection and Alignment Module:
Projection Module:
1. Lightweight learnable convolutional sub-network.

Alignment Module:
1. Aligns intermediate semantic features with image encoder's representation.
2. Applies a final 1x1 convolutional layer.
3. Maps 16-channel feature map to a 256-dimensional embedding.

5. Output tensor shape: 256x64x64.

paper2.title: Dense Out-of-Distribution Detection by Robust Learning on Synthetic Negative Data
paper2.abstract:
Standard machine learning is unable to accommodate inputs which do not belong to the training distribution. The
                        resulting models often give rise to confident incorrect predictions
                        which may lead to devastating consequences. This problem is
                        especially demanding in the context of dense prediction since
                        input images may be only partially anomalous. Previous work has
                        addressed dense out-of-distribution detection by discriminative
                        training with respect to off-the-shelf negative datasets. However,
                        real negative data are unlikely to cover all modes of the
                        entire visual world. To this end, we extend this approach by
                        generating synthetic negative patches along the border of the
                        inlier manifold. We leverage a jointly trained normalizing flow
                        due to coverage-oriented learning objective and the capability to
                        generate samples at different resolutions. We detect anomalies
                        according to a principled information-theoretic criterion which
                        can be consistently applied through training and inference. The
                        resulting models set the new state of the art on benchmarks for
                        out-of-distribution detection in road-driving scenes and remote
                        sensing imagery, in spite of minimal computational overhead.

**Visualization of Synthetic Outliers**
Our method generates samples at multiple resolutions with the same normalizing flow. These samples have limited variety compared to datasets like ImageNet or COCO. Training with them reduces overconfidence by explicitly training the model to produce uncertain predictions on outliers.

Figure 10 shows synthetic outliers generated by our normalizing flow after joint training on aerial images.

**Fig. 10. Samples of DenseFlow-25-6 after joint training on aerial images.**

Figure 11 shows samples of a normalizing flow after joint training on road-driving scenes. The appearance of synthetic negative samples depends on the underlying inlier dataset. Samples from Figure 10 resemble lakes and forests, while samples from Figure 11 resemble road, sky, cars, and buildings. This is because our normalizing flows are trained to generate data points along the border of the inlier distribution, patching the open-space risk of a segmentation model by adapting synthetic negative data to the training dataset.

**Fig. 11. Samples of DenseFlow-25-6 after joint training on road-driving images as proposed in section III-A.**

**Synthetic Negatives and Feature Space Separation**
For softmax-activated models, softmax can assign arbitrarily large probabilities regardless of feature space distance, failing to bound open-space risk. We analyze synthetic negatives in open-set recognition using a max-logit baseline. Max-logit value is proportional to the projection of a feature vector onto the closest class prototype vector and can be thresholded to bound open-space risk.

SegmentMeIfYouCan (SMIYC) [11] quantifies dense outlier detection performance. It comprises three datasets: AnomalyTrack, ObstacleTrack, and LostAndFound [79]. AnomalyTrack features large objects aligned with the environment (e.g., a leopard on a dirt road). LostAndFound [79] detects small hazardous objects in urban scenes. ObstacleTrack detects small objects on various road types, with inconsistent surfaces potentially increasing false positives. ObstacleTrack and LostAndFound assess OOD detection on the driving surface, while AnomalyTrack considers the whole image. SMIYC provides a measure of OOD segmentation performance in real-world deployment.

StreetHazards [58] is a synthetic dataset generated with CARLA, simulating urban environments with inserted anomalies (e.g., a horse carriage or helicopter on the road). Synthetic anomaly simulation offers flexibility and cost-effectiveness but suffers from a quality mismatch with the real world. It has potential for evaluating outlier-aware segmentation due to cheap ground truth with K+1 classes. StreetHazards is used for measuring outlier-aware segmentation performance via open-mIoU [80].

BSB [16] is a remote sensing dataset of aerial images of Brasilia, containing 3400 labeled images (512x512 pixels), split into 3000 train, 200 validation, and 200 test. Labels include 3 stuff classes (street, permeable area, lake) and 11 thing classes (e.g., swimming pool, vehicle, sports court). Boats and harbors are extracted into the OOD test set, resulting in the BSB-OOD dataset with 2840 training images (12 inlier classes) and 184 OOD test images. This approach mirrors [28], [58], [81] in selecting a subset of classes as OOD samples. Other remote sensing datasets like Vaihingen and Potsdam have fewer labels and images, while So2Sat LCZ42 [82] has small-resolution images and image-level labels. BSB was chosen for its larger dataset size and better performance estimates.

Metrics:
OOD segmentation performance is measured using average precision (AP) [1], false-positive rate at a true-positive rate of 95% (FPR95) [40], and AUROC. AP [11], [12], [83] is suitable for OOD detection as it highlights the minority class, with a perfect score of one. FPR95 [40] is crucial for real-world applications, as high false-positive rates necessitate human intervention. Outlier-aware segmentation performance is measured by open-mIoU [80], which penalizes misclassifications between inliers and outliers. Unlike mIoU on K+1 classes, open-mIoU does not count true positive outlier predictions and averages over K classes. Ideal outlier-aware segmentation performance with perfect OOD detection would yield an open-mIoU equal to the closed-set mIoU, with the difference quantifying the performance gap caused by outliers [80].

Implementation Details:
Models are based on Ladder DenseNet-121 (LDN-121) for memory efficiency and rapid experimentation [84], but the framework supports other dense prediction architectures. Experiments involve two training stages using Cityscapes [85], Vistas [86], and Wilddash 2 [9], totaling 25,231 images. Images are resized to 1024 pixels (shorter edge), randomly flipped (p=0.5), randomly resized ([0.5, 2]), and randomly cropped to 768x768 pixels. Optimization uses Adam. The first stage trains for 25 epochs without synthetic negatives, with a batch size of 16 [84]. The initial learning rate is 10⁻⁴ for the feature extractor and 4 × 10⁻⁴ for the upsampling path, annealed via a cosine schedule to a minimum of 10⁻⁷ by epoch 50. The second stage trains for 15 epochs on mixed content.

C. Sensitivity of OOD detection to depth

Self-driving applications require early and distant anomaly detection. Distant anomalies are harder to detect due to fewer pixels. Analysis performed from 5 to 50 meters due to disparity limitations. Figure 9 shows histograms of inlier and outlier pixels. Over 60% of anomalous pixels are closer than 15 meters, biasing usual metrics (AP and FPR95) towards closer ranges. Many methods fail to detect anomalies at larger depths.

VI. ABLATIONS
We ablate the impact of loss in negative pixels, the choice of generative model, the impact of pretraining, as well as the impact of temperature scaling on dense OOD detection.

A. Impacts of the loss function and OOD score
Table VII analyzes the impact of the loss function Lneg and the OOD score sδ on AnomalyTrack val and ObstacleTrack val. The two chosen datasets feature large and small anomalies, respectively. We separately validate the modulation factor λ for each choice of the negative loss, as well as the temperature parameter. We use T=10 for max-softmax and T=2 for divergence-based scoring functions. We report average performance over last three epochs. Row 1 shows the standard setting with KL divergence as Lneg and max-softmax as the OOD score [26], [33]. Row 2 uses KL divergence both as the loss function and the OOD score. Row 3 features the reverse KL divergence. Minimizing the reverse divergence between the uniform distribution and the softmax distribution is equivalent to maximizing the softmax entropy [50]. Rows 4 and 5 feature the JS divergence. We observe that the reversed KL divergence outperforms the standard KL-MSP setup in 3 out of 4 metrics. However, JS divergence substantially outperforms all alternatives both as the loss function (JSD-MSP vs KL-MSP) and as the OOD score (JSD-JSD vs JSD-MSP and RKL-RKL). We explain this advantage with robust response in synthetic outliers which resemble inliers, as well as with improved consistency during training and scoring (cf. sections III-B and III-C).

B. Impact of the choice of generative model
Table VIII compares synthetic negative data generated by normalizing flow with synthetic negative data generated by GAN [26] and synthetic negative pre-logit features generated by GMM [44]. Normalizing flows model the likelihood as a bijective mapping towards a predefined latent distribution $p(z)$, typically a fully factorized Gaussian. Given a diffeomorphism $f_\gamma$, the likelihood is defined by the change of variables formula:
$p_\gamma(x) = p(z) \det \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$, where $z = f_\gamma(x)$.

Stochastic skip connections can improve training efficiency and convergence speed.

A normalizing flow $f_\gamma$ is sampled in two steps:
1. Sample the latent distribution to obtain a factorized latent tensor $z$.
2. Recover the corresponding image through the inverse transformation $x = f_\gamma^{-1}(z)$.
Both the latent representation and the generated image have the same dimensionality ($R^{3 \times H \times W} \to [0, 1]^{3 \times H \times W}$). This property is useful for generating synthetic negatives at different spatial resolutions.

## Dense OOD Detection with NFlowJS

Dense OOD detection is trained on mixed-content images created by pasting synthetic negatives into regular training images. These negatives are generated by a jointly trained normalizing flow. Models are trained to recognize outliers using a robust information-theoretic criterion, which also serves as the OOD score during inference. A theoretical analysis advocates for training with synthetic negatives generated through likelihood maximization.

### Training with Synthetic Negative Data

A mixed-content image $x'$ is assembled by sampling a randomly sized negative patch $x^-$ from a jointly trained normalizing flow $f_\gamma$ and pasting it onto an inlier image $x^+$:
$x' = (1 - s) \cdot x^+ + \text{pad}(x^-, s)$, where $x^- = f_\gamma^{-1}(z)$.

The binary mask $s$ identifies pixels of the pasted synthetic negative patch. $z$ is sampled from a factorized Gaussian and reshaped to the desired spatial resolution. The negative patch $x^-$ is zero-padded to allow pasting by addition. The pasting location is randomly selected.

**Figure 1.** The proposed training setup. The normalizing flow generates the synthetic negative patch $x^-$ which is pasted onto the inlier image $x^+$. The resulting mixed-content image $x'$ is fed to a dense classifier trained to discriminate inlier pixels ($L_{cls}$) and produce uniform predictions in negative pixels ($L_{neg}$). This formulation enables gradient flow from $L_{neg}$ to the normalizing flow while maximizing the likelihood of inlier patches ($L_{gen}$).

The discriminative model is trained by minimizing cross-entropy over inliers ($s_{ij} = 0$) and maximizing prediction entropy in pasted negatives ($s_{ij} = 1$):
$L_{disc}(\theta; \gamma) = \sum_{i,j} \left( (s_{ij} - 1) \cdot \log p_\theta(y_{ij}|x') + \lambda \cdot s_{ij} \cdot L_{neg}(\theta, \gamma) \right)$.

The normalizing flow is jointly trained with the primary discriminative model to satisfy two criteria:
1. The normalizing flow should maximize the likelihood of inlier patches.
2. The discriminative model should yield uniform distributions in generated pixels.
This training encourages the generation of synthetic samples at the boundary of the training distribution and incorporates outlier awareness within the discriminative model. The total loss applied to the generative model is:
$L_{gen}(\gamma; \theta) = L_{nll}(\gamma) + \lambda \sum_{i,j} s_{ij} \cdot L_{neg}(\theta, \gamma)$.

$L_{nll}$ is the negative log-likelihood of the inlier patch, defined as $L_{nll}(\gamma) = -\log p_\gamma(x_c)$, where $p_\gamma$ is defined in (1). $L_{neg}$ is scrutinized further. The end-to-end training procedure minimizes:
$L(\theta, \gamma) = L_{disc}(\theta; \gamma) + L_{gen}(\gamma; \theta)$.

With sufficient training data and capacity, synthetic negatives encompass the inlier manifold. This allows the method to detect visual anomalies not seen during training, as they are closer to synthetic negatives than inliers. Figure 2 illustrates this on a 2D toy example, where red indicates higher OOD scores. The left plot shows the max-softmax baseline, which assigns high OOD scores only at the border between inlier classes. The right plot, corresponding to this setup, discourages low OOD scores outside the inlier manifold. Synthetic negatives are red stars, and inlier classes are blue.

**Figure 2.** Softmax-activated discriminative models do not bound the input-space.

paper1.abstract:
With the emergence of transformer-based architectures and large
                        language models (LLMs), the accuracy of road scene perception has
                        substantially advanced. Nonetheless, current road scene segmentation approaches are predominantly trained on closed-set data,
                        resulting in insufficient detection capabilities for out-of-distribution
                        (OOD) objects. To overcome this limitation, road anomaly detection
                        methods have been proposed. However, existing methods primarily depend on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection
                        techniques, facing two critical issues: (1) inadequate consideration of the objectiveness attributes of anomalous regions, causing incomplete segmentation when anomalous objects share similarities
                        with known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, leading to the detection of anomalies irrelevant
                        to autonomous driving tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel
                        framework termed Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness
                        (SOTA) for autonomous driving scenes. Specifically, SOTA enhances
                        the segmentation of objectiveness through a Semantic Fusion Block
                        (SFB) and filters anomalies irrelevant to road navigation tasks using
                        a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA).
                        Extensive empirical evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets, including Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and
                        RoadAnomaly, demonstrate that the proposed SOTA consistently
                        improves OOD detection performance across diverse detectors,
                        achieving robust and accurate segmentation outcomes.

4.2 Main Results
Pixel-level Results. As summarized in Table 6, our method significantly outperforms the baseline RbA [35] and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets. While RPL+CoroCL [28] achieves slightly better AuROC and FPR on the Fishyscapes Lost&Found dataset, SOTA improves the AuPRC by a significant margin of 5.5% compared to RPL+CoroCL. Furthermore, SOTA consistently outperforms RPL+CoroCL across all other datasets.

Component-level Results. Table 2 presents the component-level evaluation on the SMIYC RA-21 and SMIYC RO-21 benchmarks. Compared to RbA, our method achieves substantial improvements on RA-21, including a 5.58% increase in sIoU, an 18.31% boost in PPV, and a 14.67% gain in F1*. Similarly, on RO-21, our method yields an 8.00% improvement in PPV and a 9.55% increase in F1*. While Mask2Anomaly achieves a higher performance on RO-21, our approach surpasses it on RA-21, achieving a 0.88% improvement in sIoU and a 12.87% increase in F1*. Moreover, while ContMAV achieves higher PPV and F1* scores on RA-21, it does not report results on RO-21, whereas our approach consistently enhances performance across both datasets.

Qualitative Results. Figure 3 presents a visual comparison of anomaly segmentation results produced by three representative methods: RPL [28], RbA [35], and our proposed method SOTA. In the figure, the first column shows the original input images, while the subsequent columns display the corresponding anomaly maps of various approaches. It can be observed that RPL tends to generate diffused predictions with substantial false positives, particularly along object boundaries and in areas outside the road region. Although RbA improves upon RPL by offering sharper delineation, it still suffers from incomplete segmentation and residual noise. In contrast, SOTA delivers more accurate and comprehensive segmentation of OOD objects while effectively suppressing extraneous pixel predictions beyond the road area. These qualitative findings underscore the advantages of our approach, which unifies attribute-aware feature learning and scene-guided context modeling to achieve a superior balance between precise anomaly localization and noise reduction.

Figure 4: SOTA Qualitative Ablation. Compared to the original outputs, SFB improves the segmentation completeness of OOD objects, while SG-PCA reduces false positives outside the road. When both modules are used together, we achieve the best results, simultaneously reducing false detections outside the road and enhancing the segmentation accuracy of OOD objects on the road.

In configuration (a), no additional modules are applied, representing the baseline RbA output. In configuration (b), only the SG-PCA variant using the raw OOD prompt fusion (˜y) is applied, effectively using RbA’s anomaly score as the mask prompt input to SAM. Abstract
Transformer-based architectures and large language models (LLMs) have advanced road scene perception accuracy. However, current road scene segmentation approaches are trained on closed-set data, limiting detection of out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Road anomaly detection methods exist but rely on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection, facing two issues: (1) inadequate consideration of anomalous region objectiveness, leading to incomplete segmentation when anomalies resemble known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, causing detection of anomalies irrelevant to autonomous driving. This paper proposes a novel framework, Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness (SOTA), for autonomous driving. SOTA enhances objectiveness segmentation with a Semantic Fusion Block (SFB) and filters irrelevant anomalies using a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA). Evaluations on Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and RoadAnomaly datasets show SOTA consistently improves OOD detection performance and achieves robust segmentation.

1 Introduction
Transformer-based architectures [10, 11, 38, 40, 51] and large-scale pretrained models [15, 21, 30] have significantly advanced semantic segmentation in road scene perception. These methods perform well in closed-set environments with predefined object categories. However, real-world environments are open and contain out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Misclassifying or ignoring these anomalies poses safety risks in autonomous driving. Reliably identifying and segmenting OOD objects is crucial.

Task-aware Aggregation Module:
1. Identifies road class from semantic segmentation output.
2. Generates a binary road mask.
3. Refines mask using a 15x15 convolutional kernel filled with ones, applied iteratively 15 times.
4. Each iteration involves padded convolution followed by thresholding at 0 to maintain binary format.
5. Results in an expanded road prompt $y_t$ capturing uncertain boundary regions.

Projection and Alignment Module:
Projection Module:
1. Lightweight learnable convolutional sub-network.
2. Transforms raw OoD confidence map into an intermediate semantic representation.
3. Input: 1x256x256 single-channel.
4. Processed through two 2x2 convolutional layers with stride 2.
5. Spatial resolution reduced to 64x64.
6. Channel dimension expanded to 16.
7. Each layer followed by LayerNorm and GELU activation.
8. Output feature map shape: 16x64x64.

Alignment Module:
1. Aligns intermediate semantic features with image encoder's representation.
2. Applies a final 1x1 convolutional layer.
3. Maps 16-channel feature map to a 256-dimensional embedding.
4. Preserves spatial structure.
5. Output tensor shape: 256x64x64.
6. Used for downstream fusion with image features.

Outlier Exposure:
1. Training dataset preparation uses Outlier Exposure (OE) strategy.
2. Cityscapes dataset used as inlier background (2,975 training images).
3. Objects selected from COCO dataset as OoD objects (excluding categories overlapping with Cityscapes).
4. COCO objects pasted onto Cityscapes images with 0.9 probability per image to simulate anomaly scenarios.
5. RbA framework [35] applied to composite images to compute anomaly scores and semantic logits.

Method demonstrates superior anomaly segmentation across multiple datasets compared to RPL and RbA.

paper2.title: Detecting the Unexpected via Image Resynthesis
paper2.abstract:
Classical semantic segmentation methods, including the
                        recent deep learning ones, assume that all classes observed
                        at test time have been seen during training. In this paper, we
                        tackle the more realistic scenario where unexpected objects
                        of unknown classes can appear at test time. The main trends
                        in this area either leverage the notion of prediction uncertainty to flag the regions with low confidence as unknown, or
                        rely on autoencoders and highlight poorly-decoded regions.
                        Having observed that, in both cases, the detected regions
                        typically do not correspond to unexpected objects, in this
                        paper, we introduce a drastically different strategy: It relies on the intuition that the network will produce spurious
                        labels in regions depicting unexpected objects. Therefore,
                        resynthesizing the image from the resulting semantic map
                        will yield significant appearance differences with respect to
                        the input image. In other words, we translate the problem
                        of detecting unknown classes to one of identifying poorlyresynthesized image regions. We show that this outperforms
                        both uncertainty- and autoencoder-based methods.

We evaluate the road-specific approach of [8], which trains a shallow Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) autoencoder to resynthesize road texture patches corrupted by Gaussian noise. Regions with differing appearance are expected to be reconstructed poorly, yielding an anomaly score from the difference between input and output. The original implementation is not public; we re-implemented it and will make our code available. We use 8x8 patches with stride 6 and a hidden layer of size 20, consistent with [8]. Empty road patches for training are extracted from Cityscapes images using ground-truth road labels. This approach is referred to as RBM.

Our full discrepancy detector uses the original image, the resynthesized image, and predicted semantic labels as input. To assess the importance of each input source, we also report results for variants using only one source: Ours (Resynthesis only) and Ours (Labels only).

**4.2. Anomaly Detection Results**

We evaluate our method's ability to detect unexpected objects on two separate datasets not used during training, focusing on novel object detection.

**4.2.1. Lost and Found**

The Lost And Found [35] dataset comprises images of small items on streets with per-pixel annotations for obstacles and free space. We use the test set, excluding 17 frames with missing annotations. Images are downscaled to 1024x512. A region of interest excludes the ego-vehicle and boundary artifacts. We focus on monocular approaches, not comparing against stereo-based methods from [35].

ROC curves (Fig. 5, left column) show our method outperforms baselines. The Labels-only and Resynthesis-only variants are competitive but less accurate. Uncertainty-based methods are ill-suited for this task. Qualitative examples are in Fig. 6. Our method has fewer false positives than baselines; some false positives represent valid unexpected objects not annotated as obstacles (e.g., a garbage bin).

Restricting evaluation to the road area (union of obstacle and freespace annotations) for the RBM method [8] improves ROC scores (Fig. 5, middle column), indicating easier anomaly detection within the road. Our method still outperforms RBM in this restricted scenario.

**4.2.2. Our Road Anomaly Dataset**

Motivated by data scarcity for unexpected object detection, we collected online images of anomalous objects (animals, rocks, tires, trash cans, construction equipment) on or near roads. We manually annotated these objects per-pixel, using Grab Cut [37] for speed. The dataset contains 60 images.

Resynthesizing an image from the semantic map will therefore result in discrepancies with the input image. A network was developed to detect meaningful discrepancies. The discrepancy detector is trained to identify pixels within the outlines of altered objects. At each feature pyramid level, features from all streams are concatenated and passed through 1x1 convolution filters for channel reduction. Pointwise correlations between real and resynthesized image features are computed and, along with the reduced concatenated features, are passed to an upconvolution pyramid for the final discrepancy score.

Training the discrepancy network on synthetic data simulates the presence of unexpected objects. The semantic segmentation network incorrectly labels regions belonging to unknown classes. To replicate this, random object instances are replaced with a different random label from known classes. The input image is then resynthesized from this altered semantic map using a pix2pixHD generator trained on the dataset. This creates real and synthesized image pairs for training the discrepancy network without needing to observe unexpected objects during training.

Comparing an input image to a resynthesized one detects adversarial attacks. A semantic map is computed from the input image, and the scene is resynthesized using the pix2pixHD generator. For adversarial examples, the predicted semantic map is incorrect, resulting in a distorted resynthesized image. Attack detection is simplified, allowing for a non-differentiable heuristic: the L2 distance between HOG features of the input and resynthesized images. A logistic regressor is trained on these distances to classify images as adversarial or not. This heuristic is more robust to attacks than deep learning-based methods.

Experiments evaluate the approach on detecting unexpected objects (e.g., lost cargo, animals, rocks) in traffic scenes, a target application domain and evaluation area for semantic segmentation. Methods output per-pixel anomaly scores, compared with ground-truth annotations using ROC curves and AUROC. Results for adversarial attack detection are also presented.

Evaluations use Bayesian SegNet and PSP Net, trained on the BDD100K dataset for generalization to anomaly datasets. The image synthesizer and discrepancy detector are trained on the Cityscapes training set, downscaled to 1024x512 due to GPU memory limitations.

Baselines include an uncertainty-based semantic segmentation network, Bayesian SegNet, which uses random dropouts to compute uncertainty as sample variance. This method requires dropout layers, absent in networks like PSP. For PSP, uncertainty is calculated using an ensemble method: four PSP models are trained with different random initializations, and the variance of their outputs serves as a proxy for uncertainty. A road-specific approach using a shallow Restricted Boltzmann Machine autoencoder to resynthesize noisy road patches is also evaluated.

Image resynthesis is used for detecting traffic obstacles in road scenes.
Methods like [32] predict non-anomalous road appearance in the current frame based on the previous frame.
[8, 33] compare input patches to the output of a shallow autoencoder trained on road texture to localize obstacles.
These road-specific methods lack generality. Patch-based approaches like [8] produce many false positives, which our approach outperforms.
Autoencoders in these approaches often perform image compression, generating lower-quality versions of the input, independent of content.
Our method resynthesizes images from semantic label maps; incorrect class predictions lead to appearance variations between input and resynthesized images.

Adversarial attacks in semantic segmentation are also detectable by comparing original and resynthesized images.
Adversarial attack literature primarily focuses on image classification [13, 3, 31], with defense strategies [23, 41] and detection methods [30, 25, 27].
Classification attack schemes have been extended to semantic segmentation networks [44, 6].
[43] is the only known defense scheme proposing an attack detection method in this scenario, analyzing spatial consistency of predictions from overlapping image patches. Our approach outperforms this technique.

**Approach**
Our objective is to handle unexpected objects at test time in semantic segmentation and predict the probability that a pixel belongs to a never-seen-before class.
This contrasts with most semantic segmentation literature, which assigns pixels to classes seen during training, without provisions for unexpected classes.

Figure 3 illustrates the Discrepancy Network.
It takes the original image, predicted semantic labels, and resynthesized image as input to detect meaningful differences caused by mislabeled objects.
A VGG [39] network extracts features from both images, correlated at all pyramid levels.
Image and label features are fused using 1x1 convolutions.
Features and their correlations are fed to a decoder via skip connections to produce the final discrepancy map.

Figure 2 summarizes our approach.
A semantic segmentation algorithm [2, 47] generates a semantic map.
This map is passed to a generative network [42] to resynthesize the input image.
If the image contains objects from a class not seen during segmentation training, these pixels are mislabeled in the semantic map and poorly resynthesized.
Unexpected objects are identified by detecting significant differences between the original and synthetic images.
We then assess which differences are significant.

**Discrepancy Network**
After synthesizing a new image, we compare it to the original to detect meaningful differences indicating unexpected objects not captured by the semantic map.
While known object layouts are preserved in the synthetic image, precise scene appearance information is lost. Simple image differencing is insufficient.
We train a second network, the discrepancy network, to detect significant image discrepancies.

Figure 3 shows the discrepancy network architecture, inspired by the co-segmentation network of [26] which uses feature correlations for detecting co-occurring objects.
Our network has a three-stream architecture for feature extraction.
A pre-trained VGG [39] network processes the original and resynthesized images.
A custom CNN processes the one-hot representation of the predicted labels.

Figure 4 illustrates the creation of training examples for the discrepancy detector:
(a) Ground-truth semantic map.
(b) Map altered by replacing object instances with random labels.
(c) Original image with outlines of altered objects overlaid.
(d) Image resynthesized using the altered map.
The discrepancy detector is trained to find pixels within the altered object outlines shown in (c).

paper1.abstract:
With the emergence of transformer-based architectures and large
                        language models (LLMs), the accuracy of road scene perception has
                        substantially advanced. Nonetheless, current road scene segmentation approaches are predominantly trained on closed-set data,
                        resulting in insufficient detection capabilities for out-of-distribution
                        (OOD) objects. To overcome this limitation, road anomaly detection
                        methods have been proposed. However, existing methods primarily depend on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection
                        techniques, facing two critical issues: (1) inadequate consideration of the objectiveness attributes of anomalous regions, causing incomplete segmentation when anomalous objects share similarities
                        with known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, leading to the detection of anomalies irrelevant
                        to autonomous driving tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel
                        framework termed Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness
                        (SOTA) for autonomous driving scenes. Specifically, SOTA enhances
                        the segmentation of objectiveness through a Semantic Fusion Block
                        (SFB) and filters anomalies irrelevant to road navigation tasks using
                        a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA).
                        Extensive empirical evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets, including Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and
                        RoadAnomaly, demonstrate that the proposed SOTA consistently
                        improves OOD detection performance across diverse detectors,
                        achieving robust and accurate segmentation outcomes.

4.2 Main Results
Pixel-level Results. As summarized in Table 6, our method significantly outperforms the baseline RbA [35] and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets. While RPL+CoroCL [28] achieves slightly better AuROC and FPR on the Fishyscapes Lost&Found dataset, SOTA improves the AuPRC by a significant margin of 5.5% compared to RPL+CoroCL. Furthermore, SOTA consistently outperforms RPL+CoroCL across all other datasets.

Component-level Results. Table 2 presents the component-level evaluation on the SMIYC RA-21 and SMIYC RO-21 benchmarks. Compared to RbA, our method achieves substantial improvements on RA-21, including a 5.58% increase in sIoU, an 18.31% boost in PPV, and a 14.67% gain in F1*. Similarly, on RO-21, our method yields an 8.00% improvement in PPV and a 9.55% increase in F1*. While Mask2Anomaly achieves a higher performance on RO-21, our approach surpasses it on RA-21, achieving a 0.88% improvement in sIoU and a 12.87% increase in F1*. Moreover, while ContMAV achieves higher PPV and F1* scores on RA-21, it does not report results on RO-21, whereas our approach consistently enhances performance across both datasets.

Qualitative Results. Figure 3 presents a visual comparison of anomaly segmentation results produced by three representative methods: RPL [28], RbA [35], and our proposed method SOTA. In the figure, the first column shows the original input images, while the subsequent columns display the corresponding anomaly maps of various approaches. It can be observed that RPL tends to generate diffused predictions with substantial false positives, particularly along object boundaries and in areas outside the road region. Although RbA improves upon RPL by offering sharper delineation, it still suffers from incomplete segmentation and residual noise. In contrast, SOTA delivers more accurate and comprehensive segmentation of OOD objects while effectively suppressing extraneous pixel predictions beyond the road area. These qualitative findings underscore the advantages of our approach, which unifies attribute-aware feature learning and scene-guided context modeling to achieve a superior balance between precise anomaly localization and noise reduction.

Figure 4: SOTA Qualitative Ablation. Compared to the original outputs, SFB improves the segmentation completeness of OOD objects, while SG-PCA reduces false positives outside the road. When both modules are used together, we achieve the best results, simultaneously reducing false detections outside the road and enhancing the segmentation accuracy of OOD objects on the road.

4.3 Ablation Studies
SOTA Ablation Analysis. Table 3 presents an ablation study comparing different configurations of our proposed method SOTA. In configuration (a), no additional modules are applied, representing the baseline RbA output. In configuration (b), only the SG-PCA variant using the raw OOD prompt fusion (˜y) is applied, effectively using RbA’s anomaly score as the mask prompt input to SAM. Configuration (c) incorporates only the SFB along with mask decoder finetuning, thereby directly integrating the enhanced image features with the anomaly cues. In configuration (d), only the SG-PCA variant using the raw OOD prompt fusion (˜y) is applied with finetuning. Configuration (e) applies SG-PCA with both the raw OOD prompt fusion (˜y) and the road semantic prompt (y′t); here, the dual cues help refine the spatial context, yielding a distinct performance pattern. Subsequent rows show the anomaly score map for different methods, namely RPL [28], RbA [35] and our approach SOTA. Abstract
Transformer-based architectures and large language models (LLMs) have advanced road scene perception accuracy. However, current road scene segmentation approaches are trained on closed-set data, limiting detection of out-of-distribution (OOD) objects. Road anomaly detection methods exist but rely on image inpainting and OOD distribution detection, facing two issues: (1) inadequate consideration of anomalous region objectiveness, leading to incomplete segmentation when anomalies resemble known classes, and (2) insufficient attention to environmental constraints, causing detection of anomalies irrelevant to autonomous driving. This paper proposes a novel framework, Segmenting Objectiveness and Task-Awareness (SOTA), for autonomous driving. SOTA enhances objectiveness segmentation with a Semantic Fusion Block (SFB) and filters irrelevant anomalies using a Scene-understanding Guided Prompt-Context Adaptor (SG-PCA). Evaluations on Fishyscapes Lost and Found, Segment-Me-If-You-Can, and RoadAnomaly datasets show SOTA consistently improves OOD detection performance and achieves robust segmentation.
