paper1.title: RbA: Segmenting Unknown Regions Rejected by All
paper1.abstract:
Standard semantic segmentation models owe their success
                        to curated datasets with a fixed set of semantic categories,
                        without contemplating the possibility of identifying unknown
                        objects from novel categories. Existing methods in outlier
                        detection suffer from a lack of smoothness and objectness
                        in their predictions, due to limitations of the per-pixel classification paradigm. Furthermore, additional training for
                        detecting outliers harms the performance of known classes.
                        In this paper, we explore another paradigm with region-level
                        classification to better segment unknown objects. We show
                        that the object queries in mask classification tend to behave
                        like one vs. all classifiers. Based on this finding, we propose
                        a novel outlier scoring function called RbA by defining the
                        event of being an outlier as being rejected by all known
                        classes. Our extensive experiments show that mask classification improves the performance of the existing outlier
                        detection methods, and the best results are achieved with
                        the proposed RbA. We also propose an objective to optimize
                        RbA using minimal outlier supervision. Further fine-tuning
                        with outliers improves the unknown performance, and unlike
                        previous methods, it does not degrade the inlier performance.

This improvement, discussed in Section 3.2, stems from reducing overconfidence due to the independent behavior of object queries. Our method, RbA, outperforms other methods across all metrics. Crucially, RbA achieves this Out-of-Distribution (OoD) performance without degrading closed-set performance, unlike methods like PEBAL which cause a significant drop in mIoU. This demonstrates RbA's superior utilization of mask classification properties.

**Alternative Loss Functions:**
Our chosen squared hinge loss is verified against other common loss functions. Table 4 shows squared hinge loss outperforms others. Mean Squared Error (MSE) and L1 result in higher false positive rates. Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE), used by treating OoD as a binary classification problem with RbA's outlier score as the positive class logit, improves FPR over MSE and L1 but performs worse than squared hinge loss across all metrics. KL Divergence, which minimizes the distance between class probabilities of outlier pixels and a fixed maximum entropy distribution, shows comparable FPR but poor AP, particularly on Fishyscapes LaF. Detailed formulations are in the Supplementary.

**Different Backbones:**
We use Mask2Former with a Swin-B backbone for all experiments. Table 5 reports results with various backbones: transformer-based Multiscale ViT (MViT) and Mix Transformer (MixT), and convolutional WideResnet38 (WR38) and ResNet101 (R101).

Fine-tuning with RbA consistently improves all metrics across all backbones. Swin-B performs best, but R101, MViT, and MixT still outperform previous methods on Road Anomaly and achieve competitive results on Fishyscapes LaF. This indicates RbA's scoring function enhances performance irrespective of the backbone.

**5. Conclusion and Future Work**
This work explores using mask classification for unknown class segmentation. Object queries, acting as one-vs-all classifiers, independently reduce overconfidence in predicted scores, improving existing scoring-based methods like max logit and energy-based methods. We propose RbA, a novel outlier scoring function based on known class probabilities, treating mask classification results as multiple one-vs-all classifiers. We also introduce an objective to optimize RbA with limited outlier data, achieving significant performance gains without impacting closed-set performance. RbA eliminates uncertainty from inlier boundaries and ambiguous background regions, considerably reducing false positive rates. Furthermore, RbA preserves objectness and smoothness due to the region-level inductive biases learned by the mask classifier.

As this is an initial exploration of mask classification for unknown segmentation, its properties can be further investigated. The improved objectness preservation makes open-world incremental learning more feasible, with unknown masks serving as more reliable supervision. Current work is limited to static images; incorporating temporal or depth information could provide significant cues for detecting unknowns.

C. Details of Experiments

C.1. Specialization of Object Queries

Our method's foundation is the observation that object queries in mask classification exhibit independence. Each object query within a subset specializes in segmenting a specific class from the closed set. This behavior is predictable due to the bipartite matching between queries and ground truth class masks during training. We empirically verify this using the BDD100K dataset. For each object query, we count its high-confidence predictions for specific classes. Figure 8 illustrates the heatmap of counts for a Mask2Former model with 100 object queries, showing that a single object query predominantly predicts each closed-set class.

The main paper tests query independence using hard and soft masking, evaluating per-class IoU on Cityscapes. Figure 9 visually explains hard and soft masking.

Figure 9: Illustration of hard vs. soft masking of object queries. In hard masking, for predicting class k, object queries specialized for class k interact with image features while others are masked. In soft masking, all queries interact within the transformer decoder, but only the specialized query predicts class k afterwards.

C.2. Other Loss Functions

The main paper includes an ablation study comparing different loss functions against squared hinge loss. This section details the formulation and parameter settings for each loss function. Ωout denotes outlier pixels, and Ωin denotes inlier pixels.

Mean-Squared Error (MSE): We optimize RbA to approach α = 5 for outlier pixels.
$$LMSE = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} (R_bA(x) - \alpha)^2$$ (8)

L1: Similar to MSE, we optimize RbA with L1 loss, setting α to 5.
$$L_{L1} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} |R_bA(x) - \alpha|$$ (9)

Binary Cross Entropy (BCE): We treat outlier scoring as a per-pixel binary classification problem, with outliers as the positive class. RbA score serves as the logit for the positive class. Assuming y is the binary label (outlier/inlier) for pixel x, we optimize BCE loss:
$$L_{BCE} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} y \cdot \log(R_bA(x)) + (1 - y) \cdot \log(1 - R_bA(x))$$ (10)

KL Divergence: We use KL Divergence to minimize the distance between the predicted class distribution and a fixed distribution. For inlier pixels, we minimize distance to a Dirac delta function (correct class probability of 1.0). For outlier pixels, we minimize distance to a uniform distribution (maximum entropy). While not directly optimizing RbA, this loss helps estimate RbA's contribution by pushing predicted class probabilities toward ideal distributions for outliers and inliers.
Let Lp(x) be the class probability distribution for pixel x with ground truth label y. Let Pin(y) be a fixed probability distribution where class y has probability 1.0. Let U be a fixed uniform probability distribution. The loss function is defined as:
$$L_{in} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{in}} D_{KL}(L_p(x) \parallel P_{in}(y))$$
$$L_{out} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} D_{KL}(L_p(x) \parallel U)$$
$$L_{KL} = \frac{1}{2} (L_{in} + L_{out})$$ (11)

C.3. Other Methods with Mask2Former

To isolate the contribution of our scoring function RbA from the architecture, we present results for state-of-the-art methods PEBAL and DenseHybrid using the Mask2Former architecture. This section details this ablation experiment for each method. For fair comparison, both methods are trained by fine-tuning the same components as RbA: the MLP+Linear layers as shown in Figure 6.

Methods PEBAL [65] and DenseHybrid [25] were implemented using the Mask2Former architecture.

Ablation Experiment Details:
Both methods were fine-tuned using the same components as RbA (MLP+Linear layers) and the same outlier data supervision method.

PEBAL:
The optimized objective consists of three components:

1.  **Pixel-wise Anomaly Abstention Loss (PAL):**
    *   Loss function: $L_{PAL} = -\sum_{x \in \Omega} \log\left(\frac{L_{y(x)} + L_{K+1}(x)}{a(x)}\right)$
    *   $\Omega$: Set of all pixels in an image.
    *   $y \in \{1, \dots, K+1\}$: Ground truth class of pixel $x$.
    *   $K+1$: Class for outliers. In Mask2Former, $K+1$ is the "no object" class. This class is not dropped from region class probabilities $P$ during fine-tuning with the PEBAL objective.
    *   Abstention penalty term $a(x)$: $a(x) = (-E(x))^2$
    *   Free energy function $E(x)$: $E(x) = -\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(L_k(x))\right)$
    *   High penalty discourages abstention; low penalty encourages it.

2.  **Energy Term Optimization:**
    *   Loss function: $L_{energy} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{in}} \max(0, E(x) - \min)^2 + \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} \max(0, \text{mout} - E(x))^2$
    *   $\Omega_{in}$: Set of inlier pixels.
    *   $\Omega_{out}$: Set of outlier pixels.
    *   $\min$, $\text{mout}$: Hyper-parameters. Experimentally set to $\text{mout} = -2.5$ and $\min = -3.5$.

3.  **Regularization Term:**
    *   For smoothness and sparsity of the predicted energy map.
    *   Loss function: $L_{reg} = \sum_{x \in \Omega} \beta_1|E(x) - E(N(x))| + \beta_2|E(x)|$
    *   $N(x)$: Set of vertical and horizontal neighboring pixels of $x$.
    *   $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$: Hyper-parameters. Set to $\beta_1 = 3 \times 10^{-7}$ and $\beta_2 = 5 \times 10^{-5}$.

Full Objective:
*   $L_{PEBAL} = L_{PAL} + \beta L_{energy} + L_{reg}$
*   $\beta$: Weighted sum coefficient, set to $\beta = 0.1$.
*   Training: Started from the same checkpoint as RbA, optimized for 5K iterations with $L_{PEBAL}$. Other hyper-parameters were the same as RbA.

DenseHybrid:
*   An additional outlier prediction head $D(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times H \times W}$ was added to Mask2Former.
*   Outlier Prediction Head: $D(x) = \text{Conv}_{3 \times 3}(\text{ReLU}(\text{BatchNorm}(x)))$
    *   Takes the highest resolution feature map from the pixel decoder.
    *   Predicts a binary output for each pixel indicating outlier probability.

Objective Function:
*   $L_{DH} = \text{CE}(L(x_{in}), Y_{in}) + \beta_1 \text{CE}(D(x), Y_{out}) + \beta_2 L_o$
*   $\text{CE}$: Cross-entropy loss.
*   $x_{in} \in \Omega_{in}$: Set of inlier pixels.
*   $Y_{in}$: Ground truth for closed-set.
*   $Y_{out}$: Binary map where outlier pixels are 1.
*   $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$: Hyper-parameters. Experimentally set to $\beta_1 = 0.3$ and $\beta_2 = 0.03$.
*   $L_o$: $L_o = \frac{1}{|\Omega_{out}|} \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} \log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(L_k(x))\right) + \text{sg}[\text{mean}(L(x))]$
    *   $\text{sg}$: Stop gradient operation.
    *   $\text{mean}$: Mean of all elements in the input tensor.

Additional Qualitative Results (Fig. 10, Fig. 11):

We explore a region-level classification paradigm for object segmentation using mask-classification models like Mask2Former. These models predict regions and classify them, promoting spatial smoothness through region-level supervision. We investigate their properties for improved confidence value calibration, leveraging this to enhance existing Out-of-Distribution (OoD) detection methods that rely on predicted class scores.

Existing methods struggle with high false positive rates due to their inability to separate uncertainty sources, particularly on real-world datasets like Road Anomaly. Segmentation models often produce weak scores for inlier classes at boundaries, leading these regions to be misclassified as OoD. Our analysis of object queries in mask classification reveals their "one vs. all" classifier-like behavior. This observation inspires a novel outlier scoring function where a pixel is considered an outlier if rejected by all known classes, defined as a complementary event to being a known class. This scoring function mitigates irrelevant uncertainty sources, such as those at boundaries, significantly reducing false positive rates.

State-of-the-art OoD methods often use outlier data for supervision, which can improve unknown segmentation but degrades closed-set performance. Our goal is to identify unknowns without compromising inlier accuracy. We propose an objective to optimize our outlier scoring function with limited outlier data. Fine-tuning a small portion of the model with this objective, our method surpasses current state-of-the-art on datasets with high distribution shifts like Road Anomaly and SMIYC, without impacting closed-set performance.

Our contributions include:
* Studying the inherent uncertainty expression capabilities of mask classification models and using this to improve existing OoD segmentation methods.
* Proposing a novel outlier scoring function, based on the "one vs. all" behavior of object queries, which defines outliers as pixels not belonging to any known class. This function reduces uncertainty in ambiguous regions like semantic boundaries.
* Introducing a loss function that optimizes our scoring function using minimal outlier data, outperforming existing methods by fine-tuning only a small model portion and preserving closed-set performance.

**2. Related Work**
**Semantic Segmentation Paradigms:**
Since the advent of Fully Convolutional Networks (FCN), semantic segmentation has predominantly used per-pixel classification. This paradigm has been optimized through convolution, pooling operations, and multi-scale contextual information aggregation. More recent advancements involve transformer-based architectures and attention mechanisms.

Mask classification, prevalent in instance segmentation and object detection, allows pixels to belong to multiple proposals and detects a variable number of objects. Max-DeepLab uses mask classification for panoptic segmentation with auxiliary losses. While earlier attempts applied mask classification to semantic segmentation, they were surpassed by per-pixel methods until recently. MaskFormer variants employ mask classification.

Figure 3 illustrates the impact of masking object queries on per-class IoU in Cityscapes, comparing hard masking (no inter-query interaction) and soft masking (allowing interactions).

paper2.title: DenseHybrid: Hybrid Anomaly Detection for Dense Open-set Recognition
paper2.abstract:
Anomaly detection can be conceived either through generative modelling of regular training data or by discriminating with respect to negative training data. These two approaches exhibit different
                        failure modes. Consequently, hybrid algorithms present an attractive research goal. Unfortunately, dense anomaly detection requires translational equivariance and very large input resolutions. These requirements
                        disqualify all previous hybrid approaches to the best of our knowledge.
                        We therefore design a novel hybrid algorithm based on reinterpreting
                        discriminative logits as a logarithm of the unnormalized joint distribution ˆp(x, y). Our model builds on a shared convolutional representation from which we recover three dense predictions: i) the closedset class posterior P(y|x), ii) the dataset posterior P(din|x), iii) unnormalized data likelihood ˆp(x). The latter two predictions are trained
                        both on the standard training data and on a generic negative dataset.
                        We blend these two predictions into a hybrid anomaly score which allows dense open-set recognition on large natural images. We carefully
                        design a custom loss for the data likelihood in order to avoid backpropagation through the untractable normalizing constant Z(θ). Experiments evaluate our contributions on standard dense anomaly detection benchmarks as well as in terms of open-mIoU - a novel metric for dense open-set performance. Our submissions achieve state-ofthe-art performance despite neglectable computational overhead over
                        the standard semantic segmentation baseline. Official implementation:
                        https://github.com/matejgrcic/DenseHybrid

Measuring performance using the proposed open-IoU requires datasets with K+1 labels. Creating such taxonomy requires substantial resources. Currently, only StreetHazards [23] offers appropriate taxonomy for measuring open-IoU.
5 Experiments
We report dense anomaly detection and open-set recognition performance of the proposed DenseHybrid approach, and compare them with the state of the art. We also explore influence of distance, show computational requirements of the proposed module, and ablate the design choices.
5.1 Benchmarks and Datasets
We evaluate performance on standard benchmarks for dense anomaly detection. Fishyscapes [5] considers urban scenarios on a subset of LostAndFound [44] and on Cityscapes validation images with pasted anomalies (FS Static). SegmentMeIfYouCan (SMIYC) [9] moves away from anomaly injection. Instead, appropriate images are collected from the real world and grouped based on the anomaly size into AnomalyTrack (large) and ObstacleTrack (small). Additionally, the benchmark encapsulates all LostAndFound images. Unfortunately, both benchmarks only have binary labels which makes them insufficient for measuring the recognition performance as proposed in Sec. 4. StreetHazards [23] is a synthetic dataset created by CARLA virtual environment. The simulated environment enables smooth anomaly injection and low-cost label extraction. Consequently, the dataset contains K +1 labels which makes it suitable for measuring both anomaly detection and dense recognition.

**Implementation Details**

Standard segmentation networks are adapted for co-operation with the hybrid anomaly detector by appending an additional branch $g_\gamma$ (BN-ReLU-Conv1x1) that computes the discriminative anomaly output. Generative anomaly output is obtained by summing exponentiated logits. Recognition models are built based on dense classifiers and fine-tuned on mixed-content images with pasted negative instances from ADE20k. For SMIYC, LDN-121 [30] is fine-tuned for 10 epochs on images from Cityscapes [12], Vistas [42], and Wilddash2 [52]. For Fishyscapes, DeepLabV3+ with WideResNet38 [55] is fine-tuned for 10 epochs on Cityscapes. LDN-121 is trained on Street-Hazards for 120 epochs in a closed world, then the recognition model is fine-tuned on mixed-content images. Further details are provided in the supplement.

**Conclusion**

Discriminative and generative approaches to dense anomaly detection have different failure modes. This work proposes a synergy by fusing the data posterior and data likelihood derived from a standard discriminative model. The proposed hybrid setup relies on unnormalized distributions, avoiding the evaluation of intractable normalization constants during training and inference. The DenseHybrid architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard anomaly segmentation benchmarks and competitive dense recognition performance in the open world, measured by the novel open-mIoU score. Future work will focus on reducing the performance gap between closed-world and open-world recognition to improve autonomous driving safety.

Hybrid Anomaly Detection for Dense Open-set Recognition

Related Work
Detecting samples deviating from training data generation is a long-standing problem [22], also known as anomaly detection or out-of-distribution (OOD) detection [24]. Early image-wide approaches used max-softmax probability [24], input perturbations [34], ensembling [31], or Bayesian uncertainty [40]. Improved performance was achieved through discriminative training against broad negative datasets [14, 25, 2, 37] or appropriately trained generative models [32, 21, 54].

Another research direction detects anomalies by estimating likelihood with a generative model. This revealed anomalies can have higher likelihood than inliers [41, 47, 53]. Group-wise anomaly detection [27] shows promise but has less practical importance. Generative models can be trained to assign low likelihood to negative data [25], potentially mitigating sub-optimal probability volume dispersion [38].

Image-wide anomaly detection methods are adaptable to dense prediction with varying success. Existing generative approaches do not provide dense likelihood estimates. Max-softmax and discriminative training with negative data are easily ported to dense prediction. Many dense anomaly detectors are trained on mixed-content images by pasting negatives (e.g., ImageNet, COCO, ADE20k) onto training images [2, 10, 4]. Discriminative anomaly detection can use a dedicated OOD head sharing features with the standard classification head. Shared features enhance OOD performance with negligible computational overhead compared to baseline semantic segmentation [2]. Recent work [10] promotes high softmax entropy in negative pixels.

Anomalies can be recognized in feature space [6]. However, this complicates detecting small objects due to subsampled features and feature collapse [38, 1]. Alternatively, anomaly detectors can use the dissimilarity between the input and a resynthesized image [36, 4, 50]. Resynthesis uses a generative model conditioned on predicted labels, but this is suitable only for uniform backgrounds like roads [36] and adds significant computational overhead, making it unsuitable for real-time applications.

Our dense anomaly detection approach combines discriminative detection and likelihood evaluation. Discriminative OOD detection was introduced in [2, 25, 14]. We improve it through synergy with likelihood testing. Dense likelihood evaluation was done by fitting a generative model to discriminative features [6]. However, their method is vulnerable to feature collapse [38, 1] due to two-phase training, and detecting small outliers is hindered by subsampling. Our method allows joint training with the standard dense prediction model and anomaly detection at full resolution.

We perform dense likelihood evaluation by reinterpreting logits as unnormalized joint likelihood [20]. However, method [20] is unsuitable for dense prediction due to the intractability of Langevin sampling at large resolutions. We reformulate their method to allow training on mixed-content images, which simplifies training by precluding backpropagation through the intractable normalizing constant Z(θ). To our knowledge, our design is the first approach for dense likelihood evaluation suitable for end-to-end training.

We build an open-set recognition model by thresholding our hybrid anomaly score and combining it with standard semantic segmentation predictions [7]. This model detects anomalies and recognizes inlier scenery simultaneously. Standard dense recognition metrics [16] do not account for accuracy on anomalous samples, as outlier pixels are recent additions to dense prediction benchmarks [52, 5, 9]. Previous work on discrimination with anomalous pixels focused more on algorithm robustness than recognition performance [52]. Thus, we propose a novel anomaly-aware performance metric called open-mIoU.

7.1 Limitations

Our method is termed hybrid because it optimizes two distinct training objectives:
i) dense discrimination between inliers and negatives, and ii) achieving a high likelihood for inliers and a low likelihood for negative data. While likelihood evaluation is a standard feature of generative models (excluding GANs) and might suggest sample generation capabilities, our formulation is not suitable for this purpose due to its handling of unnormalized distributions. This would necessitate MCMC sampling, which is infeasible at large resolutions with current techniques. Furthermore, even if sample generation were possible, the resulting approach would likely be too slow for real-time inference, as demonstrated by other image resynthesis methods.

7.2 Impact of Known Inliers on Anomaly Detection

Many real-world autonomous systems operate in environments with limited variability, such as warehouses or industrial plants. These environments typically exhibit perfectly aligned training and test distributions. Anomalous objects can still occur in such settings. We demonstrate that anomaly detection performance is significantly enhanced when known inlier instances from the test set are available. Table 7 illustrates this scenario using two DLv3+ segmentation networks. The first network was trained on the Cityscapes training set, while the second was trained on both the Cityscapes training and validation splits. Given that the Fishyscapes Static dataset is generated by overlaying negative objects onto Cityscapes validation images, we can assess anomaly detection performance with known inlier instances from the test set. The results show a drastic improvement in the average precision of anomaly detection, increasing from 60% to 89%. This indicates that the DenseHybrid anomaly detector is practical for scenarios with limited scene variety.

| train | 60.0 ± 2.0 | 4.9 ± 0.6 | 81.0 |

7.3 More Results

Table 8 presents the dense open-set recognition performance of generative and discriminative anomaly detectors on the StreetHazards dataset. The proposed hybrid anomaly score, calculated as the ratio of these two distributions, surpasses the performance of each individual component. Notably, the generative and discriminative outputs are trained using identical mixed-content images.

7.4 Implementation Details

Mixed-content training samples are created by pasting negative data onto inlier crops. Inlier crops are generated by jittering images within a range of [0.5, 2], applying random horizontal flips, and performing random square cropping to a size of 768. ADE20k instances are used as negative content. The negative images are resized to 768 pixels, and a random jittered crop of size 384 is extracted. Subsequently, two instances from the negative crop are pasted onto the inlier crop at random positions. For LDN-121, a batch size of 16 is used, along with the Adam optimizer and an initial learning rate of 10⁻⁵, which is decayed through a cosine schedule down to 10⁻⁷. The loss modulation hyper-parameter β is set to 0.03. For DLv3+, a batch size of 8 and inlier crops of 512 are used. The Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10⁻⁶ is employed, without decay. The loss modulation hyper-parameter β is set to 0.01.

In the case of Fishyscapes, DLv3+ with a WRN38 backbone, pre-trained by NVIDIA, is fine-tuned. However, due to hardware constraints, training from scratch to achieve the desired robustness for SMIYC was not feasible. Therefore, LDN-121 was chosen as an efficient alternative that can be trained on a single GPU. Utilizing the larger DLv3+ model would likely result in further improvements on SMIYC.

7.5 Visualizations

Figure 7 visualizes the anomaly detection performance of DenseHybrid on the SMIYC-AnomalyTrack and SMIYC-ObstacleTrack datasets. Anomalies detected by DenseHybrid are highlighted above the input images. The corresponding ground truth designates anomalies in orange, inlier pixels in white, and ignored pixels in black.

Fig. 7. Anomaly detection performance of DenseHybrid on SMIYC validation subsets.

We build our hybrid anomaly detector upon the discriminative dataset posterior P(din|x) and the generative data likelihood p(x). We express a novel hybrid anomaly score as log-ratio between P(dout|x) = 1 −P(din|x) and p(x):
$s(\mathbf{x}) := \ln \frac{P(d_{out}|\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x})} = \ln P(d_{out}|\mathbf{x}) - \ln \hat{p}(\mathbf{x}) + \ln Z \cong \ln P(d_{out}|\mathbf{x}) - \ln \hat{p}(\mathbf{x})$.

We can neglect Z since ranking performance is invariant to monotonic transformations. Other formulations of s(x) may also be effective, which is an interesting direction for future work.

Figure 3 illustrates the inference with the proposed open-set recognition setup. RGB input is fed to a hybrid dense model which produces pre-logit activations t and logits s. Then, we obtain the closed-set class posterior P(y|x) = softmax(s) and the unnormalized data likelihood ˆp(x). A distinct head g transforms pre-logits t into the dataset posterior P(dout|x). The anomaly score s(x) is a log-ratio between latter two distributions. The resulting anomaly map is thresholded and fused with the discriminative output into the final dense open-set recognition map.

The developed hybrid model aims at achieving a synergy between generative and discriminative modelling. However, the proposed hybrid interpretation requires specific training objectives. Dense class posteriors require a discriminative loss over the inlier data Din:
$L_{cls}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in D_{in}}[- \ln P(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})] = - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in D_{in}}[\mathbf{s}_y] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in D_{in}}[\ln \sum_i \exp{\mathbf{s}_i}]$.

The discriminative loss corresponds to the standard training in the closed world. We introduce the negative data Dout into the training procedure to ensure the desired behaviour of P(din|x) and p(x). Both distributions should yield low probability in negative pixels. We propose to train p(x) to maximize the likelihood in inliers and to minimize the likelihood in outliers. We derive the upper bound of the desired loss as follows:
$L_{\mathbf{x}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{in}}[- \ln p(\mathbf{x})] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{out}}[-\ln p(\mathbf{x})] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{in}}[- \ln \hat{p}(\mathbf{x})] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{out}}[-\ln \hat{p}(\mathbf{x})] = - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in D_{in}}[\mathbf{s}_y] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{out}}[\ln \sum_i\exp(\mathbf{s}_i)] \leq - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in D_{in}}[\mathbf{s}_y] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \in D_{out}}[\ln \sum_i\exp(\mathbf{s}_i)]$.

We eschew the backpropagation into the normalization constant Z, and derive the upper bound according to the following inequality:
$\ln \sum_i\exp{\mathbf{s}_i} \geq \max_i \mathbf{s}_i \geq \mathbf{s}_y$.

Proof of inequality (13) can be easily derived by recalling that log-sum-exp is a smooth upper bound of the max function. By comparing the standard classification loss (7) and the upper bound (12) we realize that minimizing the standard classification loss increases p(x) for inlier pixels. Indeed, minimizing the negative logarithm of softmax output increases the value of logit for the correct class.

paper1.title: RbA: Segmenting Unknown Regions Rejected by All
paper1.abstract:
Standard semantic segmentation models owe their success
                        to curated datasets with a fixed set of semantic categories,
                        without contemplating the possibility of identifying unknown
                        objects from novel categories. Existing methods in outlier
                        detection suffer from a lack of smoothness and objectness
                        in their predictions, due to limitations of the per-pixel classification paradigm. Furthermore, additional training for
                        detecting outliers harms the performance of known classes.
                        In this paper, we explore another paradigm with region-level
                        classification to better segment unknown objects. We show
                        that the object queries in mask classification tend to behave
                        like one vs. all classifiers. Based on this finding, we propose
                        a novel outlier scoring function called RbA by defining the
                        event of being an outlier as being rejected by all known
                        classes. Our extensive experiments show that mask classification improves the performance of the existing outlier
                        detection methods, and the best results are achieved with
                        the proposed RbA. We also propose an objective to optimize
                        RbA using minimal outlier supervision. Further fine-tuning
                        with outliers improves the unknown performance, and unlike
                        previous methods, it does not degrade the inlier performance.

Crucially, RbA achieves this Out-of-Distribution (OoD) performance without degrading closed-set performance, unlike methods like PEBAL which cause a significant drop in mIoU. This demonstrates RbA's superior utilization of mask classification properties.

**Alternative Loss Functions:**
Our chosen squared hinge loss is verified against other common loss functions. Table 4 shows squared hinge loss outperforms others. Mean Squared Error (MSE) and L1 result in higher false positive rates. Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE), used by treating OoD as a binary classification problem with RbA's outlier score as the positive class logit, improves FPR over MSE and L1 but performs worse than squared hinge loss across all metrics. KL Divergence, which minimizes the distance between class probabilities of outlier pixels and a fixed maximum entropy distribution, shows comparable FPR but poor AP, particularly on Fishyscapes LaF. Detailed formulations are in the Supplementary.

**Different Backbones:**
We use Mask2Former with a Swin-B backbone for all experiments. Table 5 reports results with various backbones: transformer-based Multiscale ViT (MViT) and Mix Transformer (MixT), and convolutional WideResnet38 (WR38) and ResNet101 (R101).

Fine-tuning with RbA consistently improves all metrics across all backbones. Swin-B performs best, but R101, MViT, and MixT still outperform previous methods on Road Anomaly and achieve competitive results on Fishyscapes LaF. This indicates RbA's scoring function enhances performance irrespective of the backbone.

**5. Conclusion and Future Work**
This work explores using mask classification for unknown class segmentation. Object queries, acting as one-vs-all classifiers, independently reduce overconfidence in predicted scores, improving existing scoring-based methods like max logit and energy-based methods. We propose RbA, a novel outlier scoring function based on known class probabilities, treating mask classification results as multiple one-vs-all classifiers. We also introduce an objective to optimize RbA with limited outlier data, achieving significant performance gains without impacting closed-set performance. RbA eliminates uncertainty from inlier boundaries and ambiguous background regions, considerably reducing false positive rates. Furthermore, RbA preserves objectness and smoothness due to the region-level inductive biases learned by the mask classifier.

As this is an initial exploration of mask classification for unknown segmentation, its properties can be further investigated. The improved objectness preservation makes open-world incremental learning more feasible, with unknown masks serving as more reliable supervision. Current work is limited to static images; incorporating temporal or depth information could provide significant cues for detecting unknowns.

C. Details of Experiments

C.1. Specialization of Object Queries

Our method's foundation is the observation that object queries in mask classification exhibit independence. Each object query within a subset specializes in segmenting a specific class from the closed set. This behavior is predictable due to the bipartite matching between queries and ground truth class masks during training. We empirically verify this using the BDD100K dataset. For each object query, we count its high-confidence predictions for specific classes. Figure 8 illustrates the heatmap of counts for a Mask2Former model with 100 object queries, showing that a single object query predominantly predicts each closed-set class.

The main paper tests query independence using hard and soft masking, evaluating per-class IoU on Cityscapes. Figure 9 visually explains hard and soft masking.

Figure 9: Illustration of hard vs. soft masking of object queries. In hard masking, for predicting class k, object queries specialized for class k interact with image features while others are masked. In soft masking, all queries interact within the transformer decoder, but only the specialized query predicts class k afterwards.

C.2. Other Loss Functions

The main paper includes an ablation study comparing different loss functions against squared hinge loss. This section details the formulation and parameter settings for each loss function. Ωout denotes outlier pixels, and Ωin denotes inlier pixels.

Mean-Squared Error (MSE): We optimize RbA to approach α = 5 for outlier pixels.
$$LMSE = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} (R_bA(x) - \alpha)^2$$ (8)

L1: Similar to MSE, we optimize RbA with L1 loss, setting α to 5.
$$L_{L1} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} |R_bA(x) - \alpha|$$ (9)

Binary Cross Entropy (BCE): We treat outlier scoring as a per-pixel binary classification problem, with outliers as the positive class. RbA score serves as the logit for the positive class. Assuming y is the binary label (outlier/inlier) for pixel x, we optimize BCE loss:
$$L_{BCE} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} y \cdot \log(R_bA(x)) + (1 - y) \cdot \log(1 - R_bA(x))$$ (10)

KL Divergence: We use KL Divergence to minimize the distance between the predicted class distribution and a fixed distribution. For inlier pixels, we minimize distance to a Dirac delta function (correct class probability of 1.0). For outlier pixels, we minimize distance to a uniform distribution (maximum entropy). While not directly optimizing RbA, this loss helps estimate RbA's contribution by pushing predicted class probabilities toward ideal distributions for outliers and inliers.
Let Lp(x) be the class probability distribution for pixel x with ground truth label y. Let Pin(y) be a fixed probability distribution where class y has probability 1.0. Let U be a fixed uniform probability distribution. The loss function is defined as:
$$L_{in} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{in}} D_{KL}(L_p(x) \parallel P_{in}(y))$$
$$L_{out} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} D_{KL}(L_p(x) \parallel U)$$
$$L_{KL} = \frac{1}{2} (L_{in} + L_{out})$$ (11)

C.3. Other Methods with Mask2Former

To isolate the contribution of our scoring function RbA from the architecture, we present results for state-of-the-art methods PEBAL and DenseHybrid using the Mask2Former architecture. This section details this ablation experiment for each method. For fair comparison, both methods are trained by fine-tuning the same components as RbA: the MLP+Linear layers as shown in Figure 6.

Methods PEBAL [65] and DenseHybrid [25] were implemented using the Mask2Former architecture.

Ablation Experiment Details:
Both methods were fine-tuned using the same components as RbA (MLP+Linear layers) and the same outlier data supervision method.

PEBAL:
The optimized objective consists of three components:

1.  **Pixel-wise Anomaly Abstention Loss (PAL):**
    *   Loss function: $L_{PAL} = -\sum_{x \in \Omega} \log\left(\frac{L_{y(x)} + L_{K+1}(x)}{a(x)}\right)$
    *   $\Omega$: Set of all pixels in an image.
    *   $y \in \{1, \dots, K+1\}$: Ground truth class of pixel $x$.
    *   $K+1$: Class for outliers. In Mask2Former, $K+1$ is the "no object" class. This class is not dropped from region class probabilities $P$ during fine-tuning with the PEBAL objective.
    *   Abstention penalty term $a(x)$: $a(x) = (-E(x))^2$
    *   Free energy function $E(x)$: $E(x) = -\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(L_k(x))\right)$
    *   High penalty discourages abstention; low penalty encourages it.

2.  **Energy Term Optimization:**
    *   Loss function: $L_{energy} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{in}} \max(0, E(x) - \min)^2 + \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} \max(0, \text{mout} - E(x))^2$
    *   $\Omega_{in}$: Set of inlier pixels.
    *   $\Omega_{out}$: Set of outlier pixels.
    *   $\min$, $\text{mout}$: Hyper-parameters. Experimentally set to $\text{mout} = -2.5$ and $\min = -3.5$.

3.  **Regularization Term:**
    *   For smoothness and sparsity of the predicted energy map.
    *   Loss function: $L_{reg} = \sum_{x \in \Omega} \beta_1|E(x) - E(N(x))| + \beta_2|E(x)|$
    *   $N(x)$: Set of vertical and horizontal neighboring pixels of $x$.
    *   $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$: Hyper-parameters. Set to $\beta_1 = 3 \times 10^{-7}$ and $\beta_2 = 5 \times 10^{-5}$.

Full Objective:
*   $L_{PEBAL} = L_{PAL} + \beta L_{energy} + L_{reg}$
*   $\beta$: Weighted sum coefficient, set to $\beta = 0.1$.
*   Training: Started from the same checkpoint as RbA, optimized for 5K iterations with $L_{PEBAL}$. Other hyper-parameters were the same as RbA.

DenseHybrid:
*   An additional outlier prediction head $D(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times H \times W}$ was added to Mask2Former.
*   Outlier Prediction Head: $D(x) = \text{Conv}_{3 \times 3}(\text{ReLU}(\text{BatchNorm}(x)))$
    *   Takes the highest resolution feature map from the pixel decoder.
    *   Predicts a binary output for each pixel indicating outlier probability.

Objective Function:
*   $L_{DH} = \text{CE}(L(x_{in}), Y_{in}) + \beta_1 \text{CE}(D(x), Y_{out}) + \beta_2 L_o$
*   $\text{CE}$: Cross-entropy loss.
*   $x_{in} \in \Omega_{in}$: Set of inlier pixels.
*   $Y_{in}$: Ground truth for closed-set.
*   $Y_{out}$: Binary map where outlier pixels are 1.
*   $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$: Hyper-parameters. Experimentally set to $\beta_1 = 0.3$ and $\beta_2 = 0.03$.
*   $L_o$: $L_o = \frac{1}{|\Omega_{out}|} \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} \log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(L_k(x))\right) + \text{sg}[\text{mean}(L(x))]$
    *   $\text{sg}$: Stop gradient operation.
    *   $\text{mean}$: Mean of all elements in the input tensor.

We explore a region-level classification paradigm for object segmentation using mask-classification models like Mask2Former. These models predict regions and classify them, promoting spatial smoothness through region-level supervision. We investigate their properties for improved confidence value calibration, leveraging this to enhance existing Out-of-Distribution (OoD) detection methods that rely on predicted class scores.

Existing methods struggle with high false positive rates due to their inability to separate uncertainty sources, particularly on real-world datasets like Road Anomaly. Segmentation models often produce weak scores for inlier classes at boundaries, leading these regions to be misclassified as OoD. Our analysis of object queries in mask classification reveals their "one vs. all" classifier-like behavior. This observation inspires a novel outlier scoring function where a pixel is considered an outlier if rejected by all known classes, defined as a complementary event to being a known class. This scoring function mitigates irrelevant uncertainty sources, such as those at boundaries, significantly reducing false positive rates.

State-of-the-art OoD methods often use outlier data for supervision, which can improve unknown segmentation but degrades closed-set performance. Our goal is to identify unknowns without compromising inlier accuracy. We propose an objective to optimize our outlier scoring function with limited outlier data. Fine-tuning a small portion of the model with this objective, our method surpasses current state-of-the-art on datasets with high distribution shifts like Road Anomaly and SMIYC, without impacting closed-set performance.

Our contributions include:
* Studying the inherent uncertainty expression capabilities of mask classification models and using this to improve existing OoD segmentation methods.
* Proposing a novel outlier scoring function, based on the "one vs. all" behavior of object queries, which defines outliers as pixels not belonging to any known class. This function reduces uncertainty in ambiguous regions like semantic boundaries.
* Introducing a loss function that optimizes our scoring function using minimal outlier data, outperforming existing methods by fine-tuning only a small model portion and preserving closed-set performance.

**2. Related Work**
**Semantic Segmentation Paradigms:**
Since the advent of Fully Convolutional Networks (FCN), semantic segmentation has predominantly used per-pixel classification. This paradigm has been optimized through convolution, pooling operations, and multi-scale contextual information aggregation. More recent advancements involve transformer-based architectures and attention mechanisms.

Mask classification, prevalent in instance segmentation and object detection, allows pixels to belong to multiple proposals and detects a variable number of objects. Max-DeepLab uses mask classification for panoptic segmentation with auxiliary losses. While earlier attempts applied mask classification to semantic segmentation, they were surpassed by per-pixel methods until recently. MaskFormer variants employ mask classification.

Figure 3 illustrates the impact of masking object queries on per-class IoU in Cityscapes, comparing hard masking (no inter-query interaction) and soft masking (allowing interactions).

paper2.title: Entropy Maximization and Meta Classification for Out-Of-Distribution Detection in Semantic Segmentation
paper2.abstract:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) for the semantic segmentation of images are usually trained to operate on a predefined closed set of object classes. This is in contrast to
                        the “open world” setting where DNNs are envisioned to be
                        deployed to. From a functional safety point of view, the ability to detect so-called “out-of-distribution” (OoD) samples,
                        i.e., objects outside of a DNN’s semantic space, is crucial
                        for many applications such as automated driving. A natural baseline approach to OoD detection is to threshold on
                        the pixel-wise softmax entropy. We present a two-step procedure that significantly improves that approach. Firstly,
                        we utilize samples from the COCO dataset as OoD proxy
                        and introduce a second training objective to maximize the
                        softmax entropy on these samples. Starting from pretrained
                        semantic segmentation networks we re-train a number of
                        DNNs on different in-distribution datasets and consistently
                        observe improved OoD detection performance when evaluating on completely disjoint OoD datasets. Secondly, we
                        perform a transparent post-processing step to discard false
                        positive OoD samples by so-called “meta classification.”
                        To this end, we apply linear models to a set of hand-crafted
                        metrics derived from the DNN’s softmax probabilities. In
                        our experiments we consistently observe a clear additional
                        gain in OoD detection performance, cutting down the number of detection errors by 52% when comparing the best
                        baseline with our results. We achieve this improvement sacrificing only marginally in original segmentation performance. Therefore, our method contributes to safer DNNs
                        with more reliable overall system performance.

Conclusion & Outlook:
A novel re-training approach for deep neural networks combines improved OoD detection with state-of-the-art semantic segmentation. This OoD training significantly enhances detection efficiency via softmax entropy thresholding, outperforming existing methods. Meta classifiers for entropy-based OoD object predictions, using lightweight logistic regressions, reliably classify OoD segments. The increased sensitivity from entropy maximization further enhances meta classifier efficiency. The combination of OoD training and meta classification can significantly improve safety-critical deep learning applications.

Future work includes applying OoD training for OoD object retrieval to assess their importance and the need for new concepts. Code is available at https://github.com/robin-chan/meta-ood.

**C. Segment-wise Metrics for Meta Classifiers**

Meta classifiers are trained using hand-crafted metrics derived from softmax probabilities $f(x) \in (0, 1)^{|Z| \times |C|}$ and other information from deep convolutional neural networks. Let $\hat{Z}_{out}(x)$ be the set of pixel locations predicted as OoD in image $x$. An OoD segment/object prediction, $k \in \hat{K}(x) \subseteq P(\hat{Z}_{out}(x))$, is a connected component where entropy exceeds a given threshold. This differs from other segment-wise meta classification approaches that consider connected components with the same class label as segments.

Uncertainty per OoD segment $k$ is estimated by averaging pixel-wise scores for pixels $z \in k$. In addition to softmax probabilities $f_z(x)$, three pixel-wise dispersion measures are used:

1.  **Normalized Entropy:**
    $\bar{E}(f_z(x)) = -\frac{1}{|C|} \sum_{j \in C} f_{z_j}(x) \log(f_{z_j}(x))$

2.  **Variation Ratio:**
    $V(f_z(x)) = 1 - f_{z_{\hat{c}(z)}}(x)$

3.  **Probability Margin:**
    $M(f_z(x)) = V(f_z(x)) + \max_{j \in C \setminus \{\hat{c}(z)\}} f_{z_j}(x)$
    where $\hat{c}(z) := \arg \max_{j \in C} f_{z_j}(x)$ is the class label with the highest a posteriori probability.

Segment size $S(k) = |k|$ is used for averaging and as a direct meta classification input. Interior pixel locations $k_{in} = \{(h, w) \in k : [h \pm 1] \times [w \pm 1] \in k\}$ and boundary pixel locations $k_{bd} = k \setminus k_{in}$ are considered. Relative sizes of the boundary and interior are used as geometry features:
$\tilde{S} = S/S_{bd}$ and $\tilde{S}_{in} = S_{in}/S_{bd}$

Variances of pixel-wise scores are also considered, measuring deviation from the segment score mean, and significantly impact OoD detection meta classifiers.

The neighborhood of segment $k$ is defined as $k_{nb} = \{z' \in [h \pm 1] \times [w \pm 1] \subset |H| \times |W| : (h, w) \in k, z' \notin k\}$, where $Z = H \times W$ is the image. A metric for misplaced segments is:
$N(j|k) = \frac{1}{|k_{nb}|} \sum_{z \in k_{nb}} \mathbf{1}_{\{j=\hat{c}(z)\}} \forall j \in C$
This is the proportion of neighborhood pixels with class $j$ having the highest softmax score, relative to the neighborhood size.

The segment's geometric center is calculated as:
$C_h(k) = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{i=1}^{S} h_i$ and $C_w(k) = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{i=1}^{S} w_i$
where $z_i = (h_i, w_i) \in k$ for $i = 1, \dots, |k|$.

For each segment $k$, there are $m=83$ metrics in total (assuming $|C|=19$). This forms a structured dataset:
$\mu \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{|\cup_{x \in X} \hat{K}(x)| \times m} = \mathbb{R}^{|\cup_{x \in X} \hat{K}(x)| \times 83}$

6.2. Original Task Performance
To monitor that the baseline model does not unlearn its original task due to Out-of-Distribution (OoD) training, we evaluate the model’s performance on in-distribution data with OoD predictions at different entropy thresholds. The original task is the semantic segmentation of Cityscapes images, evaluated using the mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) metric. In addition to Cityscapes class predictions obtained via the standard maximum a posteriori (MAP) decision principle, we consider an extra OoD class prediction if the softmax entropy is above a given threshold $t$. We compute mIoU for the Cityscapes validation dataset, averaging only over the 19 Cityscapes class IoUs.

The state-of-the-art DeepLabv3+ model, serving as our baseline, achieves an mIoU score of 0.90 on the Cityscapes validation dataset without OoD predictions ($t = 1.0$). Retraining the CNN with entropy maximization on OoD inputs improves OoD-AUPRC scores, indicating better detection of OoD samples. This gain comes with a marginal drop in Cityscapes validation mIoU to 0.89. These mIoU scores remain nearly constant (deviations less than 1 percent point) for thresholds $t = 0.3, \dots, 1.0$. Generally, lower entropy thresholds result in more pixels predicted as OoD. At $t = 0.2$, a noticeable performance decrease is observed: 0.05 for the baseline and 0.03 for the retrained model. Further lowering the threshold leads to a more significant sacrifice of original performance. Therefore, we consider entropy thresholds of at least $t = 0.3$, as the performance loss appears acceptable given substantially improved OoD detection capability.

7. Segment-wise Evaluation
This section evaluates the meta-classification performance on LostAndFound. The main metrics for segment-wise evaluation are the numbers of False Positives (FPs) and False Negatives (FNs) with respect to an OoD object prediction. The F1-score ($F1 = \frac{2TP}{2TP + FP + FN}$) summarizes error rates. As removing FP OoD predictions should not significantly impact original performance, we also consider the miss rate of road pixels:
$$ \epsilon := 1 - \frac{|\hat{Z}_{in}(x) \cap Z_{in}(x)|}{|Z_{in}(x)|} - 1 $$
where $X$ is the dataset, $\hat{Z}_{in}$ are pixel locations predicted as in-distribution, and $Z_{in}$ are pixels annotated as in-distribution. $\epsilon$ measures the fraction of actual road pixels incorrectly identified.

We compute per-segment metrics for OoD object predictions in the LostAndFound test set and feed them into simple logistic regression meta-classification models. Segments are leave-one-out cross-validated for TP or FP classification. Least angle regression is used to analyze metrics most impactful on meta-classification. The analysis shows that after OoD training, the entropy metric $E(f(x))$ has the most impact.

Generally, higher entropy thresholds predict fewer OoD objects, consequently reducing data for linear models. This explains why meta-classifiers identify FPs more reliably at lower $t$. topic: Image segmentation anomaly detection aims to identify and segment unusual or unexpected regions in images, supporting safety-critical applications in medical imaging, manufacturing, and autonomous systems. What is the better method for image segmentation anomaly detection tasks: RbA or ATTA?

paper1.title: RbA: Segmenting Unknown Regions Rejected by All
paper1.abstract:
Standard semantic segmentation models owe their success
                        to curated datasets with a fixed set of semantic categories,
                        without contemplating the possibility of identifying unknown
                        objects from novel categories. Existing methods in outlier
                        detection suffer from a lack of smoothness and objectness
                        in their predictions, due to limitations of the per-pixel classification paradigm. Furthermore, additional training for
                        detecting outliers harms the performance of known classes.
                        In this paper, we explore another paradigm with region-level
                        classification to better segment unknown objects. We show
                        that the object queries in mask classification tend to behave
                        like one vs. all classifiers. Based on this finding, we propose
                        a novel outlier scoring function called RbA by defining the
                        event of being an outlier as being rejected by all known
                        classes. Our extensive experiments show that mask classification improves the performance of the existing outlier
                        detection methods, and the best results are achieved with
                        the proposed RbA. We also propose an objective to optimize
                        RbA using minimal outlier supervision. Further fine-tuning
                        with outliers improves the unknown performance, and unlike
                        previous methods, it does not degrade the inlier performance.

Crucially, RbA achieves this Out-of-Distribution (OoD) performance without degrading closed-set performance, unlike methods like PEBAL which cause a significant drop in mIoU. This demonstrates RbA's superior utilization of mask classification properties.

**5. Conclusion and Future Work**
This work explores using mask classification for unknown class segmentation. Object queries, acting as one-vs-all classifiers, independently reduce overconfidence in predicted scores, improving existing scoring-based methods like max logit and energy-based methods. We propose RbA, a novel outlier scoring function based on known class probabilities, treating mask classification results as multiple one-vs-all classifiers. We also introduce an objective to optimize RbA with limited outlier data, achieving significant performance gains without impacting closed-set performance. RbA eliminates uncertainty from inlier boundaries and ambiguous background regions, considerably reducing false positive rates. Furthermore, RbA preserves objectness and smoothness due to the region-level inductive biases learned by the mask classifier.

As this is an initial exploration of mask classification for unknown segmentation, its properties can be further investigated. The improved objectness preservation makes open-world incremental learning more feasible, with unknown masks serving as more reliable supervision. Current work is limited to static images; incorporating temporal or depth information could provide significant cues for detecting unknowns.

C. Details of Experiments

C.1. Specialization of Object Queries

Our method's foundation is the observation that object queries in mask classification exhibit independence. Each object query within a subset specializes in segmenting a specific class from the closed set. This behavior is predictable due to the bipartite matching between queries and ground truth class masks during training. We empirically verify this using the BDD100K dataset. For each object query, we count its high-confidence predictions for specific classes. Figure 8 illustrates the heatmap of counts for a Mask2Former model with 100 object queries, showing that a single object query predominantly predicts each closed-set class.

The main paper tests query independence using hard and soft masking, evaluating per-class IoU on Cityscapes. Figure 9 visually explains hard and soft masking.

Figure 9: Illustration of hard vs. soft masking of object queries. In hard masking, for predicting class k, object queries specialized for class k interact with image features while others are masked. In soft masking, all queries interact within the transformer decoder, but only the specialized query predicts class k afterwards.

C.2. Other Loss Functions

The main paper includes an ablation study comparing different loss functions against squared hinge loss. This section details the formulation and parameter settings for each loss function. Ωout denotes outlier pixels, and Ωin denotes inlier pixels.

Mean-Squared Error (MSE): We optimize RbA to approach α = 5 for outlier pixels.
$$LMSE = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} (R_bA(x) - \alpha)^2$$ (8)

L1: Similar to MSE, we optimize RbA with L1 loss, setting α to 5.
$$L_{L1} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} |R_bA(x) - \alpha|$$ (9)

Binary Cross Entropy (BCE): We treat outlier scoring as a per-pixel binary classification problem, with outliers as the positive class. RbA score serves as the logit for the positive class. Assuming y is the binary label (outlier/inlier) for pixel x, we optimize BCE loss:
$$L_{BCE} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} y \cdot \log(R_bA(x)) + (1 - y) \cdot \log(1 - R_bA(x))$$ (10)

KL Divergence: We use KL Divergence to minimize the distance between the predicted class distribution and a fixed distribution. For inlier pixels, we minimize distance to a Dirac delta function (correct class probability of 1.0). For outlier pixels, we minimize distance to a uniform distribution (maximum entropy). While not directly optimizing RbA, this loss helps estimate RbA's contribution by pushing predicted class probabilities toward ideal distributions for outliers and inliers.
Let Lp(x) be the class probability distribution for pixel x with ground truth label y. Let Pin(y) be a fixed probability distribution where class y has probability 1.0. Let U be a fixed uniform probability distribution. The loss function is defined as:
$$L_{in} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{in}} D_{KL}(L_p(x) \parallel P_{in}(y))$$
$$L_{out} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} D_{KL}(L_p(x) \parallel U)$$
$$L_{KL} = \frac{1}{2} (L_{in} + L_{out})$$ (11)

C.3. Other Methods with Mask2Former

To isolate the contribution of our scoring function RbA from the architecture, we present results for state-of-the-art methods PEBAL and DenseHybrid using the Mask2Former architecture. This section details this ablation experiment for each method. For fair comparison, both methods are trained by fine-tuning the same components as RbA: the MLP+Linear layers as shown in Figure 6.

Methods PEBAL [65] and DenseHybrid [25] were implemented using the Mask2Former architecture.

Ablation Experiment Details:
Both methods were fine-tuned using the same components as RbA (MLP+Linear layers) and the same outlier data supervision method.

PEBAL:
The optimized objective consists of three components:

1.  **Pixel-wise Anomaly Abstention Loss (PAL):**
    *   Loss function: $L_{PAL} = -\sum_{x \in \Omega} \log\left(\frac{L_{y(x)} + L_{K+1}(x)}{a(x)}\right)$
    *   $\Omega$: Set of all pixels in an image.
    *   $y \in \{1, \dots, K+1\}$: Ground truth class of pixel $x$.
    *   $K+1$: Class for outliers. In Mask2Former, $K+1$ is the "no object" class. This class is not dropped from region class probabilities $P$ during fine-tuning with the PEBAL objective.
    *   Abstention penalty term $a(x)$: $a(x) = (-E(x))^2$
    *   Free energy function $E(x)$: $E(x) = -\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(L_k(x))\right)$
    *   High penalty discourages abstention; low penalty encourages it.

2.  **Energy Term Optimization:**
    *   Loss function: $L_{energy} = \sum_{x \in \Omega_{in}} \max(0, E(x) - \min)^2 + \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} \max(0, \text{mout} - E(x))^2$
    *   $\Omega_{in}$: Set of inlier pixels.
    *   $\Omega_{out}$: Set of outlier pixels.
    *   $\min$, $\text{mout}$: Hyper-parameters. Experimentally set to $\text{mout} = -2.5$ and $\min = -3.5$.

3.  **Regularization Term:**
    *   For smoothness and sparsity of the predicted energy map.
    *   Loss function: $L_{reg} = \sum_{x \in \Omega} \beta_1|E(x) - E(N(x))| + \beta_2|E(x)|$
    *   $N(x)$: Set of vertical and horizontal neighboring pixels of $x$.
    *   $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$: Hyper-parameters. Set to $\beta_1 = 3 \times 10^{-7}$ and $\beta_2 = 5 \times 10^{-5}$.

Full Objective:
*   $L_{PEBAL} = L_{PAL} + \beta L_{energy} + L_{reg}$
*   $\beta$: Weighted sum coefficient, set to $\beta = 0.1$.
*   Training: Started from the same checkpoint as RbA, optimized for 5K iterations with $L_{PEBAL}$. Other hyper-parameters were the same as RbA.

DenseHybrid:
*   An additional outlier prediction head $D(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times H \times W}$ was added to Mask2Former.
*   Outlier Prediction Head: $D(x) = \text{Conv}_{3 \times 3}(\text{ReLU}(\text{BatchNorm}(x)))$
    *   Takes the highest resolution feature map from the pixel decoder.
    *   Predicts a binary output for each pixel indicating outlier probability.

Objective Function:
*   $L_{DH} = \text{CE}(L(x_{in}), Y_{in}) + \beta_1 \text{CE}(D(x), Y_{out}) + \beta_2 L_o$
*   $\text{CE}$: Cross-entropy loss.
*   $x_{in} \in \Omega_{in}$: Set of inlier pixels.
*   $Y_{in}$: Ground truth for closed-set.
*   $Y_{out}$: Binary map where outlier pixels are 1.
*   $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$: Hyper-parameters. Experimentally set to $\beta_1 = 0.3$ and $\beta_2 = 0.03$.
*   $L_o$: $L_o = \frac{1}{|\Omega_{out}|} \sum_{x \in \Omega_{out}} \log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(L_k(x))\right) + \text{sg}[\text{mean}(L(x))]$
    *   $\text{sg}$: Stop gradient operation.
    *   $\text{mean}$: Mean of all elements in the input tensor.

We explore a region-level classification paradigm for object segmentation using mask-classification models like Mask2Former. These models predict regions and classify them, promoting spatial smoothness through region-level supervision. We investigate their properties for improved confidence value calibration, leveraging this to enhance existing Out-of-Distribution (OoD) detection methods that rely on predicted class scores.

Existing methods struggle with high false positive rates due to their inability to separate uncertainty sources, particularly on real-world datasets like Road Anomaly. Segmentation models often produce weak scores for inlier classes at boundaries, leading these regions to be misclassified as OoD. Our analysis of object queries in mask classification reveals their "one vs. all" classifier-like behavior. This observation inspires a novel outlier scoring function where a pixel is considered an outlier if rejected by all known classes, defined as a complementary event to being a known class. This scoring function mitigates irrelevant uncertainty sources, such as those at boundaries, significantly reducing false positive rates.

State-of-the-art OoD methods often use outlier data for supervision, which can improve unknown segmentation but degrades closed-set performance. Our goal is to identify unknowns without compromising inlier accuracy. We propose an objective to optimize our outlier scoring function with limited outlier data. Fine-tuning a small portion of the model with this objective, our method surpasses current state-of-the-art on datasets with high distribution shifts like Road Anomaly and SMIYC, without impacting closed-set performance.

Our contributions include:
* Studying the inherent uncertainty expression capabilities of mask classification models and using this to improve existing OoD segmentation methods.
* Proposing a novel outlier scoring function, based on the "one vs. all" behavior of object queries, which defines outliers as pixels not belonging to any known class. This function reduces uncertainty in ambiguous regions like semantic boundaries.
* Introducing a loss function that optimizes our scoring function using minimal outlier data, outperforming existing methods by fine-tuning only a small model portion and preserving closed-set performance.

**2. Related Work**
**Semantic Segmentation Paradigms:**
Since the advent of Fully Convolutional Networks (FCN), semantic segmentation has predominantly used per-pixel classification. This paradigm has been optimized through convolution, pooling operations, and multi-scale contextual information aggregation. More recent advancements involve transformer-based architectures and attention mechanisms.

Mask classification, prevalent in instance segmentation and object detection, allows pixels to belong to multiple proposals and detects a variable number of objects. Max-DeepLab uses mask classification for panoptic segmentation with auxiliary losses. While earlier attempts applied mask classification to semantic segmentation, they were surpassed by per-pixel methods until recently. MaskFormer variants employ mask classification.

Figure 3 illustrates the impact of masking object queries on per-class IoU in Cityscapes, comparing hard masking (no inter-query interaction) and soft masking (allowing interactions).

paper2.title: ATTA: Anomaly-aware Test-Time Adaptation for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Segmentation
paper2.abstract:
Recent advancements in dense out-of-distribution (OOD) detection have primarily
                        focused on scenarios where the training and testing datasets share a similar domain,
                        with the assumption that no domain shift exists between them. However, in realworld situations, domain shift often exits and significantly affects the accuracy of
                        existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection models. In this work, we propose a
                        dual-level OOD detection framework to handle domain shift and semantic shift
                        jointly. The first level distinguishes whether domain shift exists in the image by
                        leveraging global low-level features, while the second level identifies pixels with
                        semantic shift by utilizing dense high-level feature maps. In this way, we can
                        selectively adapt the model to unseen domains as well as enhance model’s capacity
                        in detecting novel classes. We validate the efficacy of our method on several OOD
                        segmentation benchmarks, including those with significant domain shifts and those
                        without, observing consistent performance improvements across various baseline
                        models. Code is available at https://github.com/gaozhitong/ATTA.

Compared to other methods, our method with PEBAL achieves new state-of-the-art performance across three datasets. Figure 3 provides qualitative results. Our ATTA approach improves OOD detection by mitigating domain-shift impact and encouraging model prediction confidence for inliers and outliers.

Appendix E presents time and memory overhead, and additional ablation results.

5 Conclusion

This work proposes dense OOD detection under domain shift, highlighting limitations of existing methods in wild scenarios. We introduce a dual-level OOD detection framework to jointly handle domain and semantic shift, enabling selective adaptation to unseen domains and enhancing detection of novel classes. We validate our method on OOD segmentation benchmarks with and without significant domain shifts, demonstrating substantial performance gains, especially in cases with notable domain shifts.

ATTA can be further refined. Similar to other self-training methods, ATTA relies on a well-initialized model. While our adaptation method shows strong results on state-of-the-art models, improvement is less noticeable with weaker backbones. Test-time adaptation also adds computational time. Future research could focus on developing more efficient algorithms to reduce inference time. Our study introduces a more realistic setting for dense OOD detection under domain shift and aims to guide future work.

G.1 Specific Domain Shift in the Road Anomaly Dataset

The domain shift in the Road Anomaly dataset compared to Cityscapes includes adverse road conditions, diverse weather and lighting conditions, and various camera perspectives and conditions.

Adverse Road Conditions: Road Anomaly includes diverse rural locations with varied textures and colors due to different materials, wear, soil types, and vegetation, unlike the well-paved urban scenes in Cityscapes. Previous OOD detection methods often mistake these variations for anomalies, while our algorithm reduces such errors.

Weather and Lighting Variations: Road Anomaly includes snowy, rainy, foggy weather, and nighttime scenes, which affect surrounding areas and the sky, leading to more false positive errors in existing OOD detection models. Our method enhances adaptability to changes in weather and lighting.

Various Camera Conditions: Road Anomaly images can be captured from various angles and locations, such as alongside the road, differing from the typical road-centered perspective in Cityscapes. This variance can disrupt previously learned biases in road surface predictions.

**Constructing FS Static-C Dataset:**
The FS Static-C dataset was created by simulating domain shift through random smog, color shifting, and Gaussian blur. The fog function from Hendrycks and Dietterich [16] was incorporated. The ‘ColorJitter’ and ‘GaussianBlur’ transformations from the torchvision library were utilized. Each transformation was applied independently with a 50% probability. Random combinations of these transformations generated the final transformed images. This process created a diverse dataset encompassing various forms and levels of domain shift, enabling comprehensive evaluation and demonstration of robustness.

**Additional Results on Simulated FS Static-C Dataset**

**ATTA Combined with Other OOD Detection Methods:**
Evaluation extended to include PEBAL [44] and five other OOD detection methods. The results demonstrated that the method consistently enhances the robustness of these OOD detection techniques under potential domain shifts. Significant performance gains were achieved on the FS Static-C dataset for all OOD detection methods. Average increases were approximately 20% in AUC, 10% in AP, and a decrease of nearly 80% in FPR95. Some results on FS Static-C surpassed original performance on the non-domain-shift FS-Static dataset for methods like MSP, Entropy, and Meta-OOD. Combination with various OOD detection methods demonstrated efficacy and general applicability.

A Pseudo Code of ATTA
The pseudo code for Anomaly-aware Test-Time Adaptation (ATTA) is presented in Algorithm 1. Each test image xt utilizes a same pre-trained network parameter θ for initialization. The adaptation process consists of two stages: a domain-aware selective Batch Normalization (BN) updating stage and an online self-training stage based on an anomaly-aware entropy loss. The final output includes the inlier probability map and outlier score map for each test image.

Algorithm 1: Anomaly-aware Test-Time Adaptation (ATTA)
Input: Test samples Dtest = {xt}T t=1, seen-class classifier fθ, unseen-class detector gθ with pretrained θ, number of iterations N, learning rate η, confidence thresholds τ1, τ2.
Output: Inlier probability maps {Ft}T t=1, outlier score maps {Gt}T t=1.

for xt ∈ Dtest do
Initialize parameters θt ← θ.
Compute the domain-shift probability based on Eq.(1).
Update the BN statistics using the probability as in Eq.(2,3).
for i = 1, · · · , N do
Get inlier probability map Ft ← fθt(xt) and outlier score map Gt ← gθt(xt).
Calculate anomaly-aware entropy loss L(Ft, Gt, τ1, τ2) as in Eq.(10,11).
Update model parameters: θt ← Adam(∇L, θt, η).
end
Output inlier probability map Ft ← fθt(xt) and outlier score map Gt ← gθt(xt).
end

B More Implementation Details
Experimental Results of Previous OOD Methods: Experimental results for previous dense OOD detection methods are obtained by running pretrained model weights from official code repositories or as officially reported in original papers.

Implementation Details for Tent: For Tent [46], instructions from their original paper on segmentation tasks are followed. This includes considering affine transformation parameters in Batch Normalization layers as trainable parameters, using transductive batch normalization [36], and adopting episodic training. For fair comparison, the model is updated once per test image, Adam optimizer is used, and the learning rate is tuned on the FS Static-C dataset.

Implementation Details for GMM Modeling in Our Method: During Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) fitting, a peak-finding algorithm identifies the right-most peak in the OOD score distribution. This peak is used as the initial mean for the right GMM component before Expectation-Maximization (EM) optimization. This approach mitigates issues from multiple peaks in the inlier distribution, leveraging prior knowledge that the right-most peak likely represents outliers.

Details in Constructing FS Static-C Dataset: Domain shift in the FS Static-C dataset is simulated by introducing random smog, color shifting, and Gaussian noise, as described in Section 4.1.

paper1.title: RbA: Segmenting Unknown Regions Rejected by All
paper1.abstract:
Standard semantic segmentation models owe their success
                        to curated datasets with a fixed set of semantic categories,
                        without contemplating the possibility of identifying unknown
                        objects from novel categories. Existing methods in outlier
                        detection suffer from a lack of smoothness and objectness
                        in their predictions, due to limitations of the per-pixel classification paradigm. Furthermore, additional training for
                        detecting outliers harms the performance of known classes.
                        In this paper, we explore another paradigm with region-level
                        classification to better segment unknown objects. We show
                        that the object queries in mask classification tend to behave
                        like one vs. all classifiers. Based on this finding, we propose
                        a novel outlier scoring function called RbA by defining the
                        event of being an outlier as being rejected by all known
                        classes. Our extensive experiments show that mask classification improves the performance of the existing outlier
                        detection methods, and the best results are achieved with
                        the proposed RbA. We also propose an objective to optimize
                        RbA using minimal outlier supervision. Further fine-tuning
                        with outliers improves the unknown performance, and unlike
                        previous methods, it does not degrade the inlier performance.

Crucially, RbA achieves this Out-of-Distribution (OoD) performance without degrading closed-set performance, unlike methods like PEBAL which cause a significant drop in mIoU. This demonstrates RbA's superior utilization of mask classification properties.

**Alternative Loss Functions:**
Our chosen squared hinge loss is verified against other common loss functions. Table 4 shows squared hinge loss outperforms others. Mean Squared Error (MSE) and L1 result in higher false positive rates. Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE), used by treating OoD as a binary classification problem with RbA's outlier score as the positive class logit, improves FPR over MSE and L1 but performs worse than squared hinge loss across all metrics. KL Divergence, which minimizes the distance between class probabilities of outlier pixels and a fixed maximum entropy distribution, shows comparable FPR but poor AP, particularly on Fishyscapes LaF. Detailed formulations are in the Supplementary.

**Different Backbones:**
We use Mask2Former with a Swin-B backbone for all experiments. Table 5 reports results with various backbones: transformer-based Multiscale ViT (MViT) and Mix Transformer (MixT), and convolutional WideResnet38 (WR38) and ResNet101 (R101).
