A Pseudo Code of ATTA
The pseudo code for Anomaly-aware Test-Time Adaptation (ATTA) is presented in Algorithm 1. Each test image xt utilizes a same pre-trained network parameter θ for initialization. The adaptation process consists of two stages: a domain-aware selective Batch Normalization (BN) updating stage and an online self-training stage based on an anomaly-aware entropy loss. The final output includes the inlier probability map and outlier score map for each test image.

Algorithm 1: Anomaly-aware Test-Time Adaptation (ATTA)
Input: Test samples Dtest = {xt}T t=1, seen-class classifier fθ, unseen-class detector gθ with pretrained θ, number of iterations N, learning rate η, confidence thresholds τ1, τ2.
Output: Inlier probability maps {Ft}T t=1, outlier score maps {Gt}T t=1.

for xt ∈ Dtest do
Initialize parameters θt ← θ.
Compute the domain-shift probability based on Eq.(1).
Update the BN statistics using the probability as in Eq.(2,3).
for i = 1, · · · , N do
Get inlier probability map Ft ← fθt(xt) and outlier score map Gt ← gθt(xt).
Calculate anomaly-aware entropy loss L(Ft, Gt, τ1, τ2) as in Eq.(10,11).
Update model parameters: θt ← Adam(∇L, θt, η).
end
Output inlier probability map Ft ← fθt(xt) and outlier score map Gt ← gθt(xt).
end

B More Implementation Details
Experimental Results of Previous OOD Methods: Experimental results for previous dense OOD detection methods are obtained by running pretrained model weights from official code repositories or as officially reported in original papers.

Implementation Details for Tent: For Tent [46], instructions from their original paper on segmentation tasks are followed. This includes considering affine transformation parameters in Batch Normalization layers as trainable parameters, using transductive batch normalization [36], and adopting episodic training. For fair comparison, the model is updated once per test image, Adam optimizer is used, and the learning rate is tuned on the FS Static-C dataset.

Implementation Details for GMM Modeling in Our Method: During Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) fitting, a peak-finding algorithm identifies the right-most peak in the OOD score distribution. This peak is used as the initial mean for the right GMM component before Expectation-Maximization (EM) optimization. This approach mitigates issues from multiple peaks in the inlier distribution, leveraging prior knowledge that the right-most peak likely represents outliers.

Details in Constructing FS Static-C Dataset: Domain shift in the FS Static-C dataset is simulated by introducing random smog, color shifting, and Gaussian noise, as described in Section 4.1.

paper2.title: A Simple Unified Framework for Detecting Out-of-Distribution Samples and Adversarial Attacks
paper2.abstract:
Detecting test samples drawn sufficiently far away from the training distribution
                        statistically or adversarially is a fundamental requirement for deploying a good
                        classifier in many real-world machine learning applications. However, deep neural networks with the softmax classifier are known to produce highly overconfident
                        posterior distributions even for such abnormal samples. In this paper, we propose
                        a simple yet effective method for detecting any abnormal samples, which is applicable to any pre-trained softmax neural classifier. We obtain the class conditional
                        Gaussian distributions with respect to (low- and upper-level) features of the deep
                        models under Gaussian discriminant analysis, which result in a confidence score
                        based on the Mahalanobis distance. While most prior methods have been evaluated for detecting either out-of-distribution or adversarial samples, but not both,
                        the proposed method achieves the state-of-the-art performances for both cases in
                        our experiments. Moreover, we found that our proposed method is more robust
                        in harsh cases, e.g., when the training dataset has noisy labels or small number of
                        samples. Finally, we show that the proposed method enjoys broader usage by applying it to class-incremental learning: whenever out-of-distribution samples are
                        detected, our classification rule can incorporate new classes well without further
                        training deep models.
methodology:
A confidence score M(x) is computed on a test sample x. If M(x) is above a threshold, it is classified as positive (in-distribution). The Euclidean distance, using only empirical class means, is used for comparison. ResNet is trained on CIFAR-10. Tiny-ImageNet is used as an out-of-distribution dataset. The Mahalanobis distance-based metric outperforms the Euclidean and maximum softmax score methods.

Calibration Techniques:
Input pre-processing involves adding controlled noise to test samples. For each test sample x, a pre-processed sample bx is calculated:
bx = x + εsign(▽xM(x)) = x − εsign(▽x(f(x) − bµbc)⊤bΣ−1(f(x) − bµbc))
Here, ε is the noise magnitude, and bc is the index of the closest class. The confidence score is then measured using bx. This noise is generated to increase the confidence score, not for adversarial attacks. This perturbation can better separate in- and out-of-distribution samples. Similar input pre-processing in [21] aims to increase the softmax score of the predicted label. Our method differs as the noise is generated to increase the proposed metric.

Algorithm 2: Updating Mahalanobis distance-based classifier for class-incremental learning.
Input: Samples from a new class {xi : ∀i = 1 . . . NC+1}, means and covariances of observed classes {bµc : ∀c = 1 . . . C}, bΣ
1. Compute the new class mean: bµC+1 ← 1/NC+1 * Σ_i f(xi)
2. Compute the covariance of the new class: bΣC+1 ← 1/NC+1 * Σ_i (f(xi) − bµC+1)(f(xi) − bµC+1)⊤
3. Update the shared covariance: bΣ ← (C/(C+1)) * bΣ + (1/(C+1)) * bΣC+1
Output: Means and covariances of all classes {bµc : ∀c = 1 . . . C + 1}, bΣ

Feature ensemble: To enhance performance, confidence scores from low-level features, in addition to final features, are measured and combined. For training data, ℓ-th hidden features fℓ(x) are extracted, and their empirical class means bµℓ,c and tied covariances bΣℓ are computed. For each test sample x, the confidence score from the ℓ-th layer is measured using formula (2). This method can improve calibration by extracting more input-specific information from low-level features. The area under ROC (AUROC) curves for a threshold-based detector using confidence scores from different basic blocks of DenseNet trained on CIFAR-10 are measured. Similar trends are observed on ResNet. Performance on various OOD samples (SVHN, LSUN, TinyImageNet, and adversarial samples from DeepFool) is shown in Figure 2. Intermediate feature dimensions are reduced using average pooling. Confidence scores from low-level features often provide better calibration than final features (e.g., for LSUN, TinyImageNet, and DeepFool). A feature ensemble method is designed to further improve performance. Confidence scores from all layers are extracted and integrated by weighted averaging: Σℓ αℓMℓ(x), where Mℓ(·) is the confidence score at the ℓ-th layer and αℓ is its weight. Weights are chosen by training a logistic regression detector on validation samples. This weighted averaging of confidence scores can prevent performance degradation if some layer scores are ineffective; their trained weights would be near zero.

Class-incremental learning using Mahalanobis distance-based score: The Mahalanobis distance-based confidence score can be used in class-incremental learning. A classifier pre-trained on base classes is updated with new classes and samples. This is challenging due to catastrophic forgetting and limited memory. Existing methods often involve generative models or data sampling, which can be computationally expensive. Based on the proposed confidence score, a simple classification method is developed without complex training. It assumes the classifier is well-trained.

**3.3 Class-Incremental Learning**

**Setup:**
*   ResNet-34 is trained for CIFAR-100 and downsampled ImageNet classification.
*   A classifier is pre-trained on base classes; new classes are incrementally added.
*   **Scenario 1:** Half of CIFAR-100 classes are base, the rest are new.
*   **Scenario 2:** All CIFAR-100 classes are base, 100 ImageNet classes are new.
*   All scenarios are tested five times and averaged. Class splits are randomly generated per trial.
*   **Comparison Methods:**
    *   Softmax classifier (fine-tuned for new classes, only softmax layer updated for near-zero cost training).
    *   Euclidean classifier (accommodates new classes by computing class mean).
*   **Memory Management (Softmax Classifier):** Follows Rebuffi & Kolesnikov [29]. A small number of old class samples are kept in memory. Memory size matches that for Mahalanobis distance-based classifier (sum of learned classes and hidden feature dimension, 512 in experiments).
*   **Evaluation:**
    *   Base-new class accuracy curve adjusted by a bias to new class scores (similar to [18]).
    *   Area Under Curve (AUC) measured to provide an imbalanced measure of performance.

**Comparison with Other Classifiers:**
*   Figure 4 compares incremental learning performance (AUC) in two scenarios.
*   Each sub-figure shows AUC vs. number of learned classes (left) and base-new class accuracy curve after last new class addition (right).
*   Mahalanobis distance-based classifier (ours) significantly outperforms other methods, especially as the number of new classes increases.
*   A crossing is observed in the right figure of Figure 4(b) in small regimes due to catastrophic forgetting.
*   **AUC Performance:**
    *   Our method: 40.0% (22.1%)
    *   Softmax classifier: 32.7% (15.6%)
    *   Euclidean distance classifier: 32.9% (17.1%)
    *   (First experiment (Second experiment) results)
*   Similar trends observed when CIFAR-100 classes are base and CIFAR-10 classes are new (reported in supplementary material).
*   Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our confidence score compared to others.

**4 Conclusion**
*   Propose a simple yet effective method for detecting abnormal test samples (out-of-distribution and adversarial).
*   Core idea: Induce a generative classifier under LDA assumption and define a new confidence score.
*   With calibration techniques (input pre-processing, feature ensemble), the method performs strongly across tasks: OOD detection, adversarial attack detection, and class-incremental learning.
*   Method is more robust to hyperparameter choices and extreme scenarios (noisy labels, small datasets).
*   Approach has potential for broader application.

C
More experimental results
C.1
Robustness of our method in detecting adversarial samples
To verify robustness, we measured detection performance by training ResNet on CIFAR-10 with varying numbers of training data and random labels. Our method (blue bar) outperforms LID (green bar) across all experiments (Figure 5).
C.2
Class-incremental learning
Figure 6 compares AUCs when CIFAR-100 is pre-trained and CIFAR-10 serves as new classes. Our Mahalanobis distance-based classifier significantly outperforms others as the number of new classes increases. With all new classes added, our method achieves an AUC of 47.7%, compared to 41.0% for the softmax classifier and 43.0% for the Euclidean distance classifier.
C.3
Experimental results on joint confidence loss
The proposed detector using a softmax neural classifier trained with standard cross-entropy loss typically outperforms the ODIN detector, which uses a softmax classifier trained with confidence loss [19]. The latter involves jointly training a generator and classifier to calibrate the posterior distribution. Our detector further improves performance when used with a model trained by confidence loss, indicating our method enhances any pre-trained softmax neural classifier.

paper1.title: Dense Out-of-Distribution Detection by Robust Learning on Synthetic Negative Data
paper1.abstract:
Standard machine learning is unable to accommodate inputs which do not belong to the training distribution. The
                        resulting models often give rise to confident incorrect predictions
                        which may lead to devastating consequences. This problem is
                        especially demanding in the context of dense prediction since
                        input images may be only partially anomalous. Previous work has
                        addressed dense out-of-distribution detection by discriminative
                        training with respect to off-the-shelf negative datasets. However,
                        real negative data are unlikely to cover all modes of the
                        entire visual world. To this end, we extend this approach by
                        generating synthetic negative patches along the border of the
                        inlier manifold. We leverage a jointly trained normalizing flow
                        due to coverage-oriented learning objective and the capability to
                        generate samples at different resolutions. We detect anomalies
                        according to a principled information-theoretic criterion which
                        can be consistently applied through training and inference. The
                        resulting models set the new state of the art on benchmarks for
                        out-of-distribution detection in road-driving scenes and remote
                        sensing imagery, in spite of minimal computational overhead.

**Inference Speed**
A dense OOD detector should not significantly increase computational burden. Inference speed was measured on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 for 1024 × 2048 inputs. Our approach increases inference time by only 7.8 ms over the baseline while outperforming other methods. SynthCP measurements are from [90].

**Visualization of Synthetic Outliers**
Our method generates samples at multiple resolutions with the same normalizing flow. These samples have limited variety compared to datasets like ImageNet or COCO. Training with them reduces overconfidence by explicitly training the model to produce uncertain predictions on outliers.

Figure 11 shows samples of a normalizing flow after joint training on road-driving scenes. The appearance of synthetic negative samples depends on the underlying inlier dataset. Samples from Figure 10 resemble lakes and forests, while samples from Figure 11 resemble road, sky, cars, and buildings. This is because our normalizing flows are trained to generate data points along the border of the inlier distribution, patching the open-space risk of a segmentation model by adapting synthetic negative data to the training dataset.

**Fig. 11. Samples of DenseFlow-25-6 after joint training on road-driving images as proposed in section III-A.**

**Synthetic Negatives and Feature Space Separation**
For softmax-activated models, softmax can assign arbitrarily large probabilities regardless of feature space distance, failing to bound open-space risk. We analyze synthetic negatives in open-set recognition using a max-logit baseline. Max-logit value is proportional to the projection of a feature vector onto the closest class prototype vector and can be thresholded to bound open-space risk.

SegmentMeIfYouCan (SMIYC) [11] quantifies dense outlier detection performance. It comprises three datasets: AnomalyTrack, ObstacleTrack, and LostAndFound [79]. AnomalyTrack features large objects aligned with the environment (e.g., a leopard on a dirt road). LostAndFound [79] detects small hazardous objects in urban scenes. ObstacleTrack detects small objects on various road types, with inconsistent surfaces potentially increasing false positives. ObstacleTrack and LostAndFound assess OOD detection on the driving surface, while AnomalyTrack considers the whole image. SMIYC provides a measure of OOD segmentation performance in real-world deployment.

StreetHazards [58] is a synthetic dataset generated with CARLA, simulating urban environments with inserted anomalies (e.g., a horse carriage or helicopter on the road). Synthetic anomaly simulation offers flexibility and cost-effectiveness but suffers from a quality mismatch with the real world. It has potential for evaluating outlier-aware segmentation due to cheap ground truth with K+1 classes. StreetHazards is used for measuring outlier-aware segmentation performance via open-mIoU [80].

BSB [16] is a remote sensing dataset of aerial images of Brasilia, containing 3400 labeled images (512x512 pixels), split into 3000 train, 200 validation, and 200 test. Labels include 3 stuff classes (street, permeable area, lake) and 11 thing classes (e.g., swimming pool, vehicle, sports court). Boats and harbors are extracted into the OOD test set, resulting in the BSB-OOD dataset with 2840 training images (12 inlier classes) and 184 OOD test images. This approach mirrors [28], [58], [81] in selecting a subset of classes as OOD samples. Other remote sensing datasets like Vaihingen and Potsdam have fewer labels and images, while So2Sat LCZ42 [82] has small-resolution images and image-level labels. BSB was chosen for its larger dataset size and better performance estimates.

Metrics:
OOD segmentation performance is measured using average precision (AP) [1], false-positive rate at a true-positive rate of 95% (FPR95) [40], and AUROC. AP [11], [12], [83] is suitable for OOD detection as it highlights the minority class, with a perfect score of one. FPR95 [40] is crucial for real-world applications, as high false-positive rates necessitate human intervention. Outlier-aware segmentation performance is measured by open-mIoU [80], which penalizes misclassifications between inliers and outliers. Unlike mIoU on K+1 classes, open-mIoU does not count true positive outlier predictions and averages over K classes. Ideal outlier-aware segmentation performance with perfect OOD detection would yield an open-mIoU equal to the closed-set mIoU, with the difference quantifying the performance gap caused by outliers [80].

Implementation Details:
Models are based on Ladder DenseNet-121 (LDN-121) for memory efficiency and rapid experimentation [84], but the framework supports other dense prediction architectures. Experiments involve two training stages using Cityscapes [85], Vistas [86], and Wilddash 2 [9], totaling 25,231 images. Images are resized to 1024 pixels (shorter edge), randomly flipped (p=0.5), randomly resized ([0.5, 2]), and randomly cropped to 768x768 pixels. Optimization uses Adam. The first stage trains for 25 epochs without synthetic negatives, with a batch size of 16 [84]. The initial learning rate is 10⁻⁴ for the feature extractor and 4 × 10⁻⁴ for the upsampling path, annealed via a cosine schedule to a minimum of 10⁻⁷ by epoch 50. The second stage trains for 15 epochs on mixed content.

Normalizing flows model the likelihood as a bijective mapping towards a predefined latent distribution $p(z)$, typically a fully factorized Gaussian. Given a diffeomorphism $f_\gamma$, the likelihood is defined by the change of variables formula:
$p_\gamma(x) = p(z) \det \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$, where $z = f_\gamma(x)$.

Stochastic skip connections can improve training efficiency and convergence speed.

A normalizing flow $f_\gamma$ is sampled in two steps:
1. Sample the latent distribution to obtain a factorized latent tensor $z$.
2. Recover the corresponding image through the inverse transformation $x = f_\gamma^{-1}(z)$.
Both the latent representation and the generated image have the same dimensionality ($R^{3 \times H \times W} \to [0, 1]^{3 \times H \times W}$). This property is useful for generating synthetic negatives at different spatial resolutions.

## Dense OOD Detection with NFlowJS

Dense OOD detection is trained on mixed-content images created by pasting synthetic negatives into regular training images. These negatives are generated by a jointly trained normalizing flow. Models are trained to recognize outliers using a robust information-theoretic criterion, which also serves as the OOD score during inference. A theoretical analysis advocates for training with synthetic negatives generated through likelihood maximization.

### Training with Synthetic Negative Data

A mixed-content image $x'$ is assembled by sampling a randomly sized negative patch $x^-$ from a jointly trained normalizing flow $f_\gamma$ and pasting it onto an inlier image $x^+$:
$x' = (1 - s) \cdot x^+ + \text{pad}(x^-, s)$, where $x^- = f_\gamma^{-1}(z)$.

The binary mask $s$ identifies pixels of the pasted synthetic negative patch. $z$ is sampled from a factorized Gaussian and reshaped to the desired spatial resolution. The negative patch $x^-$ is zero-padded to allow pasting by addition. The pasting location is randomly selected.

**Figure 1.** The proposed training setup. The normalizing flow generates the synthetic negative patch $x^-$ which is pasted onto the inlier image $x^+$. The resulting mixed-content image $x'$ is fed to a dense classifier trained to discriminate inlier pixels ($L_{cls}$) and produce uniform predictions in negative pixels ($L_{neg}$). This formulation enables gradient flow from $L_{neg}$ to the normalizing flow while maximizing the likelihood of inlier patches ($L_{gen}$).

The discriminative model is trained by minimizing cross-entropy over inliers ($s_{ij} = 0$) and maximizing prediction entropy in pasted negatives ($s_{ij} = 1$):
$L_{disc}(\theta; \gamma) = \sum_{i,j} \left( (s_{ij} - 1) \cdot \log p_\theta(y_{ij}|x') + \lambda \cdot s_{ij} \cdot L_{neg}(\theta, \gamma) \right)$.

The normalizing flow is jointly trained with the primary discriminative model to satisfy two criteria:
1. The normalizing flow should maximize the likelihood of inlier patches.
2. The discriminative model should yield uniform distributions in generated pixels.
This training encourages the generation of synthetic samples at the boundary of the training distribution and incorporates outlier awareness within the discriminative model. The total loss applied to the generative model is:
$L_{gen}(\gamma; \theta) = L_{nll}(\gamma) + \lambda \sum_{i,j} s_{ij} \cdot L_{neg}(\theta, \gamma)$.

$L_{nll}$ is the negative log-likelihood of the inlier patch, defined as $L_{nll}(\gamma) = -\log p_\gamma(x_c)$, where $p_\gamma$ is defined in (1). $L_{neg}$ is scrutinized further. The end-to-end training procedure minimizes:
$L(\theta, \gamma) = L_{disc}(\theta; \gamma) + L_{gen}(\gamma; \theta)$.

With sufficient training data and capacity, synthetic negatives encompass the inlier manifold. This allows the method to detect visual anomalies not seen during training, as they are closer to synthetic negatives than inliers. Figure 2 illustrates this on a 2D toy example, where red indicates higher OOD scores. The left plot shows the max-softmax baseline, which assigns high OOD scores only at the border between inlier classes. The right plot, corresponding to this setup, discourages low OOD scores outside the inlier manifold. Synthetic negatives are red stars, and inlier classes are blue.

**Figure 2.** Softmax-activated discriminative models do not bound the input-space.

paper2.title: Detecting the Unexpected via Image Resynthesis
paper2.abstract:
Classical semantic segmentation methods, including the
                        recent deep learning ones, assume that all classes observed
                        at test time have been seen during training. In this paper, we
                        tackle the more realistic scenario where unexpected objects
                        of unknown classes can appear at test time. The main trends
                        in this area either leverage the notion of prediction uncertainty to flag the regions with low confidence as unknown, or
                        rely on autoencoders and highlight poorly-decoded regions.
                        Having observed that, in both cases, the detected regions
                        typically do not correspond to unexpected objects, in this
                        paper, we introduce a drastically different strategy: It relies on the intuition that the network will produce spurious
                        labels in regions depicting unexpected objects. Therefore,
                        resynthesizing the image from the resulting semantic map
                        will yield significant appearance differences with respect to
                        the input image. In other words, we translate the problem
                        of detecting unknown classes to one of identifying poorlyresynthesized image regions. We show that this outperforms
                        both uncertainty- and autoencoder-based methods.

We evaluate the road-specific approach of [8], which trains a shallow Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) autoencoder to resynthesize road texture patches corrupted by Gaussian noise. Regions with differing appearance are expected to be reconstructed poorly, yielding an anomaly score from the difference between input and output. The original implementation is not public; we re-implemented it and will make our code available. We use 8x8 patches with stride 6 and a hidden layer of size 20, consistent with [8]. Empty road patches for training are extracted from Cityscapes images using ground-truth road labels. This approach is referred to as RBM.

Our full discrepancy detector uses the original image, the resynthesized image, and predicted semantic labels as input. To assess the importance of each input source, we also report results for variants using only one source: Ours (Resynthesis only) and Ours (Labels only).

**4.2. Anomaly Detection Results**

We evaluate our method's ability to detect unexpected objects on two separate datasets not used during training, focusing on novel object detection.

**4.2.1. Lost and Found**

The Lost And Found [35] dataset comprises images of small items on streets with per-pixel annotations for obstacles and free space. We use the test set, excluding 17 frames with missing annotations. Images are downscaled to 1024x512. A region of interest excludes the ego-vehicle and boundary artifacts. We focus on monocular approaches, not comparing against stereo-based methods from [35].

ROC curves (Fig. 5, left column) show our method outperforms baselines. The Labels-only and Resynthesis-only variants are competitive but less accurate. Uncertainty-based methods are ill-suited for this task. Qualitative examples are in Fig. 6. Our method has fewer false positives than baselines; some false positives represent valid unexpected objects not annotated as obstacles (e.g., a garbage bin).

Restricting evaluation to the road area (union of obstacle and freespace annotations) for the RBM method [8] improves ROC scores (Fig. 5, middle column), indicating easier anomaly detection within the road. Our method still outperforms RBM in this restricted scenario.

**4.2.2. Our Road Anomaly Dataset**

Motivated by data scarcity for unexpected object detection, we collected online images of anomalous objects (animals, rocks, tires, trash cans, construction equipment) on or near roads. We manually annotated these objects per-pixel, using Grab Cut [37] for speed. The dataset contains 60 images.

The approach is based on the intuition that typical semantic segmentation networks produce spurious labels for unseen objects. Resynthesizing an image from the semantic map will therefore result in discrepancies with the input image. A network was developed to detect meaningful discrepancies. Experiments show this approach detects unexpected objects more reliably than uncertainty- and autoencoder-based techniques. A new dataset with annotated road anomalies was contributed to facilitate research in this field. The approach still has false positives, which could be distracting in autonomous driving. Reducing false positives is a focus of future research.

The discrepancy detector is trained to identify pixels within the outlines of altered objects. At each feature pyramid level, features from all streams are concatenated and passed through 1x1 convolution filters for channel reduction. Pointwise correlations between real and resynthesized image features are computed and, along with the reduced concatenated features, are passed to an upconvolution pyramid for the final discrepancy score.

Training the discrepancy network on synthetic data simulates the presence of unexpected objects. The semantic segmentation network incorrectly labels regions belonging to unknown classes. To replicate this, random object instances are replaced with a different random label from known classes. The input image is then resynthesized from this altered semantic map using a pix2pixHD generator trained on the dataset. This creates real and synthesized image pairs for training the discrepancy network without needing to observe unexpected objects during training.

Comparing an input image to a resynthesized one detects adversarial attacks. A semantic map is computed from the input image, and the scene is resynthesized using the pix2pixHD generator. For adversarial examples, the predicted semantic map is incorrect, resulting in a distorted resynthesized image. Attack detection is simplified, allowing for a non-differentiable heuristic: the L2 distance between HOG features of the input and resynthesized images. A logistic regressor is trained on these distances to classify images as adversarial or not. This heuristic is more robust to attacks than deep learning-based methods.

Experiments evaluate the approach on detecting unexpected objects (e.g., lost cargo, animals, rocks) in traffic scenes, a target application domain and evaluation area for semantic segmentation. Methods output per-pixel anomaly scores, compared with ground-truth annotations using ROC curves and AUROC. Results for adversarial attack detection are also presented.

Evaluations use Bayesian SegNet and PSP Net, trained on the BDD100K dataset for generalization to anomaly datasets. The image synthesizer and discrepancy detector are trained on the Cityscapes training set, downscaled to 1024x512 due to GPU memory limitations.

Baselines include an uncertainty-based semantic segmentation network, Bayesian SegNet, which uses random dropouts to compute uncertainty as sample variance. This method requires dropout layers, absent in networks like PSP. For PSP, uncertainty is calculated using an ensemble method: four PSP models are trained with different random initializations, and the variance of their outputs serves as a proxy for uncertainty. A road-specific approach using a shallow Restricted Boltzmann Machine autoencoder to resynthesize noisy road patches is also evaluated.

Image resynthesis is used for detecting traffic obstacles in road scenes.
Methods like [32] predict non-anomalous road appearance in the current frame based on the previous frame.
[8, 33] compare input patches to the output of a shallow autoencoder trained on road texture to localize obstacles.
These road-specific methods lack generality. Patch-based approaches like [8] produce many false positives, which our approach outperforms.
Autoencoders in these approaches often perform image compression, generating lower-quality versions of the input, independent of content.
Our method resynthesizes images from semantic label maps; incorrect class predictions lead to appearance variations between input and resynthesized images.

Adversarial attacks in semantic segmentation are also detectable by comparing original and resynthesized images.
Adversarial attack literature primarily focuses on image classification [13, 3, 31], with defense strategies [23, 41] and detection methods [30, 25, 27].
Classification attack schemes have been extended to semantic segmentation networks [44, 6].
[43] is the only known defense scheme proposing an attack detection method in this scenario, analyzing spatial consistency of predictions from overlapping image patches. Our approach outperforms this technique.

**Approach**
Our objective is to handle unexpected objects at test time in semantic segmentation and predict the probability that a pixel belongs to a never-seen-before class.
This contrasts with most semantic segmentation literature, which assigns pixels to classes seen during training, without provisions for unexpected classes.

Figure 3 illustrates the Discrepancy Network.
It takes the original image, predicted semantic labels, and resynthesized image as input to detect meaningful differences caused by mislabeled objects.
A VGG [39] network extracts features from both images, correlated at all pyramid levels.
Image and label features are fused using 1x1 convolutions.
Features and their correlations are fed to a decoder via skip connections to produce the final discrepancy map.

Figure 2 summarizes our approach.
A semantic segmentation algorithm [2, 47] generates a semantic map.
This map is passed to a generative network [42] to resynthesize the input image.
If the image contains objects from a class not seen during segmentation training, these pixels are mislabeled in the semantic map and poorly resynthesized.
Unexpected objects are identified by detecting significant differences between the original and synthetic images.
We then assess which differences are significant.

**Discrepancy Network**
After synthesizing a new image, we compare it to the original to detect meaningful differences indicating unexpected objects not captured by the semantic map.
While known object layouts are preserved in the synthetic image, precise scene appearance information is lost. Simple image differencing is insufficient.
We train a second network, the discrepancy network, to detect significant image discrepancies.

Figure 3 shows the discrepancy network architecture, inspired by the co-segmentation network of [26] which uses feature correlations for detecting co-occurring objects.
Our network has a three-stream architecture for feature extraction.
A pre-trained VGG [39] network processes the original and resynthesized images.
A custom CNN processes the one-hot representation of the predicted labels.

Figure 4 illustrates the creation of training examples for the discrepancy detector:
(a) Ground-truth semantic map.
(b) Map altered by replacing object instances with random labels.
(c) Original image with outlines of altered objects overlaid.
(d) Image resynthesized using the altered map.
The discrepancy detector is trained to find pixels within the altered object outlines shown in (c).

paper1.title: Dense Out-of-Distribution Detection by Robust Learning on Synthetic Negative Data
paper1.abstract:
Standard machine learning is unable to accommodate inputs which do not belong to the training distribution. The
                        resulting models often give rise to confident incorrect predictions
                        which may lead to devastating consequences. This problem is
                        especially demanding in the context of dense prediction since
                        input images may be only partially anomalous. Previous work has
                        addressed dense out-of-distribution detection by discriminative
                        training with respect to off-the-shelf negative datasets. However,
                        real negative data are unlikely to cover all modes of the
                        entire visual world. To this end, we extend this approach by
                        generating synthetic negative patches along the border of the
                        inlier manifold. We leverage a jointly trained normalizing flow
                        due to coverage-oriented learning objective and the capability to
                        generate samples at different resolutions. We detect anomalies
                        according to a principled information-theoretic criterion which
                        can be consistently applied through training and inference. The
                        resulting models set the new state of the art on benchmarks for
                        out-of-distribution detection in road-driving scenes and remote
                        sensing imagery, in spite of minimal computational overhead.

**Inference Speed**
A dense OOD detector should not significantly increase computational burden. Inference speed was measured on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 for 1024 × 2048 inputs. SynBoost and SynthCP are not suitable for real-time inference due to significant overhead. The baseline model LDN-121 achieves near real-time inference (46.5 ms, 21.5 FPS). ODIN requires an additional forward-backward pass, resulting in a 3-fold slowdown. MC Dropout requires K forward passes, resulting in 45.8 ms overhead for K=2. Our approach increases inference time by only 7.8 ms over the baseline while outperforming other methods. SynthCP measurements are from [90].

**Visualization of Synthetic Outliers**
Our method generates samples at multiple resolutions with the same normalizing flow. These samples have limited variety compared to datasets like ImageNet or COCO. Training with them reduces overconfidence by explicitly training the model to produce uncertain predictions on outliers.

Figure 10 shows synthetic outliers generated by our normalizing flow after joint training on aerial images.

**Fig. 10. Samples of DenseFlow-25-6 after joint training on aerial images.**

Figure 11 shows samples of a normalizing flow after joint training on road-driving scenes. The appearance of synthetic negative samples depends on the underlying inlier dataset. Samples from Figure 10 resemble lakes and forests, while samples from Figure 11 resemble road, sky, cars, and buildings. This is because our normalizing flows are trained to generate data points along the border of the inlier distribution, patching the open-space risk of a segmentation model by adapting synthetic negative data to the training dataset.

**Fig. 11. Samples of DenseFlow-25-6 after joint training on road-driving images as proposed in section III-A.**

**Synthetic Negatives and Feature Space Separation**
For softmax-activated models, softmax can assign arbitrarily large probabilities regardless of feature space distance, failing to bound open-space risk. We analyze synthetic negatives in open-set recognition using a max-logit baseline. Max-logit value is proportional to the projection of a feature vector onto the closest class prototype vector and can be thresholded to bound open-space risk.

Similar effects are seen with real negative data, but our approach avoids bias towards test anomalies related to training data and is a great alternative for non-standard domains. SegmentMeIfYouCan (SMIYC) [11] quantifies dense outlier detection performance. It comprises three datasets: AnomalyTrack, ObstacleTrack, and LostAndFound [79]. AnomalyTrack features large objects aligned with the environment (e.g., a leopard on a dirt road). LostAndFound [79] detects small hazardous objects in urban scenes. ObstacleTrack detects small objects on various road types, with inconsistent surfaces potentially increasing false positives. ObstacleTrack and LostAndFound assess OOD detection on the driving surface, while AnomalyTrack considers the whole image. SMIYC provides a measure of OOD segmentation performance in real-world deployment.

StreetHazards [58] is a synthetic dataset generated with CARLA, simulating urban environments with inserted anomalies (e.g., a horse carriage or helicopter on the road). Synthetic anomaly simulation offers flexibility and cost-effectiveness but suffers from a quality mismatch with the real world. It has potential for evaluating outlier-aware segmentation due to cheap ground truth with K+1 classes. StreetHazards is used for measuring outlier-aware segmentation performance via open-mIoU [80].

BSB [16] is a remote sensing dataset of aerial images of Brasilia, containing 3400 labeled images (512x512 pixels), split into 3000 train, 200 validation, and 200 test. Labels include 3 stuff classes (street, permeable area, lake) and 11 thing classes (e.g., swimming pool, vehicle, sports court). Boats and harbors are extracted into the OOD test set, resulting in the BSB-OOD dataset with 2840 training images (12 inlier classes) and 184 OOD test images. This approach mirrors [28], [58], [81] in selecting a subset of classes as OOD samples. Other remote sensing datasets like Vaihingen and Potsdam have fewer labels and images, while So2Sat LCZ42 [82] has small-resolution images and image-level labels. BSB was chosen for its larger dataset size and better performance estimates.

Metrics:
OOD segmentation performance is measured using average precision (AP) [1], false-positive rate at a true-positive rate of 95% (FPR95) [40], and AUROC. AP [11], [12], [83] is suitable for OOD detection as it highlights the minority class, with a perfect score of one. FPR95 [40] is crucial for real-world applications, as high false-positive rates necessitate human intervention. Outlier-aware segmentation performance is measured by open-mIoU [80], which penalizes misclassifications between inliers and outliers. Unlike mIoU on K+1 classes, open-mIoU does not count true positive outlier predictions and averages over K classes. Ideal outlier-aware segmentation performance with perfect OOD detection would yield an open-mIoU equal to the closed-set mIoU, with the difference quantifying the performance gap caused by outliers [80].

Implementation Details:
Models are based on Ladder DenseNet-121 (LDN-121) for memory efficiency and rapid experimentation [84], but the framework supports other dense prediction architectures. Experiments involve two training stages using Cityscapes [85], Vistas [86], and Wilddash 2 [9], totaling 25,231 images. Images are resized to 1024 pixels (shorter edge), randomly flipped (p=0.5), randomly resized ([0.5, 2]), and randomly cropped to 768x768 pixels. Optimization uses Adam. The first stage trains for 25 epochs without synthetic negatives, with a batch size of 16 [84]. The initial learning rate is 10⁻⁴ for the feature extractor and 4 × 10⁻⁴ for the upsampling path, annealed via a cosine schedule to a minimum of 10⁻⁷ by epoch 50. The second stage trains for 15 epochs on mixed content.

We ablate the impact of loss in negative pixels, the choice of generative model, the impact of pretraining, as well as the impact of temperature scaling on dense OOD detection.

A. Impacts of the loss function and OOD score
Table VII analyzes the impact of the loss function Lneg and the OOD score sδ on AnomalyTrack val and ObstacleTrack val. The two chosen datasets feature large and small anomalies, respectively. We separately validate the modulation factor λ for each choice of the negative loss, as well as the temperature parameter. We use T=10 for max-softmax and T=2 for divergence-based scoring functions. We report average performance over last three epochs. Row 1 shows the standard setting with KL divergence as Lneg and max-softmax as the OOD score [26], [33]. Row 2 uses KL divergence both as the loss function and the OOD score. Row 3 features the reverse KL divergence. Minimizing the reverse divergence between the uniform distribution and the softmax distribution is equivalent to maximizing the softmax entropy [50]. Rows 4 and 5 feature the JS divergence. We observe that the reversed KL divergence outperforms the standard KL-MSP setup in 3 out of 4 metrics. However, JS divergence substantially outperforms all alternatives both as the loss function (JSD-MSP vs KL-MSP) and as the OOD score (JSD-JSD vs JSD-MSP and RKL-RKL). Normalizing flows model the likelihood as a bijective mapping towards a predefined latent distribution $p(z)$, typically a fully factorized Gaussian. Given a diffeomorphism $f_\gamma$, the likelihood is defined by the change of variables formula:
$p_\gamma(x) = p(z) \det \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$, where $z = f_\gamma(x)$.

Stochastic skip connections can improve training efficiency and convergence speed.

A normalizing flow $f_\gamma$ is sampled in two steps:
1. Sample the latent distribution to obtain a factorized latent tensor $z$.
2. Recover the corresponding image through the inverse transformation $x = f_\gamma^{-1}(z)$.
Both the latent representation and the generated image have the same dimensionality ($R^{3 \times H \times W} \to [0, 1]^{3 \times H \times W}$). This property is useful for generating synthetic negatives at different spatial resolutions.

## Dense OOD Detection with NFlowJS

Dense OOD detection is trained on mixed-content images created by pasting synthetic negatives into regular training images. These negatives are generated by a jointly trained normalizing flow. Models are trained to recognize outliers using a robust information-theoretic criterion, which also serves as the OOD score during inference. A theoretical analysis advocates for training with synthetic negatives generated through likelihood maximization.

### Training with Synthetic Negative Data

A mixed-content image $x'$ is assembled by sampling a randomly sized negative patch $x^-$ from a jointly trained normalizing flow $f_\gamma$ and pasting it onto an inlier image $x^+$:
$x' = (1 - s) \cdot x^+ + \text{pad}(x^-, s)$, where $x^- = f_\gamma^{-1}(z)$.

The binary mask $s$ identifies pixels of the pasted synthetic negative patch. $z$ is sampled from a factorized Gaussian and reshaped to the desired spatial resolution. The negative patch $x^-$ is zero-padded to allow pasting by addition. The pasting location is randomly selected.

**Figure 1.** The proposed training setup. The normalizing flow generates the synthetic negative patch $x^-$ which is pasted onto the inlier image $x^+$. The resulting mixed-content image $x'$ is fed to a dense classifier trained to discriminate inlier pixels ($L_{cls}$) and produce uniform predictions in negative pixels ($L_{neg}$). This formulation enables gradient flow from $L_{neg}$ to the normalizing flow while maximizing the likelihood of inlier patches ($L_{gen}$).

The discriminative model is trained by minimizing cross-entropy over inliers ($s_{ij} = 0$) and maximizing prediction entropy in pasted negatives ($s_{ij} = 1$):
$L_{disc}(\theta; \gamma) = \sum_{i,j} \left( (s_{ij} - 1) \cdot \log p_\theta(y_{ij}|x') + \lambda \cdot s_{ij} \cdot L_{neg}(\theta, \gamma) \right)$.

The normalizing flow is jointly trained with the primary discriminative model to satisfy two criteria:
1. The normalizing flow should maximize the likelihood of inlier patches.
2. The discriminative model should yield uniform distributions in generated pixels.
This training encourages the generation of synthetic samples at the boundary of the training distribution and incorporates outlier awareness within the discriminative model. The total loss applied to the generative model is:
$L_{gen}(\gamma; \theta) = L_{nll}(\gamma) + \lambda \sum_{i,j} s_{ij} \cdot L_{neg}(\theta, \gamma)$.

$L_{nll}$ is the negative log-likelihood of the inlier patch, defined as $L_{nll}(\gamma) = -\log p_\gamma(x_c)$, where $p_\gamma$ is defined in (1). $L_{neg}$ is scrutinized further. The end-to-end training procedure minimizes:
$L(\theta, \gamma) = L_{disc}(\theta; \gamma) + L_{gen}(\gamma; \theta)$.

With sufficient training data and capacity, synthetic negatives encompass the inlier manifold. This allows the method to detect visual anomalies not seen during training, as they are closer to synthetic negatives than inliers. Figure 2 illustrates this on a 2D toy example, where red indicates higher OOD scores. The left plot shows the max-softmax baseline, which assigns high OOD scores only at the border between inlier classes. The right plot, corresponding to this setup, discourages low OOD scores outside the inlier manifold. Synthetic negatives are red stars, and inlier classes are blue.

**Figure 2.** Softmax-activated discriminative models do not bound the input-space.

paper2.title: Pixel-wise Anomaly Detection in Complex Driving Scenes
paper2.abstract:
The inability of state-of-the-art semantic segmentation
                        methods to detect anomaly instances hinders them from being deployed in safety-critical and complex applications,
                        such as autonomous driving. Recent approaches have
                        focused on either leveraging segmentation uncertainty to
                        identify anomalous areas or re-synthesizing the image from
                        the semantic label map to find dissimilarities with the input image. In this work, we demonstrate that these two
                        methodologies contain complementary information and can
                        be combined to produce robust predictions for anomaly
                        segmentation. We present a pixel-wise anomaly detection
                        framework that uses uncertainty maps to improve over existing re-synthesis methods in finding dissimilarities between
                        the input and generated images. Our approach works as
                        a general framework around already trained segmentation
                        networks, which ensures anomaly detection without compromising segmentation accuracy, while significantly outperforming all similar methods. Top-2 performance across
                        a range of different anomaly datasets shows the robustness
                        of our approach to handling different anomaly instances.
methodology:
The dissimilarity module in the proposed framework acts as a wrapper for segmentation and synthesis networks. The architecture is independent of specific segmentation and synthesis approaches, provided the segmentation network outputs a softmax layer. This generalization is validated by retraining the dissimilarity network with different segmentation (ICNet) and synthesis (SPADE) techniques, creating a lighter version named "Ours Light." While "Ours Light" is significantly faster, it exhibits lower performance compared to the original framework.

Table 3 compares the performance of "Ours Light," the original framework ("Ours"), and the "Image Resynthesis++" baseline. "Ours Light" outperforms the baseline despite using lower-performing segmentation and synthesis modules (e.g., 83.5% vs. 70.6% class mIOU on Cityscapes). This demonstrates that the dissimilarity network generalizes to various segmentation and synthesis networks, performing well even with lower-quality outputs.

A direct correlation exists between the performance of the segmentation and synthesis modules and anomaly detection accuracy. "Ours" outperforms "Ours Light" across all metrics, as "Ours" utilizes state-of-the-art networks. This aligns with the intuition that resynthesis methods are highly dependent on the quality of segmentation and synthesis networks; better predictions from these modules facilitate the dissimilarity module in differentiating input and synthesized images. Future improvements in segmentation and synthesis networks are expected to enhance the performance of the anomaly detector. Inference time analysis of "Ours" and "Ours Light" is available in Appendix A.3.

The research investigates pixel-level anomaly detection in complex driving scenes. An anomaly segmentation framework is designed, combining uncertainty and resynthesis approaches. The framework utilizes uncertainty measurement maps (softmax entropy, softmax distance, perceptual differences) to guide a dissimilarity network in identifying differences between an input image and a generated image from the predicted semantic map. The presented approach significantly outperforms re-synthesis and uncertainty-based methods on the Fishyscapes benchmark, achieving the best overall performance across datasets. It is compatible with any pre-trained segmentation model due to no constraints on the segmentation network. The method also performs well with lighter segmentation and synthesis networks, making it suitable for deployment in autonomous machines.

References are provided for related works in anomaly segmentation, out-of-distribution detection, image synthesis, and benchmarks like Fishyscapes and Cityscapes.

Fusion Module: Concatenates input, synthesized, and semantic feature maps at each resolution level. Applies a 1x1 convolution to extract important areas and reduce complexity. Performs point-wise correlation between the dispersion feature map and the 1x1 convolution output. Outputs four feature maps, one per resolution.

Decoder Blocks: Four decoder blocks are used.
- Blocks 1 & 2: c256 −s1, sp −19, c256 −s1, sp −19, t256.
- Block 3: c384−s1, sp−19, c128−s1, sp−19, t1258.
- Block 4: c192 −s1, sp−19, c64−s1, sp−19, r2.
The first decoder block uses the lowest resolution feature map. Subsequent blocks take the concatenation of the fusion module output and the previous decoder block's output.

Training: Dissimilarity network trained for 50 epochs using the Adam solver with a learning rate of 0.0001. Learning rate reduced on plateau with a patience of 10 epochs. Training images augmented by vertical flipping and normalized using ImageNet mean and standard deviation.

Re-Implementation of Image Re-Synthesis: Image Re-synthesis [24] is a synthesis-based framework for anomaly segmentation, consisting of segmentation model S, synthesis model G, and discrepancy network D. It predicts a semantic label map with S, re-synthesizes the map with G, and detects anomalies by comparing natural and synthesized images with D. It uses Bayesian SegNet/PSPNet for segmentation and Pix2PixHD for synthesis.

Performance of re-synthesis methods depends on segmentation and synthesis quality. To isolate contributions, Image Re-synthesis was re-implemented with state-of-the-art networks: [42] for segmentation and [25] for synthesis.

Table 4 compares Image Resynthesis++ (our re-implementation) with [24]. Experiments used the same datasets (Lost & Found [30], Road Anomaly [24]) and performance metric (AUC ROC). A variation of Lost & Found was used, restricting evaluation to the road area.

Image Resynthesis++ shows improved performance across datasets. It was submitted to the Fishyscapes Benchmark (private test set) using FS Lost & Found and FS Static.

AUC ROC was used in these experiments as it was the only metric reported in the original work [24]. However, ROC metrics are not ideal for imbalanced problems like anomaly detection [5]. Main experiments use average precision (AP) and false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95).

The Road Anomaly Dataset was not used in main experiments due to its small size (60 images), insufficient for proper generalization.

The synthesis module, trained with a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) [37, 25], aims to match the generative distribution to the distribution of input images from the semantic model. While capable of producing photorealistic images of common objects like cars, buildings, or pedestrians, the semantic map lacks crucial information such as color or appearance for direct per-pixel value comparison.

Therefore, a perceptual difference (V) is calculated between the original and synthesized images. This feature map is inspired by perceptual loss methods [16, 8] used in cGANs. The approach utilizes an ImageNet [32] pre-trained VGG network [33] as a feature extractor to identify pixels with significantly different feature representations. This allows for comparison based on image content and spatial structure, rather than low-level features like color and texture. Discrepancies between the input and synthesized images, caused by undetected or misclassified anomaly objects, should be detectable by this perceptual difference.

The perceptual difference V for each pixel x in the input image and corresponding pixel r in the synthesized image is calculated as:
$V(x, r) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{M_i} \|F^{(i)}(x) - F^{(i)}(r)\|$ (3)
where $F^{(i)}$ denotes the i-th layer with $M_i$ elements of the VGG network and N layers. For consistency, this dispersion measure is normalized to [0, 1].

### Dissimilarity Module

The dissimilarity module receives the original image, generated image, semantic map, and uncertainty maps (softmax entropy, softmax distance, perceptual difference) as input. It then combines these features to predict an anomaly segmentation map. The module comprises an encoder, a fusion module, and a decoder (Figure 3). Implementation details are provided in Appendix A.1.

**Encoder:** Each image is processed by an encoder for feature extraction. A pre-trained VGG [33] network is used for both the original and re-synthesized images, following [24]. A simple Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) processes the semantic map, and another CNN encodes the concatenated uncertainty maps.

**Fusion Module:** At each level of the feature pyramid, the input, synthesis, and semantic feature maps are concatenated and passed through a 1x1 convolution. This initial step trains the network to distinguish between original and generated images, a common practice in re-synthesis methods. Subsequently, the resulting feature map is used for point-wise correlation with the uncertainty feature map, guiding the network to focus on high-uncertainty areas.

**Decoder:** Feature maps are decoded and concatenated with corresponding higher levels in the pyramid to produce the anomaly segmentation prediction. The decoder block incorporates the semantic map using a spatial-aware normalization technique [29] to preserve semantic information during the decoding process.

Figure 3 illustrates the Dissimilarity Module Architecture. Input, synthesized, semantic, and uncertainty images are processed by CNNs to extract features from high to low levels. At each level, input (blue), synthesized (yellow), and semantic (red) features are concatenated and fused via a 1x1 convolution. This fused map is then correlated with uncertainty map features (green). The output of the fusion module (purple) feeds into a decoder that generates the predicted anomaly segmentation. The semantic map is used in the decoder block with SPADE normalization [29] for spatially aware predictions.

### Training Procedure

Anomaly instances, by definition, are objects not belonging to the training classes. Thus, the methodology must be robust to detect any anomaly and avoid overfitting to specific objects from out-of-distribution (OoD) datasets. The training should also be general enough to encompass all three anomaly scenarios depicted in Figure 1.

The segmentation and synthesis modules are trained solely on the inlier segmentation dataset. This approach makes no assumptions about anomalies and ensures the segmentation module focuses exclusively on the segmentation task, without being influenced by other factors.

To train the dissimilarity module, a method similar to [24] is employed to circumvent the need for an OoD dataset. This involves generating synthetic data to simulate segmentation maps in the presence of anomalies. This is achieved by replacing randomly chosen object instances in the ground truth semantic map with alternative random classes. These altered semantic maps are then synthesized using the previously trained module.

Our proposed approach was compared against methods impacting segmentation network performance. Our model achieved the best performance on FS L&F in both AP and FPR95. Additionally, our approach achieved the second-best AP, behind Outlier Head [3] by 16% and 4% in FS Static and FS Web, respectively. Our framework achieves comparable state-of-the-art performance on anomaly segmentation while maintaining state-of-the-art performance in semantic segmentation. Our pipeline works as a general framework that can be implemented on top of different segmentation models. Wrapper methods have extended running times compared to methods that predict anomaly and segmentation in a single model. Inference time details are in Appendix A.3.

Our technique is the only method achieving top-2 performance on the Fishyscapes benchmark, demonstrating generalization across different test sets. Previous methods like Dirichlet DeepLab [26] have high AP in FS L&F but low AP in FS Static and FS Web. Outlier Head [3] has high AP in FS Static and FS Web but does not generalize well to FS L&F.

Qualitative comparisons with uncertainty methods [14] and image-resynthesis methods [24] are in Appendix A.5.

**5. Discussion**

Comparing all methods in Table 1 (excluding ours), a trade-off between segmentation performance and anomaly detection might be inferred. Our framework refutes this, showing that state-of-the-art anomaly detection does not compromise segmentation quality. The following discusses key insights contributing to this result.

**5.1. Ablation Study**

Table 2 presents results from an ablation study analyzing the contribution of individual components. Both our training data generator and the addition of uncertainty maps significantly improve the framework. The improvement from training data highlights the importance of covering all three anomaly scenarios (Figure 1), unlike methods focusing on only one [24]. Further improvement from uncertainty maps confirms that resynthesis and uncertainty carry complementary information, leading to better overall performance when combined. Removing the training data generator prevents the dissimilarity network from training with uncertainty maps.

Combining uncertainty maps (softmax entropy, softmax distance, and perceptual difference) with the dissimilarity model's output greatly reduces FPR95 on both datasets. This indicates that our dissimilarity module, like many deep CNNs, tends to be overconfident [11]. The ensemble mitigates this issue. The FPR95 improvement does not correlate with AP; a drop in AP for FS Lost & Found is expected when combining our framework's prediction with a weaker detector to reduce FPR95 for safety-critical applications. Conversely, AP improves for FS Static, likely because uncertainty methods perform better on images with artificially blended anomaly objects, making them easier to detect. Generally, ensemble predictions may lead to a small drop in AP but significant improvements in FPR95.

The ensemble demonstrates more consistent performance across trainings on all metrics. This is expected as the dissimilarity module's training impact on the ensemble's overall performance is limited compared to standalone use, which is a desirable property for safety-critical applications.

**5.2. Framework Generalization**

The dissimilarity module in our framework acts as a wrapper for segmentation and synthesis networks. The architecture is independent of the specific segmentation and synthesis networks.

Test Set Sizes:
*   FS Static: 275 images
*   FS Web: 1,000 images

*   FS Web: Dynamically changing dataset with objects crawled from the internet using keywords. Performance is reported only on data crawled after submission.

Table 1 Summary:
*   Our method achieves higher AP and lower FPR95 than previous methods that do not compromise segmentation performance (measured by class mIOU on Cityscapes).
*   Our method achieves second-best performance when compared to all existing approaches.

Performance Summary:
*   Against methods that do not compromise segmentation: Our technique outperforms previous best methods on all three FS datasets (FS L&F, FS Static, FS Web) for AP. FPR95 is reduced for FS L&F and FS Web by 50%, with comparable performance to the previous best on FS Static.

Computational Complexity (Table 5):

paper1.title: Dense Out-of-Distribution Detection by Robust Learning on Synthetic Negative Data
paper1.abstract:
Standard machine learning is unable to accommodate inputs which do not belong to the training distribution. The
                        resulting models often give rise to confident incorrect predictions
                        which may lead to devastating consequences. This problem is
                        especially demanding in the context of dense prediction since
                        input images may be only partially anomalous. Previous work has
                        addressed dense out-of-distribution detection by discriminative
                        training with respect to off-the-shelf negative datasets. However,
                        real negative data are unlikely to cover all modes of the
                        entire visual world. To this end, we extend this approach by
                        generating synthetic negative patches along the border of the
                        inlier manifold. We leverage a jointly trained normalizing flow
                        due to coverage-oriented learning objective and the capability to
                        generate samples at different resolutions. We detect anomalies
                        according to a principled information-theoretic criterion which
                        can be consistently applied through training and inference. The
                        resulting models set the new state of the art on benchmarks for
                        out-of-distribution detection in road-driving scenes and remote
                        sensing imagery, in spite of minimal computational overhead.

For softmax-activated models, softmax can assign arbitrarily large probabilities regardless of feature space distance, failing to bound open-space risk. Max-logit value is proportional to the projection of a feature vector onto the closest class prototype vector and can be thresholded to bound open-space risk.

SegmentMeIfYouCan (SMIYC) [11] quantifies dense outlier detection performance. It comprises three datasets: AnomalyTrack, ObstacleTrack, and LostAndFound [79]. AnomalyTrack features large objects aligned with the environment (e.g., a leopard on a dirt road). LostAndFound [79] detects small hazardous objects in urban scenes. ObstacleTrack detects small objects on various road types, with inconsistent surfaces potentially increasing false positives. ObstacleTrack and LostAndFound assess OOD detection on the driving surface, while AnomalyTrack considers the whole image. SMIYC provides a measure of OOD segmentation performance in real-world deployment.

StreetHazards [58] is a synthetic dataset generated with CARLA, simulating urban environments with inserted anomalies (e.g., a horse carriage or helicopter on the road). Synthetic anomaly simulation offers flexibility and cost-effectiveness but suffers from a quality mismatch with the real world. It has potential for evaluating outlier-aware segmentation due to cheap ground truth with K+1 classes. StreetHazards is used for measuring outlier-aware segmentation performance via open-mIoU [80].

BSB [16] is a remote sensing dataset of aerial images of Brasilia, containing 3400 labeled images (512x512 pixels), split into 3000 train, 200 validation, and 200 test. Labels include 3 stuff classes (street, permeable area, lake) and 11 thing classes (e.g., swimming pool, vehicle, sports court). Boats and harbors are extracted into the OOD test set, resulting in the BSB-OOD dataset with 2840 training images (12 inlier classes) and 184 OOD test images. This approach mirrors [28], [58], [81] in selecting a subset of classes as OOD samples. Other remote sensing datasets like Vaihingen and Potsdam have fewer labels and images, while So2Sat LCZ42 [82] has small-resolution images and image-level labels. BSB was chosen for its larger dataset size and better performance estimates.

Metrics:
OOD segmentation performance is measured using average precision (AP) [1], false-positive rate at a true-positive rate of 95% (FPR95) [40], and AUROC. AP [11], [12], [83] is suitable for OOD detection as it highlights the minority class, with a perfect score of one. FPR95 [40] is crucial for real-world applications, as high false-positive rates necessitate human intervention. Outlier-aware segmentation performance is measured by open-mIoU [80], which penalizes misclassifications between inliers and outliers. Unlike mIoU on K+1 classes, open-mIoU does not count true positive outlier predictions and averages over K classes. Ideal outlier-aware segmentation performance with perfect OOD detection would yield an open-mIoU equal to the closed-set mIoU, with the difference quantifying the performance gap caused by outliers [80].

Implementation Details:
Models are based on Ladder DenseNet-121 (LDN-121) for memory efficiency and rapid experimentation [84], but the framework supports other dense prediction architectures. Experiments involve two training stages using Cityscapes [85], Vistas [86], and Wilddash 2 [9], totaling 25,231 images. Images are resized to 1024 pixels (shorter edge), randomly flipped (p=0.5), randomly resized ([0.5, 2]), and randomly cropped to 768x768 pixels. Optimization uses Adam. The first stage trains for 25 epochs without synthetic negatives, with a batch size of 16 [84]. The initial learning rate is 10⁻⁴ for the feature extractor and 4 × 10⁻⁴ for the upsampling path, annealed via a cosine schedule to a minimum of 10⁻⁷ by epoch 50. The second stage trains for 15 epochs on mixed content.

Normalizing flows model the likelihood as a bijective mapping towards a predefined latent distribution $p(z)$, typically a fully factorized Gaussian. Given a diffeomorphism $f_\gamma$, the likelihood is defined by the change of variables formula:
$p_\gamma(x) = p(z) \det \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$, where $z = f_\gamma(x)$.

Stochastic skip connections can improve training efficiency and convergence speed.

A normalizing flow $f_\gamma$ is sampled in two steps:
1. Sample the latent distribution to obtain a factorized latent tensor $z$.
2. Recover the corresponding image through the inverse transformation $x = f_\gamma^{-1}(z)$.
Both the latent representation and the generated image have the same dimensionality ($R^{3 \times H \times W} \to [0, 1]^{3 \times H \times W}$). This property is useful for generating synthetic negatives at different spatial resolutions.

## Dense OOD Detection with NFlowJS

Dense OOD detection is trained on mixed-content images created by pasting synthetic negatives into regular training images. These negatives are generated by a jointly trained normalizing flow. Models are trained to recognize outliers using a robust information-theoretic criterion, which also serves as the OOD score during inference. A theoretical analysis advocates for training with synthetic negatives generated through likelihood maximization.

### Training with Synthetic Negative Data

A mixed-content image $x'$ is assembled by sampling a randomly sized negative patch $x^-$ from a jointly trained normalizing flow $f_\gamma$ and pasting it onto an inlier image $x^+$:
$x' = (1 - s) \cdot x^+ + \text{pad}(x^-, s)$, where $x^- = f_\gamma^{-1}(z)$.

The binary mask $s$ identifies pixels of the pasted synthetic negative patch. $z$ is sampled from a factorized Gaussian and reshaped to the desired spatial resolution. The negative patch $x^-$ is zero-padded to allow pasting by addition. The pasting location is randomly selected.

**Figure 1.** The proposed training setup. The normalizing flow generates the synthetic negative patch $x^-$ which is pasted onto the inlier image $x^+$. The resulting mixed-content image $x'$ is fed to a dense classifier trained to discriminate inlier pixels ($L_{cls}$) and produce uniform predictions in negative pixels ($L_{neg}$). This formulation enables gradient flow from $L_{neg}$ to the normalizing flow while maximizing the likelihood of inlier patches ($L_{gen}$).

The discriminative model is trained by minimizing cross-entropy over inliers ($s_{ij} = 0$) and maximizing prediction entropy in pasted negatives ($s_{ij} = 1$):
$L_{disc}(\theta; \gamma) = \sum_{i,j} \left( (s_{ij} - 1) \cdot \log p_\theta(y_{ij}|x') + \lambda \cdot s_{ij} \cdot L_{neg}(\theta, \gamma) \right)$.

The normalizing flow is jointly trained with the primary discriminative model to satisfy two criteria:
1. The normalizing flow should maximize the likelihood of inlier patches.
2. The discriminative model should yield uniform distributions in generated pixels.
This training encourages the generation of synthetic samples at the boundary of the training distribution and incorporates outlier awareness within the discriminative model. The total loss applied to the generative model is:
$L_{gen}(\gamma; \theta) = L_{nll}(\gamma) + \lambda \sum_{i,j} s_{ij} \cdot L_{neg}(\theta, \gamma)$.

$L_{nll}$ is the negative log-likelihood of the inlier patch, defined as $L_{nll}(\gamma) = -\log p_\gamma(x_c)$, where $p_\gamma$ is defined in (1). $L_{neg}$ is scrutinized further. The end-to-end training procedure minimizes:
$L(\theta, \gamma) = L_{disc}(\theta; \gamma) + L_{gen}(\gamma; \theta)$.

With sufficient training data and capacity, synthetic negatives encompass the inlier manifold. This allows the method to detect visual anomalies not seen during training, as they are closer to synthetic negatives than inliers. Figure 2 illustrates this on a 2D toy example, where red indicates higher OOD scores. The left plot shows the max-softmax baseline, which assigns high OOD scores only at the border between inlier classes. The right plot, corresponding to this setup, discourages low OOD scores outside the inlier manifold. Synthetic negatives are red stars, and inlier classes are blue.

paper2.title: A Baseline for Detecting Misclassified and Out-of-Distribution Examples in Neural Networks
paper2.abstract:
We consider the two related problems of detecting if an example is misclassified or
                        out-of-distribution. We present a simple baseline that utilizes probabilities from
                        softmax distributions. Correctly classified examples tend to have greater maximum softmax probabilities than erroneously classified and out-of-distribution examples, allowing for their detection. We assess performance by defining several tasks in computer vision, natural language processing, and automatic speech
                        recognition, showing the effectiveness of this baseline across all. We then show
                        the baseline can sometimes be surpassed, demonstrating the room for future research on these underexplored detection tasks.

Mixing TIMIT audio with realistic noises from the Aurora-2 dataset (Hirsch & Pearce, 2000) with TIMIT audio volume at 100% and noise volume at 30% yields a mean SNR of approximately 5. Speakers remain audible but confuse the phone recognizer as prediction edit distance more than doubles. For further out-of-distribution examples, test examples from the THCHS-30 dataset (Wang & Zhang, 2015), a Chinese speech corpus, are used. Table 9 presents the results. When performing detection, softmax probabilities are computed while ignoring the blank symbol's logit. Without the blank symbol, softmax prediction probabilities allow differentiation between normal and abnormal distributions, enabling out-of-distribution detection.

4. ABNORMALITY DETECTION WITH AUXILIARY DECODERS

Softmax prediction probabilities enable abnormality detection. Other information may be more useful. Exploiting learned internal representations of neural networks, a normal classifier is trained with an appended auxiliary decoder that reconstructs the input (Figure 1). Auxiliary decoders can improve classification performance (Zhang et al., 2016). The decoder and scorer are trained jointly on in-distribution examples. Subsequently, blue layers in Figure 1 are frozen. Red layers are trained on clean and noised training examples. The sigmoid output of the red layers scores input normality. Noised examples are classified as abnormal, clean examples as normal, and the sigmoid is trained to output the input's class. This process results in a normal classifier, an auxiliary decoder, and an abnormality module. The gains from the abnormality module suggest research avenues for outperforming the baseline.

4.1. TIMIT

The abnormality module is tested on the TIMIT task with a different architecture, demonstrating how auxiliary components can significantly improve detection. The system is a three-layer, 1024-neuron wide classifier with an auxiliary decoder and abnormality module. This network takes 11 frames as input and predicts the phone of the center frame, with 26 features per frame. Weights are initialized according to (Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016c). The network trains for 20 epochs, and the abnormality module trains for two. The abnormality module is trained on clean examples and, as negative examples, TIMIT examples distorted with white noise, brown noise (spectral density proportional to 1/f²), or pink noise (spectral density proportional to 1/f) at various volumes.

The abnormality module is not trained on the same type of noise as the test examples. Nevertheless, Table 10 shows that simple noised examples effectively detect realistically distorted audio. Abnormal examples are detected by comparing the typical abnormality
