Fine-tuning
Fine-tune BERT-base model on DisSent tasks with 2e-5 learning rate for 1 epoch. Fine-tuning for longer epochs did not yield improvement as all DisSent tasks corpora are quite large. Fine-tune BERT on other supervised learning datasets for multiple epochs and select the epoch providing best performance on evaluation task. Fine-tuning on MNLI is better than on SNLI or both combined, a phenomenon also discussed in Phang et al. (2018).
Discourse Marker Set
Experimented with three subsets of discourse markers (Table 4). First trained over all markers in the ALL marker set. Model achieved 67.5% test accuracy on this classification task. Markers with similar meanings tended to be confusable. Detailed analysis of performance on this classification task is presented in Appendix A.4.
Because of intrinsic conceptual overlap in ALL markers, experimented on different subsets of discourse markers. Chose sets of 5 and 8 discourse markers that were non-overlapping and frequent. Sentence pair sets for each smaller dataset are strict subsets of those in any larger dataset. Chosen sets are shown in Table 4.
Marked vs Unmarked Prediction Task
Adjacent sentences always have a relationship, some marked with discourse markers, others not. Humans perform well above chance at guessing whether a discourse marker is marked vs. unmarked (Patterson and Kehler, 2013; Yung et al., 2017), indicating systematicity.
Hypothesize that high quality sentence embeddings contain useful information to determine whether a discourse relation is explicitly marked. Success at this task could help natural language generation models generate more human-like long sequences.
To test this, created additional tasks based on Penn Discourse Treebank (Rashmi et al., 2008). This hand-annotated dataset contains expert discourse relation annotations between sentences. Collected 34,512 sentences from PDTB3 (see Appendix), where 16,224 sentences are marked with implicit relation type, and 18,459 are marked with explicit relation type.
Implicit Relation Prediction Task
Sporleder and Lascarides (2008) argued sentence pairs with explicitly marked relations are qualitatively different from those where the relation is implicit. Qin et al. (2017) used an adversarial network to leverage explicit discourse data for training to increase performance on implicit discourse relation prediction. Use the same dataset split scheme for this task as for the implicit vs explicit task.
Following Ji and Eisenstein (2015) and Qin et al. (2017), predict the 11 most frequent relations. There are 13,445 pairs for training, and 1,188 pairs for evaluation.
SentEval Tasks
Evaluate performance of generated sentence embeddings from fixed sentence encoder model on natural language understanding benchmark tests (Conneau et al., 2017).
Tasks include sentiment analysis (MR, SST), question-type (TREC), product reviews (CR), subjectivity-objectivity (SUBJ), opinion polarity (MPQA), entailment (SICK-E), relatedness (SICK-R), and paraphrase detection (MRPC). These are classification tasks with 2-6 classes, except for relatedness, for which the model predicts human similarity judgments.

topic: General language understanding tasks evaluate models on a broad set of natural language processing challenges, such as sentiment analysis, inference, and textual similarity, to measure overall language comprehension. What is the better method for general language understanding tasks: ConvBERT base or ALBERT?

paper1.title: ConvBERT: Improving BERT with Span-based Dynamic Convolution
paper1.abstract:
Pre-trained language models like BERT and its variants have recently achieved
                        impressive performance in various natural language understanding tasks. However,
                        BERT heavily relies on the global self-attention block and thus suffers large
                        memory footprint and computation cost. Although all its attention heads query on
                        the whole input sequence for generating the attention map from a global perspective,
                        we observe some heads only need to learn local dependencies, which means the
                        existence of computation redundancy. We therefore propose a novel span-based
                        dynamic convolution to replace these self-attention heads to directly model local
                        dependencies. The novel convolution heads, together with the rest self-attention
                        heads, form a new mixed attention block that is more efficient at both global
                        and local context learning. We equip BERT with this mixed attention design and
                        build a ConvBERT model. Experiments have shown that ConvBERT significantly
                        outperforms BERT and its variants in various downstream tasks, with lower training
                        costs and fewer model parameters. Remarkably, ConvBERTBASE model achieves
                        86.4 GLUE score, 0.7 higher than ELECTRABASE, using less than 1/4 training
                        cost.
methodology:
We measure accuracy for MNLI, QNLI, QQP, RTE, SST. Spearman correlation is measured for STS, and Matthews correlation for CoLA. The GLUE score is the average of all 8 tasks. For SQuAD, we compare with other models on the development set. We report Exact Match and F1 score on both v1.1 and v2.0 development sets. Unless stated otherwise, we use the same configuration as ELECTRA [9] for fair comparison. In addition to BERT and ELECTRA, we also compare with knowledge distillation methods: TinyBERT [25], MobileBERT [60], and DistillBERT [53]. All results are from single-task fine-tuning.

**Ablation Study**

To investigate each component, we add bottleneck structure, span-based dynamic convolution, and grouped linear operation one by one to the original BERT [14] architecture. We also increase the hidden dimension to assess performance gains from increased parameter size. Detailed configuration and results are in Table 1.

**Table 1: Detailed configuration of different sized models.** GLUE score is the average score on the GLUE dev set. BNK: bottleneck structure; GL: grouped linear operator; SDConv: span-based dynamic convolution. Larger: increased hidden and head dimensions.

**Bottleneck Structure and Grouped Linear Operation**

Introducing bottleneck structure and grouped linear operation reduces parameters and computation cost without significant performance degradation. This may even benefit small models by forcing attention heads to learn more compact, generalizable representations.

**Kernel Size**

We investigate the kernel size of dynamic convolution. Figure 5 shows results for different kernel sizes on a small ConvBERT model. Larger kernels improve results until the receptive field covers the entire input sentence. Beyond that, benefits diminish. We set the convolution kernel size to 9 for dynamic convolution, as it yielded the best results.

**Ways to Integrate Convolution**

Table 2 compares different methods of integrating convolution into self-attention. Directly adding conventional depth-wise separable convolution parallel to self-attention hurts performance. Inserting dynamic convolution offers minor improvement over the baseline BERT architecture. Span-based dynamic convolution further improves performance significantly by increasing local dependency.

**Comparison Results**

We compare our ConvBERT model with BERT [14], ELECTRA [9], and state-of-the-art methods [25, 53, 60, 50] on GLUE [63] and SQuAD [52] to demonstrate our method's advantages.

**Results on GLUE**

We evaluate performance on GLUE development and test sets. Due to space limitations, detailed results are on the test set; development set results are in the Appendix. Our small and base-sized models outperform comparable baseline models while requiring less pre-training cost. For example, compared to ELECTRABASE, our models show superior performance.

ConvBERT offers multiple positive impacts by prioritizing model efficiency and reduced training costs over increased complexity. This approach benefits applications with limited computational resources. Unlike distillation methods requiring a large teacher model, ConvBERT focuses on backbone designs for efficiency. It is particularly suitable for tasks like text-based counseling.

Negative Impact: While ConvBERT is more efficient and cost-effective than BERT, its ability to detect and understand personal text posts on social platforms can pose a privacy threat.

Conclusion
ConvBERT integrates a novel span-based dynamic convolution operator into the self-attention mechanism for language pre-training. It also includes a bottleneck structure in the self-attention module and a grouped linear operation in the feed-forward module. Experiments demonstrate that ConvBERT achieves consistent performance improvements with significantly less pre-training computation.

Broader Impact
The proposed pre-training scheme, widely used in NLP, involves self-supervised learning on large corpora followed by fine-tuning on downstream tasks. ConvBERT, a new pre-training based language understanding model, offers smaller size, lower training cost, and better performance compared to BERT. It promotes model efficiency and cost savings, benefiting applications with limited computational resources, contrary to the trend of increasing model complexity for performance gains.

Reduce the number of attention heads by ratio γ, saving computation cost and yielding more compact attention information.

Grouped Feed-Forward Module:
The large parameter count in transformers originates from the feed-forward module. To maintain representation power while reducing parameters and computation cost, a grouped linear (GL) operator is applied:
M = Π_{i=0}^{g-1} f_{d_g → m_g}(H[:, i-1:i×d_g])
M′ = GeLU(M)
H′ = Π_{i=0}^{g-1} f_{m_g → d_g}(M′[:, i-1:i×m_g])
where H, H′ ∈ R^{n×d}, M, M′ ∈ R^{n×m}, f_{d1→d2} is a fully connected layer transforming dimension d1 to d2, g is the group number, and Π denotes concatenation. This splits input features into groups, processes them independently, and concatenates them, which is more efficient than a standard fully connected layer with negligible performance drop.

ConvBERT is built by stacking mixed attention and grouped feed-forward modules iteratively. Experiments show ConvBERT is lighter, more efficient at capturing global and local contexts, and performs better.

Experiment
Implementation:
The architecture is evaluated on replaced token detection pre-training.
Model sizes:
- Small-sized: hidden dimension 256, word embedding dimension 128, intermediate feed-forward layer 1024, 12 layers, 4 attention heads.
- Medium-small-sized: 384 dimension embedding, 8 attention heads.
- Base-sized: BERT-base configuration (768 hidden dimension, 12 layers), 12 attention heads.
When applying bottleneck structure (reducing hidden space dimension for self-attention), head number is reduced by γ = 2.

Pre-training:
- Batch size: 128 (small-sized), 256 (base-sized).
- Input sequence length: 128.
- Model updates: 1M and 4M.

Pre-training Dataset:
- Open-sourced dataset OpenWebText (32G) is used for reproduction.
- Results on WikiBooks (English Wikipedia + BooksCorpus) are in Appendix.
- Corpus information and data collection/filtering details are in [48].

Evaluation:
- General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark.
- Question answering task SQuAD.
- GLUE tasks: MNLI, QNLI, QQP, RTE, SST (accuracy), STS (Spearman correlation), CoLA (Matthews correlation). GLUE score is the average of all 8 tasks.
- SQuAD: context, question, answer location. SQuAD V1.1 answers are in context; V2.0 may not include answers.

SST-2: Stanford Sentiment Treebank, sentences from movie reviews with human-annotated sentiment (POSITIVE/NEGATIVE).
MRPC: Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus, sentence pairs from online news annotated for semantic equivalence.
CoLA: Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability, binary classification of grammatical English sentences.
SST-B: Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark, sentence pairs annotated with similarity scores (1-5).
WNLI: Winograd NLI, excluded due to construction issues.

SQuAD dataset:
SQuAD v1.1: Stanford Question Answering Dataset, over 100K questions where each answer is a text span from the context.
SQuAD v2.0: Combines SQuAD v1.1 with over 50K unanswerable questions.

Pre-training details:
Replaced Token Detection task: Trains model to predict if a token in a sequence is replaced. Uses a generator trained with masked language modeling to create training examples with replaced tokens. The target model acts as a discriminator. Generator and discriminator are jointly trained with masked language modeling loss and replaced token detection loss.
Pre-training configuration follows ELECTRA, with most hyper-parameters from [9].
For downstream tasks with longer context, pre-training with input sequence length of 512 for 10% more updates is used to improve positional embedding generalization.

paper2.title: ALBERT: A Lite BERT for Self-supervised Learning of Language Representations
paper2.abstract:
Increasing model size when pretraining natural language representations often results in improved performance on downstream tasks. However, at some point further model increases become harder due to GPU/TPU memory limitations and
                        longer training times. To address these problems, we present two parameterreduction techniques to lower memory consumption and increase the training
                        speed of BERT (Devlin et al., 2019). Comprehensive empirical evidence shows
                        that our proposed methods lead to models that scale much better compared to
                        the original BERT. We also use a self-supervised loss that focuses on modeling
                        inter-sentence coherence, and show it consistently helps downstream tasks with
                        multi-sentence inputs. As a result, our best model establishes new state-of-the-art
                        results on the GLUE, RACE, and SQuAD benchmarks while having fewer parameters compared to BERT-large.

The single-model ALBERT configuration incorporates the best-performing settings: an ALBERT-xxlarge configuration using combined MLM and SOP losses, and no dropout.
Fine-tuning for RTE, STS, and MRPC uses an MNLI checkpoint.
Checkpoints for the final ensemble model are selected based on development set performance; the number of checkpoints ranges from 6 to 17, depending on the task.
For GLUE and RACE, predictions for ensemble models are averaged, where candidates are fine-tuned from different training steps using 12-layer and 24-layer architectures.
For SQuAD, prediction scores for spans with multiple probabilities are averaged, along with the scores of the "unanswerable" decision.
ALBERT improves state-of-the-art on all three benchmarks: GLUE score of 89.4, SQuAD 2.0 test F1 score of 92.2, and RACE test accuracy of 89.4.
ALBERT's RACE test accuracy is a +17.4% absolute points improvement over BERT, +7.6% over XLNet, +6.2% over RoBERTa, and 5.3% over DCMI+.
ALBERT single model achieves 86.5% accuracy, 2.4% better than the state-of-the-art ensemble model.

**Downstream Evaluation Tasks**

**GLUE:** GLUE comprises 9 tasks: Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA), Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST), Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC), Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark (STS), Quora Question Pairs (QQP), Multi-Genre NLI (MNLI), Question NLI (QNLI), Recognizing Textual Entailment (RTE), and Winograd NLI (WNLI). It evaluates natural language understanding capabilities. For MNLI, only the "match" condition (MNLI-m) is reported. Finetuning procedures from prior work are followed, reporting held-out test set performance from GLUE submissions. Task-specific modifications for WNLI and QNLI, as described by Liu et al. (2019) and Yang et al. (2019), are performed for test set submissions.

**SQuAD:** SQuAD is an extractive question-answering dataset from Wikipedia, where answers are context paragraph segments. The task is to predict answer spans. Evaluation is performed on SQuAD v1.1 (100,000 human-annotated question/answer pairs) and SQuAD v2.0 (adds 50,000 unanswerable questions). For SQuAD v1.1, the training procedure matches BERT. For SQuAD v2.0, models are jointly trained with a span extraction loss and an additional classifier for predictabilty. Both development and test set performance are reported.

**RACE:** RACE is a large-scale, multi-choice reading comprehension dataset from English examinations in China, containing nearly 100,000 questions. Each instance has 4 candidate answers. Following prior work, the passage, question, and each candidate answer are concatenated as model input. Representations from the “[CLS]” token predict the probability of each answer. The dataset has two domains: middle school and high school. Models are trained on both domains, with accuracies reported on both development and test sets.

Our loss is most similar to the sentence ordering objective of Jernite et al. (2017), where sentence embeddings are learned to determine the ordering of two consecutive sentences. Unlike most of the above work, our loss is defined on textual segments rather than sentences. BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) uses a loss based on predicting whether the second segment in a pair has been swapped with a segment from another document. Sentence ordering is a more challenging pretraining task and more useful for certain downstream tasks. Concurrently, Wang et al. (2019) also predict the order of two consecutive segments of text, but combine it with next sentence prediction in a three-way classification task.

THE ELEMENTS OF ALBERT
We present ALBERT's design decisions and compare them against corresponding configurations of BERT (Devlin et al., 2019).

MODEL ARCHITECTURE CHOICES
The ALBERT architecture uses a transformer encoder (Vaswani et al., 2017) with GELU nonlinearities (Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016). We use E for vocabulary embedding size, L for encoder layers, and H for hidden size. The feed-forward/filter size is 4H and the number of attention heads is H/64.

ALBERT makes three main contributions over BERT:

Factorized embedding parameterization.
In BERT, XLNet (Yang et al., 2019), and RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), the WordPiece embedding size E is tied with the hidden layer size H (E ≡ H). This is suboptimal because WordPiece embeddings learn context-independent representations, while hidden-layer embeddings learn context-dependent representations. Untying E from H allows for more efficient parameter usage, as H ≫ E. Natural language processing requires a large vocabulary size V. If E ≡ H, increasing H increases the embedding matrix size (V × E), potentially leading to billions of parameters updated sparsely during training. ALBERT factorizes embedding parameters into two smaller matrices, projecting one-hot vectors to a lower dimensional embedding space (E) and then to the hidden space (H). This reduces embedding parameters from O(V × H) to O(V × E + E × H), a significant reduction when H ≫ E. We use the same E for all word pieces as they are more evenly distributed than whole-word embeddings.

Cross-layer parameter sharing.
ALBERT proposes cross-layer parameter sharing to improve parameter efficiency. Sharing all parameters across layers is the default decision. Similar strategies were explored by Dehghani et al. (2018) (Universal Transformer) and Bai et al. (2019) (Deep Equilibrium Models). Unlike our observations, Dehghani et al. (2018) show UT outperforms a vanilla Transformer. Bai et al. (2019) show DQEs reach an equilibrium where input and output embeddings of a layer are the same. Our measurements show our embeddings are oscillating rather than converging.

paper1.title: AMBERT: A Pre-trained Language Model with Multi-Grained Tokenization
paper1.abstract:
Pre-trained language models such as BERT
                        have exhibited remarkable performances in
                        many tasks in natural language understanding (NLU). The tokens in the models are usually fine-grained in the sense that for languages like English they are words or subwords and for languages like Chinese they are
                        characters. In English, for example, there
                        are multi-word expressions which form natural
                        lexical units and thus the use of coarse-grained
                        tokenization also appears to be reasonable.
                        In fact, both fine-grained and coarse-grained
                        tokenizations have advantages and disadvantages for learning of pre-trained language models. In this paper, we propose a novel pretrained language model, referred to as AMBERT (A Multi-grained BERT), on the basis
                        of both fine-grained and coarse-grained tokenizations. For English, AMBERT takes both
                        the sequence of words (fine-grained tokens)
                        and the sequence of phrases (coarse-grained
                        tokens) as input after tokenization, employs
                        one encoder for processing the sequence of
                        words and the other encoder for processing
                        the sequence of the phrases, utilizes shared
                        parameters between the two encoders, and finally creates a sequence of contextualized representations of the words and a sequence of
                        contextualized representations of the phrases.
                        Experiments have been conducted on benchmark datasets for Chinese and English, including CLUE, GLUE, SQuAD and RACE. The
                        results show that AMBERT can outperform
                        BERT in all cases, particularly the improvements are significant for Chinese. We also develop a method to improve the efficiency of
                        AMBERT in inference, which still performs
                        better than BERT with the same computational
                        cost as BERT.

Our BERT models and AMBERT alternatives (AMBERT-Combo and AMBERT-Hybrid) use the same hyper-parameters in pre-training. The optimizer is Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014). Mixed precision is used for all models to enhance efficiency. Training is performed on Nvidia V-100 with 32 to 64 GPUs, depending on model sizes.

**Hyper-parameters in Fine-tuning**

For Chinese tasks, where original papers did not report detailed fine-tuning hyper-parameters for baseline models, we uniformly use the same hyper-parameters as in Table 11, except for the training epoch. AMBERT and AMBERT-Combo, having more parameters, require more training for convergence. Training epochs for all models are chosen when performance on development sets stops improving.

Table 11 also lists fine-tuning hyper-parameters for English models. We adopt the best hyper-parameters from original papers for baselines. For AMBERT‡, we tune learning rate ([1e-5, 2e-5, 3e-5]) and batch size ([16, 32]) for GLUE using the RoBERTa method (Liu et al., 2019).

**Data Augmentation**

Data augmentation is performed for three Chinese classification tasks: TNEWS, CSL, and CLUEWSC2020, to enhance performance. In TNEWS, both keywords and titles are used. For CSL, keywords are concatenated with a special token “ ”. In CLUEWSC2020, a few instances with pronouns like “她 (she)” are duplicated in the training data.

Discussions: AMBERT is superior to AMBERT-Combo. Figure 3 shows distances between [CLS] representations of fine-grained and coarse-grained encoders in AMBERT-Combo and AMBERT. AMBERT-Combo has larger distances than AMBERT. This indicates that representations of fine-grained and coarse-grained encoders are closer in AMBERT due to parameter sharing across encoders. This parameter sharing allows AMBERT to learn and represent similar ways of combining tokens, regardless of granularity. Intuitively, the ways of combining fine-grained and coarse-grained token representations "in the same contexts" are the same.

AMBERT works better than AMBERT-Hybrid, despite both exploiting multi-grained tokenization. Figure 2 shows attention weights of first layers. In AMBERT-Hybrid, fine-grained tokens attend more to corresponding coarse-grained tokens, weakening attention among fine-grained tokens. In AMBERT, attention weights among fine-grained tokens and among coarse-grained tokens remain intact. Attentions among single-grained tokens (fine-grained or coarse-grained) appear crucial for downstream tasks.

Improvements of AMBERT on Chinese are larger than on English. Tokenizing 10,000 English sentences from GLUE tasks shows an average proportion of phrases (coarse-grained tokens) of only 13.1%, indicating significantly fewer coarse-grained tokens than fine-grained tokens in English. ## 3.4 Inference

Two inference methods for AMBERT:
1.  Utilize AMBERT itself: Better performance, higher computational cost.
2.  Utilize only one encoder of AMBERT: Slightly worse performance, computational cost comparable to BERT.

Choice of encoder to drop can be determined via development dataset evaluation, reducing computational cost to BERT-level.

## 3.5 Alternatives

Two alternatives to AMBERT based on multi-grained tokenization: AMBERT-Combo and AMBERT-Hybrid.

**AMBERT-Combo:**
*   Two individual BERT encoders: one for fine-grained tokens, one for coarse-grained tokens.
*   No parameter sharing between encoders.
*   Combines output layers of the two encoders during learning and inference.
*   Fine-tuning is similar to AMBERT.

**AMBERT-Hybrid:**
*   One BERT encoder works on both fine-grained and coarse-grained token sequences.
*   Creates representations on the concatenation of the two sequences.
*   Representations of the two sequences interact at each layer.

paper2.title: SesameBERT: Attention for Anywhere
paper2.abstract:
Fine-tuning with pre-trained models has achieved exceptional results for many
                        language tasks. In this study, we focused on one such self-attention network
                        model, namely BERT, which has performed well in terms of stacking layers
                        across diverse language-understanding benchmarks. However, in many downstream tasks, information between layers is ignored by BERT for fine-tuning. In
                        addition, although self-attention networks are well-known for their ability to capture global dependencies, room for improvement remains in terms of emphasizing
                        the importance of local contexts. In light of these advantages and disadvantages,
                        this paper proposes SesameBERT, a generalized fine-tuning method that (1) enables the extraction of global information among all layers through Squeeze and
                        Excitation and (2) enriches local information by capturing neighboring contexts
                        via Gaussian blurring. Furthermore, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach in the HANS dataset, which is used to determine whether models have
                        adopted shallow heuristics instead of learning underlying generalizations. The experiments revealed that SesameBERT outperformed BERT with respect to GLUE
                        benchmark and the HANS evaluation set.

**EXPERIMENTS**
The SesameBERT model was evaluated on multiple classification tasks. The BERT model was reimplemented in TensorFlow for comparison. Parameters were set similar to the original BERT model: batch size (16, 32), learning rate (5e-5, 3e-5, 2e-5), and epochs (3, 4). Results are replicable within 12 hours on a GPU. All models were trained on NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs.

**GLUE DATASETS**
The GLUE benchmark consists of nine natural language understanding tasks, including question-answering, sentiment analysis, textual similarity, and textual entailment. These datasets evaluate model performance across diverse NLU tasks. Specific datasets and metrics are detailed in Appendix A.

**HANS DATASET**
The HANS dataset was used to diagnose fallible structural heuristics based on syntactic properties. Models might learn to label instances based on word overlap rather than meaning. Instances contradicting lexical overlap heuristics in MNLI are rare, potentially preventing models from learning beyond heuristics.

Gaussian blurring was analyzed for its effect on the context layer, showing higher accuracy in lower layers. This suggests capturing short-range dependencies among neighboring words in lower layers is effective. Even with self-attention models capturing long-range dependencies in higher layers, modeling localness remains a helpful metric. SesameBERT, though performing poorly in lower layers, outperformed other methods in higher layers, indicating Squeeze and Excitation alongside Gaussian blurring helps self-attention models capture global information.

On the MNLI-m dataset, BERT achieved 84.6% accuracy, surpassing SesameBERT. In the HANS dataset, both models performed well on Entailment heuristics, assigning correct labels nearly 100% of the time. For Non-entailment heuristics, BERT performed poorly, assigning labels based on heuristics rather than inference rules. SesameBERT performed significantly better than BERT, especially on "Lexical overlap."

Table 3 compares layer-specific accuracies on the RTE dataset for BERT, SE-BERT (BERT with Squeeze and Excitation), BLUR-BERT (BERT with Gaussian blurring), and SesameBERT. SesameBERT shows the highest weighted average accuracy across layers.

Figure 3 illustrates BERT and SesameBERT performance on heuristics-entailed and non-entailment cases. BERT's poor performance on non-entailment cases suggests it adopted shallow heuristics instead of learning latent information.

This work proposes that capturing local contexts with Gaussian blurring in self-attention networks can prevent models from adopting heuristics. While models performed poorly on "Subsequence" and "Constituent" heuristics, these may be hierarchical cases of "Lexical overlap," where performance might not directly match.

SesameBERT, a fine-tuning approach for BERT, aims to improve self-attention network performance by identifying high-quality attention output layers, extracting information through Squeeze and Excitation, and using Gaussian blurring for local contexts. Experiments on GLUE datasets showed SesameBERT outperformed BERT. HANS dataset analysis indicated SesameBERT learns intended information rather than shallow heuristics, highlighting an advantage over BERT in handling lexical overlap. SesameBERT can help prevent models from adopting shallow heuristics.

References include work on neural machine translation, modeling localness for self-attention, behavior analysis of NLI models, compositionality in sentence embeddings, BERT pre-training, and efficient BERT training.

Models may learn heuristics, such as assuming entailment when words overlap between premise and hypothesis (Dasgupta et al., 2018; Naik et al., 2018) or contradiction when negation appears only in the premise (McCoy & Linzen, 2019). BERT's strong performance on MNLI but poor performance on HANS suggests reliance on such heuristics.

MNLI has three labels: Entailment, Neutral, and Contradiction. HANS simplifies this to two: Entailment and Non-entailment, by translating Contradiction and Neutral instances into non-entailment. HANS targets three heuristics: Lexical overlap, Subsequence, and Constituent. It aids in measuring progress and visualizing model shortcomings.

**4.3 RESULTS**

**4.3.1 GLUE DATASETS RESULTS**
Experiments involved Gaussian blurring on attention outputs, a batch size of 32, learning rates of 3e-5, and 3 epochs for all GLUE tasks. The SesameBERT model was fine-tuned on 9 downstream tasks. Gaussian blur kernel sigmas of 1e-2, 1e-1, 3e-1, and 5e-1 were tested, selecting the best performance on the dev set. Predictions were uploaded to the GLUE server for evaluation as test set labels are not distributed.

Table 1 presents the results, with the GLUE benchmark provided for reference. SesameBERT generally outperformed BERT-Base (Devlin et al., 2019), showing improvements of 1.2% on RTE and 1.6% on AX.

Table 2 shows accuracy on the dev set for Gaussian blurring alongside BERT on value and context layers across four GLUE datasets. The effectiveness of Gaussian blurring on self-attention layers varied.

Gong et al. (2019) showed that different layers have varying abilities to capture local and global dependencies. Weights indicated that lower layers, which have weaker context (Baosong Yang, 2018), may struggle with encoding global context and learning localness in self-attention. Table 3, showing accuracy by attention output layer, confirms that lower layers had lower accuracy.

Three ablation studies were conducted:
1.  **Without blurring:** Squeeze and Excitation improved higher layers more than lower layers.
2.  **Gaussian blurring on context layer:** This method achieved higher accuracy in lower layers, suggesting that capturing short-range dependencies among neighboring words is effective.

Convolution applied with a fixed window size for sentence embedding allows words to focus on their importance and relationships with neighboring words, maintaining both global and local dependencies.

Experiments with the proposed method aimed to outperform BERT. SesameBERT showed marked improvement on most GLUE tasks. The HANS evaluation set, designed to diagnose fallible structural heuristics (lexical overlap, subsequent, constituent), was used. Models relying on these heuristics fail on HANS. BERT, despite high performance on test sets, performs poorly on HANS, potentially by assuming entailment based on word overlap rather than meaning. SesameBERT performs well on HANS, indicating it does not solely rely on heuristics. The final model proved competitive on multiple downstream tasks.

**RELATED WORK**

**UNSUPERVISED PRETRAINING IN NLP**
Most studies use pretrained word vectors (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014), which capture semantics only from surrounding text. This results in the same embedding for a word across different contexts, even with different meanings. Pretrained contextualized word representations address this by capturing context-dependent meanings. ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) uses stacked LSTMs' hidden states for context-sensitive representations. Generative pretraining (Radford et al., 2018) uses the Transformer encoder but is unidirectional and predicts future left-to-right contexts. BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) uses masked language modeling for high performance on natural language understanding tasks. However, BERT's varied information in different layer outputs makes pooling strategy selection a challenge.

**SQUEEZE AND EXCITATION**
Introduced by Hu et al. (2018) to enhance representation quality. Convolutional neural networks traditionally fuse spatial and channel-wise image information. However, their convolutional features' channels lack interdependencies, leading to equal weighting. Squeeze and Excitation enables feature recalibration using global information to emphasize informative features and suppress less important ones.

**LOCALNESS MODELING**
Self-attention networks capture global dependencies regardless of distance using an attention mechanism. The Gaussian-blurring method focuses on learning local contexts while retaining long-range dependency capture. Localness modeling was conceptualized as a learnable Gaussian bias (Yang et al., 2019) predicting a central position and dynamic window alongside intermediate representations. Instead of masking logit similarity with Gaussian bias, this method applies it element-wise after the embedding layer to improve model performance.

**DIAGNOSING SYNTACTIC HEURISTICS**
A study by McCoy et al. (2019) investigated whether neural networks adopt shallow heuristics instead of learning underlying generalizations. Similar to computer vision where networks are misled by contextual heuristics (e.g., monkey recognition; Wang et al., 2017), in natural language inference (NLI), a model might predict a contradictory label due to words like "not" appearing in training examples.

SESAMEBERT: ATTENTION FOR ANYWHERE
Ta-Chun Su, Hsiang-Chih Cheng
Cathay Financial Holdings Lab
{bgg, alberthcc}@cathayholdings.com.tw

ABSTRACT
Fine-tuning pre-trained models has yielded exceptional results for many language tasks. BERT, a self-attention network model, has performed well on diverse language-understanding benchmarks. However, BERT often ignores inter-layer information during fine-tuning for downstream tasks. While self-attention networks capture global dependencies, local context importance can be improved. This paper proposes SesameBERT, a generalized fine-tuning method that:
1. Extracts global information among all layers using Squeeze and Excitation.
2. Enriches local information by capturing neighboring contexts via Gaussian blurring.

SesameBERT's effectiveness is demonstrated on the HANS dataset, used to determine if models adopt shallow heuristics or learn generalizations. Experiments show SesameBERT outperforms BERT on the GLUE benchmark and the HANS evaluation set.

1 INTRODUCTION
Unsupervised pre-trained models have become dominant in natural language processing (NLP). Model construction involves pretraining on large-scale unlabeled data to learn word embeddings, followed by fine-tuning with labeled data for downstream tasks.

Traditional word embeddings represent each word with an independent vector, ignoring morphological similarities. Contextualized word representation techniques (Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019) overcome this by learning sentence-level information from sentence encoders, generating multiple word embeddings per word, and extracting local semantic information more effectively than conventional methods. Pre-trained contextual representations like BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), OpenAI GPT (Radford et al., 2018), and ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) have achieved high accuracy on GLUE tasks (Wang et al., 2019). BERT, utilizing the Transformer encoder architecture, leads in GLUE benchmark performance, suggesting self-attention's effectiveness in extracting latent meanings from sentence embeddings.

This study aims to improve contextualized word embeddings output by encoder layers. Using BERT's pretraining stage, we introduce a new architecture for the fine-tuning process: Squeeze and Excitation alongside Gaussian blurring with symmetrically SAME padding ("SESAME").
1. The Squeeze and Excitation method (Hu et al., 2018) focuses on information between layer weights, enabling feature recalibration and improving representation quality by emphasizing informative features and suppressing redundant ones.
2. The self-attention mechanism captures global dependencies. To enhance local context focus, we introduce Gaussian blurring. A Gaussian matrix and convolution with a fixed window size are applied to sentence embeddings. This allows words to consider their own importance and relationships with neighboring words, maintaining both global and local dependencies.

Models trained to recognize objects are misled by contextual heuristics. In natural language inference (NLI), a model may predict a label that contradicts the input because the word "not" is present. Our study aimed to make SesameBERT robust with respect to all training sets. Consequently, we used HANS datasets to diagnose fallible structural heuristics.

METHODS
We focused on BERT, a multilayer Transformer encoder with improvements. The encoder consists of L encoder layers, each with a multihead self-attention layer and a feed-forward network. The multihead mechanism uses a scaled dot product attention function:
Attention(Q, K, V ) = softmax(QKT/√d) · V
where Q, K, and V are query, key, and value vectors of dimension l x d, with l being the input sentence length and d the embedding dimension. For subsequent layers, Q, K, V come from the previous layer's output. The attention weights A = softmax( QKT/√d ) ∈Rl×l indicate the importance of key-value pairs with respect to a query. During fine-tuning, we used the output encoder layer from a pre-trained BERT model to create contextualized word embeddings. We addressed limitations in existing methods for extracting these embeddings by applying Squeeze and Excitation.

SQUEEZE AND EXCITATION
We proposed the application of Squeeze and Excitation to the output of the encoder layer, treating the number of channels as equivalent to the number of layers.
Let U:,:,k be the output of the k-th encoder layer, for 1 ≤ k ≤ n. To acquire global information, we concatenated all encoder layer outputs to form feature maps U ∈ Rl×d×n.
In the squeeze step, global average pooling on the k-th layer compresses spatial information into a layer descriptor:
Z:,:,k = fsq(Uk) = 1/(l × d) * Σ(i=1 to l) Σ(j=1 to d) Ui,j,k
In the excitation step, we capture layer-wise dependencies using a gating mechanism with sigmoid activation and two fully connected layers. Let W1 ∈ Rⁿˣⁿ/r and W2 ∈ Rⁿ/rˣⁿ be the weights of these layers, and r be the bottleneck parameter. The excitation function is:
s = fex(z) = σ(ReLU(z, W1), W2)
where z is the vector from the squeezed tensor Z.
Finally, we rescale the output Z:,:,k by multiplying it by sk:
euk = fscale(sk, U:,:,k)
All rescaled outputs form the rescaled feature maps eu. We then calculated a weighted average layer:
euavg = Σ(k=1 to n) fscale(sk, U:,:,k) / Σ(k=1 to n) sk
We employed n = 12 attention layers.

GAUSSIAN BLURRING
Given an input sequence X = {x1, x2, ..., xl} ∈ Rl×d, the model transforms it into queries Q, keys K, and values V, where Q, K, and V ∈ Rl×d. Multihead attention allows the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions by splitting these into h subspaces of size d.

paper1.title: AMBERT: A Pre-trained Language Model with Multi-Grained Tokenization
paper1.abstract:
Pre-trained language models such as BERT
                        have exhibited remarkable performances in
                        many tasks in natural language understanding (NLU). The tokens in the models are usually fine-grained in the sense that for languages like English they are words or subwords and for languages like Chinese they are
                        characters. In English, for example, there
                        are multi-word expressions which form natural
                        lexical units and thus the use of coarse-grained
                        tokenization also appears to be reasonable.
                        In fact, both fine-grained and coarse-grained
                        tokenizations have advantages and disadvantages for learning of pre-trained language models. In this paper, we propose a novel pretrained language model, referred to as AMBERT (A Multi-grained BERT), on the basis
                        of both fine-grained and coarse-grained tokenizations. For English, AMBERT takes both
                        the sequence of words (fine-grained tokens)
                        and the sequence of phrases (coarse-grained
                        tokens) as input after tokenization, employs
                        one encoder for processing the sequence of
                        words and the other encoder for processing
                        the sequence of the phrases, utilizes shared
                        parameters between the two encoders, and finally creates a sequence of contextualized representations of the words and a sequence of
                        contextualized representations of the phrases.
                        Experiments have been conducted on benchmark datasets for Chinese and English, including CLUE, GLUE, SQuAD and RACE. The
                        results show that AMBERT can outperform
                        BERT in all cases, particularly the improvements are significant for Chinese. We also develop a method to improve the efficiency of
                        AMBERT in inference, which still performs
                        better than BERT with the same computational
                        cost as BERT.

**Hyper-parameters in Fine-tuning**

For Chinese tasks, where original papers did not report detailed fine-tuning hyper-parameters for baseline models, we uniformly use the same hyper-parameters as in Table 11, except for the training epoch. AMBERT and AMBERT-Combo, having more parameters, require more training for convergence. Training epochs for all models are chosen when performance on development sets stops improving.

Table 11 also lists fine-tuning hyper-parameters for English models. We adopt the best hyper-parameters from original papers for baselines. For AMBERT‡, we tune learning rate ([1e-5, 2e-5, 3e-5]) and batch size ([16, 32]) for GLUE using the RoBERTa method (Liu et al., 2019).

**Data Augmentation**

Data augmentation is performed for three Chinese classification tasks: TNEWS, CSL, and CLUEWSC2020, to enhance performance. In TNEWS, both keywords and titles are used. For CSL, keywords are concatenated with a special token “ ”. In CLUEWSC2020, a few instances with pronouns like “她 (she)” are duplicated in the training data.

**Case Study**

We qualitatively study the results of BERT and AMBERT, finding they support our claims. Examples from entailment tasks (QNLI and CMNLI) are provided in Table 12. Observations:
1. Fine-grained models (e.g., Our BERT word) struggle with complete lexical units like “Doctor Who” and “打死”, potentially leading to incorrect predictions.
2. Coarse-grained models (e.g., Our BERT phrase) have difficulty with incorrect tokenizations, exemplified by “the blind” and “格式”.
3. AMBERT effectively utilizes complete lexical units such as “sister station” and “员工/工人”, and is robust to incorrect tokenizations.

AMBERT outperforms both RoBERTa and ALBERT in the CLUE benchmark. Comparisons with base models trained with different datasets and procedures should be taken as references, with settings matching Xu et al. (2020). AMBERT's average score is higher than all other models, indicating multi-grained tokenization is beneficial for pre-trained language models.

**English Tasks**

**Benchmarks**
The General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark, a collection of nine NLU tasks, is used. The WNLI task is excluded due to undifferentiated results. Three MRC tasks (SQuAD v1.1, SQuAD v2.0, and RACE) are included.

**Experimental Results**
AMBERT is compared with BERT models on GLUE tasks. Multi-grained models, especially AMBERT, achieve better results than single-grained models. AMBERT performs best among multi-grained models with fewer parameters and less computation.

On MRC tasks, AMBERT outperforms Google BERT on SQuAD. "Our BERT (word)" performs well, while "Our BERT (phrase)" performs poorly in span detection. AMBERT performs best on RACE for both development and test sets. AMBERT is the best multi-grained model.

Comparisons with state-of-the-art models on GLUE and MRC benchmarks show AMBERT outperforming all models on average without using advanced training techniques.

**Enhancement of Inference Speed**
Experiments on inference speed for AMBERT on CLUE/GLUE/SQuAD/RACE are conducted. The fine-grained encoder is chosen for span detection tasks (CMRC2018 and SQuAD) due to superior performance. Discussions: AMBERT is superior to AMBERT-Combo. Figure 3 shows distances between [CLS] representations of fine-grained and coarse-grained encoders in AMBERT-Combo and AMBERT. AMBERT-Combo has larger distances than AMBERT. This indicates that representations of fine-grained and coarse-grained encoders are closer in AMBERT due to parameter sharing across encoders. This parameter sharing allows AMBERT to learn and represent similar ways of combining tokens, regardless of granularity. Intuitively, the ways of combining fine-grained and coarse-grained token representations "in the same contexts" are the same.

AMBERT works better than AMBERT-Hybrid, despite both exploiting multi-grained tokenization. Figure 2 shows attention weights of first layers. In AMBERT-Hybrid, fine-grained tokens attend more to corresponding coarse-grained tokens, weakening attention among fine-grained tokens. In AMBERT, attention weights among fine-grained tokens and among coarse-grained tokens remain intact. Attentions among single-grained tokens (fine-grained or coarse-grained) appear crucial for downstream tasks.

Improvements of AMBERT on Chinese are larger than on English. Analysis of 10,000 randomly selected Chinese sentences from CLUE tasks shows an average proportion of words (fine-grained tokens) of 51.5%, meaning roughly half fine-grained and half coarse-grained tokens. Tokenizing 10,000 English sentences from GLUE tasks shows an average proportion of phrases (coarse-grained tokens) of only 13.1%, indicating significantly fewer coarse-grained tokens than fine-grained tokens in English. ## 3.4 Inference

Two inference methods for AMBERT:
1.  Utilize AMBERT itself: Better performance, higher computational cost.
2.  Utilize only one encoder of AMBERT: Slightly worse performance, computational cost comparable to BERT.

Choice of encoder to drop can be determined via development dataset evaluation, reducing computational cost to BERT-level.

## 3.5 Alternatives

Two alternatives to AMBERT based on multi-grained tokenization: AMBERT-Combo and AMBERT-Hybrid.

**AMBERT-Combo:**
*   Two individual BERT encoders: one for fine-grained tokens, one for coarse-grained tokens.
*   No parameter sharing between encoders.
*   Combines output layers of the two encoders during learning and inference.
*   Fine-tuning is similar to AMBERT.

**AMBERT-Hybrid:**
*   One BERT encoder works on both fine-grained and coarse-grained token sequences.
*   Creates representations on the concatenation of the two sequences.
*   Representations of the two sequences interact at each layer.

paper2.title: Learning General Purpose Distributed Sentence Representations via Large Scale Multi-task Learning
paper2.abstract:
A lot of the recent success in natural language processing (NLP) has been driven
                        by distributed vector representations of words trained on large amounts of text
                        in an unsupervised manner. These representations are typically used as general
                        purpose features for words across a range of NLP problems. However, extending this success to learning representations of sequences of words, such as sentences, remains an open problem. Recent work has explored unsupervised as well
                        as supervised learning techniques with different training objectives to learn general purpose fixed-length sentence representations. In this work, we present a
                        simple, effective multi-task learning framework for sentence representations that
                        combines the inductive biases of diverse training objectives in a single model. We
                        train this model on several data sources with multiple training objectives on over
                        100 million sentences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that sharing a single recurrent sentence encoder across weakly related tasks leads to consistent improvements over previous methods. We present substantial improvements in the context
                        of transfer learning and low-resource settings using our learned general-purpose
                        representations.

CONCLUSION & FUTURE WORK
We present a multi-task framework for learning general-purpose fixed-length sentence representations. Our primary motivation is to encapsulate the inductive biases of several diverse training signals used to learn sentence representations into a single model. Our multi-task framework includes a combination of sequence-to-sequence tasks such as multi-lingual NMT, constituency parsing and skip-thought vectors as well as a classification task - natural language inference. We demonstrate that the learned representations yield competitive or superior results to previous general-purpose sentence representation methods. We also observe that this approach produces good word embeddings.

In future work, we would like to understand and interpret the inductive biases that our model learns and observe how it changes with the addition of different tasks beyond just our simple analysis of sentence characteristics and syntax. Having a rich, continuous sentence representation space could allow the application of state-of-the-art generative models of images such as that of Nguyen et al. (2016) to language. One could also consider controllable text generation by directly manipulating the sentence representations and realizing it by decoding with a conditional language model.

EVALUATION STRATEGIES, EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS & DISCUSSION

We describe our approach to evaluate the quality of learned representations, present the results of our evaluation, and discuss our findings.

EVALUATION STRATEGY

We use learned representations as features for a low-complexity classifier (typically linear) on novel supervised tasks/domains unseen during training without updating the parameters of our sentence representation model. We also consider transfer learning evaluation in an artificially constructed low-resource setting. Additionally, we evaluate the quality of individual word representations using standard benchmarks.

The choice of transfer tasks and evaluation framework are borrowed from Conneau et al. (2017). A summary of the tasks is provided in the Appendix.

EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS & DISCUSSION

Table 2 presents the results of training logistic regression on 10 different supervised transfer tasks using different fixed-length sentence representations. Supervised approaches trained from scratch are also presented for comparison. We present performance ablations when adding more tasks and increasing the number of hidden units in our GRU (+L).

Adding more tasks improves transfer performance. Increasing the capacity of our sentence encoder with more hidden units (+L) and an additional layer (+2L) also leads to improved transfer performance. We observe gains of 1.1-2.0% on sentiment classification tasks (MR, CR, SUBJ & MPQA) over Infersent. We demonstrate substantial gains on TREC (6% over Infersent and roughly 2% over CNN-LSTM), outperforming a competitive supervised baseline. Similar gains (2.3%) are seen on paraphrase identification (MRPC), closing the gap on supervised approaches trained from scratch. The addition of constituency parsing improves performance on sentence relatedness (SICK-R) and entailment (SICK-E), consistent with observations by Bowman et al. (2016).

Table 4 shows that training an MLP on top of our fixed sentence representations outperforms several strong & complex supervised approaches that use attention mechanisms, even on a fairly large dataset. We observe a 0.2-0.5% improvement over the decomposable attention model (Parikh et al., 2016). Using a small fraction of the training data (columns 1k-25k), we outperform the Siamese and Multi-Perspective CNN using roughly 6% of the available training set. We also outperform the Deconv LVM model proposed by Shen et al. (2017) in this low-resource setting.

Unlike Conneau et al. (2017), who use pretrained GloVe word embeddings, we learn our word embeddings from scratch. Table 3 shows that the learned word embeddings are competitive with popular methods such as GloVe, word2vec, and fasttext (Bojanowski et al., 2016) on the benchmarks presented by Faruqui & Dyer (2014) and Tsvetkov et al. (2015).

In Table 5, we probe our sentence representations to determine if certain sentence characteristics and syntactic properties can be inferred, following work by Adi et al. (2016) and Shi et al. (2016). Syntactic properties are better encoded with the addition of multi-lingual NMT and parsing. Representations learned solely from NLI appear to encode syntax, but incorporation into our multi-task framework does not amplify this signal. Sentence characteristics such as length and word order are better encoded with the addition of parsing.

In Appendix Table 6, our sentence representations outperform skip-thoughts and are on par with Infersent for image-caption retrieval. Comparing sentences using different approaches shows varied results.

VOCABULARY EXPANSION & REPRESENTATION POOLING:
10-fold cross-validation was performed to determine L2 regularization penalty for logistic regression models. Sentence representation generation from hidden states was tuned. Approaches considered include the last hidden state (Kiros et al., 2015) and max-pooling across all hidden states (Conneau et al., 2017). Max-pooling performed best on sentiment tasks (MR, CR, SUBJ, MPQA), while the last hidden state performed better on other tasks. Vocabulary expansion was employed on all tasks, mapping pre-trained GloVe embeddings to model word embeddings via linear regression (Kiros et al., 2015).

**10.1 Supervised Classification**

*   **Method:** Train a logistic regression classifier with 10-fold cross-validation to tune the L2 weight penalty.
*   **Evaluation Metric:** Classification accuracy.

**10.2 Paraphrase Identification**

*   **Task:** Binary classification to identify if two sentences are paraphrases of each other.
*   **Corpus:** Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC).
*   **Evaluation Metrics:** Classification accuracy and F1.

**10.3 Entailment and Semantic Relatedness**

*   **SICK-R Task:** Train a linear model to output a score from 1 to 5 indicating the relatedness of two sentences.
*   **SICK-E Task:** Binary classification using entailment labels.
*   **Evaluation Metrics:** Pearson correlation for SICK-R, classification accuracy for SICK-E.

**10.4 Semantic Textual Similarity**

*   **Task:** Measure sentence relatedness using cosine similarity between their representations.
*   **Datasets:** STS benchmark tasks (STS12-STS16, STSB).
*   **Evaluation Criterion:** Pearson correlation.

**10.5 Image-Caption Retrieval**

*   **Task:** Ranking task where images are retrieved based on text, and vice-versa.
*   **Data:** 113k training images from MSCOCO, 5k for validation, 5k for testing.
*   **Image Features:** Extracted using a pre-trained 110-layer ResNet.
*   **Evaluation Criteria:** Recall@K and median K across 5 splits.

**10.6 Quora Duplicate Question Classification**

*   **Task:** Binary classification to identify duplicate question pairs.
*   **Dataset:** Quora duplicate question dataset (approx. 400,000 question pairs).
*   **Classifier:** 4-layer MLP with 1024 hidden units, dropout 0.5 after each hidden layer.
*   **Evaluation Criterion:** Classification accuracy.
*   **Low-Resource Setting:** Training examples reduced to 1,000-25,000.

**10.7 Sentence Characteristics & Syntax**

*   **Objective:** Understand information encoded in sentence representations by predicting sentence characteristics and syntactic properties.

    *   **Sentence Characteristic Tasks:**
        *   **Length:** 8-way classification based on binned sentence lengths.
        *   **Content:** Binary classification determining if a word is contained in a sentence (using sentence representation `u` and word representation `w`).
        *   **Order:** Extension of content task to determine the order of two words in a sentence.
        *   **Dataset:** Random subset of the 1-billion-word dataset (not used for training multi-task representations).

    *   **Syntactic Properties Tasks:**
        *   **Passive:** Binary classification to determine active/passive voice.
        *   **Tense:** Binary classification to determine past tense.
        *   **Top Syntactic Sequence (TSS):** 20-way classification (19 most frequent sequences + 1 miscellaneous).
        *   **Dataset:** Same as Shi et al. (2016), with different training, validation, and test splits.

ABSTRACT
Recent success in natural language processing (NLP) has been driven by distributed vector representations of words trained on large amounts of text unsupervised. These representations are typically used as general purpose features for words across NLP problems. Extending this success to learning representations of sequences of words, such as sentences, remains an open problem. Recent work has explored unsupervised and supervised learning techniques with different training objectives to learn general purpose fixed-length sentence representations. This work presents a simple, effective multi-task learning framework for sentence representations that combines the inductive biases of diverse training objectives in a single model. The model is trained on several data sources with multiple training objectives on over 100 million sentences. Experiments demonstrate that sharing a single recurrent sentence encoder across weakly related tasks leads to consistent improvements over previous methods. Substantial improvements are presented in transfer learning and low-resource settings using the learned general-purpose representations.

1 INTRODUCTION
Transfer learning has driven recent successes in computer vision and NLP. Computer vision tasks like image captioning and visual question answering typically use CNNs pretrained on ImageNet to extract representations of the image. Several natural language tasks such as reading comprehension and sequence labeling have benefited from pretrained word embeddings that are either fine-tuned for a specific task or held fixed. Many neural NLP systems are initialized with pretrained word embeddings but learn their representations of words in context from scratch, in a task-specific manner from supervised learning signals. Learning these representations reliably from scratch is not always feasible, especially in low-resource settings, where using general purpose sentence representations is believed to be beneficial.

Some recent work has addressed this by learning general-purpose sentence representations. However, there is no clear consensus yet on what training objective or methodology is best suited to this goal. Understanding the inductive biases of distinct neural models is important for guiding progress in representation learning. Neural machine translation (NMT) systems appear to capture morphology and some syntactic properties. Sequence-to-sequence parsers more strongly encode source language syntax. Adi et al. (2016) probe representations extracted by sequence autoencoders, word embedding averages, and skip-thought vectors with a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) classifier to study whether sentence characteristics such as length, word content, and word order are encoded.

To generalize across a diverse set of tasks, it is important to build representations that encode several aspects of a sentence. Neural approaches to tasks such as skip-thoughts, machine translation, natural language inference, and constituency parsing likely have different inductive biases. This work exploits this in the context of a simple one-to-many multi-task learning (MTL) framework, wherein a single recurrent sentence encoder is shared across multiple tasks. The hypothesis is that sentence representations learned by training on a reasonably large number of weakly related tasks will generalize better to novel tasks unseen during training, since this process encodes the inductive biases of multiple models. This hypothesis is based on theoretical work by Baxter et al. (2000). While this work aims at learning fixed-length distributed sentence representations, it is not always practical to assume that the entire "meaning" of a sentence can be encoded into a fixed-length vector.

Discussions: AMBERT is superior to AMBERT-Combo. Figure 3 shows distances between [CLS] representations of fine-grained and coarse-grained encoders in AMBERT-Combo and AMBERT. AMBERT-Combo has larger distances than AMBERT. This indicates that representations of fine-grained and coarse-grained encoders are closer in AMBERT due to parameter sharing across encoders. This parameter sharing allows AMBERT to learn and represent similar ways of combining tokens, regardless of granularity. Intuitively, the ways of combining fine-grained and coarse-grained token representations "in the same contexts" are the same.

AMBERT works better than AMBERT-Hybrid, despite both exploiting multi-grained tokenization. Figure 2 shows attention weights of first layers. In AMBERT-Hybrid, fine-grained tokens attend more to corresponding coarse-grained tokens, weakening attention among fine-grained tokens. In AMBERT, attention weights among fine-grained tokens and among coarse-grained tokens remain intact. Attentions among single-grained tokens (fine-grained or coarse-grained) appear crucial for downstream tasks.

Improvements of AMBERT on Chinese are larger than on English. Tokenizing 10,000 English sentences from GLUE tasks shows an average proportion of phrases (coarse-grained tokens) of only 13.1%, indicating significantly fewer coarse-grained tokens than fine-grained tokens in English. ## 3.4 Inference

Two inference methods for AMBERT:
1.  Utilize AMBERT itself: Better performance, higher computational cost.
2.  Utilize only one encoder of AMBERT: Slightly worse performance, computational cost comparable to BERT.

Choice of encoder to drop can be determined via development dataset evaluation, reducing computational cost to BERT-level.

## 3.5 Alternatives

Two alternatives to AMBERT based on multi-grained tokenization: AMBERT-Combo and AMBERT-Hybrid.

**AMBERT-Combo:**
*   Two individual BERT encoders: one for fine-grained tokens, one for coarse-grained tokens.
*   No parameter sharing between encoders.
*   Combines output layers of the two encoders during learning and inference.
*   Fine-tuning is similar to AMBERT.

**AMBERT-Hybrid:**
*   One BERT encoder works on both fine-grained and coarse-grained token sequences.
*   Creates representations on the concatenation of the two sequences.
*   Representations of the two sequences interact at each layer.

paper2.title: Supervised Learning of Universal Sentence Representations from Natural Language Inference Data
paper2.abstract:
Many modern NLP systems rely on word
                        embeddings, previously trained in an unsupervised manner on large corpora, as
                        base features. Efforts to obtain embeddings for larger chunks of text, such as
                        sentences, have however not been so successful. Several attempts at learning unsupervised representations of sentences have
                        not reached satisfactory enough performance to be widely adopted. In this paper,
                        we show how universal sentence representations trained using the supervised data of
                        the Stanford Natural Language Inference
                        datasets can consistently outperform unsupervised methods like SkipThought vectors (Kiros et al., 2015) on a wide range
                        of transfer tasks. Much like how computer vision uses ImageNet to obtain features, which can then be transferred to
                        other tasks, our work tends to indicate the
                        suitability of natural language inference
                        for transfer learning to other NLP tasks.
                        Our encoder is publicly available.

BiLSTM-max trained on SNLI outperforms SkipThought vectors on MR, CR, MPQA, SST, MRPC-accuracy, SICK-R, SICK-E, STS14.
BiLSTM-max also outperforms SkipThought-LN on MR, CR, MPQA (except SUBJ).
Cosine metrics in BiLSTM-max embedding space are more semantically informative than SkipThought embedding space (0.68 vs. 0.29 and 0.44 Pearson scores for STS14).
Hypothesis: SNLI matching method (element-wise product, absolute difference) incorporates distance, enhancing semantic informativeness.

NLI as a supervised training set:
Model trained on SNLI achieves better overall results than models trained on COCO, dictionary definitions, NMT, PPDB, and SST.
SST is smaller than NLI; models used were identical.
Representations provide higher-quality features for classification and similarity tasks.
Explanation: NLI constrains the model to encode semantic information, which is generally discriminative and informative.

Domain adaptation on SICK tasks:
Transfer learning approach yields better results than state-of-the-art on SICK (out-domain version of SNLI) for entailment and relatedness.
SICK-R: 0.885 Pearson score (vs. 0.868 by Tai et al., 2015).
SICK-E: 86.3% test accuracy (vs. 84.5% by Lai and Hockenmaier, 2014).
Significantly outperformed previous transfer learning approaches on SICK-E (Bowman et al., 2015) which fine-tuned an LSTM trained on SNLI (80.8% accuracy).
Hypothesis: Embeddings already contain in-domain information; learning only the classifier on the small out-domain task limits parameters learned.

Image-caption retrieval results (COCO):
When trained with ResNet features and 30k more data, SkipThought vectors improved from 33.8 to 37.9 (caption R@1) and 25.9 to 30.6 (image R@1).
Our approach achieved 42.4 (caption retrieval) and 33.2 (image retrieval).
Results are comparable to Ma et al. (2015) who learned directly on the task.
Pre-trained representations (ResNet, sentence embeddings) achieve competitive results compared to features learned directly on the objective task.

MultiGenre NLI:
MultiNLI corpus (Williams et al., 2017) is a multi-genre version of SNLI (433K sentence pairs).
Covers ten distinct genres, increasing language complexity coverage.
Model trained on SNLI + MultiNLI (AllNLI) shows significant overall performance boost compared to SNLI alone.
AllNLI model reaches AdaSent performance on CR.
Larger training task coverage improves general representation learning.
Competitive on STS14 (0.70 Pearson score) with PPDB based paragramphrase embeddings.
Training on MultiNLI genres does not degrade performance on COCO image caption retrieval, confirming generalization power of embeddings.

Conclusion:
Studied effects of supervised sentence embedding training on 12 transfer tasks.
Models learned on NLI outperform models trained in unsupervised conditions or on other supervised tasks.
BiLSTM network with max pooling is the best current universal sentence embedding architecture.

Architecture impact:
BiLSTM-4096 with max-pooling performs best on SNLI and transfer tasks.
It significantly outperforms LSTM, GRU, BiGRU-last, BiLSTM-Mean, inner-attention, and HConvNet in micro and macro averages.
Better training task performance doesn't always translate to better transfer task results (e.g., inner-attention vs. BiLSTM-Mean).

Transfer quality is sensitive to the optimization algorithm. Adam (vs. SGD) leads to faster convergence on SNLI for BiLSTM-max but worse transfer task results due to increased over-specialization.

The model captures hierarchical abstractions of an input sentence in a fixed-size representation.

Training details
For all models trained on SNLI, SGD is used with a learning rate of 0.1 and a weight decay of 0.99. The learning rate is divided by 5 each epoch if dev accuracy decreases. Mini-batches of size 64 are used, and training stops when the learning rate falls below 10⁻⁵. The classifier is a multi-layer perceptron with 1 hidden layer of 512 hidden units. Open-source GloVe vectors trained on Common Crawl 840B with 300 dimensions are used as fixed word embeddings.

Evaluation of sentence representations
The aim is to obtain general-purpose sentence embeddings that capture generic information useful for a broad set of tasks. To evaluate these representations, they are used as features in 12 transfer tasks. The sentence-embedding evaluation procedure is presented.

SentEval, an open-source sentence evaluation tool, is used to automate evaluation on all tasks. SentEval uses Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) to fit a logistic regression classifier with a batch size of 64.

Binary and multi-class classification
A set of binary classification tasks is used, covering sentiment analysis (MR, SST), question-type (TREC), product reviews (CR), subjectivity/objectivity (SUBJ), and opinion polarity (MPQA). Sentence vectors are generated and a logistic regression is trained on top. A linear classifier is suitable for small datasets due to its fewer parameters compared to an MLP. The L2 penalty of the logistic regression is tuned with grid-search on the validation set.

Entailment and semantic relatedness
Evaluation is performed on the SICK dataset for both entailment (SICK-E) and semantic relatedness (SICK-R). The same matching methods as in SNLI are used, and a Logistic Regression is learned on top of the joint representation. For semantic relatedness, the approach of Tai et al. (2015) is followed to predict the probability distribution of relatedness scores. Pearson correlation is reported.

STS14 - Semantic Textual Similarity
While semantic relatedness is supervised in SICK-R, embeddings are also evaluated on the 6 unsupervised SemEval tasks of STS14 (Agirre et al., 2014). This dataset includes pairs of sentences from news articles, forum discussions, image descriptions, and headlines, labeled with a similarity score from 0 to 5. These tasks evaluate how the cosine distance between sentences correlates with human-labeled similarity scores through Pearson and Spearman correlations.

Paraphrase detection
The Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus consists of sentence pairs extracted from web news sources. Sentence pairs are human-annotated for paraphrase/semantic equivalence. The approach used is similar to SICK-E, with a classifier having 2 classes.

Caption-Image retrieval
The caption-image retrieval task evaluates joint image and language feature models (Hodosh et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2014). The goal is to rank images by relevance to a query caption (Image Retrieval) or rank captions by relevance to a query image (Caption Retrieval). A pairwise ranking-loss Lcir(x, y) is used:

U and V are learned linear transformations projecting caption x and image y to the same embedding space. A margin α = 0.2 and 30 contrastive terms are used. Supervised tasks are best for embedding whole-sentence semantics. Neural networks excel at capturing task biases but can overspecialize, forgetting input data semantics. Learning on large unsupervised tasks makes specialization harder. Co-adaptation of encoders and classifiers, trained end-to-end, can negatively impact the generalization power of encoder-generated image features. A loss incorporating multiple orthogonal classifiers can counteract this.

Recent sentence embedding generation models include those composing word embeddings and more complex neural network architectures. SkipThought vectors adapt the skip-gram model for words to the sentence level by encoding a sentence to predict surrounding sentences. Features from this are used in a linear model, demonstrating good performance on transfer tasks. Layer-norm regularization further improved results. The task on which sentence embeddings are trained significantly impacts their quality.

Supervised training on machine translation data, dictionary definitions, and image captioning data yielded significantly lower results compared to unsupervised Skip-Thought. Recent work has explored training sentence encoders on the SNLI corpus and applying them to the SICK corpus using multi-task learning or pretraining. Results were inconclusive and did not match simpler approaches that directly learn a classifier on top of unsupervised sentence embeddings. This work is the first to fully exploit the SNLI corpus for building generic sentence encoders, consistently outperforming unsupervised approaches even with less human-annotated data.

This work combines two research directions: using the NLI task to train universal sentence encoding models and exploring various sentence encoder architectures. Architectures investigated include standard recurrent models (LSTMs, GRUs) with mean and max-pooling, self-attentive networks incorporating different sentence views, and hierarchical convolutional networks blending levels of abstraction.

The SNLI dataset contains 570k human-generated English sentence pairs labeled as entailment, contradiction, or neutral. It captures natural language inference (Recognizing Textual Entailment - RTE) and is a large, high-quality labeled resource requiring sentence semantics understanding. The semantic nature of NLI is hypothesized to make it suitable for learning universal sentence embeddings in a supervised way, capturing universally useful features.

Generic NLI training involves a shared sentence encoder outputting representations for premise `u` and hypothesis `v`. Three matching methods extract relations between `u` and `v`: concatenation of the two representations. Models can be trained on SNLI using sentence encoding-based models that separate sentence encoding or joint methods that use encoding of both sentences for cross-features or attention. For generic sentence encoders, a sentence encoding-based approach is adopted, as illustrated in Figure 1.

For each time step t, we report the number of times the max-pooling operation selected the hidden state ht (which can be seen as a sentence representation centered around word wt).
Without any training, the max-pooling is rather even across hidden states, although it seems to focus consistently more on the first and last hidden states. When trained, the model learns to focus on speciﬁc words that carry most of the meaning of the sentence without any explicit attention mechanism.

paper1.title: AMBERT: A Pre-trained Language Model with Multi-Grained Tokenization
paper1.abstract:
Pre-trained language models such as BERT
                        have exhibited remarkable performances in
                        many tasks in natural language understanding (NLU). The tokens in the models are usually fine-grained in the sense that for languages like English they are words or subwords and for languages like Chinese they are
                        characters. In English, for example, there
                        are multi-word expressions which form natural
                        lexical units and thus the use of coarse-grained
                        tokenization also appears to be reasonable.
                        In fact, both fine-grained and coarse-grained
                        tokenizations have advantages and disadvantages for learning of pre-trained language models. In this paper, we propose a novel pretrained language model, referred to as AMBERT (A Multi-grained BERT), on the basis
                        of both fine-grained and coarse-grained tokenizations. For English, AMBERT takes both
                        the sequence of words (fine-grained tokens)
                        and the sequence of phrases (coarse-grained
                        tokens) as input after tokenization, employs
                        one encoder for processing the sequence of
                        words and the other encoder for processing

AMBERT-Combo has larger distances than AMBERT. This indicates that representations of fine-grained and coarse-grained encoders are closer in AMBERT due to parameter sharing across encoders. This parameter sharing allows AMBERT to learn and represent similar ways of combining tokens, regardless of granularity.
